# Dozable — the manual and privacy policy

> Dozable runs teams of AI coding agents on your Mac. Each agent runs where you choose: in its own micro VM or held to its folder on your Mac, where your keys never go inside, or as you. Free and open source.

The complete user manual (every chapter, in reading order) followed by the privacy policy. Each part starts with the URL of its page.

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/getting-started

# Getting started

Dozable runs teams of AI coding agents on your Mac. A **workspace** holds the agents, their chat room, the folders they
work in and a brief that says what the work is for. Agents from any vendor (Claude Code, Codex and more) take on the
work one **unit of work** at a time; each is recorded in a journal, and the lessons you approve carry into the next. You
watch, talk to them in the room and decide what matters. You work through `doz`, a command-line tool, and a web
dashboard (`doz ui`).

Where each agent runs is one setting of the workspace, not the first thing you decide: in its own Linux micro VM, held
by macOS's sandbox to its folder on your Mac (**fenced**, the default for a workspace's agents), or as you. Start with
the default; [Sessions on this Mac](https://dozable.com/docs/sessions-on-this-mac.md) and [Sandboxes](https://dozable.com/docs/sandboxes-and-lifecycle.md) compare
the choices.

**What you'll have in about 15 minutes:** a workspace with an agent in it, a chat room where you talk to it, and a
folder it works in. Most of the time is a one-off download.

**Know three things before you start:**

- **Agents need an account.** `doz onboard` uses this Mac's own Claude Code login by default. That login expires after
  some hours unless the Mac's Claude Code renews it; for unattended work, add a setup-token account
  ([Agents and accounts](https://dozable.com/docs/agents-and-accounts.md)).
- **Workers talk through chat.** Turn it on with `doz chat on`. Without it you drive the agents yourself.
- **Long jobs need room.** `doz exec` stops a command after 120 s unless you pass `--timeout`; start a long one in the
  background with `doz run NAME -d`.

```sh
brew trust --tap dozable/tap && brew install dozable/tap/doz
doz onboard --first none        # this Mac: the checks, the base image, your agents' account
doz chat on --name ada          # rooms for you and your agents; ada is your name there
doz workspace new hello --preset blank --brief "Read this project and write NOTES.md: what it is and how to build it" --folder ~/code/my-app --worker "Do what the brief asks" --dry-run
doz workspace new hello --preset blank --brief "Read this project and write NOTES.md: what it is and how to build it" --folder ~/code/my-app --worker "Do what the brief asks"
doz workspace start hello       # the brief posted in the room, the first unit of work open, the worker started
doz ui                          # watch it, and talk to it in the room
```

The steps, one at a time, are below: [Your first workspace](#your-first-workspace).

> **If you are an agent setting this up for someone,** read [Workspaces](https://dozable.com/docs/workspaces.md) and then [Letting another
> agent drive Dozable](14-letting-another-agent-drive.md) first.

**On this page:** [What you need](#what-you-need) · [Install](#install) ·
[Set up this Mac](#set-up-this-mac) · [Your first workspace](#your-first-workspace) ·
[A sandbox on its own](#a-sandbox-on-its-own) · [Talk to your agent](#talk-to-your-agent) ·
[Day to day](#day-to-day) · [When the agent needs a website](#when-the-agent-needs-a-website) ·
[Undo](#undo-with-restore-points) · [Next steps](#next-steps)

## What you need

- A Mac with **Apple silicon** (M1 or later) running **macOS 26 or later**.
- About **5 GB of free disk** for the first image. Sandboxes share their disks with the image they
  came from, so each extra sandbox usually adds only megabytes.
- An internet connection for the first setup.
- **Optional:** [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) installed and signed in on your Mac.
  Your sandboxes can then use that login, with nothing to paste. You can use an API key or a
  long-lived token instead, or decide later.
  That login (the account `mac`) gives out access that **expires** after some hours, and only the Mac's
  own Claude Code renews it — Dozable never does. `doz account keepalive always` keeps it fresh: when it
  expires, Dozable runs the Mac's own `claude` once to renew it. It can't do that for a daemon started
  over SSH (the login keychain is locked there). For long unattended work, use a **setup-token**
  account instead: `claude setup-token` makes a token valid for a year, and
  `doz account add NAME --setup-token` adds it
  ([Agents and accounts](https://dozable.com/docs/agents-and-accounts.md)).

## Install

With [Homebrew](https://brew.sh):

```sh
brew trust --tap dozable/tap   # once per Mac: Homebrew loads a third-party tap's formulas only once trusted
brew install dozable/tap/doz
doz --version
```

The install takes seconds (a prebuilt, signed `doz`) and ends with a hint: `doz onboard`. More on
installing, upgrading and removing: [Installing, upgrading and uninstalling](https://dozable.com/docs/install-upgrade-uninstall.md).

## Set up this Mac

Setup happens once per Mac. It checks that your Mac can run sandboxes, connects your Claude account,
and prepares the agent's image so your first sandbox starts in seconds. Do it in the terminal or in
your browser; both do the same thing.

**In the terminal:**

```sh
doz onboard
```

At each question the recommended answer is already selected: press **Enter** to take it.

1. **Checks.** Apple silicon, macOS, the virtualization permission, disk space. A required check
   that fails stops setup and says why; an optional one (Claude Code not installed, for example) is
   a warning.
2. **Base image.** Node.js, the Linux system every tool runs on — **Enter** starts its download (about
   380 MB) in the background, once; every tool you try is added to it. The next questions come at once.
3. **Models & keys.** The sign-ins Dozable found on this Mac (Claude Code, Codex), then a key if you want
   one — Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, Google or an OpenRouter key (it is never echoed). **Enter** adds none.
4. **Access**, **Folder rules** and **Settings** — GitHub and your SSH agent (off unless you choose
   them), what `.dozignore` does, and the settings file. See [Setting up this Mac](https://dozable.com/docs/setting-up.md).
5. **Usage statistics.** What an official build sends — counts and ranges about how Dozable is used,
   never names, paths, contents or anything inside a sandbox — and where to see it exactly
   (`doz telemetry show`). **Enter** keeps them on; answer **n** to turn them off. A build from the
   open-source repository sends nothing and skips this step.
6. **Stay in touch (optional).** Release news, tool news, early access and tips and tricks by email — skip it
   with **Enter**. See [Usage statistics and sign-up](#usage-statistics-and-sign-up).
7. **Your first sandbox.** `claude`, `pi` or `opencode` — a name (`claude`) and a new empty folder
   (`~/doz-workspaces/claude`). Dozable waits for the base if it is still downloading (**Ctrl-C** leaves it
   running; `doz onboard --status` shows it again), adds the tool and attaches you to it. Going straight to a
   workspace? Answer **none** here (or run `doz onboard --first none`).

**In your browser:**

```sh
doz ui
```

The dashboard opens on the **setup wizard**: the same steps — the base downloading at the foot while you answer —
the **Usage statistics** switch (on unless you turn it off), an optional **Stay in touch**, and the **First sandbox**.

![The setup wizard's first step](https://dozable.com/docs/images/wizard-welcome.png)

Details: [Setting up](https://dozable.com/docs/setting-up.md).

### What you just set up



- **Each sandbox is a small Linux virtual machine,** not a container, with its own kernel and disk.
  It can't see your Mac's files, apart from the one project folder you share at `/workspace`.
- **A workspace's agents run fenced on this Mac by default** — no VM: macOS's own sandbox holds each one to its
  project folder, its own temp and caches, and Dozable's proxy for the network, with your Keychain closed. A preset or
  `--worker-isolation vm` puts them in micro VMs instead; [Where an agent runs](https://dozable.com/docs/sessions-on-this-mac.md#where-an-agent-runs-the-three-choices)
  compares the three choices.
- **The Dozable daemon runs the sandboxes and sessions.** It's a background program that the first command starts, and
  it keeps running when nothing is (the setting `daemon.always_on`, on by default; off, it exits once nothing runs).
  `doz` and the dashboard are remote controls for it.
- **Sandboxes and fenced sessions sit behind a network proxy on your Mac.** A sandbox has no network card of its own:
  every connection goes through the proxy, which allows only what you permit, and logs it.
- **Your credentials never enter a sandbox or a fenced session.** The agent sees a stand-in; the proxy adds your real
  login as each request leaves for Anthropic. An unfenced agent is the exception: it acts as you.
- **Two files hold your choices:** `~/.config/doz/doz.toml` (your settings for this Mac)
  and a project's `doz_project.yaml` (its sandbox). Everything else is kept by the daemon.

## Your first workspace

Four steps: set up this Mac, make the workspace, start it, and then give it its next unit of work.

1. **`doz onboard`** checks this Mac and sets up the account your agents use (above). Once per Mac.
2. **`doz workspace new NAME --preset …`** says what the work is: the brief, the folders, the workers, and a preset for
   where they run and what network they get — `blank` (choose yourself: fenced on this Mac, a locked network), `research`,
   `swift-tests`, `mac-admin` or `remotion-video` ([what each sets up](https://dozable.com/docs/workspaces.md#presets)). Add `--dry-run` first:
   it shows what would be made, what would be refused and what the start would still need, each with its fix, and makes
   nothing. A worker needs chat on (`doz chat on`).

   ```sh
   doz workspace new hello --preset blank --brief "Read this project and write NOTES.md" --folder ~/code/my-app --worker "Do what the brief asks" --dry-run
   ```

3. **`doz workspace start NAME`** runs the set-up check (it lists every gap with the command that fixes it), posts your
   brief as your first message in the workspace's room, opens the first unit of work and starts the worker, in the place
   the preset chose. Watch it on the dashboard (`doz ui`, then the workspace on **Home**), or follow its room from a
   terminal: `doz chat read hello --follow`. Write in the room to talk to it.
4. **When it is done, finish it and go on.** `doz workspace finish NAME` closes the unit of work and archives it — the
   room's messages, the agents' conversations, its journal. `doz workspace run NAME "next goal"` opens the next one,
   with every lesson you approved from the ones before:

   ```sh
   doz workspace finish hello
   doz workspace retro hello --propose --addendum "Keep NOTES.md under one page"   # a lesson; you decide it in the room
   doz workspace run hello "Now add a section on running the tests"
   ```

More: [Workspaces](https://dozable.com/docs/workspaces.md), [Runs, the journal and lessons](https://dozable.com/docs/runs-the-journal-and-lessons.md), and a worked
example of a whole process in [Bring your own process](https://dozable.com/docs/bring-your-own-process.md).

## Usage statistics and sign-up

**Official builds** (Homebrew, the release download) **send anonymous usage statistics**, so we can see
what to fix and improve: at most once a day, counts and ranges about how Dozable itself is used — which
commands ran and how often they failed (by exit code), which agents, bases and network presets new
sandboxes use, the size of your setup as ranges, typical start and wake times rounded to 50 ms, how long
sandboxes ran and slept and how long agents worked (as ranges), which features you used (the dashboard,
the installed app, the dashboard on your network (`doz ui --lan`), folder rules, GitHub access, restore points, saved disks), which built-in
image-preparation step failed, and your Mac's macOS version, chip family, memory and cores as ranges — with
a random install id. **Never**
a sandbox, image or project name, a file or folder name or path, anything inside a sandbox, anything
you type or a program prints, a command's arguments, a host or website, an account, email or key.
Our server adds your country from the connection and does not keep your IP address.

Setup tells you about them and lets you turn them off there and then: the **Usage statistics** step of
`doz onboard` (or `doz onboard --usage-stats off` in a script) and of the dashboard's setup wizard. If you
never ran the setup, the first command says so in one line instead. See exactly what would be sent, and
turn it off with any one of these:

```sh
doz telemetry show                                      # on or off, why, and the exact messages
doz config set telemetry.send_anonymous_usage_stats false   # off (or the switch in the dashboard's Settings)
DO_NOT_TRACK=1 doz ls                                   # off whenever DO_NOT_TRACK is set
doz ls --no-send-anonymous-usage-stats                  # off for one command
doz telemetry reset                                     # a new random install id
```

**Signing up is optional**: `doz signup` (or the setup's *Stay in touch*) asks for an email and what you
want — release news, tool news (new and updated tools you can try), early access, tips and tricks. A confirmation email comes first; every email has a
one-click unsubscribe, and your email is never linked to the statistics.

**Builds from the open-source repository send nothing.** The statistics and sign-up code is part of the
official builds only and is not open source; this repository holds the list of what may be sent and
every switch. The full policy: [dozable.com/privacy](https://dozable.com/privacy).

## A sandbox on its own

You don't need a workspace to use one agent: a sandbox on its own is a single agent in its own micro VM, which you
attach to and talk to in your terminal. A sandbox works on one project folder, shared into it at `/workspace`: the agent's changes appear on
your Mac at once, and your editor sees them live.

```sh
cd ~/code/my-app
doz init
```

`doz init` asks for the sandbox's name (from the folder's) and its image, and writes
`doz_project.yaml` in the folder. It holds no secrets, so you can commit it: anyone who runs
`doz up` in the project gets the same sandbox.

```sh
doz up
```

The first time, this creates the sandbox and starts it in a few seconds (setup prepared the image
already). After that, `doz up` in the folder wakes the same sandbox. Either way it opens the agent
in your terminal.

> **Detach, don't quit.** Press **Ctrl-]** twice to leave the sandbox (once opens a small menu at
> the bottom: `d detach · n next · p prev · s sessions · Esc back`). The agent keeps running, and
> `doz up` brings you straight back to it.

Your terminal's title shows where you are, for example `my-app · claude · 14:05`, and goes back to
what it was when you detach. Details: [Projects](https://dozable.com/docs/projects.md) and
[Terminals and sessions](https://dozable.com/docs/terminals-and-sessions.md).

> **No project yet?** `doz new` — or **Quick add** in the dashboard — makes a sandbox with every
> default and puts you in it: a free name like `claude-sandbox`, and its own folder in your projects
> folder (`~/doz-workspaces/claude-sandbox`). See
> [The quickest way](https://dozable.com/docs/sandboxes-and-lifecycle.md#the-quickest-way-quick-add-and-doz-new).

## Talk to your agent

You're now in Claude Code, inside the sandbox. Its first-run screens are done and it doesn't stop to
ask permission for each command: inside a sandbox, the VM and its network are the boundary. (To have
Claude ask first anyway, see `recipes.anthropic.claude-code.approvals` in the [settings](https://dozable.com/docs/settings-reference.md).)

Claude also knows where it runs. Ask it:

> where are you running, and where is /workspace on my Mac?

It should tell you it is in a Dozable sandbox (a Linux VM on your Mac), that `/workspace` is your
`~/code/my-app`, that its network only reaches what you allow, and that your credentials are added
by your Mac and never stored in the sandbox. It learns this from a short note Dozable gives it at every
start. See [Agents and accounts](https://dozable.com/docs/agents-and-accounts.md).

A few things work as you'd hope:

- **It can install system packages.** The agent has passwordless `sudo` inside its sandbox, so
  `sudo apt-get install -y …` works (Debian-based images) — and never stops to ask questions.
- **Its clock is yours.** A sandbox follows your Mac's time zone, even after it slept while you
  travelled.
- **Copying works.** When Claude copies something, it lands on your Mac's clipboard and a notice
  says so.
- **Browser sign-ins work.** If a tool in the sandbox opens a sign-in page, it opens in your Mac's
  browser, and the login completes. See [Signing in from a sandbox](https://dozable.com/docs/signing-in-from-a-sandbox.md).

## Day to day

A sandbox you're not using doesn't have to hold your Mac's memory. Each of these brings the agent
back exactly where it was: same conversation, same running programs.

| | what happens | memory | back in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `doz pause my-app` | frozen instantly | kept | ~1 ms |
| `doz sleep my-app` | frozen and saved to disk, so it survives a crash | kept | ~0.3 s |
| `doz hibernate my-app` | saved to disk, and the VM stops | **given back to your Mac** | ~0.3 s |

`doz wake my-app`, or simply `doz up` in the project folder, brings it back. `doz ls` lists your
sandboxes; the dashboard (`doz ui`) shows the same thing with a live terminal for each.

`doz shutdown` is a real power-off: running programs end but the disk is kept. `doz reset` goes back
to a fresh copy of the image. Neither touches your project folder or the agent's own settings and
history. Details: [Sandboxes and their lifecycle](https://dozable.com/docs/sandboxes-and-lifecycle.md).

## When the agent needs a website

A sandbox has no network card of its own. Every connection goes through a proxy on your Mac that
checks a short list of **permissions** and logs the connection. The **Standard** permissions let a
coding agent talk to its AI model, update itself, install system packages and your language's
packages, use GitHub and send its own error reports. Anything else is refused and logged.

```sh
doz net my-app                              # what the agent may do, and what it was refused lately
doz net allow my-app install:python         # a permission, live
doz net allow my-app site:api.example.com   # one site
```

In the dashboard, the sandbox's details show **What the agent can do** as switches, with a one-click
suggestion when the agent was refused something. The agent can't change its own permissions; only
you can. Details: [What the agent can do](https://dozable.com/docs/permissions-and-network.md).

## Undo with restore points

Before letting an agent loose on something risky, take a restore point. It takes milliseconds and
uses almost no disk until things change:

```sh
doz point take my-app before-refactor
doz point revert my-app before-refactor        # go back
doz point fork my-app before-refactor try-2    # or try again in a new sandbox, from the same moment
```

Restore points cover the sandbox's own disk. Your project folder is on your Mac, so use git for that.
Details: [Restore points, duplicates and saved disks](https://dozable.com/docs/restore-points-duplicates-templates.md).

## Next steps

- Something not working? `doz doctor`, then [Troubleshooting and FAQ](https://dozable.com/docs/troubleshooting-and-faq.md).
- Let the agent you already use on your Mac drive Dozable: [Letting another agent drive Dozable](https://dozable.com/docs/letting-another-agent-drive.md).
- How your Mac is kept safe: [Security model](https://dozable.com/docs/security-model.md).
- Everything else: the [manual's index](https://dozable.com/docs/index.md).

# Installing, upgrading and uninstalling

`doz` is one command-line program. It comes with everything it needs inside it: the small Linux
programs each sandbox uses, the Linux kernel sandboxes boot (so the first start downloads no kernel), the web
dashboard, and the permission macOS requires to run virtual machines. You install it with Homebrew.

## Concepts

- **The `doz` program** is what you install. It is signed with Apple's virtualization entitlement;
  without that, macOS refuses to boot virtual machines. A copy you build yourself without signing can
  run every command except the ones that boot a VM, and `doz doctor` says so.
- **The store** is where your sandboxes, images and restore points live:
  `~/Library/Application Support/doz` unless you choose another (see
  [Settings reference](https://dozable.com/docs/settings-reference.md), `store.path`). Upgrading `doz` never touches it
  (0.37 is the one exception: it starts with a new store — see [Upgrading to 0.37](#upgrading-to-037-a-fresh-start)).
- **The settings** live in `~/.config/doz/doz.toml`, beside your agent prompt template
  (`agent-prompt.md`). Upgrading never touches them either.
- **The daemon** is a background `doz` process that runs your sandboxes. A running daemon keeps using the
  version of `doz` it started as, which is why upgrading has one extra step (below).

## Install

You need a Mac with Apple silicon and macOS 26 or later.

```sh
brew trust --tap dozable/tap   # once per Mac: Homebrew loads a third-party tap's formulas only once trusted
brew install dozable/tap/doz
doz --version
```

Recent Homebrew loads formulas from a third-party tap only after you trust it — `brew trust` is needed
once per Mac (without it `brew install` refuses the formula). Homebrew then adds Dozable's tap and installs
a prebuilt, signed and notarised `doz` in seconds — no compiler is needed. It ends with a hint: run `doz onboard` ([Setting up](https://dozable.com/docs/setting-up.md)).

The tap used to be called `dozer-sandbox/tap`. If you installed from it, nothing changes: it still gets every
update, and `doz upgrade` uses it.

### Release channels

There is one formula per release channel; they install the same `doz` command, so you have one at a time:

| formula | channel | what you get |
|---|---|---|
| `dozable/tap/doz` | stable | releases |
| `dozable/tap/doz-beta` | beta | beta builds first, and every release |
| `dozable/tap/doz-canary` | canary | every build, first |

`doz upgrade --channel beta` switches: it asks, then Homebrew uninstalls one formula and installs the other.
Your store, sandboxes and settings are not Homebrew's and stay. doz never installs an older build — switching
to a channel whose newest build is older than yours waits until that channel catches up.

### Without Homebrew

Each release also has a tarball on the project's GitHub releases page: `doz-VERSION-macos-arm64.tar.gz` (and
its `.sha256`). Unpack it anywhere and put its `bin` on your `PATH`; keep the folder as it is (`bin/doz` is a
link into `libexec/doz`, where doz finds its parts). `doz upgrade -y` updates such an install itself: it downloads
the new tarball, checks it against the signed feed and Apple's signature, and swaps it in, keeping the
previous version as `libexec/doz.previous`.

The releases page also lists a `doz-VERSION-macos-arm64-helper.tar.gz`. That one is **not for you** unless you build a
Mac app that carries `doz` inside it: it has no dashboard and never updates itself. See
[Bundling doz in an app](https://dozable.com/docs/bundling-doz-in-an-app.md). Each tarball also has a `.dSYM.zip` beside it — its symbols,
for reading crash reports; you don't need it to run doz.

## Upgrade

doz tells you when a new release is out — one line after a command on your terminal, and a banner on the
dashboard:

> doz 0.31.1 is available — upgrade: doz upgrade -y (notes: https://updates.dozable.com/v1/notes/0.31.1.html)

```sh
doz upgrade -y            # or doz upgrade: it shows the version and the notes, and asks first
doz daemon restart
```

`doz upgrade` refreshes Dozable's tap first, then runs `brew upgrade` for your channel's formula. It always asks the
feed itself (past any cached copy), so a release is there the minute it is published. Its first name, `doz update`,
still works. Homebrew's own output stays off the screen: no update of your other taps first, and what brew prints
goes to `brew.log` in doz's settings folder (`~/.config/doz/brew.log`) — shown when brew fails, or as it
runs with `doz upgrade --verbose`. When a daemon of the previous version is running, `doz upgrade` (without `-y`)
then asks whether to restart it now. Homebrew refreshes
its taps only now and then, so a plain `brew upgrade doz` can say there is nothing new for up to a day; with brew
directly, run `brew update` first.

- **How it knows.** At most once a day (and when `doz ui` starts), doz reads one small file,
  `https://updates.dozable.com/v1/feed.json`, signed with Dozable's own key; anything that doesn't verify
  is ignored. Nothing about you or your sandboxes is sent — only the request, with doz's version and channel
  in its user agent. Offline, it says nothing. Never with `--json` or `-q`, or when not on a terminal.
- **The setting `updates.mode`**: `notify` (the default), `auto` — doz also installs the update itself (through
  Homebrew for a Homebrew install), but only while no sandbox is running and no session is attached, and then says
  `Updated to 0.31.1 — restart to apply: doz daemon restart` — or `off` (never look). `doz upgrade --check` looks
  now, whatever the mode.
- Homebrew installs the new version beside the old one, then removes the old one.
- **A running daemon keeps its old version.** After an upgrade, Homebrew runs `doz daemon upgrade-check`,
  which says when a daemon of the previous version is still running. You can run it yourself at any time;
  it never starts or stops anything.
- **`doz daemon restart`** hibernates every running sandbox and starts a daemon of the new version (`doz daemon
  stop` does the same and leaves the next command to start it). Each sandbox wakes on the new daemon when you
  use it — with its programs and sessions where they were:

```sh
doz wake my-app        # or doz up, doz attach, or just use the dashboard
```

Until you do, every command that talks to the old daemon says so, once, on stderr (never in its output,
and not with `-q`):

```
note: the doz daemon is 0.12.0-rc.9 (this doz is 0.12.0-rc.10) — `doz daemon stop` switches to 0.12.0-rc.10; sandboxes hibernate and wake
```

(If the daemon is the *newer* one — you ran an older `doz` — the note says to upgrade this `doz`.)

If you skip `doz daemon stop`, nothing breaks right away: your sandboxes keep running. But the old
daemon can no longer boot anything once Homebrew has removed its files, so a start, a wake or a new
sandbox is refused with a message that tells you to run `doz daemon stop`. Once nothing runs and
nobody is attached, the old daemon replaces itself with one of the new version — no command needed (with
`daemon.always_on` off it just exits, and the next command starts the new one). A daemon that only holds
sessions on this Mac hands them over to a daemon of the new version the same way, the sessions running on.

### The daemon stays running

The daemon does not exit when nothing runs: `daemon.always_on` is on by default, and while it is on
`daemon.idle_timeout_minutes` has no effect. The idle timeout's default is 5 minutes, and it applies only when
`daemon.always_on` is off; `0` disables it. If you turned `daemon.always_on` off and never set a timeout, the daemon
now exits after 5 idle minutes again. To have the daemon exit when idle:

```sh
doz config set daemon.always_on off               # it then exits after daemon.idle_timeout_minutes (default 5)
```

Always-on off together with a timeout of `0` means the daemon never switches off by idling, and once it is stopped it
does not come back until the next doz command runs — `doz config show`, `doz daemon status` and `doz doctor` warn.

### Upgrading to 0.51: stop the old daemon

In 0.51 a doz and a daemon of an earlier version no longer talk to each other (what a sandbox works on is now called
its folder everywhere, and the two would misread each other). A command of the new doz that reaches the old daemon
says `the running daemon is 0.50.x, this doz is 0.51.0: doz daemon stop (the next command starts the new one)`.
`doz daemon status` and `doz daemon stop` still work across the two. See the renamed flags and settings in the
[manual's index](https://dozable.com/docs/index.md#renamed-in-051).

A daemon started over ssh (where the login Keychain is locked) is never kept running: it still exits after 5
minutes with nothing running, so the next command from the Mac itself starts one that can read your Claude login.
`doz daemon status` says which it is.

### Start the daemon when you log in

An upgrade never adds anything to `~/Library/LaunchAgents`. The first command you type in Terminal after it says once:

```text
doz: the daemon now stays running. To also start it when you log in (sandboxes and kept sessions come back after the Mac restarts): doz daemon login-item on
```

`doz daemon login-item on` adds ONE login item for your store, `~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.dozable.daemon.<8 letters
and digits>.plist` (macOS shows "Background Items Added"). At login, and every 15 minutes after, it runs
a short doz command that starts the daemon from your desktop session — where it can read your login
Keychain — and exits; launchd never runs the daemon itself. It runs the doz Homebrew keeps current
(`…/opt/doz/libexec/doz/doz`), so an upgrade needs nothing more.

```sh
doz daemon login-item           # is it there, loaded, switched off?
doz daemon login-item on        # add it (daemon.login_item = on)
doz daemon login-item off       # remove it (daemon.login_item = off)
```

`doz daemon stop` keeps the daemon stopped until a doz command or your next login (the 15-minute look starts nothing
meanwhile). `doz config set daemon.always_on off` removes the login item too: with nothing kept running there is
nothing to start at login. A new install's `doz onboard` asks "Start Dozable when you log in?" (`--start-at-login on|off`
answers it). Over ssh, a command that needs the daemon starts it in your desktop session through the login item, and
`doz daemon restart` never replaces a daemon started from your desktop with one that could not read the Keychain.

### The menu bar app

doz comes with a small menu bar app, Dozable.app: the daemon's state at a glance, Start, Stop and Restart, and Open
Dashboard. Nothing is added to your Mac until you ask for it:

```sh
doz app install          # puts Dozable.app in /Applications (or ~/Applications), then open it from Finder
doz app install --open   # … and opens it
```

The app updates with doz: after `doz upgrade` its menu offers **Update Menu Bar App**. Its **Start at Login** starts
the daemon (and the menu) when you log in; it replaces doz's own login item, so there is only ever one. See
[The menu bar app](https://dozable.com/docs/the-menu-bar-app.md).

### The background process is now called the daemon

The background process that runs your sandboxes is called **the daemon**, and its commands are `doz daemon start|stop|restart|status|upgrade-check`. The old command name `host` no longer exists (there is no alias: doz answers it with `unexpected arguments: 'host', …`), and `DOZ_HOST_IDLE` is replaced by `DOZ_DAEMON_IDLE`. A 0.40 store and its settings are carried over automatically, once: the first daemon takes over the old lock and log, the `host.*` settings are read and written back as `daemon.*` the next time `doz.toml` is saved, and an older daemon that is still running keeps serving until it exits by itself when idle (or until `doz daemon stop` switches).

### Upgrading to 0.37: a fresh start

0.37 is the first release with Dozable's own names on disk, and it **starts fresh**: nothing from an earlier
install is read — not your sandboxes, images, restore points, accounts, settings, prompt template or dashboard
links. There is no migration. Before you upgrade, with the version you have:

```sh
doz get my-app /workspace/notes.md ~/Desktop/   # copy out anything a sandbox holds that you want to keep
doz ui stop
doz daemon stop
```

Then upgrade and run `doz onboard` again: it makes the new store, settings and images (every image is built
afresh). New sandboxes' folders go to `~/doz-workspaces`; your project folders, wherever they are, are never
touched. When you no longer need the old install, remove its folders:

```sh
rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/dozer-sandbox   # the old store: sandboxes, images, restore points, accounts list
rm -rf ~/.config/dozer-sandbox                        # the old settings and agent prompt template
rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/dozer-sandbox                 # the old download cache
```

The keys an earlier version saved stay in your login keychain (items named `doz-…`) until you delete them in
Keychain Access. Images an earlier version built with Apple's `container` are named `dozer/…` there:
`container image ls` lists them and `container image delete NAME` removes one.

### Your images after an upgrade

A new version of Dozable may prepare its images differently (it may add a tool, for example). Your
existing images are **never rebuilt without you**: Dozable says an image is out of date — in
`doz image ls`, `doz doctor`, when you create a sandbox, and on the dashboard's Images page — and
you rebuild it when it suits you. See [Images and bases](https://dozable.com/docs/images-and-bases.md#out-of-date-images).

### A sandbox that slept through an upgrade

A sandbox asleep or hibernated when you upgraded wakes on the new version with everything where it
was. Each snapshot remembers the exact virtual machine it was taken in, and the wake rebuilds that
machine, including the Linux kernel it slept under. If a new version ever can't rebuild the same
machine, the wake is refused rather than risk the snapshot, and says so.

## In the dashboard

The dashboard watches the daemon. If a daemon of another version takes over, a banner says so; if the
daemon is **older** than the dashboard, the banner offers **Restart daemon**: it asks first, hibernates
the running sandboxes and starts the newer daemon (they wake when you use them). If the dashboard itself is
the older one — the daemon is newer, or you upgraded doz while it ran — the banner offers **Restart dashboard**
(in this Mac's own browser; or `doz ui restart`), which starts the doz installed now, and the page reloads by
itself. A dashboard in the background with no page open restarts into the new doz by itself. See
[The dashboard](https://dozable.com/docs/the-dashboard.md).

## Uninstall

```sh
doz uninstall
brew uninstall doz
```

`doz uninstall` lists exactly what it will delete and asks once:

- **the store**: every sandbox, image, kernel and restore point, and the daemon's log and metrics;
- **the settings folder**: `doz.toml` and `agent-prompt.md`;
- **the login item**, if you added one (`doz daemon login-item on`) — only this store's; another store's is listed
  and left alone;
- **the menu bar app**, if you installed it (`doz app install`) — its Start at Login is turned off and it is quit first.
  `doz app uninstall` removes only it.

Run `doz uninstall` BEFORE `brew uninstall doz` (Homebrew's note says so): a login item left behind only fails
harmlessly at each login, but it is yours to remove (`doz daemon login-item off`, or delete the plist).

Keep either with `--keep-store` or `--keep-config`; `--yes` skips the question (without a terminal
and without `--yes` it refuses). A running daemon is stopped first; a running `doz ui` must be stopped
by you (Ctrl-C in its terminal). For a Homebrew install, the `doz` program itself is Homebrew's to
remove: `doz uninstall` says so and ends with the `brew uninstall doz` command.

It **never** touches:

- your project folders;
- your keychain. Remove accounts you added first if you want their keychain items gone:
  `doz account rm NAME` (it deletes the item `doz account add` made). `doz uninstall` names any left;
- Claude Code's own files and login.

## Start over: doz nuke

```sh
doz inventory        # what Dozable keeps on this Mac, where, and how big — changes nothing
doz nuke --dry-run   # what doz nuke would remove
doz nuke             # remove it all (asks first)
```

`doz nuke` puts this Mac back to a fresh install of Dozable and keeps `doz` installed. It lists each item with
its place and size, then asks once:

- **the store**: every sandbox, image, kernel, restore point and saved disk, and the daemon's log and metrics;
- **the settings folder**: `doz.toml`, `agent-prompt.md`, and the update and usage records;
- **the download cache** (`~/Library/Caches/doz`);
- **the keychain items Dozable made**: your accounts' keys and the default GitHub key.

`--dry-run` lists and removes nothing; `--yes` skips the question. A running daemon is stopped first; a running
`doz ui` must be stopped by you (`doz ui stop`). Your next `doz` command starts
from the beginning: `doz onboard` or `doz ui`.

It **never** touches your sandboxes' folders, the Mac's own Claude Code and Codex logins, or Apple's `container`
data. `doz inventory` prints the same list and changes nothing.

## Build from source (contributors)

The source is on GitHub (`dozable/dozable`). `make install-cli` builds and signs `doz` into
`~/.local/bin`; `make cli` builds a signed development copy. A source build is never updated by doz itself.
Don't have a Homebrew `doz` and a source-built one on your `PATH` at the same time. See the repository's README.

## Settings

| key | default | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `store.path` | `~/Library/Application Support/doz` | Where the store lives (`--store`, `$DOZ_STORE`). |
| `daemon.always_on` | `true` | The daemon keeps running when nothing runs (`$DOZ_DAEMON_ALWAYS_ON`). |
| `daemon.idle_timeout_minutes` | `5` | With `daemon.always_on` off: minutes with nothing running before the daemon exits (`0` disables it). |
| `updates.mode` | `notify` | `notify`, `auto` or `off` (`$DOZ_UPDATES`). |
| `updates.channel` | `stable` | `stable`, `beta` or `canary` — a Homebrew install's formula decides while it is not set. |

## Troubleshooting

| symptom | what to do |
|---|---|
| `brew install` says another doz formula is installed | One channel at a time: `doz upgrade --channel …` switches (or `brew uninstall` the other first). |
| "the update feed was ignored" / "do not verify" | Nothing is installed from it; doz keeps working. If it persists, check your network isn't rewriting `updates.dozable.com`. |
| `doz: command not found` | `brew list doz`, then open a new terminal window. |
| The menu bar app says doz is not installed | It looks for doz at `/opt/homebrew/bin/doz`, `/usr/local/bin/doz` and `~/.local/bin/doz` — install doz there (Homebrew does). |
| "this daemon's program … is gone — an upgrade removed it" | `doz daemon stop`, then run your command again. |
| "cannot boot a VM" or a message about the entitlement | `doz doctor`. Reinstall: `brew reinstall doz`. |
| Start over, keeping doz installed | `doz nuke`, then `doz onboard`. |
| Start over from nothing | `doz uninstall`, `brew uninstall doz`, then `brew trust --tap dozable/tap`, `brew install dozable/tap/doz` and `doz onboard`. |

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/setting-up

# Setting up this Mac

Setup — **onboarding** — is what you do once after installing: it checks your Mac, prepares the **base image**
every tool is added to, adds the **keys** your tools use, chooses and confirms what sandboxes may use as you
(**Access**: GitHub, your SSH agent), explains **folder rules** and lets you choose what they do, writes your
settings, and makes your **first sandbox**. You can do it in the terminal (`doz onboard`) or in the browser (the
dashboard's setup wizard). Both are safe to run again.

## Concepts

- **The base image** is the Linux system every tool runs on: Node.js on Debian by default (`doz base ls` lists
  the others). It is downloaded and prepared **once**; each tool you try — Claude Code, pi, OpenCode … — is added
  to it as a layer, so a second tool downloads only itself. The store's base is the setting `defaults.base`. See
  [Images and bases](https://dozable.com/docs/images-and-bases.md).
- **Preparation runs in the daemon**, not in your terminal. Setup starts the base's download at the Base image step
  and goes on asking; you can close the terminal or leave the wizard and it carries on. A tool prepared while the
  base is still being prepared waits for it instead of downloading it a second time.
- **An account** is how a tool pays for its AI model: your Mac's Claude Code or Codex login, a long-lived token, or
  a key of a provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, Google) or a gateway (OpenRouter). The secret stays on your Mac; a
  sandbox only ever sees a stand-in. See [Agents and accounts](https://dozable.com/docs/agents-and-accounts.md).
- **Onboard uses this Mac's Claude Code login by default.** When Claude Code is signed in on this Mac, that login —
  the account `mac` — is what your agents use, with nothing to paste; the Models & keys step shows it. To set up with
  another account instead, give it: `doz onboard --key setup-token` (or another provider's key) adds that one and runs
  no Claude Code checks. To set up **without** the Mac's login at all, say so: `doz onboard --claude-account none --yes`
  leaves no account `mac` (the default account is then none; nothing of the Mac's is read), `--claude-account later`
  changes nothing, and `--claude-account mac` (or later `doz account default mac`) takes it back. After onboarding, `doz account default none --decline-mac` declines it the same way. A declined store never uses the Mac's login: agents fenced on this Mac use the store's default account, or none. That login **expires** after some
  hours, and only the Mac's own Claude Code renews it: `doz account keepalive always` has Dozable run it when the login
  expires (not for a daemon started over SSH), and a setup-token account (`claude setup-token`, valid a year) suits long
  unattended work. See [How the Mac login stays fresh](https://dozable.com/docs/agents-and-accounts.md#how-the-mac-login-stays-fresh).
- **Access** is every other credential a sandbox may use as you — **GitHub as you**
  ([GitHub](https://dozable.com/docs/github.md)) and **SSH agent forwarding**. Each is a choice of yours (both are off until you choose
  them), and each is **confirmed live** when you choose it. A credential that can't be confirmed can be
  **skipped**: the choice is kept, marked *not confirmed*, and setup goes on. The choices are the defaults for new
  sandboxes; `doz access` and **Settings** › **Access** check them again later.
- **Folder rules** are two small files you can put in a project folder: `.dozignore` (paths the agent
  must not use) and `.dozreadonly` (paths it may read but not change). Setup explains them and asks one
  question: should a `.dozignore` **lock** the paths it lists (still listed, but nothing can open them —
  the default) or **hide** them (not there at all)? See [Folder rules](https://dozable.com/docs/workspace-rules.md).

## In the terminal

```sh
doz onboard
doz onboard --no-color      # the same, without colour (doz config set ui.color never keeps it so)
```

On a terminal it asks, one step at a time — each headed **Step N of M** with the same names as the dashboard's setup.
A choice is a list: **↑**/**↓** move, **Enter** picks, a number picks at once; the recommended answer is marked and
already selected, so **Enter** alone accepts it. A name or a folder is typed, its default shown dimmed (**Enter** keeps
it); a name that can't be used is refused right under the field. While the base downloads, a line between two steps
says how far it is — never under a question. With `--no-color` (or `doz config set ui.color never`, or `NO_COLOR` set)
it looks the same without colour; with its output in a pipe (`doz onboard | cat`) it asks for typed answers instead.

1. **Welcome** — what Dozable is and what these steps set up; **Enter** starts.
2. **This Mac** — the same checks as `doz doctor`. The required ones stop setup when they fail: Apple
   silicon, macOS 26 or later, virtualization, the signed program, the store on an APFS disk with room
   for the base (about 2 GB with a first sandbox), and a store path short enough. The rest only warn: Claude
   Code missing or signed out (you can add a key instead), and the NAT network helper (only `--network nat`
   needs it). Setup waits here for **Enter**, so you can read them.
3. **Base image** — every base, with its size and what it is for; Node.js (`node:22-bookworm`, ↓ 381 MiB) is
   selected. **Enter** starts its download and preparation in the daemon at once, and the next questions follow
   straight away; **None now** prepares none (each tool's first start prepares its own).
4. **Models & keys** — the sign-ins found on this Mac (Claude Code, Codex), then **Add a key?**: every provider and
   gateway, each with the tools it serves, asked again until **No more keys**. A key
   is pasted at a hidden prompt and added exactly as `doz account add` adds it: checked with one tiny request
   and stored in your login keychain. An OpenRouter key works for every tool that can use OpenRouter (pi,
   OpenCode). **Claude subscription token** adds one (from `claude setup-token`); **Sign in with ChatGPT** signs
   Codex in (official builds). An Anthropic key becomes the store's default only when Claude Code
   is not signed in on this Mac — it never quietly replaces your subscription.
5. **GitHub & SSH** — what sandboxes may use as you, each offered and never done behind your back:
   - **GitHub as you**: *Off* (the default), *Read-only* or *Read and push* — and where the token
     comes from: this Mac's `gh` login, or a token you paste (best: a fine-grained one).
   - **SSH agent forwarding**: *Off* (the default) or *On*.

   Each choice has a one-line consequence beside it. Then each is **confirmed**:

   ```
   ✓ Claude account        mac              confirmed — this Mac's Claude Code login (you@example.com), max
   ✓ GitHub as you         read (gh login)  confirmed — signed in as you — scopes: repo, read:org (from this Mac's gh login)
   ✗ SSH agent forwarding  on               not confirmed — this Mac has no ssh-agent to forward
   ```

   A failure says why, and offers **Skip** (keep the choice, not confirmed — `doz access` checks
   again later), **Turn it off**, or **Check again**. Setup is never blocked by it.
6. **Folder rules** — what `.dozignore` and `.dozreadonly` do, in a few lines: the benefit (keep an
   agent out of your secrets, or stop it changing some files, without moving anything), and the
   consequences — **lock** keeps a path listed but unreadable, so the agent knows it exists; **hide**
   removes it altogether; only a folder with one of the files changes, and nothing costs anything without
   them; the first look through many files is a little slower when rules exist; and it is **not a security
   boundary** (root in the sandbox can get round it). Then: *Lock* (recommended) or *Hide* — the default
   for every sandbox (the setting `folder.ignore_mode`; a sandbox can choose its own).
7. **Settings** — `doz.toml` (every setting at its default, plus your answers) and `agent-prompt.md`
   beside it, each written **only if it doesn't exist yet**. Your base (when it is not Node.js), Access and
   Folder rules answers are then set in it — only the ones you chose.

Then, in an official build, two questions:

- **Usage statistics** — what is sent (counts and ranges about how Dozable is used, never names, paths,
  contents or anything inside a sandbox), `doz telemetry show` to see it exactly, and the privacy
  policy; then *Send anonymous usage statistics?* (**y**/**n**). **Enter** keeps them on and changes nothing;
  **n** sets `telemetry.send_anonymous_usage_stats = false`. When `DO_NOT_TRACK` or
  `$DOZ_SEND_ANONYMOUS_USAGE_STATS` already decides, it says so and does not ask. A build from the
  open-source repository sends nothing and skips the step.
- **Stay in touch** (optional) — release news, tool news, early access and tips and tricks by email; **Enter**
  skips it.

And last:

- **First sandbox** — *Make your first sandbox?*: Claude Code, pi, OpenCode (Codex too, once it has a sign-in or a
  key) or *Not now*. Then its **Name** (`claude`) and **Folder** (`~/doz-workspaces/claude`) — **Enter** keeps a new
  empty folder of its own; type a path to use a project folder of yours. It is made the quick way, like `doz try`: the tool on the
  store's base, a new sandbox's network (**Standard**, `defaults.permissions`: its model, software packages and
  GitHub), and files it opens from its folder open on this Mac (`sandbox.open_files`). Setup says the same in one
  command — `Same in Terminal: doz new claude --agent claude-code` — and waits for **Enter** before it makes anything
  (**Ctrl-C** stops there, with nothing made); then it waits for the base (its progress shown; **Ctrl-C** leaves it running),
  starts the sandbox and attaches you to the tool. When you leave it: `Leaving claude — [S]leep / [d]elete / [k]eep
  running`; **d** removes it, and its folder while that is still empty.

Without a first sandbox, setup waits for the base at the end. Press **Ctrl-C** to leave it running in the
background. Then:

```sh
doz onboard --status      # show the base and follow a preparation that is running
doz onboard --cancel      # stop the base being prepared
```

When the base is ready, the store is marked as set up — even if you'd detached. Setup then sums up what it set up
(the base, sign-ins, keys added, GitHub, the SSH agent, the folder rules, the settings file) and, without a first
sandbox, what to run next.

### Without questions (scripts)

```sh
doz onboard --yes                                     # the Node.js base, no key, no sandbox
doz onboard --base python --yes
doz onboard --no-base --yes                           # prepare nothing now
doz onboard --key openrouter --key-name or-work --secret-stdin --yes < key.txt
doz onboard --key setup-token --key-name work --plan max --secret-stdin --yes < token.txt
doz onboard --first claude                            # the first sandbox without asking for it
doz onboard --github read --ssh-agent on --yes
doz onboard --ignore-mode hide --yes
doz onboard --github push --github-key-stdin --yes < github-token.txt
```

`--yes`, `--json`, or no terminal: nothing is asked and the defaults are taken — the Node.js base, no key, no
sandbox. A key or token is read from standard input only with `--secret-stdin` (`--github-key-stdin` for a GitHub
token); it is never a command-line argument. Each credential chosen is still confirmed; one that can't be is
**skipped with a note** and the exit code stays 0. Without `--github` / `--ssh-agent` / `--ignore-mode` /
`--usage-stats`, `--yes` leaves those settings exactly as they are.

| option | what it does |
|---|---|
| `--base ID` | The base image without asking: `node` (the default), `python`, `go` … (`doz base ls`). Sets `defaults.base`. |
| `--no-base` | Prepare no base now (each tool's first start prepares its own). |
| `--key PROVIDER` | Add a key without asking: `anthropic`, `openai`, `xai`, `google`, `openrouter`, or `setup-token` (the Claude Code checks are then skipped). |
| `--key-name NAME` · `--plan PLAN` · `--force` | For the key: its name (default: the provider's name), a setup token's plan (`max`, `pro`, `team`, `enterprise`), replace an existing account. |
| `--first AGENT\|none` | The first sandbox without asking: `claude`, `pi`, `opencode`, `codex` (any tool `doz try` takes), or `none`. |
| `--openai-account mac\|chatgpt\|openai-key\|later` | Codex's account without asking. |
| `--github off\|read\|push` | Answer "GitHub as you" (the setting `defaults.github`). |
| `--github-source gh\|key` · `--github-key-stdin` | Where the GitHub token comes from: this Mac's `gh` login, or a token read from standard input (kept in the login keychain as `doz-github`). |
| `--ssh-agent on\|off` | Answer "SSH agent forwarding" (the setting `sandbox.ssh_agent`). |
| `--ignore-mode lock\|hide` | Answer the Folder rules step (the setting `folder.ignore_mode`). |
| `--usage-stats on\|off` | Answer the Usage statistics step (official builds; the setting `telemetry.send_anonymous_usage_stats`, written only when it changes). |
| `--status` · `--cancel` | Follow · stop the preparation. |

## In the dashboard

```sh
doz ui
```

A store that was never set up opens on the **setup wizard**, in a window over the dashboard (its steps
across the top; **✕** or **Escape** closes it, asking first once you have chosen something). Each step's title is
centred over a column of the step's own width — narrow for a switch or a form, wide for two columns:

1. **Welcome** — what Dozable is, and **This Mac**: the doctor's checks, inline. A failing required check stops here,
   with what to fix and **Check again**; the others only say what will not work yet.
2. **Base image** — one card, **Node.js** (recommended), how each tool is added to it as a layer, and
   **Another base** folded (Python, Go, Rust, …). **Download and continue** starts its download and preparation in the
   host and moves on at once.
3. **Models & keys** — two columns. On the left the sign-ins found on this Mac (Claude Code, Codex) and **Tools you can
   use now**; on the right the keys by **Providers** (Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, Google), **Gateways** (OpenRouter) and
   **No key** (OpenCode Zen's free models), each row naming the tools it serves. **Add a key** opens a masked field
   under its row; the key is checked once and kept in the login keychain, and the tools it serves turn ready.
   **Decide later** moves on.
4. **GitHub & SSH** — **GitHub as you** (off, read-only, read and push — from this Mac's `gh` login or a token in a
   masked field) and **SSH agent forwarding**, each with its consequence. **Next** confirms each one: *confirmed* with
   what was found, or *not confirmed* with the reason and **Skip** · **Turn it off** · **Check again**.
5. **Folder rules** — the same description as in the terminal, and the same choice: **Lock** (recommended) or
   **Hide**. Its **Next** writes the settings (the base too, when it is not Node.js).
6. **Usage statistics** (official builds) — the same text as in the terminal and one switch, **Send anonymous usage
   statistics**, on. **Next** saves it only if you changed it.
7. **Stay in touch** (optional, official builds) — an email and what you'd like; **Skip** moves on.
8. **First sandbox** — the tools' cards (one you cannot use yet is dimmed, with what it needs) and its plan: a
   **Name** (the tool's: `claude`), its folder — **a new empty folder** (`~/doz-workspaces/claude`, the default) or
   **a project folder on this Mac** (typed, or **Choose…**) — then Model, Network (Standard), Image, what Delete does,
   and **Same in Terminal** (`doz new claude --agent claude-code`). **Open what it makes on this Mac**
   is on (the setting `sandbox.open_files`). **Create and start claude** makes it and opens its page; **Finish
   without a sandbox** goes to Sandboxes. **What setup wrote** (folded) says what went where.

From the step after Base image, the base's progress is a strip at the foot, just above the buttons: downloading (a
bar, the bytes, the time left) → preparing (step N of 4) → ready (green). **Details** opens a popover over the step —
the steps with their times, the last lines of output, **Operations** and **Cancel…**; **✕**, **Escape** or a click
outside closes it. If the download stops, the strip turns red with **Retry**, and the questions go on. Reach First
sandbox before the base is ready and its Image line says it *waits for the base*: Create and start does not wait —
the sandbox's page opens, and its build's first step is the wait.

![The wizard's checks](https://dozable.com/docs/images/wizard-checks.png)

You can run the wizard again at any time: **Onboarding** under **Setup** in the sidebar (with a dot beside it until
the store is set up), or **Doctor** › **Run onboarding again**.

## Checking access again

```sh
doz access                       # each credential, confirmed now
doz access --no-check            # the last confirmation only
doz access set --github push     # change a choice (and confirm it)
doz access set --ssh-agent off
```

In the dashboard: **Settings** › **Access** shows each credential as last confirmed, with **Check
again**; the choices themselves are the settings `defaults.github`, `github.credentials` and
`sandbox.ssh_agent` further down the page.

## What was written where

| what | where |
|---|---|
| Your settings | `~/.config/doz/doz.toml` (under `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` if set) — see [Settings reference](https://dozable.com/docs/settings-reference.md) |
| Your agent prompt template | `agent-prompt.md` beside it — everything inside an HTML comment, so it changes nothing until you write your own text. See [Agents and accounts](https://dozable.com/docs/agents-and-accounts.md#the-agents-environment-facts) |
| The store (images, sandboxes) | `~/Library/Application Support/doz` |
| Accounts with a secret | your login keychain, `doz-claude:NAME` (tokens) or `doz-anthropic:NAME` (API keys) |
| A GitHub token you gave | your login keychain, `doz-github` |
| The last access check | `access.json` in the store — states and reasons, never a secret |

## Settings

| key | default | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `defaults.image` | `lab` | The image `doz up NAME`, `doz init` and the dashboard's New sandbox use when you don't name one. Onboarding sets it to `claude-code`. |
| `defaults.base` | `node` | The store's base: the base a quick-made sandbox's tool is added to (Quick try, `doz try`, the first sandbox). The Base image step's choice. |
| `defaults.projects_dir` | `~/doz-workspaces` | Your projects folder: Quick add, `doz new` and New sandbox make each new sandbox's folder in it. `doz onboard` says where it is; the dashboard's **Settings** › **Choose…** or `doz config set defaults.projects_dir DIR` moves it. |
| `defaults.account` | `mac` | The account of a store that hasn't chosen one. `doz account default` decides for a store once it has. |
| `defaults.github` | `off` | "GitHub as you" for new sandboxes: `off`, `read` or `push`. The Access step's choice. |
| `github.credentials` | `gh` | Where the GitHub token comes from: `gh` (this Mac's login), `key` (a token you gave), `off`. |
| `sandbox.ssh_agent` | `off` | Forward this Mac's ssh-agent into sandboxes (github.com only). |
| `folder.ignore_mode` | `lock` | What a `.dozignore` does to the paths it lists: `lock` or `hide`. The Folder rules step's choice. |
| `ui.allow_secret_entry` | `true` | The dashboard may take an API key or setup token in a masked field. `false`: it shows the `doz account add` command instead. The dashboard can turn this off, never on. |
| `recipes.anthropic.claude-code.version` · `recipes.earendil-works.pi.version` | `latest` | Which agent version its image is baked with. See [Agents and accounts](https://dozable.com/docs/agents-and-accounts.md#agent-versions). |

## Limits and notes

- Setup never signs you in to Claude Code, and never touches Claude Code's own refresh token.
- Re-running `doz onboard` is safe: it re-checks, leaves existing settings files alone and prepares
  only what is missing.
- The first preparation needs the internet: it downloads the base (about 380 MB for Node.js; `doz base ls` lists
  each base's download), then each tool the first time it is used.

## Troubleshooting

| symptom | what to do |
|---|---|
| A required check fails | Read its message; `doz doctor` shows every check with what to do. |
| Preparation fails part way | `doz onboard --status` shows the failed step. Run `doz onboard` again: it continues with what's missing (a download resumes). |
| "latest" can't be resolved (offline) | Set an exact agent version: `doz config set recipes.anthropic.claude-code.version 2.1.227`. |
| The wizard shows commands instead of a key field | `ui.allow_secret_entry` is off: use `doz account add NAME --api-key` in a terminal. |
| GitHub *not confirmed: gh is not logged in* | Run `gh auth login` on the Mac, then `doz access` — or give a token: `doz access set --github-key`. |
| SSH *not confirmed: no ssh-agent* or *no keys* | Start an agent and `ssh-add` your key on the Mac, then `doz access`. Or turn it off: `doz access set --ssh-agent off`. |
| You want to start over | [Uninstall](https://dozable.com/docs/install-upgrade-uninstall.md#uninstall), then install and onboard again. |

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/projects

# Projects

A **project** is a folder with a `doz_project.yaml` file in it. The file describes the folder's
sandbox — which agent, how much memory, what it may reach, which sessions to start — and `doz up` in
that folder creates, starts or wakes exactly that sandbox, with the folder shared at `/workspace`.
Use projects when you work on the same code day after day, or want everyone on a team to get the same
sandbox from a checkout.

## Concepts

- **The project folder is the sandbox's folder.** A project's sandbox always shares its own folder — the folder
  appears inside the sandbox at `/workspace` — live: what the agent writes is on your Mac at once, and the other way round.
- **The file holds choices, never secrets.** You can commit it. Credentials come from your
  [accounts](https://dozable.com/docs/agents-and-accounts.md), which stay on your Mac.
- **Some choices are made when the sandbox is made.** Its image, CPUs and memory — and a `nat` or
  `none` network — are the virtual machine's make-up. Changing them in the file affects a **new**
  sandbox only; `doz up` tells you so. Other keys apply at once or from the next session (below).
- **Your projects folder is not a project.** The setting `defaults.projects_dir`
  (`~/doz-workspaces`) is where **Quick add**, **New sandbox** and `doz new` make a
  folder for each new sandbox that has none of its own — `claude-sandbox`, `claude-sandbox-2`, … —
  with no `doz_project.yaml`. Run `doz init` in one of them to make it a project. Change the folder in
  **Settings** › **Choose…** or with `doz config set defaults.projects_dir DIR`
  ([The quickest way](https://dozable.com/docs/sandboxes-and-lifecycle.md#the-quickest-way-quick-add-and-doz-new)).

## Make a folder a project

```sh
cd ~/code/my-app
doz init
```

On a terminal `doz init` walks the same steps as the dashboard's **New sandbox** wizard, each saying
`Step N of 10`:

1. **Project folder** — the folder, and the sandbox's name (suggested from the folder's);
2. **Agent and base** — the image (suggested from the setting `defaults.image`);
3. **Account** — for an agent: `default` (the store's), `none`, or an account;
4. **Access** — the same questions as onboarding's Access step, for this sandbox: GitHub as you (`off`,
   `read` or `push`; the default is the setting `defaults.github`) and SSH agent forwarding. What you
   turn on is confirmed live (as `doz access` does); one that can't be confirmed can be skipped — kept,
   not confirmed — turned off, or checked again. Where the GitHub token comes from is this Mac's choice
   (`doz access set`), not the project's;
5. **Folder rules** — onboarding's description of `.dozignore` and `.dozreadonly`, what the folder
   already has (each rule file, how many patterns and its first lines — or *none — the folder is shared
   as is*, with how to add one), and this sandbox's choice: **Lock** or **Hide** (`ignore_mode` in the
   file; the default is the setting `folder.ignore_mode`). See [Folder rules](https://dozable.com/docs/workspace-rules.md);
6. **Permissions and network** — the network, and what the agent may do (`standard`, `locked`,
   `open`, or changes like `+web,-error-reports`);
7. **Resources** — CPUs and memory (the disk is the image's own; it isn't set per sandbox);
8. **Bridges** — the clipboard, links in your browser, the folder's files opened on the Mac;
9. **Session** — tmux, and the agent's sudo;
10. **Review** — the file it will write, and **Write?**

Each question shows its default; **Enter** keeps it. It sets this Mac up first if it never was. The
file lists every key: what you chose is set, and what you left at its default stays commented out — it
follows your settings.

In a folder that already has a project file, `doz init` on a terminal starts from that file, and
replaces it only after showing what changes (`- ` the line there now, `+ ` the new one) and asking.

```sh
doz init ~/code/other --name other --image python-claude-code --memory 4G --yes
doz init ~/code/api --yes --network agent --permissions +web --github read --tmux
doz init --force            # rewrite an existing doz_project.yaml without asking
```

| option | what it does |
|---|---|
| `DIR` | The folder (default: the current one; made if missing). |
| `--name` · `--image` · `--cpus` · `--memory` · `--network` · `--permissions` · `--account` | Answer those questions up front. |
| `--github` · `--ssh-agent` · `--ignore-mode` · `--clipboard` · `--browser-bridge` · `--open-files` · `--tmux` · `--agent-sudo` | The same, for access, folder rules, bridges and the session (`--no-tmux`, `--no-agent-sudo` too). |
| `--yes` | Ask nothing: every default. `--json` and no terminal ask nothing too. |
| `--force` | Rewrite an existing file without asking. |

## Use it

```sh
cd ~/code/my-app
doz up
```

With no sandbox name, in a project folder, `doz up`:

1. creates the sandbox if it doesn't exist (the folder becomes its `/workspace`);
2. starts it, or wakes it;
3. starts the file's `sessions` — the first one attached to your terminal, the others in the
   background;
4. brings the sandbox's own settings into line with the file (its agent prompt, sudo, clipboard,
   browser bridge, opening files, tmux), and says what it changed.

Options you give `up` win over the file's, for a new sandbox: `doz up --memory 8G`.
`doz up -d` does it all without attaching. When you detach (**Ctrl-]** twice), the line printed
names the shortest way back — in the project folder that is just `doz up`.

### In the dashboard

**Sandboxes** › **New sandbox** is a wizard with the same ten steps, in a window over the dashboard. It starts with the **project
folder**: a new folder in your projects folder, or a folder you have (type it, or **Choose…** in your
Mac's folder picker). If that folder has a project file, the wizard starts from it.

- Every step is filled in from your settings (or from the file). The steps run across the top, a
  check on each one done (hover it for your answer) — click one to go back to it. **Back** and **Next**
  (at the bottom, always in view) move between steps, **Enter** is Next, **Alt+←** / **Alt+→** too, and
  **Skip to review** jumps to the end keeping every default.
- **✕** or **Escape** closes the wizard; once you have chosen something it asks first. The browser's
  **Back** closes it too and keeps your choices — **Forward**, or **New sandbox** again, picks up where
  you were.
- **Folder rules** lists the folder's `.dozignore` / `.dozreadonly` as they are now; add or edit one on
  the Mac and press **Look again**.
- **Review** lists your choices and says what will happen; **The file, exactly as written** unfolds the
  `doz_project.yaml` it will write. **Write and create** writes it into the folder, makes the sandbox
  from it — as `doz up` there would — starts it, sets up its tools and opens its page. A folder that
  already has a file asks first, showing what changes.
- **One-page form** (top right) is the old single form, for an isolated sandbox with no project file.
  **Quick add** stays the no-questions way in ([The quickest way](https://dozable.com/docs/sandboxes-and-lifecycle.md#the-quickest-way-quick-add-and-doz-new)).

![The New sandbox wizard's review](https://dozable.com/docs/images/new-sandbox-wizard.png)

A project's sandbox is an ordinary sandbox there: it appears under **Sandboxes**, and its page shows
its folder.

## `doz_project.yaml` reference

The file may also be called `doz_project.yml`. A folder with both is an error — `doz up`, `doz init`
and the dashboard all say so; keep one.

```yaml
version: 1
name: webapp                # the sandbox
image: claude-code          # or: agent + base, or agent + dockerfile (below)
cpus: 4
memory: 4G
network: agent              # agent, bake, locked, open, nat, none
permissions: "+web"         # standard, locked, open, or changes on Standard
account: default            # default, none, or an account name
model_source: openrouter    # where the model comes from: a provider or gateway the agent is offered (doz models)
model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6   # a model id of that source
sessions:                   # what doz up starts; the first is attached
  - claude                  #   the image's own session
  - name: server            #   a session of your own
    command: npm run dev    #   split on spaces, no shell — or a list: [npm, run, dev]
agent_prompt: |             # this project's own lines for the agent
  The tests run with `make test`.
agent_prompt_mode: append   # or replace
agent_sudo: true
clipboard: write            # or off
browser_bridge: on          # or off
open_files: on              # or off
ssh_agent: off              # or on
github: off                 # read or push: git and gh signed in as you
tmux: false                 # or true
folder_view: on          # off: share the folder directly (programs in it lose their folder at a wake)
```

| key | value | default | when a change applies |
|---|---|---|---|
| `version` | `1` | — | — |
| `name` | the sandbox: 1–40 of `a-z 0-9 -` | the folder's name | — |
| `image` | `claude-code`, `pi`, `lab`, a base × agent image (`python-claude-code`, `go-pi`, `debian`, …) or a saved disk (`doz image save`) | `defaults.image` | when the sandbox is made |
| `agent` | `claude-code`, `codex`, `opencode`, `pi` (any tool `doz search` lists as supported) or `none` — instead of `image`, with `base` or `dockerfile`; a tool's major or exact release: `opencode@1`, `opencode@2.0.28` ([A tool's major version](https://dozable.com/docs/try-and-search.md#a-tools-major-version)); its full name: `anthropic/claude-code`, `mine/acme/tool` ([A tool's full name](https://dozable.com/docs/try-and-search.md#a-tools-full-name)) | `claude-code` | when made |
| `base` | a recommended base: `node`, `python`, `go`, `rust`, `java`, `ruby`, `dotnet`, `debian`, `ubuntu`, `alpine` | `node` | when made |
| `dockerfile` | your own Dockerfile, relative to the folder or absolute (see [Images and bases](https://dozable.com/docs/images-and-bases.md#your-own-dockerfile)) | — | when made |
| `cpus` | 1–64 | `defaults.cpus` (2) | when made |
| `memory` | `2G`, `512M` or MiB, 256 MiB – 256 GiB | per image (settings) | when made |
| `network` | `agent`, `bake`, `locked`, `open`, `nat`, `none` | per image | `agent`/`bake`/`locked`/`open`: at the next `doz up`, live (unless you edited the sandbox's permissions since); `nat`/`none`: when made |
| `permissions` | what the agent may do on a network with permissions (`agent`, `locked`, `open`): `standard`, `locked`, `open`, or changes on Standard like `+web,-error-reports` (or a list); see [What the agent can do](https://dozable.com/docs/permissions-and-network.md) | `defaults.permissions` (standard) | when made (later: `doz net allow` / `doz net deny`) |
| `account` | `default`, `none` or an account name | follow the store's default | run `doz account use NAME ACCOUNT` |
| `model_source` | where the model comes from: a provider or gateway the agent is offered — `anthropic`, `openai`, `xai`, `google`, `openrouter` (which ones depends on the tool: [Other AI tools](https://dozable.com/docs/ai-tools.md#providers-and-gateways)); `--provider` / `--gateway` on `doz up` win over it | the agent's own | when made |
| `model` | a model id of that source (`doz models --gateway openrouter`); `--model` on `doz up` wins over it | the source's default | when made |
| `sessions` | a list of session names, or `{name, command}` — at most 16 | the image's own session | every `doz up` |
| `agent_prompt` | text, at most 16 KiB | — | the next session |
| `agent_prompt_mode` | `append` or `replace` | `append` | the next session |
| `agent_sudo` | `true` or `false` | `sandbox.agent_sudo` (true) | the next session |
| `clipboard` | `write` or `off` | `sandbox.clipboard` (write) | at once |
| `browser_bridge` | `on` or `off` | `sandbox.browser_bridge` (on) | at once |
| `open_files` | `on` or `off` | `sandbox.open_files` (on) | at once |
| `ssh_agent` | `on` or `off` | `sandbox.ssh_agent` (off) | at once |
| `github` | `off`, `read` or `push` ([GitHub as you](https://dozable.com/docs/github.md)) | off | when made (later: `doz net allow NAME github:as-you`) |
| `tmux` | `true` or `false` | `sessions.tmux` (false) | the next session |
| `approvals` | `skip` or `ask`: the agent's own approval prompts | its recipe's `approvals` (skip) | the next session |

A value the file sets is recorded in its sandbox as the project's (the dashboard's badge: **project**), and
`doz up` applies it again. `doz config set --project DIR KEY VALUE` changes the file for you.

The schema is closed: an unknown key, a key given twice, a wrong type or a value out of range is an
error that names the line. One YAML document, no anchors or aliases, at most 64 KiB.

### When you change the file

`doz up` compares the file with the sandbox and says each difference and what it did, for example:

```
[doz] cpus 2 → 4 in doz_project.yaml: applies only when the sandbox is made — doz rm webapp && doz up recreates it (this folder is kept)
[doz] network agent → locked in doz_project.yaml: applied now (live — the next connection is judged by it)
[doz] clipboard off in doz_project.yaml — applies at once (the UI re-reads it)
```

To remake a sandbox with new make-up, `doz rm NAME` then `doz up`. Your folder is never touched; the
agent's history on the sandbox's state disk goes with the sandbox, so take a
[duplicate](https://dozable.com/docs/restore-points-duplicates-templates.md) with `--copy-state` first if you want to keep it.

## Limits

- One sandbox per project file. Several folders can each have their own.
- The sandbox's name must be unique in the store. Two checkouts of the same project on one Mac need
  different `name`s.
- `permissions` and `github` need a network with permissions (`agent`, `locked` or `open` — or an image
  whose default network is one): with `bake`, `nat` or `none` the file is refused, and says why.
- The disk is the image's own: there is no disk-size key.

## Troubleshooting

| symptom | what to do |
|---|---|
| "unknown key …" | The key isn't in the table above (check its spelling). |
| `doz up` says "which sandbox?" | There's no `doz_project.yaml` in this folder: `cd` into the project, or `doz init`. |
| "NAME was made from …, not this folder's doz_project.yaml — using it anyway" | Two projects use the same `name`, so they share one sandbox. Rename one. |
| A change in the file didn't apply | `doz up` prints when each change applies; image, CPUs and memory need a new sandbox. |

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/sandboxes-and-lifecycle

# Sandboxes and their lifecycle

A **sandbox** is one Linux virtual machine with its own disks. This page covers making one, the
states it can be in — running, paused, asleep, hibernated, shut down — and moving between them, and
the background **daemon** that runs them all.

A sandbox can also be adopted into a workspace, with other agents, a room and a brief — see
[Workspaces](https://dozable.com/docs/workspaces.md); adopting it changes nothing of the sandbox itself. A workspace's `doz workspace sleep`
hibernates its sandboxes (the same as `doz hibernate`, all at once) and `wake` wakes them; `finish` shuts them down, keeping
their disks — a workspace never removes a sandbox unless you say so (`--remove-sandboxes`, and never one you adopted).

A sandbox is one of three places an agent can run — a micro VM; the other two are fenced and unfenced sessions on this
Mac. [Where an agent runs: the three choices](https://dozable.com/docs/sessions-on-this-mac.md#where-an-agent-runs-the-three-choices) compares
them (what each reaches, its memory, its start time, when to pick it).

## Concepts

- **Name.** 1–40 characters of `a-z 0-9 -`, unique in the store.
- **Image.** What the sandbox starts from (Claude Code, pi, a plain shell, a saved disk…). See
  [Images and bases](https://dozable.com/docs/images-and-bases.md).
- **Three kinds of storage**, each kept differently:

  | | what's on it | kept through |
  |---|---|---|
  | the **root disk** | the system and anything installed or written outside the next two | shutdown; gone with `reset` (back to the image) and `rm` |
  | the **state disk** (agent images) | the agent's own settings, logins and history (`~/.claude`, `~/.pi/agent`) | shutdown **and** reset; gone with `rm` |
  | the **folder** | your Mac folder, shared live — it appears inside the sandbox at `/workspace` | everything — it's on your Mac |

- **Isolated.** A sandbox with no shared folder: `/workspace` is a folder on its own disk, and nothing
  on your Mac is shared. `doz ls` shows `isolated`, and the agent is told.
- **Sessions.** The terminal programs running inside (a shell, `claude`, `pi`). They survive pause,
  sleep and hibernate. See [Terminals and sessions](https://dozable.com/docs/terminals-and-sessions.md).
- **The daemon.** One background `doz` process per store. It owns every running VM, the network proxy
  and the credentials. The first command that needs it starts it, and it keeps running (`daemon.always_on`),
  so you normally never think about it.

## The states

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    [*] --> off: doz create
    off --> booting: doz start
    booting --> running
    booting --> failed
    failed --> booting: doz start
    running --> paused: doz pause
    paused --> running: doz resume
    running --> asleep: doz sleep
    asleep --> running: doz wake
    running --> hibernated: doz hibernate
    hibernated --> running: doz wake
    running --> off: doz shutdown
    running --> off: doz reset (a fresh disk)
    off --> [*]: doz rm

    note right of paused: frozen · memory kept · back in ~1 ms
    note right of asleep: frozen and saved to disk · memory kept · back in ~0.3 s
    note right of hibernated: saved to disk · memory given back · back in ~0.3 s
    note left of off: powered off · disks kept · programs ended
```

`doz ls` and the dashboard show which of these states each sandbox is in. `doz up` also wakes an
asleep or hibernated sandbox and resumes a paused one, so it's the one command to remember.

| command | what happens | typical time | memory | programs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `doz start NAME` | boots (or wakes it if asleep, resumes it if paused) | ~0.4 s (a first start may prepare the image) | used as needed | start fresh |
| `doz pause NAME` · `doz resume NAME` | the CPU stops | ~1 ms | kept | frozen, then carry on |
| `doz sleep NAME` · `doz wake NAME` | paused **and** saved to disk — survives a crash of the daemon | ~0.3 s | kept | carry on |
