isolation at all with `--unfenced`: see [Sessions on this Mac](https://dozable.com/docs/sessions-on-this-mac.md).

### Leaving: the Ctrl-] menu

Press **Ctrl-]** in an attached session. One line appears over the bottom row:

```
 doz: d detach · n next · p prev · s sessions · Esc back
```

| key | what it does |
|---|---|
| **Ctrl-]** again (or **d**) | detach — the session keeps running |
| **n** / **p** | move this terminal to the sandbox's next / previous session |
| **s** | list the sessions on that line (`1 shell* · 2 claude · …`); a number switches |
| **Esc** (or any other key) | back to the session |

While the menu shows, the screen is held; when it goes, the screen is redrawn cleanly from the
session's own, so nothing of the menu is left behind. **Ctrl-] twice, quickly, is always a plain
detach**, and the key works however the program has set up your keyboard (Claude Code uses the kitty
keyboard protocol, for example). The menu closes by itself after 15 seconds. If your input is a pipe
rather than a terminal, Ctrl-] detaches at once.

`--detach-key ctrl-x` picks another key; `--detach-key none` has none (close the terminal to leave).

On the way out your terminal is put back exactly as it was — mouse, paste and keyboard modes — and
the last line names the shortest command that comes back: `doz up` in the project folder,
`doz attach NAME` for the sandbox's own session, or `doz attach NAME SESSION`.

### Your terminal's title

While you're attached, `doz attach` sets your terminal window's (or tab's) title, by default to
`sandbox · session · time`, for example `my-app · claude · 14:05`, refreshed each minute. When you
leave, the title you had comes back (iTerm2, Ghostty, kitty and xterm keep a title stack;
Terminal.app keeps Dozable's until something else sets one). Change it with the setting
`ui.terminal_title`, using `{sandbox}` `{session}` `{image}` `{time}` `{phase}`:

```sh
doz config set ui.terminal_title "{image}:{session} ({phase})"
doz config set ui.terminal_title ""          # leave the title to the program in the session
```

While Dozable sets the title, a program's own title (Claude Code sets one) isn't shown.

### When the sandbox sleeps

If the sandbox hibernates while you're attached, the terminal waits and reattaches by itself when it
wakes. With `--no-wake`, `attach` waits for a sleeping sandbox instead of waking it.

## In the browser

On a sandbox's page in the dashboard:

- **Home**, the first tab, lists every session — the agent's as a card, the others as rows, each with
  a small picture of its screen, live while the sandbox runs (a picture is drawn from the session's
  screen, not a terminal of its own, so it never attaches to the session or changes its size).
  **Open** there attaches to a session (the image's own one is started if needed).
- **Watch** (a session's **⋯**) is read-only: nothing you type reaches the session, and it never
  resizes it.
- On the terminals' tab strip, **New shell** starts a new shell session (`shell-2`, `shell-3`, …); its
  **▾** › **Terminal…** starts a new session — a shell, or one running a command — and **Run
  detached…** one that runs without opening here.
- Terminals are **tabs**; **Split** shows two side by side (⇄ moves a tab across). Two tabs on one
  session are marked "shared with tab N". Closing a tab only closes the view — the session keeps
  running; closing the agent's tab brings you to Home, which says so.
- **All sessions** shows every session of every running sandbox as a live, read-only tile.
- **Restart session** and **End session** are on a tab's **⋯** and on a session's **⋯** on **Home**
  (**End…** is on the agent's card itself) (see [Restarting or ending a session](#restarting-or-ending-a-session)). Both ask first; for
  an agent session you can choose to start a new conversation. The tab shows "Restarting the session…" and
  reattaches when the program is back, keeping what was on screen above it.

Each tab's title follows `ui.terminal_title`, like `1 · my-app · claude · 14:05`.

**A sleeping sandbox's terminal** is covered with its state; **any key you type wakes it** (or
resumes it) and the screen comes back where it was, with a note of how long it took. What your
terminal sends by itself (focus changes, colour replies) never wakes it, and neither does a watcher.

**The mouse** works as in a native terminal. A program that tracks the mouse (Claude Code does, and
tmux) gets the wheel, clicks and drags. Hold **Shift** to select text instead, or to scroll the pane.
A program that doesn't track the mouse gets nothing: the wheel scrolls the pane's own scrollback.

**Paste** is filtered: control characters that could run commands become spaces. A multi-line paste
into a program that didn't ask for bracketed paste, or one over 64 KiB, asks first; over 1 MiB is
refused. **Cmd-C** copies a selection, **Cmd-V** pastes; other Cmd shortcuts belong to the browser
(Cmd-W closes the tab — the session runs on).

## What the agent is doing

Claude Code and pi say what they are doing — **working**, **blocked** (waiting for you), **done**, or
stopped with an **error** — and Dozable shows it, whether or not a terminal is attached:

- **The dashboard**: a chip on each session's tab, on its tile in **All sessions** and on its row in the
  **Sessions** tab (with the agent's own one-line message under it); a dot beside the sandbox in the
  sidebar for its most urgent session (blocked, then error, working, done).
- **A notice** at the top of every dashboard page when an agent finishes, gets blocked or fails — it
  names the sandbox and the session and says what it waits for: "needs permission", "has a question"
  or "needs sign-in". **Open** goes to the session; the notice goes when you dismiss it, or by itself
  once the agent is working again.
- **The terminal**: `doz ls` has an AGENT column (each sandbox's most urgent session), and
  `doz sessions NAME` one for each session:

```sh
$ doz sessions my-app
SESSION  PID  SIZE    CLIENTS  STATE    AGENT                      COMMAND
claude   41   120×36  1        running  blocked: needs permission  claude --dangerously-skip-permissions
shell    88   120×36  0        running  —                          bash -l
```

`doz events` prints each change as it happens; `--json` on `ls`, `sessions` and `inspect` carries the
full status.

Which agents say it:

| agent | reports its status |
|---|---|
| Claude Code | 2.1.295 and later (images install the newest by default) |
| pi | 1.1.0 and later |
| Grok Build | 1.0.52 and later (the version Dozable installs) |
| Codex | no — its sessions show nothing, and everything else works as usual |
| OpenCode | no (checked with 1.19.0) |
| GitHub Copilot CLI | no (checked with 1.0.96) |
| Qwen Code | no (checked with 0.25.1) |
| Goose | no (checked with 1.54.0) |
| Kilo Code CLI | no (checked with 7.8.8) |
| Mistral Vibe | no (checked with 2.26.1) |
| Factory Droid | 0.240.1 (the version Dozable installs) |
| Dirac | no (checked with 0.5.20) |
| Kimi Code | no (checked with 2.1.1) |
| Cline CLI | no (checked with 3.0.71) |
| OpenHands CLI | no (checked with 1.16.0) |
| Letta Code | no (checked with 0.34.13) |
| Docker Agent | 1.150.0 (the version Dozable installs) |
| Nanocoder | no (checked with 1.31.0) |
| mini-swe-agent | no (checked with 2.4.6) |
| Open Interpreter | no (checked with 0.0.56) |
| Crush | partly (0.98.1 reports idle and working, never done; not used yet) |
| MiMo Code | no (checked with 0.1.15) |
| CodeWhale | no (checked with 0.10.1) |
| Maki | no (checked with 0.6.3) |
| oh-my-pi | partly (18.10.4 reports idle, never working or done; not used yet) |
| Tau | no (checked with 0.4.7) |

How it works: a program reports its state with a terminal escape sequence (the *program status*
protocol, OSC 7501) — but only after the terminal answers that it understands it. Dozable's session
keeper inside the sandbox answers and keeps the latest report of each session, so the status is
there while you are detached, and after a sleep or a hibernation the agent carries on reporting. The
sequence itself still reaches your terminal unchanged when you are attached. A session's status ends
with its program, except **done** and **error**, which stay until the session starts something new
or the sandbox shuts down.

Limits:

- the agent's message is its own text, shown as plain text and never written to Dozable's log;
- tmux does not pass the status through, so a session running inside tmux shows none: tmux (3.8 too) drops
  the sequence, and the agents send it plain. tmux's `allow-passthrough` would not change that — it only
  passes on a sequence a program wraps for tmux, and Claude Code and pi don't — so Dozable leaves it off;
- a session started before an update keeps the session keeper it started with and shows no status
  until it is restarted (`doz sessions restart NAME SESSION`).

## The clipboard

When a program in a session copies — Claude Code's copy, a yank in vim or tmux — the text goes onto
**your Mac's clipboard**, and you're told every time: `my-app copied 42 chars` over the bottom row of
`doz attach` for three seconds (then the screen is redrawn), or a message in the corner of the
dashboard. When the output isn't a terminal (`doz run … > file`), the notice is a line on stderr.

![The clipboard notice in the dashboard](https://dozable.com/docs/images/clipboard-toast.png)

- **A sandbox can never read your clipboard.** A program's request to read it is dropped — it never
  even reaches your terminal app, so nothing can answer it for the sandbox — and logged once.
- **Limits:** 1 MiB per copy, at most 10 copies in 10 seconds per sandbox. More is refused, and said.
- **Only while you watch:** a copy happens only while a terminal is attached to the session.
- **The risk:** an agent could put a command on your clipboard hoping you paste it. That's why every
  copy is announced. Turn it off where you don't want it:

```sh
doz config set --sandbox my-app sandbox.clipboard off   # this sandbox (at once)
doz config set sandbox.clipboard off                    # every sandbox without its own choice
doz create my-app --clipboard off …                     # from the start (or clipboard: off in doz_project.yaml)
doz config unset --sandbox my-app sandbox.clipboard     # follow the setting again
```

## Opening your folder's files on your Mac

A sandbox has no desktop, but its files in `/workspace` are your Mac folder. So when a program (or
the agent) runs `xdg-open report.html` — or `open notes.md`, or `doz-open notes.md` — inside a
sandbox with a shared folder, the file opens **on your Mac**, in its default app: an html page in
your browser, markdown in your editor, a PDF in Preview. A relative name is the program's own folder's.

A **folder** — the shared folder itself or any folder in it — opens in the **Finder**, and
`doz-open --reveal` shows a file selected in its folder:

```sh
xdg-open report.html                    # in the sandbox: opens ~/Developer/my-app/report.html on the Mac
open docs/notes.md                      # the same
doz-open --app Typora notes.md          # in a named app — only one you allowed (below)
open .                                  # the shared folder, in the Finder
open src                                # a folder in it, in the Finder
doz-open --reveal dist/app.zip          # the Finder, with that file selected (nothing is opened)
```

Every time, your terminal (or the dashboard) says what happened: `my-app opened report.html in
Safari`, `my-app opened src/ in the Finder`, `my-app showed app.zip in the Finder`.

![The open-file notice in the dashboard](https://dozable.com/docs/images/open-file-toast.png)

What it never does:

- **Nothing outside the shared folder.** The path is mapped to your shared folder and resolved on the
  Mac; a `..` or a link (made in the sandbox or on the Mac) that leads out of it is refused.
- **Documents only:** html, md, pdf, images (png, jpg, gif, webp, svg, …), txt and log, csv and tsv,
  json, yaml, xml, toml. Never an app, script, installer or link file (`.command`, `.sh`, `.pkg`,
  `.dmg`, `.webloc`, …), never a file with its executable bit set, and never a program or `#!` script
  whatever its name says — the first bytes are checked.
- **Folders only in the Finder**, never as an app. A folder the Mac treats as a package (an `.app`, a
  bundle, an `.rtfd` …) is never opened, not even in the Finder; `doz-open --reveal` can still show it,
  selected in its parent folder.
- **No app you didn't name.** A file opens in its default app. To let a sandbox name another one, list
  it: `doz config set bridges.open_apps "Typora, Visual Studio Code"`. Any other name is refused, and
  so is naming an app for a folder.
- **An isolated sandbox** has nothing of yours to open, and says so.
- **Only while you watch:** like the clipboard, it acts only while a terminal is attached to the
  session; at most 3 files or folders in 10 seconds per sandbox.

URLs work exactly as before ([Signing in from a sandbox](https://dozable.com/docs/signing-in-from-a-sandbox.md)). Turn
files off where you don't want them:

```sh
doz config set --sandbox my-app sandbox.open_files off   # this sandbox (at once)
doz config set sandbox.open_files off                    # every sandbox without its own choice
doz create my-app --open-files off …                     # from the start (or open_files: off in doz_project.yaml)
```

## tmux inside a session

Off by default. Turn it on for every sandbox (`doz config set sessions.tmux true`) or for one
(`doz create --tmux`, `tmux: true` in `doz_project.yaml`, or
`doz config set --sandbox NAME sessions.tmux true`), and each **new** session runs its program inside
tmux: windows, panes, copy mode, its status bar and its prefix key, **Ctrl-b**.

tmux runs *inside* Dozable's own session keeper, so everything else still works: `doz attach` and
Ctrl-], sleep and wake (tmux and its programs are where they were), saved screens (tmux's screen,
status bar included), browser terminals, and the clipboard and browser bridges. Each session has a
tmux server of its own, and reopening a session finds a program tmux still holds.

It is **tmux 3.8**, on every base: Dozable brings its own (one of its [managed tools](https://dozable.com/docs/the-tools-layer.md)), so
floating panes, the fast switcher (`Ctrl-b Tab`), auto-hiding scrollbars and `remain-on-exit failed-key`
are there whatever tmux the image ships. tmux 3.8 also asks your terminal whether it is in light or dark
mode and tells the programs in its panes, so an agent inside tmux picks colours for the terminal you
attach with (Ghostty, kitty, iTerm2 and others answer; with one that doesn't, tmux guesses from its
background colour).

Limits:

- tmux takes **Ctrl-b** and the mouse (in the browser, Shift+drag still selects text);
- the kitty keyboard protocol and xterm's modifyOtherKeys don't fully pass through tmux, so a program
  that relies on them (Claude Code's richer key handling) sees less;
- the session's exit code is tmux's (0), not the program's;
- the session's program runs in Dozable's tmux once it is in the sandbox (the first start after you turn
  tmux on puts it there). If it is not there yet, the image's own tmux is used; with neither, the session
  runs without tmux and says how to get it (`doz tools NAME --apply`);
- a session that was already running in the image's tmux before Dozable's arrived keeps that tmux until it
  ends.

## Settings

| key | default | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `ui.terminal_title` | `{sandbox} · {session} · {time}` | The title of your terminal while attached, and of dashboard tabs. `""` leaves it to the program. |
| `sandbox.clipboard` | `write` | `write`: copies reach your Mac's clipboard, with a notice. `off`: never. Per sandbox too. |
| `sandbox.open_files` | `on` | `on`: `xdg-open PATH` opens a `/workspace` document in its app, or a folder in the Finder, on your Mac, with a notice. `off`: never. Per sandbox too. |
| `bridges.open_apps` | `""` | The apps a sandbox may name to open a file in (`doz-open --app NAME`). Empty: default apps only. |
| `sessions.tmux` | `false` | New sessions run inside tmux (Dozable's tmux 3.8). Per sandbox too. |
| `ui.terminals` | `true` | Terminals in the browser at all. |
| `ui.terminal_font_size` | `13` | Browser terminal font size. |
| `ui.split_default` | `shell` | What **Split** opens. |
| `ui.grid_tile_size` | `medium` | The size of All sessions' tiles (every tile is live; `ui.grid_live_tiles` is no longer used). |
| `ui.grid_refresh_ms` | `500` | How often the pictures are brought up to date, in milliseconds (200–10000; lower is livelier and costs more). |
| `daemon.screen_capture_minutes` | `5` | How often running sessions' screens are saved. |

## Troubleshooting

| symptom | what to do |
|---|---|
| Ctrl-] seems to do nothing | Look at the bottom row: the menu is there. Press Ctrl-] again (or `d`) to detach. |
| After detaching, moving the mouse types odd characters | Shouldn't happen — Dozable turns the program's mouse mode off on the way out. If a crash left it on, run `reset` in your terminal. |
| The title didn't come back (Terminal.app) | Terminal.app has no title stack; the next program that sets a title replaces it. |
| A copy didn't reach the clipboard | Check the notice: off, too large or too many. `doz config show --sandbox NAME`. |
| Keys like Shift+Enter don't work in Claude Code under tmux | A tmux limit (see above); turn tmux off for that sandbox. |
| A browser terminal won't type Chinese, Japanese or Korean | Its input-method support is incomplete; use **Open in Terminal**. |

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/images-and-bases

# Images and bases

Every sandbox starts from a **baked image**: a disk with a Linux system, a developer toolkit and,
usually, the agent a recipe installs. The layers are base → developer base → baked image, one baked image
per base × recipe. You choose an image when you create a sandbox; Dozable bakes it the first time it's
needed (the CLI and the dashboard call that *preparing* it) and then makes each sandbox an instant copy of it.
A recipe with at least one baked image on this Mac is *installed* — the dashboard's **Recipes › Installed** lists it, with its
baked images and their size.

## Concepts

- **An image is two choices: an agent and a base.**
  - The **agent** (what a recipe installs): **Claude Code**, **pi**, **Codex** ([Codex](https://dozable.com/docs/codex.md)), or **none** (a shell only).
  - The **base**: the Linux system underneath — one of the **recommended bases** (below), **your own
    Dockerfile**, or a **saved disk** — a sandbox's disk you saved with `doz image save`.
- **Image names** follow the pair: `<base>-<agent>`, for example `python-claude-code` or `go-pi`, and
  just `<base>` with no agent (`debian`). Three names predate the choice and stay:

  | name | base | agent |
  |---|---|---|
  | `claude-code` | Node.js | Claude Code |
  | `pi` | Node.js | pi |
  | `codex` | Node.js | Codex (new — on other bases `<base>-codex`) |
  | `lab` | Alpine | none (bash and a few tools) |

- **The developer baseline.** On every base, Dozable adds the tools agents expect: git, curl, jq,
  ripgrep (`rg`), fd, python3, less, vim, ssh, sudo, tmux and the package lists, so the agent can
  install more with `sudo apt-get install` (or `apk add` on Alpine). Claude Code on a base without
  Node is its standalone build; pi on a base without Node gets its own Node; Codex is its official
  static linux-arm64 build on every base.
- **Preparing** an image downloads the base (digest-pinned), installs the baseline and the agent in a
  temporary VM, and checks the result. Minutes, once, with the network. A sandbox started while its
  image is being prepared joins that preparation.
- **Copies are free.** A sandbox's disk is an APFS clone of its image: it costs almost nothing until
  it changes.

## The recommended bases

`doz base ls` lists them, with the exact image each follows, its download, how long a first
preparation takes, and which package registries its sandboxes may reach:

| base | what's in it |
|---|---|
| `node` | Node.js 22 on Debian |
| `python` | Python 3.13 on Debian |
| `go` | Go 1.25 on Debian |
| `rust` | Rust on Debian |
| `java` | Java 21 (Eclipse Temurin) |
| `ruby` | Ruby 3.4 on Debian |
| `dotnet` | .NET 9 SDK |
| `debian` | plain Debian |
| `ubuntu` | Ubuntu 24.04 |
| `alpine` | Alpine 3.20 |

A base's own package registry (PyPI for `python`, crates.io for `rust`, …) is part of what its
sandboxes may reach by default. See [What the agent can do](https://dozable.com/docs/permissions-and-network.md).

## The store's base

A store has **one base** that tools are added to: the setting `defaults.base` (`node` unless you chose another
in `doz onboard`'s Base image step). Every sandbox made the quick way — the dashboard's **Quick try**, `doz try`,
and onboarding's first sandbox — puts its tool on it, so the base is downloaded and flattened **once** and each
tool after the first adds only itself. OpenCode, whose own recipe is on Debian, becomes `node-opencode2` on a
Node.js store, and `doz try opencode` needs no `--base`. A tool that cannot run on the store's base (a glibc-only
tool on Alpine) keeps its recipe's own; `--base BASE` (or the Quick try's base choice) picks another for one
sandbox.

Onboarding prepares the base in the daemon as soon as you choose it: the base image pulled, then its disk
flattened — the same two steps a tool's first preparation would take. A tool prepared meanwhile **waits** for it
("waited for the Node.js base") instead of downloading the same layers a second time. `doz onboard --status`
shows it (`base node ready`); Operations in the dashboard shows it as "prepare the Node.js base".

New sandbox, `doz new`, `doz create` and `doz_project.yaml` keep each recipe's own base, so a project file means
the same on every Mac.

## Choose an image — in the terminal

```sh
doz create web --image claude-code --folder ~/code/web              # Node · Claude Code
doz create api --agent claude-code --base python --folder ~/code/api
doz create tools --agent none --base go --isolated                      # a Go shell, no agent
doz create mine --agent pi --dockerfile ~/code/mine/Dockerfile          # your own base
doz create tpl-copy --image my-disk                                     # a saved disk (doz image save)
```

`--image` is shorthand for `--agent` and `--base`. `doz up` takes the same options.

## Choose an image — in the dashboard

**New sandbox** shows two rows: **Agent** and **Base**. The agent is chosen in two steps: **Coding agents**,
**AI tools** or **No agent**, then one of that section's (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, pi · Fabric, llm,
promptfoo …). Choosing one that cannot run on the base chosen (Alpine, for a tool built for glibc only) moves the base
to its own. **Base**: **Recommended** (a card per base, with its download and time), **Dockerfile** (**Choose
Dockerfile…** opens the Mac's file picker) or **Saved disk**. The line under them names the image the pair makes.

![Choosing agent and base](https://dozable.com/docs/images/new-sandbox-base.png)

## Your own Dockerfile

Use a Dockerfile when a recommended base isn't close enough — your company's image, extra system
libraries, a pinned toolchain. Dozable builds it with **Apple's `container` tool**, then adds its
baseline and the agent on top as usual.

- **Apple's tool is optional**, installed and started only when you ask:

  ```sh
  doz builder status        # installed? supported? running?
  doz builder install       # opens Apple's signed installer package in macOS Installer (you approve it there)
  doz builder start         # starts its services (asks first)
  ```

  In the dashboard, choosing **Dockerfile** shows the same state, with **Install Apple's container
  tool…** or **Start its services** when needed. Dozable never uses `sudo` for it.
- **The build runs outside Dozable's network policy.** The Dockerfile's `RUN` steps run in Apple's
  builder and reach the internet directly, without Dozable's proxy or permissions. Only build
  Dockerfiles you trust. The sandbox made from the image is under your permissions as usual.
- The Dockerfile's folder is the build context, and the sandbox's shared folder unless you give one.
- An unchanged Dockerfile prepares again in seconds. When it changes, Dozable says "Dockerfile changed —
  rebuild available"; `doz image bake df-…` rebuilds (the image's name is shown in `doz image ls`),
  and `doz reset NAME` moves a sandbox onto it.
- Apple's tool keeps its own storage, shown on the Resources page (never deleted by Dozable). See
  [Resources and disk space](https://dozable.com/docs/resources-and-disk-space.md).

## See and manage images

Each image's **STATUS** (also on the Images page, and `status` in `--json`) is one of: **up to date**,
**update available** (a newer agent release), **older recipe** (an older Dozable prepared it), **not
prepared** (it's prepared the first time it's needed) or **preparing**.

```sh
doz image ls                   # every image and saved disk: baked here?, its agent version, status
doz image ls --tree            # the lineage: base → image → saved disk → sandboxes, with sizes
doz image save my-app my-disk  # a sandbox's system disk saved as an image (never its state disk)
doz image bake claude-code     # prepare (or rebuild) now rather than at the first start
doz image rm python-pi         # remove an image's prepared disk (sandboxes made from it keep working)
```

In the dashboard, **Images** shows the same with **Bake** or **Rebuild** on each row and **Remove…**
under its **⋯**, each image's
own and shared disk space as a bar, and **Lineage**, the tree.

![The Images page](https://dozable.com/docs/images/images.png)

## Out-of-date images

An image can fall behind in two ways: a **newer agent release** exists, or it was prepared by an
**older version of Dozable** whose recipe lacked something (a tool the baseline gained, for example).
Either way, **Dozable never rebuilds an image without you.** It says so:

- `doz image ls` — a STATUS column (`update available`, `older recipe`) and a line such as
  `pi: prepared by an older doz — this doz's image adds: sudo, apt-utils, tmux, package lists`;
- `doz doctor`, the **Images** page (a badge and **Rebuild**), and a sandbox's page;
- **when you create a sandbox**, which asks:

  ```
  The claude-code image is out of date: … Rebuild it first (~2 min, needs network; existing sandboxes are NOT affected)?
  ```

  **Enter** uses the current image. `--rebuild` or `--use-current` decide up front; without a terminal
  the current image is used with a warning. The dashboard's New sandbox shows the same choice.

Rebuilding never touches existing sandboxes: they keep their disks. To move a sandbox onto the new
image, `doz reset NAME` — it keeps the agent's own state (`~/.claude`, `~/.pi`) and `/workspace`, and
drops everything else installed on its system disk (save its disk first — [`doz image save`](https://dozable.com/docs/restore-points-duplicates-templates.md#saved-disks)
— if you want that).

## Saved disks

A **saved disk** is a sandbox's system disk saved as an image (`doz image save SANDBOX NAME`): set a sandbox up the way
you like, then make new sandboxes from it. It never includes the agent's state disk (logins, history). `doz image ls`
lists it (BASE · AGENT says **saved disk**) and `doz image rm NAME` removes it. These were `doz template create | ls | rm`,
which forward here for one release. See
[Restore points, duplicates and saved disks](https://dozable.com/docs/restore-points-duplicates-templates.md#saved-disks).

## Settings

| key | default | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `defaults.image` | `lab` | The image used when you don't name one (onboarding sets it to `claude-code`). |
| `defaults.base` | `node` | The store's base: quick-made sandboxes' tools go on it (see [The store's base](#the-stores-base)). |
| `recipes.anthropic.claude-code.version` | `latest` | The Claude Code version its image is baked with: `latest` (resolved when it is baked) or an exact version like `2.1.227`. |
| `recipes.earendil-works.pi.version` | `latest` | The same for pi. |
| `images.lab.memory_mib` · `recipes.anthropic.claude-code.memory_mib` · `recipes.earendil-works.pi.memory_mib` | `1024` · `2048` · `2048` | Memory of a new sandbox of each image. |
| `images.lab.network` · `recipes.anthropic.claude-code.network` · `recipes.earendil-works.pi.network` | `bake` · `agent` · `agent` | Network of a new sandbox of each image. |
| `resources.clean_unused_days` | `30` | Clean up removes a baked image no sandbox was made from in this many days. |

## Limits

- Images can't yet be pulled from or pushed to a registry (`doz image pull` / `push` answer "not yet").
- A Dockerfile base must be for `linux/arm64` and needs Apple's `container` tool on this Mac.
- A sandbox keeps the image it was made from; only `reset` (or a new sandbox) changes that.

## Troubleshooting

| symptom | what to do |
|---|---|
| The first start takes minutes | The image is being prepared (once). `doz onboard --status` or the dashboard's Operations show it. |
| A preparation failed | `doz image bake NAME -v` shows each step and its output; a network refusal during preparation is in `doz net log`. |
| "Dockerfile changed — rebuild available" | `doz image bake df-…` (the name is in `doz image ls`), then `doz reset NAME`. |
| `doz builder status` says not installed | `doz builder install`, approve it in Installer, then `doz builder start`. |
| An image says "older recipe" | Rebuild when it suits you (`doz image bake NAME` or **Rebuild**), then `doz reset` the sandboxes you want on it. |

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/agents-and-accounts

# Agents and accounts

Dozable runs three AI coding agents out of the box — **Claude Code**, **pi** and OpenAI's **Codex** — and
gives each one the account it should use, without the secret ever entering the sandbox. Codex has its
own page: [Codex](https://dozable.com/docs/codex.md). This page covers which
agent can use which account, how to add accounts, the agent's versions and its `sudo`, and what the
agent is told about where it runs.

## The words

| word | means |
|---|---|
| **recipe** | the definition: how to build, launch and configure one agent (`anthropic/claude-code`). The dashboard's **Recipes › Installed** lists the ones on this Mac. |
| **agent** | what a recipe installs and a sandbox runs: you install the Claude Code recipe and run its agent, Claude Code. |
| a recipe's **subject** | what a recipe calls its own agent, shown beside its name — pi is a *coding harness*, Fabric an *agentic tool*. Without one it is simply an agent. |
| **managed tools** | `gh`, tmux, the ssh client and GitHub's host keys: tools Dozable supports natively, each with its own settings, added to a sandbox and never baked — see [Managed tools](https://dozable.com/docs/the-tools-layer.md). |
| **baked image** | base → developer base → baked image: one per base × recipe, made once and cloned for each sandbox. |

A recipe on this Mac is **in use** (a sandbox runs its agent) or **installed** (a baked image of it is
here); the rest are **available** in the catalogue (`doz search`, Quick try). `doz recipe ls --installed`
lists the first two, and `doz recipe uninstall ID` removes a recipe's baked images (refused while a
sandbox runs it; your settings for it are kept unless `--forget-settings`). Each recipe's settings — its
agent's `version`, `approvals`, `memory_mib`, `network` and `history` — are in [the settings](https://dozable.com/docs/settings-reference.md)
under `[recipes.VENDOR.PRODUCT]`.

## Concepts

- **The agent runs as a normal user** (`agent`) in `/workspace`. Its own settings, logins and
  history (`~/.claude`, `~/.pi/agent`, Codex's `~/.codex`) are on a separate **state disk** that survives shutdown and
  reset.
- **An account** is how the agent pays for its model. Dozable's proxy on your Mac holds the secret and
  adds it to requests to Anthropic on their way out. Inside the sandbox, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or
  `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` is only a placeholder (`doz_cred_…`). A secret is never a command-line
  argument, so it never lands in shell history or `ps`.
- **Three kinds of account:**

  | kind | what it is | where the secret lives | renewal |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `mac` (built in) | your Mac's own Claude Code login | Claude Code's own keychain item — or its `~/.claude/.credentials.json` when that holds the newer login (a `claude` login over ssh renews only the file) — read-only for Dozable; `doz account show mac` says which | your Mac's Claude Code renews it |
  | setup token | a `claude setup-token` token (a Claude subscription, valid a year) | your login keychain, `doz-claude:NAME` | none — add a new one before it expires |
  | API key | an Anthropic API key | your login keychain, `doz-anthropic:NAME` | none |

  For **Codex**, OpenAI's kinds: **this Mac's Codex login** (`mac` — read-only, nothing to add; the
  default while Codex is signed in on this Mac), a **ChatGPT sign-in** (builds from source only: `doz account add NAME --chatgpt`
  — Dozable's own, in your browser; renewed by Dozable on your Mac) and an **OpenAI API key**
  (`--openai-key`). See [Codex](https://dozable.com/docs/codex.md).

- **Which agent can use which:**

  | agent | accounts it can use |
  |---|---|
  | Claude Code | `mac`, a setup token, an API key |
  | pi | an API key only (a Claude subscription is never given to it): Anthropic's (the default), or an OpenAI, xAI, Google AI or OpenRouter key (`doz try pi --gateway openrouter`); off Anthropic, Dozable puts the model on its session's command line (`--model PROVIDER/MODEL`) |
  | Codex | `mac` (this Mac's Codex login), a ChatGPT sign-in or an OpenAI API key — never an Anthropic account (and no Claude agent ever gets an OpenAI one) |

  This is checked **before** a sandbox is made. With no account pi can use, Dozable stops and tells you
  the next step (or, on a terminal and in the dashboard, offers to take a key right there).

## Claude Code in a sandbox

Claude Code starts ready to work: its first-run screens are done, the working folder is trusted, and
it runs without asking permission for each command (the VM and its network are the boundary). It
also shows your real plan ("Claude Max") and picks the same default model as on your Mac.

To have it ask first, set its recipe's `approvals` to `ask` — on this Mac
(`doz config set --agent claude-code approvals ask`), for one sandbox
(`doz config set --sandbox NAME approvals ask`, or `doz create NAME --approvals ask`), or in a project
(`approvals: ask` in `doz_project.yaml`) — or for one session:
`doz run NAME -e DOZ_CLAUDE_PERMISSIONS=ask -- claude`. A `claude` run as root always asks.

Inside a sandbox Claude Code never updates itself; the image decides its version (below).

Dozable also keeps your Claude Code conversations — see the next section.

## Conversation history

Some agents delete their own old conversations: Claude Code, on its own, deletes conversations older
than 30 days. By default Dozable keeps them — the setting **`agent.history`** is `keep`. For an agent that
deletes by itself, Dozable writes the agent's own setting into the agent's own settings file, once, when
the sandbox is set up (its next start or wake), and only where you have not set one: **your value is never
changed**, and a key you delete or change yourself is left as you made it. Nothing is rebuilt. A file
Dozable cannot read (a hand edit that is not valid JSON or TOML) is never written.

What each value does in each agent:

| agent | `keep` (the default) | `agent-default` |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | sets `cleanupPeriodDays = 36500` in `~/.claude/settings.json` | takes `cleanupPeriodDays` back if it still holds 36500 — Claude Code deletes conversations older than 30 days ([its settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#cleanupperioddays)) |
| Codex | sets `history.persistence = "save-all"` in `~/.codex/config.toml` (a `none` you set stays) | takes it back if it still holds `save-all` — Codex saves its conversations by itself |
| pi | nothing — it keeps every session by itself | nothing |
| OpenCode, OpenCode 2 | nothing — it has no clean-up of its own | nothing |
| any other agent | not known — the setting does not apply | not known |

**`agent-default`** lets each agent follow its own rule: Dozable takes back only a key that still holds
exactly the value Dozable wrote (if you happened to type that same value yourself, it goes too).
Conversations an agent already deleted are gone.

Where to choose — the most specific value that is not `follow` wins:

```sh
doz config set agent.history agent-default                 # every agent, on this Mac
doz config set --agent claude-code history keep            # one agent (follow: what agent.history says)
doz config set --project ~/code/my-app history keep        # a project (history: in doz_project.yaml)
doz config set --sandbox my-app history agent-default      # one sandbox
doz config show --agent codex                              # what each value does in Codex, and where its value comes from
```

In the dashboard: **Settings › The agent** shows **Conversation history** with a table of what each value
does in each agent; each agent's page under **Recipes** has its own drop-down and its row of that table;
a sandbox's **Config** tab shows its value and where it came from. A change applies at each sandbox's next
start or wake.

## Accounts — in the terminal

```sh
doz account ls                                    # accounts, state, expiry, which sandboxes use them — never a secret
                                                  # (state rejected: its provider refused the key at its last check)
doz account add work --setup-token --plan max     # paste the token (no echo), or pipe it in
doz account add ci --api-key                      # an API key (prompt or stdin), or --keychain SERVICE
doz account default work                          # every sandbox that follows the default moves to work
doz account use my-app work                       # this sandbox uses work (open sessions switch on their next request)
doz account use my-app default                    # follow the store's default again
doz account verify work                           # one tiny request to api.anthropic.com
doz account rename work team                      # its keychain item, the default and its sandboxes go with it
doz account set-plan team pro                     # a setup token's plan, without pasting it again
doz account add team --setup-token --force        # a new token under the same name (default, sandboxes and plan kept)
doz account rm work                               # also deletes the keychain item Dozable made
doz create my-app --image claude-code --account work
```

A rename moves everything that names the account: the keychain item Dozable made for it (written under
the new name and read back before the old one is deleted), the store's default, and every sandbox that
uses it — chosen for it or as a custom key. Open sessions keep working. A keychain item you named
yourself (`--keychain SERVICE`) keeps its name. This Mac's logins keep theirs, and so does a ChatGPT
sign-in (sign in again under the new name, then remove the old one).

A new sandbox follows the store's default account — `mac` out of the box. Sign in to Claude Code on
your Mac once, and every sandbox can use your subscription with nothing to paste.

Keys of the other providers and of the model gateways are accounts too, each with its provider:

```sh
doz account add xai --provider xai                # xAI (OpenCode, and the tools that speak xAI)
doz account add google --provider google          # the Gemini API (Fabric and the tools that speak it)
doz account add oc --provider opencode            # OpenCode (OpenCode Zen and OpenCode Go: one key; OpenCode 2)
doz account add or --provider openrouter          # OpenRouter: one key, many models (creator/name)
doz account add vg --provider vercel-ai-gateway   # Vercel AI Gateway: the same idea (unpublished for now — a key already added keeps working)
```

Each provider has its own default (`doz account default or` makes `or` OpenRouter's). An agent or tool that can use
several (the AI tools — see [Other AI tools](https://dozable.com/docs/ai-tools.md)) talks to the provider or gateway of the account it is
given: `doz try TOOL --gateway openrouter` picks OpenRouter's default key, `--account NAME` a given one. The key goes
only to that provider's or gateway's own API — a placeholder sent anywhere else is refused.

## Accounts — in the dashboard

**Accounts & keys** is built around four things you come to it for.

**Something is broken — fix it.** At the top, **Needs you** lists every problem, one line each, worst
first: a key its provider refused, a key Dozable cannot read (its keychain item is gone, the keychain is
locked, or the 1Password / AWS / command source did not answer), and this Mac's Claude login when it is
signed out or expired while a sandbox relies on it. Each line says which sandboxes get no key at their
next session and has the one fix as a button — **Copy claude** (sign in on this Mac), **Add it again…**,
**Read again**, **Replace…** — with the rest under **⋯**. The same key stored twice is one line. When
nothing is wrong, the page says **Every key works**. The **Accounts & keys** entry in the sidebar shows a
red count while a problem breaks a sandbox.

A refused or unreadable key is **replaced in place**: **Replace…** / **Add it again…** opens the paste
under the same name, and the sandboxes that use it keep using it — the new key from their next session
(what `doz account add NAME --force` does). To put a new value in a key that works, use **⋯ › Edit…**.

**Edit a key.** **⋯ › Edit…** changes a key's details in one step: its **Name** (the sandboxes that use
it and its default come along), a Claude subscription token's **Plan**, and — for a key Dozable keeps in
your keychain — **Replace the key**: paste a new value under the same name, or leave it empty to keep
the current one. A new value is checked like an added one; the sandboxes that use it get it at their next
session. A key read from 1Password, AWS or a command, a custom key, or a keychain item you named offers
the name only, with the `doz account add … --force` line for the rest. This Mac's logins and a ChatGPT
sign-in have no Edit.

**Which key does this sandbox use?** The **Sandboxes** view lists every sandbox with its tool, the key it
uses now, how it gets it (its provider's default, or chosen for it) and its status. A sandbox whose
network reaches no model provider (NAT, or no network) shows **Not needed**. **Change…** turns the row
into a choice right there — the keys its tool can use, its provider's default, or no key — and **Use it**
applies it from the sandbox's next session.

**Change a default.** The **Keys** view has a heading and a table per provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, then
each provider and gateway), naming the tools its key serves. Each key is a row:

- a **Default** radio: the key a sandbox that follows its provider's default uses. Anthropic's last row
  is **No default**.
- the key's name, and where it lives in plain words: Keychain, 1Password, AWS, a command, or this
  Mac's Claude login. **⋯ › Details** shows the keychain item, the fingerprint, the source and the last check.
- one status: **Works**, **Not checked**, **Refused** (its provider said no), **Can't read** or
  **No check for this provider** — with a second line only when it adds something (the refusal's code,
  an expiry, "read on use").
- the sandboxes that use it (each a link to its page), then the one action that helps now (**Check**,
  **Read again**, **Replace…**, **Add again…**) and **⋯** (**Set default**, **Edit…**, **Details**, **Remove…**).

The Claude Code keep-alive switch sits under Anthropic's table. **Find** filters both views by a tool,
a provider, a key or a sandbox.

**Add a key for a tool.** **Add a key** first asks which tool it is for — or which provider. Type a
tool's name (grok, codex, opencode) and it shows the providers that tool can use, with the keys you
already have for each; type a provider's name and press Enter to go straight to it. Paste the key into
the masked field: Dozable checks it with one small request and keeps it in your login keychain. The
field is there only while the setting `ui.allow_secret_entry` is on. For a key kept in 1Password or
AWS, read by a command, a custom key or a ChatGPT sign-in, the page gives the exact `doz account add`
line to copy and run in Terminal. After the check it offers what follows: to make the new key its
provider's default, and to remove an old copy of a replaced key that still fails.

A sandbox's page shows its account, with **Account…** (the details' **Keys** tab) to change it; New
sandbox offers only the accounts its agent can use.

## How the Mac login stays fresh

Dozable reads only the **access token** of your Mac's Claude Code login — never the refresh token — so
your Mac's Claude Code stays the one program that renews it. The access token lives about 8 hours;
Claude Code renews it whenever it runs on your Mac near expiry. **This is the most common reason an agent stops
working:** "this Mac's Claude login expired".

**Signing in over SSH.** Claude Code keeps its login in two places: a Keychain item, written when you sign in at the
Mac itself, and `~/.claude/.credentials.json`, the only one a sign-in over SSH writes (the Keychain is locked there).
Dozable reads both, read-only, and uses whichever holds the later login, so a sign-in over SSH counts;
`doz account show mac` says which one it reads now. What an SSH session cannot do is keep the login fresh: a daemon started over SSH
never runs the keep-alive (below). For a Mac you reach only over SSH, sign in once at the Mac, start the daemon from its
desktop (or `doz daemon login-item on`), or use a **setup-token** account, which needs no renewing for a year.

- The daemon re-reads the login every 2 minutes; a renewed token reaches every sandbox without a
  restart.
- **If it expired** (nothing ran Claude Code on the Mac overnight), Claude Code in the sandbox shows
  "this Mac's Claude login expired at 04:59 — open Claude Code on the Mac (any prompt), then retry",
  and recovers by itself once the Mac renews.
- **Keep-alive** (off by default) keeps the Mac login renewed. When the login expires, the daemon
  runs the Mac's own `claude` once: one tiny turn on your subscription, with no tools, no MCP servers and
  no hooks, in an empty folder. Claude Code renews an expired login as it starts (it leaves one that
  has not expired yet as it is); Dozable never touches the login's refresh token. If a run leaves the
  login as it was, or fails (say, the network was down), it is tried again 1, 5 and 15 minutes after
  the expiry, then every 30 minutes, six runs in all, and then said as failed until the login changes
  (or you set `doz account keepalive` again).
  - `doz account keepalive on`: only while a sandbox or a fenced session on this Mac used the login in
    the last 15 minutes.
  - `doz account keepalive always`: whether or not anything uses it. It suits a Mac left unattended,
    where sessions start later and find the login renewed. The daemon stays running by default, so it
    can renew with nothing open.
  - `doz account keepalive off` turns it off.
- **What stops a renewal** (each is said, and tried again at the next look):
  - **A Claude Code that is not fenced runs on this Mac.** It holds its own copy of the login, and a
    renewal by anyone else would cancel that copy. The reason names it: "Claude Code (pid 812, session
    admin on this Mac)", or "not Dozable's". It renews when that Claude Code is next used. A fenced
    session never stops it: it holds only a stand-in for the login.
  - **The daemon was started over ssh.** The login keychain is locked there, so it never runs the
    keep-alive. Run `doz daemon restart` from the Mac's desktop, or `doz daemon login-item on`.
  - **Claude Code isn't installed** on this Mac.
- **Seeing it:** `doz account ls` ends with a line such as "keep-alive always · last renewed 09:02
  (until 17:02) · next try 16:52", or "· last try 09:02 FAILED (exit 1: …)". `doz doctor` has a
  "Claude login keep-alive" row, and `doz daemon status` says the same. Each needs no daemon running.
- **If you sign out on the Mac**, sandboxes stop getting a token at once. **If a different account
  signs in**, sandboxes on `mac` follow it at their next request — running sessions keep working,
  with no restart and no sign-in inside the sandbox — and each sandbox's activity says which account
  it now uses. (A session's plan and rate-limit tier are read when it starts, so a session started
  before the switch still reports the earlier account's until it is restarted.)
- **Several Claude config folders:** `doz account add work-mac --claude-login --config-dir ~/.claude-work`.

**No silent fallback:** a missing or expired credential is refused with a message saying what to do.
A sandbox never switches account by itself.

## A credential the agent brings itself

If someone signs in inside the sandbox (`/login`) or pastes a key, the proxy sees it. The **key
policy** decides what happens:

```sh
doz key policy my-app allow     # let it through, and flag it
doz key policy my-app strict    # refuse it (and block the sign-in pages, so /login can't finish)
doz key policy my-app auto      # the default: strict for a token or API-key account, allow for mac
```

With `allow`, `doz key ls` lists the credential's fingerprint (never its value) and `doz ls` marks the
sandbox. Dozable never adds its own credential to a request that carries the agent's.

## A key for one sandbox

```sh
doz key set my-app --anthropic                      # prompt (no echo), or: … < keyfile
doz key set my-app --anthropic --keychain SERVICE   # read it from a keychain item
doz key ls my-app                                   # never the value
doz key rm my-app --anthropic
```

A key typed or piped in lasts while the daemon runs; after the daemon stops, set it again (or use
`--keychain`, which is read again by each new daemon).

## Keys from 1Password, AWS or a command

An API-key account (`--api-key`, `--openai-key`, `--provider xai|google|google-stitch|opencode|openrouter|vercel-ai-gateway`, `--custom`) can keep its key
where you already keep it. Dozable stores only **where** it is — never the key, not even in the keychain —
and the daemon reads it on your Mac when a sandbox needs it:

```sh
doz account add grok --provider xai --from op://Dev/xAI/credential               # 1Password (op)
doz account add grok --provider xai --from op://Dev/xAI/credential --env OP_ACCOUNT=my.1password.com
doz account add work --api-key --from aws:arn:aws:secretsmanager:eu-west-1:123456789012:secret:dev/anthropic#api_key
doz account add work --api-key --from aws:arn:… --env AWS_PROFILE=dev --env AWS_REGION=eu-west-1
doz account add ci --openai-key --from-command '~/bin/print-key openai'                 # any program; its output is the key
doz account add work --api-key --from op://Dev/Anthropic/credential --force       # switch an existing account
doz account show grok                                                             # where it comes from, the last read — never the key
doz account refresh grok                                                          # read it again now
```

- **When it is read:** once when you add it (with the provider's own key check — `--no-verify` skips
  both), then on use: kept in the daemon's memory for `--ttl` (55 minutes by default; `2h`, `90m`), read
  again right away after `doz account refresh` or a change to the account, and once more when the
  provider answers 401 (a rotated key). A sandbox's session start reads it in the background, so the
  agent's first request does not wait for 1Password.
- **`--from-command`** runs a program with arguments — never a shell: no `;`, `|`, `&`, `$(…)`, backticks
  or redirections (put a pipeline in a script and give its path). The program is found once, at add
  time, as an absolute path; `doz` shows the exact command and asks before saving it (`--yes` off a
  terminal). Its output is the key: one line, at most 8 KiB.
- **Where it runs:** on your Mac, as the daemon, with the standard `PATH`, your home, the tools' own
  sign-in variables (`OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN`, `AWS_*`) and the `--env` variables the account names —
  only `OP_ACCOUNT`, `AWS_PROFILE`, `AWS_REGION`, `AWS_CONFIG_FILE` and `AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE`
  (never a secret). Nothing is typed into it. 1Password gets 20 seconds (a Touch ID prompt), the others 10.
- **When it fails** the agent's request gets a 401 saying why, in the tool's own words (the first line it
  wrote to its errors, cleaned and shortened — never its output, never a line holding the key), the reason
  in plain words where it is known, and what to do — never another key. For example:

  ```
  the key of account demo comes from command: /usr/bin/security find-generic-password -w -s demo, but
  /usr/bin/security says: The specified item could not be found in the keychain. (the keychain has no such
  item) — run that command in Terminal to check it, then doz account refresh demo
  ```

  Known: `security`'s exits 44 (no such item), 51 (it would have to ask you) and 36 (the keychain is locked);
  `op` signed out; `aws` AccessDenied and expired credentials; `gh` not signed in. `doz account show`, the
  sandbox's page and `doz doctor` say the same; `account show` gives the last verification as history ("last
  verified 12 Oct 16:21").
- **In the dashboard** an account like this shows where its key comes from and its last read, with
  **Refresh**. Adding or changing where a key comes from is done with `doz` only.

## Custom keys for other services

A key for an API Dozable has no account kind for — your own service, a search API — goes to exactly the
hosts you name, in the header you name, and only replaces its placeholder (the sandbox never has the
key):

```sh
doz account add search --custom --host api.search.example --env-var SEARCH_API_KEY --bearer      # Authorization: Bearer KEY
doz account add maps --custom --host maps.example.com --env-var MAPS_KEY --header x-api-key      # x-api-key: KEY
doz account add search --custom --host api.search.example --env-var SEARCH_API_KEY --bearer --from op://Dev/search/key
doz create my-app --image claude-code --allow site:api.search.example --key search             # attach it (repeatable)
doz account use my-app search --extra                                                           # attach to an existing sandbox
doz account use my-app search --remove-extra
```

Each host must be one the sandbox may reach on purpose (`--allow site:HOST`, or `doz net allow`) —
Dozable refuses to attach it otherwise, and withholds it (saying how to allow it) if the policy later
denies the host. A custom key never goes to a host Dozable already holds keys for (Anthropic, OpenAI,
GitHub, xAI, Google). Sessions opened after attaching get its variable.

## Agent versions

An agent image installs its agent at one exact version, chosen by `recipes.anthropic.claude-code.version` and
`recipes.earendil-works.pi.version`:

- **`latest`** (the default) is resolved **when its image is baked** — never while a sandbox runs —
  and installed at that exact version, integrity-checked.
- **A newer release is only announced** (`doz image ls`, `doz doctor`, the Images page, `doz create`):
  "Claude Code 2.1.290 is available (image has 2.1.285)". Rebuild when it suits you:
  `doz image bake claude-code`, then `doz reset NAME` for the sandboxes you want on it.
- **An exact version** (`doz config set recipes.anthropic.claude-code.version 2.1.227`) never asks the internet,
  so it works offline.

## Sudo inside the sandbox

The agent has **passwordless `sudo`** in its sandbox, so it can install what a task needs:
`sudo apt-get install -y PACKAGE` (Debian-based images keep the package lists, and never stop to
ask configuration questions) or `sudo apk add PACKAGE` on Alpine. Root inside the VM reaches no more
than the agent: there's no network card, every connection still goes through your permissions, no
credential is inside, and nothing of your Mac but its folder. `doz reset` or a restore point
undoes what it installed.

Turn it off for every sandbox (`doz config set sandbox.agent_sudo false`) or one
(`doz create --no-agent-sudo`, `agent_sudo: false` in `doz_project.yaml`, or
`doz config set --sandbox NAME sandbox.agent_sudo false`). It applies from the next session and boot.

## The agent's environment facts

At every session start, Dozable tells the agent where it is:

- a short **facts block**, added to its system prompt: that it's in a Dozable sandbox (a Linux VM on
  your Mac, not a container) with its name, image, CPUs and memory; whether `/workspace` is your Mac
  folder (and which) or isolated; how its network works and what to do when refused; that its
  credentials are supplied by the proxy; whether it has sudo; its time zone; what the clipboard does;
  one line on what it can show you on your Mac — a URL in your browser, a document of its folder in its
  app, a folder in the Finder — saying only what is on (the `doz` skill has the details:
  types, apps, refusals); and, only when you turned it on, one line saying `git` and `gh` are signed in
  as you on GitHub, read-only or with push ([GitHub as you](https://dozable.com/docs/github.md));
- the **`doz` skill** (`~/.claude/skills/doz/SKILL.md`, pi: `~/.pi/agent/skills/doz/SKILL.md`,
  Codex: `~/.agents/skills/doz/SKILL.md`),
  which it reads when a question is about the machine: what persists, the network, credentials,
  sleep, and what it can't do from inside (and must ask you for).

```sh
doz inspect my-app --prompt          # exactly what the next session gets
doz config set agent.prompt false    # off: the next session start removes both
```

Running Claude Code with **your own `--append-system-prompt`** (`doz run my-app -- claude
--append-system-prompt "…"`) keeps the facts: Claude Code uses only one such flag, so Dozable combines
them — the facts first, then each of your values (and an `--append-system-prompt-file`'s text) — into
one. A value that already contains the facts (`"$(cat /run/doz/agent-prompt.md)"`) is passed as it is,
never doubled. `--system-prompt` is a full replacement of Claude Code's prompt: then no facts are added.

**Your own words**, in three layers: the built-in text < your **`agent-prompt.md`** (beside
`doz.toml`; text outside an HTML comment replaces the built-in text for every sandbox) < a sandbox's
own (`doz create --agent-prompt FILE`, or `agent_prompt` in `doz_project.yaml`), appended or
replacing (`--agent-prompt-mode replace`). Your text may use `{{variables}}` from a fixed list —
`sandbox.name`, `sandbox.image`, `sandbox.base`, `sandbox.cpus`, `sandbox.memory`,
`folder.shared`, `folder.host_path`, `folder.guest_path`, `folder.description`, `folder.rules`,
`network.mode`, `network.allowed_hosts`, `network.description`, `network.permissions`,
`account.name`, `agent.state`, `credentials.description`, `sandbox.sudo`, `sandbox.timezone`, `sudo.description`,
`clipboard.description`, `browser.description`, `files.description`, `mac.open`, `github.facts`, `github.description`, `dotfiles.facts`, `mac.hostname`, `doz.version` (the template
`agent-prompt.md` lists them with what each says). `doz inspect NAME --prompt` shows any mistake: an unknown variable is an error that stops the
agent's sessions from starting until it's fixed, never silently blank.

Dozable owns only those two files. The agent's own memory files (`CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`) are never
touched.

## Settings

| key | default | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `defaults.account` | `mac` | The account of a store that hasn't chosen one. |
| `daemon.keepalive` | `false` | Keep-alive for a store that hasn't chosen (`doz account keepalive`). |
| `recipes.anthropic.claude-code.approvals` | `skip` | Claude Code's own permission prompts in a sandbox: `skip` or `ask`. |
| `recipes.anthropic.claude-code.version` · `recipes.earendil-works.pi.version` · `recipes.openai.codex.version` | `latest` | The agent version its image is baked with. |
| `sandbox.agent_sudo` | `true` | The agent's passwordless sudo. Per sandbox too. |
| `agent.prompt` | `true` | Give the agent its facts block and the `doz` skill. |
| `agent.history` | `keep` | Keep the agents' conversations, or `agent-default`. Per agent, project and sandbox too ([above](#conversation-history)). |
| `ui.allow_secret_entry` | `true` | The dashboard may take a key or token. |

## Troubleshooting

| symptom | what to do |
|---|---|
| The agent says it has no key, or gets 401 | `doz key ls NAME` and `doz account ls`. A typed key is gone after the daemon stopped: set it again, or use an account. |
| "this Mac's Claude login expired" | Run `claude` on your Mac once (any prompt), or turn on keep-alive (`doz account keepalive always`). Over SSH: see [Signing in over SSH](#how-the-mac-login-stays-fresh); for unattended work, a setup-token account (`doz account add NAME --setup-token`). |
| pi can't be created: no account it can use | `doz account add NAME --api-key`, then `--account NAME`. |
| "the agent prompt does not render" | `doz inspect NAME --prompt` names the unknown `{{variable}}` and the file. |
| The agent doesn't know where it runs | `doz inspect NAME --prompt`. An image prepared by a much older Dozable may need `doz reset NAME` after a rebuild. |
| "the key of account X comes from 1Password …, but op is not signed in" | `op signin` on the Mac (or give the daemon `OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN`), then `doz account refresh X`. |
| A custom key is not used | `doz account show NAME` (its hosts); the sandbox must allow each one: `doz net allow SANDBOX site:HOST`. |
| `/login` inside the sandbox never finishes | The key policy is `strict` (it blocks the sign-in pages). That's usually what you want; to allow it: `doz key policy NAME allow`. |

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/permissions-and-network

# What the agent can do: permissions and the network

A sandbox has **no network card**. Its only way out is a proxy in Dozable's host, on your Mac, which
checks every connection against the sandbox's **permissions** — a short list of plain-language
switches — and logs it. You decide what the agent may reach; the agent can't change it.

These are a sandbox's **network** permissions (`doz net permissions`). What an agent may do in Dozable itself — start a
worker, archive a workspace — is a different list, `doz permissions` ([Workspaces](https://dozable.com/docs/workspaces.md), "What agents may do").

## Concepts

- **Permissions** are what an agent may do, each a switch:

  | permission | id | what it allows | in Standard |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Talk to its AI model | `model` | Anthropic's API | always on |
  | Talk to OpenAI | `model:openai` | Codex's model (`chatgpt.com`, `api.openai.com`) — [Codex](https://dozable.com/docs/codex.md) | always on in a Codex sandbox; never in another agent's |
  | Sign in | `sign-in` | Claude's sign-in pages, for signing in *inside* the sandbox | off (Dozable supplies the credential) |
  | Update itself | `update` | new versions of Claude Code or pi | on |
  | Install software — system packages | `install:system` | apt / apk | on |
  | Install software — Node, Python, Go, Rust, Java, Ruby, .NET | `install:node`, `install:python`, `install:go`, `install:rust`, `install:java`, `install:ruby`, `install:dotnet` (`install` = all) | that language's package registry | your base's language |
  | Install software — Swift | `install:swift` | Swift packages (the Swift download site, the Swift Package Index) | on for a fenced session on this Mac |
  | Use GitHub | `github` | clone and fetch code, Git LFS files; Claude Code's plugins | on |
  | Use GitHub as you | `github:as-you` | git and gh signed in as you — read-only ([GitHub as you](https://dozable.com/docs/github.md)) | off, in every preset |
  | Push to GitHub | `github:push` | also push and change things on GitHub as you | off, in every preset |
  | Send error reports | `error-reports` | the agent reporting its own crashes to its maker | on |
  | Browse the web | `web` | any website | off — **the agent could send your code anywhere** |
  | Sites you allow | `site:HOST`, `site:HOST:PORT`, `site:HOST:PORT,PORT` | one host — a name (`api.example.com`), a wildcard (`*.example.com`) or an IPv4 address — on every port, or only on the ports you name | none |

  `doz net permissions` lists every permission with the exact hosts behind it in your version of Dozable.
- **Presets:** **Locked** (its AI model only), **Standard**, **Open** (everything, still logged). Your
  GitHub login is never part of a preset — not even Open: it's switched on by name, and a preset you
  choose later keeps it as it was.
  New sandboxes get the setting `defaults.permissions` (`standard`).
- **Stored by name.** A sandbox remembers "Update itself", not a list of hosts, so when a new version
  of Dozable adds a host to a permission, every sandbox that has it gets it.
- **Live.** A change applies to the sandbox's next connection — no restart — and is kept for its
  next start.
- **Everything is logged:** host, verdict, rule, bytes. Never the contents.

## The default

Every new sandbox — `doz new`, `doz try`, Quick try and the setup's First sandbox alike — starts on **Standard**
(`defaults.permissions`). It's the balance most agent work needs: the agent can talk to its model, update itself,
install software (apt, npm, PyPI and its base's other package managers) and use GitHub, so `sudo apt-get install` and
`npm install` just work. It cannot browse the web at large, so it can't send your code to a site you never allowed.
Every refusal is on record, and the sandbox's **Network** tab offers to allow it.

**Locked** (its model only) is one choice away — `--network locked`, or the Network tab — for an agent you don't trust
with anything else; **Open** is for when you decide the web is fine. A sandbox runs on your Mac with your project
folder in it, which is why the default isn't Open.

## See what the agent can do

```sh
doz net my-app            # the checklist, its sites, and what it was refused lately
doz net log my-app        # the connection log
doz net log my-app --denied --follow
```

When the agent was refused something a permission would allow, `doz net` says so — "the agent tried
to install Python packages (PyPI), 3 times" — with the command that allows it.

**What a refusal looks like inside.** It depends on whether the program uses the proxy. One that does — curl, wget,
pip, npm, git and most tools read `HTTPS_PROXY` — gets an answer from Dozable: an HTTPS site refused answers `403` with
the words "refused by Dozable's network policy, not a network failure" and the `doz net` commands (curl prints them; a
tool that shows only the status says `403 Forbidden`). One that ignores the proxy and looks the name up itself — Node's
own `https` and `fetch`, for one — sees a name that does not resolve: `getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND remotion.media`, "Name or
service not known". So when a download or an API call fails with a 403 or a DNS error, look at `doz net NAME` first: it
names the host that was refused and the exact `doz net allow` command. In a workspace, `doz workspace show W --network`
lists every agent's refusals at once.

**A large refused count is often a browser's housekeeping.** A headless browser in the sandbox (a render, a test run)
makes its own background requests — Google's update, safe-browsing and font hosts — and each one refused is counted. They
are not the work: allow only the hosts the work needs (a `site:HOST` for each), never `*.googleapis.com` or **Browse the
web** to make the count go away.

This page's rules cover a sandbox and a **fenced session on this Mac** alike, each with its own proxy (see [Sessions on
this Mac](#sessions-on-this-mac), below); an unfenced session has no proxy and is not held by any of it.

## Change it — in the terminal

```sh
doz net allow my-app install:python          # switch a permission on
doz net allow my-app site:api.example.com    # one site (every port)
doz net allow my-app site:100.64.0.5:8780    # one site, one port (site:HOST:80,443 for several)
doz net deny my-app github                   # switch one off
doz net deny my-app site:tracker.example.com
doz net deny my-app site:100.64.0.5:8765    # just that port, under a site you allowed whole
doz net allow my-app locked                  # or standard, open: a preset
doz net allow my-app web --yes               # asks first without --yes
doz create my-app --allow install:rust,site:api.example.com,-error-reports
```

`--allow` on `create` and `up` adds to the default: permission ids, `-PERMISSION` to remove one,
`site:HOST` or `site:HOST:PORT[,PORT]`, or a preset name.

A site with no port is every port of that host, as it always was; with ports it is only those. **A deny beats an
allow for the same host** — a whole-host deny blocks every port, and a deny of one port blocks just that port even
where the whole host is allowed. Allowing a port of a host you had denied whole lifts that deny (the command says
"lifted: deny HOST"). An address of this Mac itself, its loopback and link-local addresses and cloud metadata stay
refused whatever a site rule says. A refused connection to a port other than 80 or 443 is offered as that host and
port (`site:HOST:PORT`), not the whole host.

## This Mac's ports

Your Mac's own addresses are never reachable from a sandbox or a fenced session — with one deliberate exception: a
port of your Mac you open to it. It then reaches the service there (a message server, a dev server, a local API) by name, as
`host.dozable.internal:PORT`, and nothing else of your Mac:

```sh
doz create my-app --host-port 8780            # at creation (repeatable); doz_project.yaml: host_ports: [8780]
doz run my-app --host-port 8780 -- bash       # a sandbox keeps it
doz run @mac --host-port 8780 -- claude       # a fenced session on this Mac
doz net allow my-app host:8780                # live, while it runs
doz net deny my-app host:8780                 # closed again, live
```

- **Only that port, only by that name.** The proxy sends `host.dozable.internal:8780` to `127.0.0.1:8780` on your
  Mac. Any other port of the name is refused with the ports that are open. `127.0.0.1:8780`, `localhost:8780` or your
  Mac's Wi-Fi or Tailscale address with the same port stay refused — only the name is the way in.
  `mac.dozable.internal` is the same route (its older name, from [Claude Code and other models](https://dozable.com/docs/claude-code-other-models.md)),
  and a model server's port is one entry of the same list.
- **Never a permission.** `host:PORT` is not a site and not part of any preset — **Open opens the internet, not your
  Mac**. `--permissions host:8780` (and `--allow`) is the same as `--host-port 8780`.
- **Never Dozable's own ports** (the dashboard's, a fenced session's proxy, a sandbox's forwarded web port), port 0
  or a port below 1024 — refused when asked, and again at each connection (a dashboard may start later on that port).
- **Plain HTTP** to it works as to any site; a credential placeholder is never sent there — but for a secret you give
  for that very port ([A secret for a service](#a-secret-for-a-service)).
- `doz net NAME` shows them ("This Mac's ports: 8780 (named), 11434 (model server)"), as does the dashboard's
  Network tab (read-only there: change them with `doz net allow|deny`). A refused connection to the name suggests
  `host:PORT`. The model server's port belongs to its model source: `doz net deny NAME host:PORT` does not take it away.
- **Live changes** follow the setting `network.host_ports_live` (on by default). Off, `doz net allow NAME host:PORT`
  is refused — the ports are fixed when the sandbox or session starts (`--host-port`); `doz net deny` always works.

**Which session is asking.** `--host-port 8780:tag` (or `host:8780:tag`) makes every plain-HTTP request through the
route carry `X-Dozable-Session` naming its sender — the sandbox's name, or `@mac/SESSION` for a fenced session; any
copy the program sent itself is removed first. It is identification, not authentication: any program on your Mac can
send the same header to the service directly. A request inside a tunnel (`CONNECT`, HTTPS) is not read by the proxy,
so it carries nothing added. Without `:tag` the route passes the program's own fields untouched.

## A secret for a service

A service your agent talks to — a message server on your Mac, an API on your Tailscale network — may want a token.
`--secret` gives it one without the token ever entering the sandbox or the fenced session: Dozable reads it from a file,
keeps it, and the session sees only a placeholder that Dozable's proxy swaps for the real token on requests to exactly
one host and port.

```sh
doz create my-app --host-port 8780 \
    --secret SERVER_TOKEN,src=~/.config/token,to=host.dozable.internal:8780,file=SERVER_TOKEN_FILE
doz run my-app --secret SERVER_TOKEN,src=~/.config/token,to=host.dozable.internal:8780 -- bash
doz run @mac --host-port 8780 --secret SERVER_TOKEN,src=~/.config/token,to=host.dozable.internal:8780 -- claude
```

Inside, `$SERVER_TOKEN` holds a placeholder (`doz_cred_…`); with `file=SERVER_TOKEN_FILE`, `$SERVER_TOKEN_FILE` names a
file holding the same placeholder. A request that carries it — `Authorization: Bearer $SERVER_TOKEN` — reaches the
service with the real token in its place.

`VAR,src=PATH,to=HOST:PORT[,header=NAME][,file=FILEVAR]`:

- **`src=PATH`** — the token's only source: a file of yours alone (`chmod go-rwx FILE`; a link, or one other users may read, is
  refused), one line of printable characters without spaces, at most 1800 bytes. Never `-e`, never the command line. A
  file inside the sandbox's folder or anything a fenced session may read is refused — the session could read the
  token itself.
- **`to=HOST:PORT`** — the one destination, port required: `host.dozable.internal:PORT` (a port of this Mac also given
  with `--host-port`), a host name or an IPv4 address the permissions already allow (`--allow site:HOST:PORT`). A
  secret never opens anything: an unreachable destination is refused at launch with the flag to add. Never
  `mac.dozable.internal`, IPv6, your Mac's own addresses or a host Dozable already holds keys for.
- **`header=NAME`** — by default the token goes as `Authorization: Bearer TOKEN`; any other header gets it as it is.
- **`file=FILEVAR`** — also a file holding the placeholder (yours alone; in a sandbox `~/.doz-secrets/VAR`, in a fenced session
  under its own folder).

At most 4 per sandbox or session; VAR and FILEVAR are never one of Dozable's own variables (`ANTHROPIC_…`, `GH_TOKEN`,
`…_PROXY`, `DOZ_…`), and `-e VAR=…` for them is refused. `--unfenced` with `--secret` is refused: an unfenced session
has no proxy to hold it.

A chat room is one such service: Dozable's own chat server, reached on its page port with a participant's token, and
`dozchat` — on the PATH of every sandbox and fenced session — is the client that sends it ([Chat](https://dozable.com/docs/chat.md#participants-and-tokens)).

**Only there.** The same placeholder sent to another port of the host, another host, or `mac.dozable.internal` is
refused (403) and logged — never forwarded with the token. A request that carries its own `Authorization` instead
passes untouched (and is noted with a fingerprint); the token is never added to it.

**Plain HTTP.** Every other credential placeholder is refused over plain HTTP. A secret's placeholder may be swapped
over plain HTTP only to this Mac's ports (`host.dozable.internal`) or a Tailscale address (`100.64.0.0/10`, a name
whose every address is in that range, or the address itself — and only while your Mac is on Tailscale itself: the
range is also used by mobile carriers), and only while the setting `network.placeholders_plain_http` is on (the
default; read when the secret is bound — at launch, a restart, or a new daemon). Anywhere else, use https:

```
refused by the sandbox proxy: a secret's placeholder is never sent over plain HTTP to 10.0.0.5:8080 — only to this
Mac's ports (host.dozable.internal) or a Tailscale address (100.64.0.0/10) while network.placeholders_plain_http is on; use https
```

**How long it lives.** The token is kept in a keychain item of its own (or, when the login keychain is locked, in the
daemon's memory — the launch says "kept until the daemon stops"), so a daemon restart and a session's restart keep it.
A sandbox's secrets end with its shutdown, reset or removal; a fenced session's when its record is removed (`doz
sessions end` of an ended session). Give the secret again to start again; giving it again for the same VAR replaces
the token (placeholders already handed out stay valid). `doz net NAME` shows each secret's destination, header and
fingerprint (`--json`: `secrets`), never the token; the agent's own facts say which variable holds a placeholder for
where.

## Change it — in the dashboard

On a sandbox's page, the details' **Network** tab › **What the agent can do** shows the presets (**Locked** ·
**Standard** · **Open**) and the permissions as switches, with its sites below. Flip a switch and it
applies at once; each permission's **hosts** unfold beneath it. When the agent was refused something, a line
says so — "The agent tried to install Python packages (PyPI)" — with **Allow** (or **Allow this
site**). A site is offered as its whole domain — the agent refused at `abc.frame.claudeusercontent.com` gets
**Allow claudeusercontent.com** (`site:*.claudeusercontent.com`), so a service that uses a new host name for
each request needs one approval, not one per address; `doz net allow NAME site:HOST` still allows a single
host. **Browse the web** asks you to confirm first. **Details: the rules and hosts** shows every
host behind the switches, and **Edit policy…** edits the raw rules with a preview of exactly what
changes.

![What the agent can do](https://dozable.com/docs/images/permissions.png)

New sandbox shows the same switches (preset from the base you chose), and the **Settings** page
edits `defaults.permissions` with them.

## The network kinds

`--network` on `create` (and `network:` in `doz_project.yaml`) chooses how a sandbox is connected:

| `--network` | what it is |
|---|---|
| `agent` | proxied, with the **Standard** permissions (the default for agent images) |
| `locked` | proxied, **Locked**: the agent's model only |
| `open` | proxied, **Open**: everything, still logged |
| `bake` | proxied, package registries only (the default for `lab`, and what image preparation uses) |
| `nat` | a real network card through macOS's NAT: **not** filtered or logged |
| `none` | no network at all |

The proxied kinds have no network card: every connection, DNS included, goes through the proxy.
`nat` and `none` are the virtual machine's make-up, fixed when the sandbox is made.

## The raw rules

Under the permissions there are rules, which you can still edit directly:

```sh
doz net policy my-app                                   # show
doz net policy my-app --allow github.com --allow '*.githubusercontent.com'
doz net policy my-app --deny example.com --remove github.com
doz net policy my-app --preset open                     # replace with a preset: locked, bake, agent, open
```

Your own rules win over a permission's hosts. A host your rules can't allow doesn't even resolve.

## Settings

| key | default | what it does |
|---|---|---|
