| `defaults.permissions` | `standard` | What a new sandbox's agent may do: `standard`, `locked`, `open`, or Standard with changes like `+web,-error-reports`. |
| `recipes.anthropic.claude-code.network` · `recipes.earendil-works.pi.network` · `images.lab.network` | `agent` · `agent` · `bake` | The network kind of a new sandbox of each image. |
| `defaults.nat_subnet` | (a free one) | The subnet of a new `nat` sandbox (`$DOZ_SUBNET`). |
| `network.host_ports_live` | `true` | Whether `doz net allow NAME host:PORT` may open a port of this Mac while a sandbox or session runs. |
| `network.placeholders_plain_http` | `true` | Whether a secret given with `--secret` may travel over plain HTTP — only ever to this Mac's ports and Tailscale addresses. |

## Limits and security

- **Browse the web** and **Open** let the agent send your code and data anywhere. Prefer a
  `site:HOST` for what the agent really needs.
- **A Dockerfile build runs outside this policy** (in Apple's builder); the sandbox made from it
  doesn't. See [Images and bases](https://dozable.com/docs/images-and-bases.md#your-own-dockerfile).
- IPv4 only; HTTP/2 isn't passed through on the hosts whose traffic the proxy inspects; UDP is refused
  (programs fall back to TCP).
- **Your Mac's own addresses are never reachable**, whatever the permissions — Open included: its localhost, its
  Wi-Fi or Ethernet address, a VPN's or Tailscale's, link-local addresses and the cloud metadata address
  `169.254.169.254`. A port of your Mac you open to it is reached by name ([This Mac's ports](#this-macs-ports)), a
  model server's among them ([Claude Code and other models](https://dozable.com/docs/claude-code-other-models.md)); other machines on your network stay reachable when the permissions allow them.
- There are no general port forwards from your Mac into a sandbox. The one exception is a sign-in's
  callback, briefly — see [Signing in from a sandbox](https://dozable.com/docs/signing-in-from-a-sandbox.md).
- A sandbox made with an older version of Dozable keeps its rules; `doz net NAME` shows them as the
  permissions they amount to, and its first permission change stores them as permissions (anything
  no permission covers stays as your own site rules).

## Sessions on this Mac

A fenced session on this Mac (`doz run @mac`, fenced by default — [Sessions on this Mac](https://dozable.com/docs/sessions-on-this-mac.md))
has the same kind of proxy, one per session: it reaches the network only through it, judged by the same permissions,
every connection logged. This Mac's **Standard** for such a session (`mac.permissions`) is its AI model, its own
updates, GitHub, error reports and the Node, Python, Go, Rust and Swift registries; `--permissions` decides for one
session, and the same commands change a running one with `--session`:

```sh
doz net @mac --session agent                      # its permissions and its refusals
doz net allow @mac --session agent install:ruby   # live
doz net log @mac --session agent --denied
doz net log @mac --session agent --fence          # what the fence itself refused (files, programs, services)
```

Inside the fence name lookups are closed (the proxy looks names up), a program that ignores the proxy has no network,
and listening is allowed only on the ports given with `--local-port N`. A service on this Mac is reached through the
proxy as `host.dozable.internal:PORT` for a port given with `--host-port PORT` (or `doz net allow @mac --session S
host:PORT`) — see [This Mac's ports](#this-macs-ports). An unfenced session (`--unfenced`) has none of
this: it reaches the network as you do, unlogged.

## Troubleshooting

| symptom | what to do |
|---|---|
| A package install fails | `doz net NAME` says what was refused and which permission allows it: `doz net allow NAME install:python`. |
| A DNS error inside (`ENOTFOUND`, "Could not resolve host") | Usually a refusal: `doz net NAME` names the host and the allow command. |
| Hundreds of refusals while a browser runs | Its own background requests: allow only the hosts the work needs. |
| The agent can't reach your company's API | `doz net allow NAME site:api.example.com`. |
| A site works in your browser but not in the sandbox | `doz net log NAME --denied` shows the refused host — sites often use a second host for assets or APIs. |
| Claude Code can't update itself | `update` must be on (it is in Standard). |
| You need the whole web for a while | `doz net allow NAME web`, then `doz net deny NAME web` when done. |

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/signing-in-from-a-sandbox

# Signing in from a sandbox

Many command-line tools sign you in through a web browser: they open a sign-in page, you sign in,
and the provider sends your browser back to the tool on `http://localhost:PORT`. A sandbox has no
browser and its `localhost` isn't your Mac's — so Dozable bridges both: the page opens in **your Mac's
browser**, and the redirect at the end finds its way back **into the sandbox**.

You rarely need this for Claude itself — Dozable supplies Claude's credential already (see
[Agents and accounts](https://dozable.com/docs/agents-and-accounts.md)). It's for everything else an agent may sign in to:
a cloud CLI, a SaaS tool's CLI, an MCP server's OAuth.

## Concepts

- **The browser bridge.** Inside every sandbox, `xdg-open` — and `$BROWSER`, `open`,
  `sensible-browser`, `www-browser` — is Dozable's own small program. It hands an **http or https**
  address to your Mac, which opens it in your default browser. You're told every time:
  `my-app opened https://example.com/docs in your browser`. Nothing is printed into the session itself
  — the agent's screen stays exactly as it drew it; when an address is refused, the program that asked
  hears why (its error output and exit status). (Given a document in `/workspace` instead of an address, the same program opens that file
  on your Mac — see [Opening your folder's files on your Mac](https://dozable.com/docs/terminals-and-sessions.md#opening-your-folders-files-on-your-mac).)
- **The sign-in callback.** When the address asks the provider to send the browser back to the
  sandbox's `localhost:PORT` (its `redirect_uri`), Dozable first opens your Mac's `localhost:PORT` and
  forwards it into the sandbox, then opens the page. The notice says
  `sign-in callback localhost:PORT forwarded (10 min)`. When your browser lands on the callback, the
  tool in the sandbox receives it and the sign-in completes.
- **It lasts the sign-in, no longer.** The forward is on your Mac's loopback only (nothing else on
  your network can reach it), one per sandbox (a new sign-in replaces it), and it closes 3 seconds
  after the callback was answered, or after 10 minutes.
- **Only while you watch.** Like the clipboard bridge, it works while a terminal (yours, or a
  dashboard tab) is attached to the session.

## Sign in

1. Attach to the session — `doz attach my-app`, `doz up`, or a terminal in the dashboard.
2. Run the tool's sign-in command in the sandbox (for example `gh auth login --web`, `gcloud auth
   login`, or the tool's `/login`).
3. Your Mac's browser opens the sign-in page, and a notice appears:
   - in `doz attach`, over the bottom row: `my-app opened https://… · sign-in callback localhost:8765 forwarded (10 min)`;
   - in the dashboard, a message in the corner.
4. Sign in as usual. The browser's last redirect reaches the tool in the sandbox; the tool says it's
   signed in. The forward closes a few seconds later.

![The browser-open notice](https://dozable.com/docs/images/browser-open-toast.png)

Programs that open a page without a sign-in (documentation, a report) just open in your browser.

## What is refused (and said)

- anything but `http` and `https` — `file:`, `javascript:`, custom schemes;
- an address on the Mac's own loopback — `http://localhost:3000` from inside a sandbox means the
  **sandbox's** own server, which your Mac's browser can't reach. (Tell the person the address; there
  are no general port forwards.)
- more than 3 addresses in 10 seconds, or an address over 2048 characters;
- a callback port already in use on your Mac: the page still opens, and the notice says the sign-in
  can't come back.

## Turn it off

```sh
doz config set --sandbox my-app sandbox.browser_bridge off    # this sandbox (applies at once)
doz config set sandbox.browser_bridge off                     # every sandbox without its own choice
doz create my-app --browser-bridge off …                      # from the start (or browser_bridge: off in doz_project.yaml)
doz config show --sandbox my-app                              # this sandbox's own values, and whose value each is
```

Off, nothing opens and nothing is forwarded; the notice says the bridge is off. The agent is told
either way, so it knows to print addresses for you instead.

## Sign-ins and permissions

The sign-in page opens on **your Mac**, outside the sandbox, so it doesn't need a permission. But the
tool inside may need to reach the provider's API afterwards: allow it as a site
(`doz net allow my-app site:api.example.com`). For Claude's own sign-in pages there is a **Sign in**
permission (off in Standard); with the default key policy a sign-in inside a sandbox that uses a
token or API key is refused on purpose. See [What the agent can do](https://dozable.com/docs/permissions-and-network.md)
and [Agents and accounts](https://dozable.com/docs/agents-and-accounts.md#a-credential-the-agent-brings-itself).

## Settings

| key | default | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `sandbox.browser_bridge` | `on` | `on`: xdg-open reaches your Mac's browser and a sign-in's callback is forwarded. `off`: never. Per sandbox too. |

## Limits and security

- **A sandbox can open web pages on your Mac.** Every one is announced and rate-limited, and only
  http(s) pages that aren't on your Mac's own loopback. If you don't want that for a sandbox, turn
  the bridge off for it.
- **The forward is narrow:** one port, on your Mac's loopback, for one sign-in, at most 10 minutes.
  The address's query (which carries the sign-in's secret state) never appears in notices or logs —
  only the scheme, host and path.
- The bridge arrives with a sandbox's next start; a sandbox woken from an older version of Dozable gets
  it at its next session.

## Troubleshooting

| symptom | what to do |
|---|---|
| Nothing opens | Is a terminal attached to the session? Is the bridge on (`doz config show --sandbox NAME`)? Does the tool use `xdg-open` or `$BROWSER`? Some print the address instead — open it yourself. |
| "localhost:PORT is in use on this Mac" | Something on your Mac uses that port. Quit it, or use the tool's device-code sign-in if it has one. |
| The browser says it can't connect at the end | The forward closed (10 minutes) or the tool in the sandbox stopped waiting. Start the sign-in again. |
| The tool signs in but then can't reach its API | `doz net NAME` shows the refusal; allow the site. |
| "only http and https URLs are opened" | The program asked to open a file or another scheme; that's never bridged. |

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/restore-points-duplicates-templates

# Restore points, duplicates and saved disks

Three ways to copy a sandbox's disk, each instant (they're APFS clones, sharing space until
something changes):

| | what it is | use it to |
|---|---|---|
| **Restore point** | a copy of a sandbox's disks at a moment, kept with the sandbox | undo: go back, or fork a new sandbox from that moment |
| **Duplicate** | a new sandbox from an existing one's disk | run the same setup on another project, or with more memory |
| **Saved disk** | a sandbox's system disk saved as an image (`doz image save`) | make many new sandboxes that start set up your way |

None of them copies your sandbox's folder (it's on your Mac — use git) or memory (a restored or
forked sandbox cold-boots).

## Restore points

```sh
doz point take my-app before-refactor --note "tests green"   # a running sandbox pauses for milliseconds
doz point ls my-app
doz point revert my-app before-refactor                       # shuts down and goes back; start boots it
doz point fork my-app before-refactor try-2                   # a new sandbox from that moment
doz point rm my-app before-refactor
```

- A point covers the sandbox's **disks** — the system disk and the agent's state disk — not what's
  running.
- **Revert takes a point first** ("before revert"), so a revert can itself be undone.
- Name a point with anything up to 64 characters (kept exactly as you type it). Wherever a command
  takes a point, you can give its name, its id (`rp-…`) or the start of either, as long as only one
  matches.
- Commands that ask first (`revert`, `rm`) check the point exists before asking, and the question
  names it, its id and when it was taken.

**In the dashboard:** a sandbox's details › **Points** has **Take a restore point…**, and per point
**Revert**, and under its **⋯** **Fork…**, **Save disk as image…**, **Duplicate…** and **Delete…** (revert
and delete ask you to tick a box first).

## Duplicates

```sh
doz duplicate my-app my-app-2 --folder ~/code/other-project --cpus 4 --memory 4G
doz duplicate my-app my-app-3 --from-point before-refactor --network locked
doz duplicate my-app my-app-4 --copy-state        # the agent's logins and history too
```

- The new sandbox is **off** until you start it. Anything you don't give is the source's, its
  permissions included.
- A `--folder` that doesn't exist is made; `--isolated` shares no folder.
- The agent's **state disk starts fresh** unless `--copy-state`.
- Keys given with `doz key set` are not copied; the account follows `--account` or the source's.

**In the dashboard:** **⋯** › **Duplicate…** on the sandbox's page (or from a restore point): new name, from
the current disk or a point, folder, CPUs, memory, network, account, and "Copy the agent's state
disk too".

## Saved disks

```sh
doz image save my-app node-tools --note "node 22 + pnpm"            # now (a live sandbox pauses for ms)
doz image save my-app base-2 --from-point before-upgrade            # or from a restore point
doz point save-image my-app before-upgrade --as base-3              # the same, from the point command
doz image ls                                                        # saved disks say "saved disk"
doz create beta --image node-tools
doz image rm node-tools                                             # sandboxes made from it keep working
```

- **Everything on the system disk is in it**: what you installed or wrote in `/root`, `/etc`,
  `/usr`, `/opt`, caches. **Don't save a secret you put there.**
- **The agent's state disk is never in it** (logins, history, tokens), so a saved disk can be shared.
  A sandbox made from a saved disk starts with a fresh state disk.
- A sandbox from a saved disk gets the agent and settings of the image the disk came from.
- **Moved:** these were `doz template create NAME --as DISK`, `doz template ls` and `doz template rm DISK`. For one
  release they still work and say where they moved; `doz template` is to mean workspace templates.

**In the dashboard:** **⋯** › **Save disk as image…** on a sandbox's page (now, or from a restore point); New
sandbox › **Base** › **Saved disk** uses one; **Images** lists saved disks and removes them.

## Seeing the family tree

```sh
doz image ls --tree
```

```
IMAGE / SANDBOX   KIND        SIZE    SHARED  OWN
alpine-3.20       prepared    34 MiB  —       116 KiB
├─ tpl-a          saved disk  36 MiB  33 MiB  160 KiB  from alpha
├─ alpha          sandbox     36 MiB  33 MiB  0 B
└─ beta           sandbox     34 MiB  34 MiB  224 KiB
```

**Shared** is what a disk shares with its parent (counted once on disk); **Own** is what removing it
would free. The dashboard's **Images** › **Lineage** draws the same tree.

## Limits

- Restore points are disk-only: a revert or fork cold-boots, and running programs start fresh.
- A saved disk can't be exported to another Mac yet (no registry push).
- A sandbox's saved screens and boot logs aren't copied by duplicate, fork or a saved disk.

## Troubleshooting

| symptom | what to do |
|---|---|
| "more than one point matches" | Give more of the name or id; the message lists the matches. |
| A reverted sandbox doesn't have my latest code | Its folder is on your Mac and isn't part of a point: use git for it. |
| A duplicate's agent has none of the conversation history | Its state disk started fresh: duplicate again with `--copy-state`. |
| Disk space after many points | Each point costs only what changed since; `doz resources` shows each one, and `doz point rm` frees it. |

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/resources-and-disk-space

# Resources and disk space

Dozable keeps everything in one folder, the **store**. `doz resources` — and the dashboard's
**Resources** page — accounts for every byte of it, shows the memory, CPUs and network your sandboxes
use, and deletes what can safely go.

## Concepts

- **Sizes are real disk use.** Dozable's disks are APFS clones: a sandbox shares most of its blocks with
  its image, and a restore point with its sandbox. So each row shows three numbers:
  - **size** — the disk space it occupies, counted in full;
  - **freed if deleted** — what deleting it would actually give back (only the blocks nobody else
    shares);
  - **used by** — what depends on it.
- **Everything adds up.** The rows add up to the total that `du` reports for the store. A last row,
  **unattributed**, is what no row explains; it should be 0.
- **Re-creatable vs. yours.** A download cache, an unused baked image or an old kernel can be made
  again (it costs time and network later). A sandbox, a restore point or a saved disk can't — those are
  yours.

## See it — in the terminal

```sh
doz resources               # every byte of the store, then memory, CPUs, traffic and kernels
doz resources --json
```

The groups: **Sandboxes** (each one's system disk, state disk, sleep snapshot, restore points, saved
screens and boot logs), **Images & saved disks**, **Caches** (the download cache, base disks, the boot
disk, kernels, preparation leftovers, and the **tools layer** — `gh`, downloaded once for sandboxes with
GitHub as you; see [Managed tools](https://dozable.com/docs/the-tools-layer.md)), **Logs & metrics**, **Stray files**, Dozable's own records — and
**Outside the store**: your settings file, keychain entries by name, the `doz` program, project
folders and Apple's `container` storage. Those outside rows are shown, never deleted here.

## Free space

```sh
doz resources clean --dry-run          # what Clean up would delete, and what each frees
doz resources clean                    # asks once
doz resources rm cache:downloads kernel:6.12.1 --dry-run
doz resources rm point:web/3           # by id, as doz resources lists them
```

- **Clean up** deletes what is **re-creatable and unused**: the download cache, the tools layer's cache, base disks, kernels
  nothing needs, images no sandbox was made from in the last `resources.clean_unused_days` (30) days,
  and leftovers. It **never** deletes saved disks, sandboxes, restore points, settings or keys; logs,
  metrics and the history file are kept too (select them yourself to clear them). Clearing the metrics clears
  their part of the history; deleting the **history** item (`timeline.sqlite`) has the daemon make it again from the
  records (see [History and retention](https://dozable.com/docs/history-and-retention.md)).
- **`rm`** deletes what you name, after showing the plan: each item, what it frees, what it costs
  later ("prepared again when next needed, about 3 min, needs network"), and anything refused and why.
- **Nothing breaks a sandbox.** Refused, always: a sandbox's own disks (remove the sandbox instead);
  the kernel and boot disk while any sandbox is asleep or running (their snapshots need them); an
  image being prepared; a folder that is a sandbox's shared folder; anything outside the store.
- The deletion waits until nothing that uses the disks is under way (a start, a wake, a preparation),
  and runs as one operation.

## In the dashboard

**Resources** in the sidebar (its total is shown beside it). The bar on top splits Dozable's total into
what it keeps, what **Clean up** would free and the blocks clones share, with the disk's free space
beside it; under it, a strip that jumps to each group (with its size) — a group's heading folds it, and
the dashboard remembers which you folded. Then the rows, each linking to where it's managed: an image to **Images**, a
sandbox's parts to **its page**, accounts to **Accounts & keys**.

1. Tick what should go, or **Select all re-creatable**.
2. **Delete selected…** — one confirmation lists each item, what it frees and what it costs later.
3. Or **Clean up…** for the safe set.

The page measures when you open it, on **Refresh**, and when an operation ends.

![The Resources page](https://dozable.com/docs/images/resources.png)

## Memory, CPUs, traffic and kernels

The same report shows the memory each running sandbox holds (and the daemon's and the dashboard's),
the CPUs given to sandboxes, each sandbox's network traffic through the proxy (today and in all), and
the Linux kernels. **Use this kernel** (or `doz resources kernel kernel:VERSION`, or `pinned` for
this version's own) picks the kernel **new** sandboxes boot; existing ones keep theirs.

## Apple's `container` storage

If you build Dockerfile bases, Apple's `container` tool keeps its own images and data outside Dozable's
store. The Resources page shows it as an **Outside** row — its data folder by part, the program, and
the images Dozable built with it — so you know where the space went. Dozable never deletes it; manage it
with Apple's `container` command.

## A second store

`--store DIR` (or `DOZ_STORE`) runs Dozable on another store — a test store beside your own, say. A second store is a
second Dozable: its own daemon, sandboxes, workspaces and chat server, with its own rooms, participants and **tokens** (a
token of one store means nothing to another). Three things to know:

- **Its chat ports.** Your settings file (`~/.config/doz/doz.toml`) is shared by every store unless you give the second
  its own settings folder (`XDG_CONFIG_HOME`); two chat servers cannot share a port, so give each store its own settings
  folder, or its own `chat.page_port` and `chat.line_port`. `doz chat status --store DIR` shows the ports it uses. An agent
  Dozable starts is given its own store's address (`CHAT_URL`); one you start yourself must be told it.
- **It keeps running.** `daemon.always_on` is on by default, for every store: the second store's daemon stays up after
  its last sandbox stops, until `doz daemon stop --store DIR`.
- **The menu bar app is for the default store only** (the one `doz` uses with no `--store`), its Start at Login
  included. A second store's daemon starts when a command needs it, or at login with a login item of its own
  (`doz daemon login-item on --store DIR`).

## Settings

| key | default | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `resources.clean_unused_days` | `30` | Clean up removes a baked image no sandbox was made from in this many days (1–3650). It's baked again when next needed. |
| `daemon.boot_logs_kept` | `5` | Boots kept per sandbox. |
| `store.path` | `~/Library/Application Support/doz` | Where the store is. |

## Troubleshooting

| symptom | what to do |
|---|---|
| The **unattributed** row isn't 0 | Something in the store no row explains. `doz resources --json` lists it under stray files; report it if it keeps growing. |
| "refused: … a sandbox's disk" | Remove or reset the sandbox instead; Resources never deletes a live sandbox's disks. |
| Clean up freed less than the sizes suggested | Sizes count shared blocks in full; "freed" counts only what nothing else shares. |
| The Mac's disk is still full | Look at **Outside the store**: Apple's container storage and your project folders are yours to manage. |

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/letting-another-agent-drive

# Letting another agent drive Dozable

So far *you* have run `doz`. But the agent you already use on your Mac — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor —
can run it too. Its job is to orchestrate a **workspace** for you: make it with a brief and your folders, start its
agents, follow the room and the journal of each unit of work, and bring you what needs your decision. A sandbox is one
place an agent of the workspace can run (a micro VM), beside a fenced session on this Mac or, only when you say, a
session that acts as you.

Before anything else, it should run `doz --version` and read the manual of that version (`doz docs`, below): commands
and flags change between releases. Then [Workspaces](https://dozable.com/docs/workspaces.md) for the model, and the rules on this page for
driving: `--json`, the exit codes, `--yes`, and what to ask you first. Four things it must know before it acts:

- **Chat on is your call.** Workers and a manager talk in the workspace's room, so they need chat (`doz chat on`); the
  agent should ask you before it turns chat on, not do it unasked.
- **`doz exec` stops after 120 s** unless it passes `--timeout`; a long job (a build, a render) goes in the background
  with `doz run NAME -d`.
- **A refused connection looks like a DNS error** inside a sandbox (`ENOTFOUND`). `doz net NAME` names what was refused
  and the command that allows it — which it asks you to run.
- **The agents inside have no `doz`.** They reach Dozable with `dozchat` and their own token ([Runs, the journal and
  lessons](41-runs-the-journal-and-lessons.md)); it never hands them its own.

## Workspaces

To get agents working on something — a brief, your folders, a helper with a task — make a **workspace**, in one
command:

```sh
doz workspace new app --brief "Fix the build" --folder ~/code/app --worker "Fix the failing test" --json
doz workspace start app --json
```

- **Create.** `--brief TEXT` (or `--brief -` for standard input, or `--prompt-file FILE`), `--folder DIR` (repeatable;
  the first is the main one), `--worker "TASK"` (repeatable: declared now, started by `doz workspace start`), `--preset
  NAME` (`blank`, `research`, `swift-tests`, `mac-admin`, `remotion-video`; a flag given wins) and `--start` to start it
  at once. `--dry-run --json` shows what would be made and makes nothing. `doz workspace create` is the same command.
  An unknown preset exits `65` (`invalid-value`), naming the real ones. Workers need chat on (`doz chat on`).
- **State.** `doz workspace state app --json` gives each agent's `condition` — `running`, `asleep`, `stopped`,
  `crashed`, `not-started` or `unknown` — with its `reason`, `role`, `place` and `since`, and `conditions.ready` (every
  agent running). With no daemon running none is started and every condition is `unknown`.
- **Add a worker.** `doz worker add app --task "Review the fix" --json` brings up a helper in a started workspace
  (refused, exit `3`, while it is still setting up); `doz worker ls app --json` lists them; `doz worker end app NAME`
  ends one. Workers run fenced on this Mac unless you say otherwise: `--isolation unfenced` acts as you, so an agent
  should never choose it for you.
- **Retry safely.** An agent that loses an answer (a timeout, a dropped connection) cannot tell whether the command
  worked, and running it again could make a second worker. So pass `--request-id ID` — an id the agent makes up once
  per request, a UUID say — to `doz workspace new`, `doz worker add`, `doz workspace adopt` and `doz permissions grant`.
  Run again with the same id and arguments, the command answers its first answer with `"replayed": true` and does
  nothing again; with other arguments it exits `3` (`request-id-reused`, naming what differs). A failed first try is not
  kept, so the retry runs for real. Ids are kept 24 hours, per command.
- **The skill.** `doz skill show doz` prints the `doz` skill — a `SKILL.md` for an agent that drives doz: workspaces,
  the exit codes, the error JSON, `--yes`, and what not to do. `doz skill show doz --json` gives its path
  (`{"kind":"Skill","schema":1,"name":"doz","path":"…/SKILL.md"}`); point your agent at it. It ships inside doz, which
  installs it nowhere.
- **This manual, of this version.** Every `doz` carries its own manual: `doz docs` says where it is (offline — no
  network, no daemon), `doz docs PAGE` prints a page by name or number (`doz docs workspaces`, `doz docs 37`; an unknown
  page exits `65` and lists them), and `doz docs --json` gives
  `{"kind":"DozDocs","schema":1,"version","local","llms","url"}`: `llms` is its index, `llms.txt` (every page, one
  line each, linked relatively), and `url` the same manual online for this version only,
  `https://dozable.com/v/VERSION/llms.txt`. `doz docs --path` prints only the folder. An agent should read this one,
  never another version's: a canary or beta has commands and flags the stable manual doesn't.

`doz create` makes a single sandbox, not a workspace: an agent asked for a workspace should use `doz workspace new`.

## Concepts

- **Every command works without a terminal to type into**, and **`--json`** gives machine-readable
  output on stdout (errors as `{"error":{"code","message","exit"}}`; fields are only ever added). A usage error is
  one too: with `--json` anywhere on the line, an unknown option or a missing argument prints
  `{"error":{"code":"usage","message":"Unknown option '--no-such-flag'","exit":64}}` on stdout and exits `64` — never
  the plain-text usage (`--help` still prints help).
- **Exit codes** say what happened, the same for every command, and they keep their meaning:

  | exit | meaning | `error.code` |
  |---|---|---|
  | `0` | done (or asked: a question was posted, the answer comes later) | — |
  | `1` | failed | `failed` |
  | `2` | not found — only that | `not-found`, `ambiguous` (several match: the message lists them) |
  | `3` | not possible now | `invalid-phase`, `conflict`, `plan-changed`, `file-changed`, `already-answered`, `not-owned`, `request-id-reused` |
  | `4` | already exists | `already-exists` (also `exists`) |
  | `5` | not confirmed (no terminal and no `--yes`) | `needs-confirmation` |
  | `6` | the daemon is unavailable | `needs-daemon` (also `unavailable`, `version`) |
  | `7` | not implemented yet | `not-implemented` |
  | `8` | supported, but not with what was asked (`doz search`) | `limited` |
  | `9` | not permitted (an agent's request) | `not-permitted` |
  | `64` | usage: an unknown command or flag, a missing argument | `usage`, `unclear-request` |
  | `65` | an invalid document or value (a space file, a name, a flag's or a setting's value) | `invalid-document`, `invalid-value`, `secret-value-in-document` (also `invalid`) |
  | `75` | partly done: `--json`'s `partial` says `done`, `remaining` and `retry` (the command that does the rest) | `partial` |
  | `124` | timed out | `timed-out` |
  | `125` | `doz` itself failed around a program (`exec`, `run`, `attach`) | — |

  `doz help exit-codes --json` prints this table (`{"kind":"ExitCodes","schema":1,"codes":[…]}`). `exec`,
  `run` and `attach` exit with the program's own code (`125` when `doz` itself failed). `exec` exits `124` when its `--timeout` passed (default 120 s, counted from when `doz`
  started — a wake or a start included); the command is killed (and anything it left running is reaped, never left
  `<defunct>`), a wake or a start goes on, and stderr says so with what to do instead: `--timeout SECONDS`, or `doz run
  -d` for a long job. A program's own `124` looks the same: `--json` says `"timedOut": true` only for the deadline.
- **Destructive commands refuse without `--yes`** when there's no terminal, so a script can't delete
  something by accident.
- **Two agents, two sets of rules.** The agent on your Mac has *your* permissions: it can run `doz`, so
  treat it as you would at the keyboard. An agent inside a sandbox or a fenced session is held by
  the proxy: it reaches Dozable only through its room and the journal, with `dozchat`, by the permissions you grant it.

## The briefing

Paste this into your project's `CLAUDE.md` (or `AGENTS.md` for other agents):

````markdown
## Sandboxes (Dozable)

This Mac has Dozable (`doz`): Linux VMs for running agents and risky commands in isolation.
Use a sandbox for anything that installs packages, runs untrusted code, or should not touch this
Mac. Always pass `--json` and read the result; never use `doz attach` or `doz up` without `--detach`
(they are interactive).

- Create one for this project: `doz create NAME --image claude-code --folder "$PWD" --json`
  (images: `claude-code`, `pi`, `lab`, or `--agent claude-code --base python|go|rust|…`; `doz base ls`).
  `/workspace` in the sandbox IS this folder, live.
  For throwaway work that must not touch this folder: `doz create NAME --isolated --json`.
- Run a command and get its output and exit code: `doz exec NAME --json -- sh -c '…'`
  (add `--timeout SECONDS` for long ones; the default is 120). It starts or wakes the sandbox if needed.
- Start a long-running agent or program and come back later:
  `doz run NAME --detach -- claude -p "…"`, then `doz sessions NAME --json` and
  `doz sessions NAME --screen SESSION` to see its terminal.
- Before anything risky: `doz point take NAME before-X`; undo with `doz point revert NAME before-X --yes`.
- Refused network: `doz net NAME --json` shows what the agent was refused and the permission that
  would allow it. Do NOT widen permissions yourself: tell me what and why, and I will run
  `doz net allow NAME …`.
- When done: `doz hibernate NAME` (keeps everything, frees memory; `doz wake NAME` brings it back).
  Ask me before `doz reset`, `doz rm` or `doz shutdown`.
- `doz ls --json` lists sandboxes; `doz doctor --json` diagnoses problems.
````

## Then ask for what you want

For example, to Claude Code on your Mac:

> Upgrade this project to React 19 in a sandbox. Take a restore point first, let a Claude in the
> sandbox do the upgrade and get the tests passing, check on it every few minutes, and show me the
> diff when it's done. Don't touch my Mac's node_modules.

Your agent will then typically run:

```sh
doz create react19 --image claude-code --folder ~/code/my-app --json
doz point take react19 before-upgrade
doz run react19 --detach -- claude -p "Upgrade to React 19 and make npm test pass"
doz sessions react19 --screen claude          # every few minutes, to see how it's going
doz exec react19 --json -- sh -c 'cd /workspace && npm test'
doz hibernate react19
```

Because `/workspace` is your project folder, the changes are already on your Mac when it finishes:
review them with `git diff`. If they're not what you wanted, `git checkout .` puts your files back
and `doz point revert` resets the sandbox.

You can watch it all in the dashboard (`doz ui`): the sandbox appears under **Sandboxes**, and
**All sessions** shows the agent working, read-only.

## Guardrails

- **Keep permission changes and deletion for yourself.** The briefing asks for that; you can make it a
  rule in your agent's own settings too (for example, only allow it `doz` subcommands that don't
  change permissions or delete).
- **Prefer `--isolated`** for work that shouldn't touch your folder at all.
- **Use restore points** before each risky step; they cost almost nothing.
- **Watch the clipboard, browser and file notices.** A sandboxed agent can put text on your clipboard,
  open a page in your browser or open a document of its folder on your Mac, and each time you're told.
  Turn any of them off for a sandbox with `doz config set --sandbox NAME sandbox.clipboard off`,
  `… sandbox.browser_bridge off` or `… sandbox.open_files off`.
- **Scripts on a schedule** should use exact agent versions (`recipes.anthropic.claude-code.version`) so an image
  never needs the internet to prepare.

## Useful JSON

| command | gives |
|---|---|
| `doz ls --json` | every sandbox: name, image, phase, RAM, disk, network, isolated, … |
| `doz inspect NAME --json` | everything about one |
| `doz exec NAME --json -- CMD` | `exitCode`, `stdout`, `stderr`, and whether it had to start or wake the sandbox |
| `doz sessions NAME --json` | its sessions, running or saved |
| `doz net NAME --json` | its permissions and recent refusals, with the suggestion for each |
| `doz resources --json` | the whole disk account |
| `doz config show --json` | every setting, value and source |

## Troubleshooting

| symptom | what to do |
|---|---|
| The agent's `doz` command hangs | It used an interactive command (`attach`, `up` without `--detach`); use `exec`, `run --detach`, `sessions --screen`. |
| Exit code 5 | A destructive command without `--yes` and without a terminal: intended. Decide yourself, or add `--yes`. |
| Exit code 6 | The daemon couldn't be reached or started: `doz doctor --json`. |
| The sandboxed agent is refused a site | Expected: it tells your Mac's agent, which tells you. `doz net NAME` shows the suggestion. |

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/settings-reference

# Settings reference

This Mac's settings are in one file, **`~/.config/doz/doz.toml`** (under `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` when that
is set). The file lists Dozable's own settings with a description and their default, commented out;
only the values you set are uncommented. A **recipe's** own settings — the settings of the agent it
installs: its `version`, `approvals`, `memory_mib`, `network`, `history`, and any the recipe declares — are a
`[recipes.VENDOR.PRODUCT]` block (`[recipes.anthropic.claude-code]`), written only while one of them is
set, so the file stays small however many recipes there are; `doz config show --agent ID` lists them.
The dashboard's **Settings** page shows and edits the same file, and its **Recipes** section lists the
recipes on this Mac.

## Where a value comes from

For each setting, the first of these that says something wins:

1. **a command-line flag** (for the settings that have one — `--store`, `--progress`, `--color`/`--no-color`,
   `doz create --cpus`, `doz create --approvals`, …);
2. **its environment variable** (`DOZ_STORE`, `DOZ_PROGRESS`, `DOZ_COLOR`, `DOZ_DAEMON_IDLE`, `DOZ_SCREEN_CAPTURE`,
   `DOZ_BOOT_LOGS`, `DOZ_SUBNET`, `DOZ_KERNEL`, `DOZ_KERNEL_CACHE`);
3. **the sandbox's own value** (a setting one sandbox can have, below);
4. **its project's** (`doz_project.yaml`: when the sandbox is made, and again at every `doz up`);
5. **this Mac's** (the file);
6. **the default** — the recipe's own, for a recipe's settings; Dozable's, for the rest.

`doz config show` names the source of every value, and the dashboard shows the same word as a badge:
**recipe** · **default** · **Mac** · **project** · **sandbox** · **env** · **flag**. A value fixed when a
sandbox is made (its agent's version, memory, network, its CPUs) is recorded in it with where it came
from; changing this Mac's value later moves no existing sandbox (`doz reset NAME` moves its version).

## Read and change settings

```sh
doz config                                  # Dozable's own settings: value, source, default — and the recipes in use
doz config show --all                       # every setting, every recipe's too
doz config get ui.theme                     # one value (--json adds its source and default)
doz config set ui.theme dark                # write it to this Mac's file (checked against its type first)
doz config unset ui.theme                   # back to the default (commented out again)
doz config init                             # write the file with every setting commented out
doz config show --agent claude-code         # one recipe's settings: value, source, the recipe's default
doz config set --agent claude-code version 2.1.290   # one of a recipe's settings, on this Mac
doz config path                             # where the file is
```

`--agent` takes a recipe's id (`claude-code`), a major (`opencode@2`) or its full name
(`anthropic/claude-code`).

In the dashboard: **Settings** lists Dozable's settings with their value, default, description and
source, and changes them in place (**Default** puts this Mac's value back to the default). Its
**Recipes** section lists the recipes in use (a sandbox runs the agent) and the ones installed (a baked
image of it is on this Mac, or you set one of its values); search the catalogue for the rest. A
recipe's page has its settings, its baked images, its sandboxes and **Uninstall**. A value set by an
environment variable, and the settings that name a folder on your Mac, are shown read-only there —
change them with `doz config set`.

### Per sandbox and per project

`sandbox.clipboard`, `sandbox.browser_bridge`, `sandbox.open_files`, `sandbox.ssh_agent`,
`sessions.tmux`, `sandbox.agent_sudo`, `sandbox.audio` and its agent's **`approvals`** and **`history`** can
also be set for one sandbox (sound only between `speakers` and `on` — whether it has sound at all is chosen
when it is made; see [Sound](https://dozable.com/docs/sound.md)):

```sh
doz config show --sandbox my-app                          # what it overrides, what it follows, what was recorded
doz config set --sandbox my-app sandbox.clipboard off
doz config set --sandbox my-app approvals ask             # its agent asks before it acts, from the next session
doz config set --sandbox my-app history agent-default     # its agent's own rule for its conversations, from its next start or wake
doz config get --sandbox my-app sessions.tmux
doz config unset --sandbox my-app sandbox.clipboard       # follow the project, else this Mac, again
doz config set --project ~/code/my-app approvals ask      # the project's doz_project.yaml
```

Or when you create it (`doz create --clipboard off --browser-bridge off --open-files off --ssh-agent on --tmux --no-agent-sudo --sound on --approvals ask`),
or in its `doz_project.yaml` (`clipboard:`, `browser_bridge:`, `open_files:`, `ssh_agent:`, `tmux:`, `agent_sudo:`, `audio:`, `approvals:`, `history:`).

**Conversation history** cascades one layer further: `agent.history` (Dozable-wide: `keep` or
`agent-default`) → the agent's own `history` (`follow`, the default, or `keep` / `agent-default`) → the
project's `history:` → the sandbox's own. The most specific value that is not `follow` wins, and
`doz config show --sandbox NAME` says which layer it came from. What each value does in each agent —
which file and key Dozable writes, or that the agent keeps its conversations by itself — is in
[Agents and accounts](https://dozable.com/docs/agents-and-accounts.md#conversation-history) and in `doz config show --agent ID`.
The sandbox page's **Config** tab shows the same: its overrides first, with this Mac's value beside each
and **Follow the Mac**.

### The names before 0.37.34

The recipe settings had other names before 0.37.34 (`images.claude_code_version`, `claude.permissions`,
`images.claude-code.memory_mib`, …; the table below lists them). They still work: the file is read with them, and
`doz config get|set|unset` takes them and says the new name. The first change written after the upgrade
moves them to their new names and keeps the file as it was, once, as `doz.toml.0.37.bak` beside it. A
base with no agent (`python`, `go`) keeps the memory and network it had: `defaults.memory_mib` and
`defaults.network`, set from Claude Code's old values.

"Use GitHub as you" is a permission, not a setting: `doz net allow NAME github:as-you` (and
`github:push`), `doz create --github read|push`, `github:` in `doz_project.yaml` — see
[GitHub as you](https://dozable.com/docs/github.md).

## About the file

- **The file is Dozable's.** `set`, `unset`, `init` and the Settings page rewrite it whole, atomically,
  readable only by you. Comments you add aren't kept.
- **A mistake never breaks Dozable.** An unknown key or a value of the wrong type is a warning (that line
  is ignored, the default applies). A file that doesn't parse at all is ignored — with the line that's
  wrong — and never overwritten until you fix it.
- **When a change applies** is part of each setting: at once, for the next command, the next sandbox
  created, the next session, the next start or wake, or after `doz daemon stop`.

## Not settable, on purpose

The dashboard's security limits and checks (session and link lifetimes, request and connection caps,
the Host/Origin/CSRF checks, the content policy); a browser terminal's one-use tickets and paste
limits; the guest programs; and any credential. `ui.terminals` can only take something away.

## Every setting

This table is generated from `doz config show` and checked against it on every build.


### `[ui]`

| key | default | values | applies | overridden by | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ui.boot_view_on_start` | `false` | boolean | at once | — | After Start the page stays on its Console tab (the kernel and vminitd), and marks the agent's tab when it is ready; false (the default): it switches to the agent's tab as soon as that has drawn its screen. |
| `ui.confirm_shutdown` | `true` | boolean | at once | — | Shut Down asks first (its dialog's "don't ask again" sets this to false). Reset and Remove always ask with a box to tick. |
| `ui.explain_tab_close` | `true` | boolean | at once | — | Closing an agent's tab returns to the sandbox's Home, which says the agent is still running and that End stops it (its "Don't say this again" sets this to false). false: Home does not say it. |
| `ui.nav_thumbnails` | `true` | boolean | at once | — | The sidebar's pictures. Hovering a session shows a screen icon; resting on it for half a second shows the session's live picture (moving to another session then shows its picture at once). An unfolded workspace that a space file made shows a small picture of it, drawn from its file and its live state. false: no icon and no picture (Home and a workspace's page still show theirs). |
| `ui.split_default` | `shell` | shell \| watch \| attach \| dialog | at once | — | What a terminal's Split opens: shell (a new shell session), watch (a read-only view of the left terminal's session), attach (a second, shared view of it), dialog (choose each time). |
| `ui.terminals` | `true` | boolean | at once | — | Terminals in the browser. false: the UI opens none and refuses a terminal ticket (Terminal.app still works). |
| `ui.terminal_title` | `{sandbox} · {session} · {time}` | a title with {sandbox} {session} {image} {time} {phase} ("" = leave the title alone) | at once | — | The title doz attach gives your terminal (window or tab) while attached, and a doz ui terminal's tab: {sandbox} {session} {image} {time} (this Mac's, HH:MM, refreshed each minute) {phase}. The terminal's own title comes back when you detach (where the terminal keeps a title stack: iTerm2, Ghostty, kitty, xterm). While doz sets it, a session's own title is not shown; "" leaves the title to the session. |
| `ui.terminal_font_size` | `13` | integer 9–32 | at once | — | The browser terminal's font size, in points (a terminal opened from now on). |
| `ui.theme` | `auto` | auto \| light \| dark | at once | — | The UI's colours: auto follows macOS. |
| `ui.density` | `comfortable` | comfortable \| compact | at once | — | The UI's spacing: comfortable, or compact — tighter rows, tabs, controls and page margins; the text stays the same size. |
| `ui.notifications` | `cards` | cards \| pills \| bell | at once | — | Where the UI shows its notifications, in its top right corner: cards (a bell, and a column hanging below it, each with its full text and buttons and, for a success, a countdown that waits while the pointer is on any card), pills (one line each along the top, the newest at the right; click one for the rest), or bell (a count; the newest shows beside it for a few seconds; click for the list). Successes go by themselves; a failure stays until you close it. The Notifications page lists every one this tab showed. |
| `ui.details_open` | `true` | boolean | at once | — | A sandbox's page shows its details panel (restore points, network, keys) beside the terminals; false: collapsed. |
| `ui.allow_secret_entry` | `true` | boolean | at once | — | The web UI takes an Anthropic API key or a Claude setup token in a masked field — an account (the setup wizard, Accounts & keys: stored exactly as doz account add stores it, the login keychain) or a sandbox's own key (its page: exactly as doz key set does, held by the daemon) — sent once, in a request body. false: the pages show the command instead. The UI can turn this off, never on. |
| `ui.open_browser` | `auto` | auto \| always \| never | next command | — | When doz ui opens a browser tab: auto (only when no page of this store's UI is open — an open page reconnects by itself instead), always (every start), never (it prints the address; doz ui link opens a page). --open and --no-open override it. |
| `ui.port` | `0` | integer 0–65535 | ui-restart | `$DOZ_UI_PORT`, `--port N` | The ONE port the dashboard (doz ui) listens on — this Mac's browser at http://127.0.0.1:<port>, and with ui.lan your other browsers at http://<this Mac>.local:<port>. 0 = automatic: without ui.lan, the port this store's last doz ui had when it is free (else one the system picks, and doz ui says so); with ui.lan, serve.port (7443), which never moves. Or a fixed port 1024–65535 (doz ui refuses to start, naming the program, when another holds it). An installed dashboard app belongs to one port: keep it fixed for one. |
| `ui.lan` | `false` | boolean | ui-restart | `$DOZ_UI_LAN`, `doz ui --lan \| --no-lan` | Also serve the dashboard to the other browsers of your network (every network interface of this Mac and Tailscale, never a sandbox's network) on the same port: each gets in once with an invite (doz ui share). false (the default): this Mac only. Where it listens and your reverse proxy: the serve.* settings. |
| `ui.grid_live_tiles` | `12` | integer 1–12 | at once | — | No longer used — every session picture is live (painted from its screen, no terminal per picture). Kept so that an older settings file still reads without a warning. |
| `ui.grid_tile_size` | `medium` | small \| medium \| large | at once | — | All sessions: the size of a tile. |
| `ui.grid_refresh_ms` | `500` | integer 200–10000 | at once | — | How often the session pictures (All sessions, All sandboxes, a sandbox's Home) are brought up to date, in milliseconds. Only pictures on screen are asked for, only while the browser tab is shown, and a screen that did not change costs almost nothing. Lower looks livelier and costs more. |
| `ui.batch_concurrency` | `3` | integer 1–8 | at once | — | How many starts, wakes, resumes, sleeps, hibernations and shut-downs the dashboard runs at once; the others wait their turn, shown as queued with a Cancel. One you start on a single sandbox (or by typing in its terminal) goes ahead of those started for many at once. A pause, and a resume from a pause, never wait. A change applies as soon as one ends. |
| `ui.progress` | `animated` | animated \| plain | at once | `$DOZ_PROGRESS`, `--progress auto\|plain` | How a start, wake or bake shows its progress — in the web UI's boot view and in the CLI on a terminal: animated (a spinner on the step under way, download bars, the output's last lines) or plain (one line per step, and a summary line per download). Not a terminal, --json or NO_COLOR: always plain. |
| `ui.color` | `auto` | auto \| always \| never | at once | `$DOZ_COLOR`, `--color auto\|always\|never, --no-color` | Colour in the CLI's output: auto (on a terminal, unless NO_COLOR is set, TERM is dumb, or with --json or -q), always (even into a pipe or a file), never (plain text; the layout and the symbols stay the same). The dashboard has its own theme (ui.theme). |

### `[serve]`

| key | default | values | applies | overridden by | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `serve.port` | `7443` | integer 1024–65535 | ui-restart | `$DOZ_SERVE_PORT`, `doz ui --lan --port N` | The dashboard's port with ui.lan while ui.port is 0 (automatic) — an earlier name for it: ui.port, when set, wins. It stays the same (devices, an installed app and a bookmark belong to it): when another program holds it, doz ui refuses and names it. |
| `serve.bind` | `lan` | lan \| loopback \| the Mac's addresses, comma-separated | ui-restart | `$DOZ_SERVE_BIND`, `doz ui --lan --bind lan\|loopback\|ADDRESSES` | Where the dashboard listens for your other browsers with ui.lan: lan (every network interface of this Mac and Tailscale — never a sandbox's network), loopback (127.0.0.1 and ::1 only: for a reverse proxy on this Mac), or this Mac's own addresses separated by commas (for a reverse proxy elsewhere on your network). This Mac's own browser is served at 127.0.0.1 in every case. |
| `serve.public_origins` | `""` | origins like https://doz.home.example, comma-separated ("" = none) | ui-restart | — | The addresses your reverse proxy serves the dashboard at, like https://doz.home.example (comma-separated). A browser may use one only through a proxy listed in serve.trusted_proxies. Over https, keys and tokens may be typed in the dashboard; over plain http they never are (except in this Mac's own browser). |
| `serve.trusted_proxies` | `""` | addresses or networks like 127.0.0.1, 192.168.1.0/24, comma-separated ("" = none) | ui-restart | — | The reverse proxies whose X-Forwarded-Proto, X-Forwarded-Host and X-Forwarded-For the dashboard believes — their addresses or networks, comma-separated (a proxy on this Mac: 127.0.0.1, ::1). From anyone else those headers are ignored. |
| `serve.mac_sessions` | `off` | off \| watch \| interactive | at once | — | With ui.lan, what your other browsers may do with the sessions on this Mac (doz run @mac — they run as you, an unfenced one with your files, Keychain and network): off (they do not see them), watch (list them and watch their screens, read-only) or interactive (also type into them, end and restart them). This Mac's own browser always has them. |
| `serve.chat` | `off` | off \| read \| write | at once | — | With ui.lan, what your other browsers may do with chat: off (they do not see it), read (read the rooms, with nothing they can send or change) or write (also post, react, edit, delete, reveal direct messages and attach files). A browser that may write acts as you in chat, the verified human: your agents take its words as yours. Each thing it sends is a line in the dashboard's audit log (never what it said). This Mac's own browser always has chat. |
| `serve.advertise` | `true` | boolean | ui-restart | — | With ui.lan, announce the dashboard on your network with Bonjour ("Dozable on <this Mac>", http://<this Mac>.local:<port>), so other Macs and phones can find it. |

### `[mac]`

| key | default | values | applies | overridden by | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `mac.fence` | `on` | off \| on | next session | `$DOZ_MAC_FENCE`, `doz run @mac --fenced \| --unfenced` | Whether a new session on this Mac (doz run @mac) runs fenced: held to its folder, its own temp and caches, your Keychain, secrets and other folders closed, its network only through Dozable's proxy (on, the default), or with no isolation at all (off). doz run @mac --fenced or --unfenced decides for one session; a session keeps its mode when it is restarted. |
| `mac.keychain` | `off` | off \| on | next session | `doz run @mac --keychain` | Whether a fenced session on this Mac may use your Keychain (signing, notarisation — and so, reading your saved logins). doz run @mac --keychain opens it for one session. |
| `mac.fence_read` | `""` | paths relative to your home, comma-separated, like "notes, src/shared" ("" = none) | next session | — | Folders or files in your home a fenced session on this Mac may read (never write), relative to your home and separated by commas, like notes, src/shared. Your secrets (~/.ssh, ~/.config, ~/Library) stay closed. |
| `mac.permissions` | `standard` | standard \| locked \| open | next session | `doz run @mac --permissions` | What a fenced session on this Mac may reach through Dozable's proxy: standard (its AI model, its own updates, GitHub, error reports and the Node, Python, Go, Rust and Swift package registries), locked (its AI model only — and no certificate checks on its behalf) or open (any site). This Mac's own addresses are never reachable. doz run @mac --permissions decides for one session; doz net allow\|deny @mac --session S changes a running one. |
| `mac.agent_config` | `private` | private \| shared | next session | `doz run @mac --agent-config` | A fenced agent's settings folder on this Mac: private (its own; your instructions and skills read-only) or shared (your own ~/.claude: less isolated). |
| `mac.account` | `mac` | mac \| none | next session | `doz run @mac --account` | The Claude login a fenced Claude Code gets through Dozable's proxy: mac (this Mac's login) or none. --account NAME picks an account. |
| `mac.agent_prompt` | `fenced` | fenced \| always \| off | next session | — | Tell Claude Code on this Mac where it runs (a facts block in its prompt): fenced sessions, always, or off. |
| `mac.open_url` | `on` | on \| off | next session | `doz run @mac --open-url` | A fenced session may open web pages in your browser, each announced (on, off). |
| `mac.open_files` | `on` | on \| off | next session | `doz run @mac --open-files` | A fenced session may open documents of its folder in your apps, each announced (on, off). |
| `mac.clipboard` | `write` | write \| off | next session | `doz run @mac --clipboard` | A fenced session may put text on your clipboard, never read it; each copy announced (write, off). |
| `mac.fence_loopback_listen` | `off` | off \| on | next session | — | Whether a fenced session on this Mac may listen on ANY port (a dev server, a test server on a free port), not only its --local-port ones (on, off). macOS's sandbox cannot keep such a server to this Mac's loopback: one that listens on every address is reachable from your network too (your firewall decides). The program still cannot connect to its own server from inside (its only way out is Dozable's proxy) — use --local-port N for that. From the next session (or restart). |

### `[network]`

| key | default | values | applies | overridden by | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `network.host_ports_live` | `true` | boolean | next command | — | Whether doz net allow NAME host:PORT may open a port of this Mac to a sandbox or a fenced session while it runs (true), or this Mac's ports are fixed when it starts — doz create/run --host-port PORT (false). Taking a port away (doz net deny NAME host:PORT) always works. |
| `network.placeholders_plain_http` | `true` | boolean | next session | — | Whether a secret given with --secret may travel over plain HTTP — only ever to this Mac's ports (host.dozable.internal) and Tailscale addresses (100.64.0.0/10), never elsewhere. |

### `[chat]`

| key | default | values | applies | overridden by | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `chat.enabled` | `false` | boolean | at once | — | Run the chat server: the doz daemon keeps it running on this Mac (127.0.0.1 only) while this is on. Turn it on and off with doz chat on\|off; while it is on, the dashboard (this Mac's own browser) shows Chat. An early feature (doz chat --help). |
| `chat.page_port` | `8790` | integer 1024–65535 | at once | — | The chat server's HTTP port on 127.0.0.1: agents call /agent/… on it with their own token. Nothing on it acts as you. When it changes, the daemon restarts the chat server within a few seconds. |
| `chat.line_port` | `8791` | integer 1024–65535 | at once | — | The chat server's line port on 127.0.0.1 (one JSON message per line). Every caller needs a token. When it changes, the daemon restarts the chat server within a few seconds. |
| `chat.remote_listen` | `""` | Tailscale addresses like 100.100.1.2, comma-separated, each one exactly ("" = none) | at once | — | This Mac's own Tailscale addresses (100.64.0.0/10) on which the chat server also listens, both ports, for agents on other machines. Only agents, each with its own token; never you. Plain HTTP: Tailscale encrypts it; any other address is refused. |
| `chat.remote_agents` | `""` | Tailscale addresses like 100.100.1.2, comma-separated, each one exactly ("" = none) | at once | — | The Tailscale addresses of the other machines that may connect to the chat server (each exactly; no range). Each is always an agent: it must send its token; it gets /agent/… and files with its token, never your page or /api. |
| `chat.refusal_reasons` | `false` | boolean | at once | — | Give a refused post its reason as an extra field (reason: space-down when the room's workspace is finished), beside the refusal the chat server always gives. Off by default: clients made for the reference never see it. |
| `chat.asks` | `true` | boolean | at once | — | Asks in chat: an agent may post a question that waits for a decision by you (or a participant you made a decider with doz chat set NAME --role decider). Off: an ask, /decide and /withdraw are refused, and open asks stay as they are until asks are on again. The chat server restarts to take it. |
| `chat.ask_max_open` | `1` | integer 1–20 | at once | — | How many open asks one participant may have in one room at once (1 to 20). The chat server restarts to take it. |
| `chat.ask_expiry_seconds` | `86400` | integer 60–604800 | at once | — | How long an ask stays open when it names no expiry of its own, in seconds (60 to 604800, a week); then its answer is decline. The chat server restarts to take it. |
| `chat.ask_cooldown_seconds` | `600` | integer -1–86400 | at once | — | How long after an ask is declined or expires its asker may not ask about the same thing again, in seconds (0 to 86400; -1 turns it off). The chat server restarts to take it. |

### `[daemon]`

| key | default | values | applies | overridden by | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `daemon.always_on` | `true` | boolean | at once | `$DOZ_DAEMON_ALWAYS_ON` | Keep the doz daemon running when nothing runs, so sessions and sandboxes are answered at once (default on). While this is on, daemon.idle_timeout_minutes (the next setting) has no effect: the daemon does not switch itself off by idling. Off: the daemon exits once it has had nothing running for daemon.idle_timeout_minutes, and when that is 0 it never does. A new doz installed under it takes over by itself once nothing runs. A daemon started where the login keychain is locked (over ssh) is never kept running: it exits after 5 minutes with nothing running, whatever these two settings say. |
| `daemon.idle_timeout_minutes` | `5` | integer 0–10080 | after `doz daemon stop` | `$DOZ_DAEMON_IDLE`, `doz daemon start --idle-timeout` | Minutes with nothing running before the daemon exits (default 5). It is read only when daemon.always_on (the previous setting) is off; while always-on is on, the daemon keeps running and this has no effect. 0 disables the timeout: with always-on off, the daemon then never switches off by idling. |
| `daemon.login_item` | `ask` | ask \| on \| off | at once | — | Start the doz daemon when you log in, from your desktop session: one login item in ~/Library/LaunchAgents, removed by off and by doz uninstall. ask: not installed; doz offers it once. Set on this Mac (doz daemon login-item on\|off), never from the dashboard. |
| `daemon.screen_capture_minutes` | `5` | integer 0–1440 | after `doz daemon stop` | `$DOZ_SCREEN_CAPTURE` | Every this many minutes, save the screen of each running sandbox's sessions that printed something since (what a sleep or hibernation falls back on); 0 = only when it pauses, sleeps or hibernates. |
| `daemon.boot_logs_kept` | `5` | integer 1–50 | next boot | `$DOZ_BOOT_LOGS` | How many boots of each sandbox to keep (its steps and kernel console — the web UI's Boot log, doz console --boot N); the oldest goes. |
| `daemon.mac_name` | `this Mac` | a name of 1–63 letters, digits, spaces or hyphens | at once | `$DOZ_MAC_NAME` | The name this Mac goes by in its history and in a space's state, e.g. "studio". It is shown, never looked up on the network. |
| `daemon.keepalive` | `false` | boolean | a store that hasn't chosen | — | When a Mac login expires, while a sandbox or fenced session uses it and no unfenced Claude Code runs, the daemon runs the Mac's claude once to renew it (doz account keepalive always: also with nothing using it). |

| `timeline.sample_seconds` | `60` | integer 0–3600 | at once | `$DOZ_TIMELINE_SAMPLE_SECONDS` | How often, in seconds, each running sandbox's CPU, memory and disk use are kept for its history (10–3600); 0 = never. Read from this Mac, never inside the sandbox. |

| `timeline.runs` | `kept/kept/kept/kept` | days EVENTS/1M/1H/1D, each a number of days or kept, like 30/30/365/kept | at once | — | Days the history keeps workspace runs and space frames: single events, then counts by minute, hour and day (kept = until you delete it). A run's frames are its record, kept as the run folder is. |
| `timeline.chat` | `30/30/365/kept` | days EVENTS/1M/1H/1D, each a number of days or kept, like 30/30/365/kept | at once | — | Days the history keeps chat times and ask outcomes: single events, then counts by minute, hour and day (kept = until you delete it). |
| `timeline.daemon_events` | `7/30/365/kept` | days EVENTS/1M/1H/1D, each a number of days or kept, like 30/30/365/kept | at once | — | Days the history keeps the daemon's event stream: single events, then counts by minute, hour and day (kept = until you delete it). |

| `timeline.resources` | `7/7/365/kept` | days EVENTS/1M/1H/1D, each a number of days or kept, like 30/30/365/kept | at once | — | Days the history keeps cpu, memory and disk samples: single events, then counts by minute, hour and day (kept = until you delete it). |
| `timeline.keys` | `30/30/365/kept` | days EVENTS/1M/1H/1D, each a number of days or kept, like 30/30/365/kept | at once | — | Days the history keeps key and proxy use: single events, then counts by minute, hour and day (kept = until you delete it). |

### `[defaults]`

| key | default | values | applies | overridden by | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `defaults.cpus` | `2` | integer 1–64 | new sandboxes | `doz create --cpus` | CPUs of a new sandbox. |
| `defaults.memory_mib` | `2048` | integer 256–262144 | new sandboxes | `doz create --memory` | Memory (MiB) of a new sandbox whose image has no agent (a base alone: python, go). A recipe's sandboxes have their recipe's own (doz config show --agent ID), the lab its own (images.lab). |
| `defaults.network` | `agent` | agent \| bake \| locked \| open \| nat \| none | new sandboxes | `doz create --network` | The network of a new sandbox whose image has no agent: agent, bake, locked, open (proxied presets), nat or none. |
| `defaults.nat_subnet` | `""` | IPv4 subnet, a.b.c.d/nn ("" = a free one) | new sandboxes | `$DOZ_SUBNET`, `doz create --subnet` | The vmnet subnet of a new --network nat sandbox. |
| `defaults.image` | `lab` | lab \| claude-code \| pi \| codex, or an agent or tool's id (doz try lists them) | new sandboxes | `doz create --image` | The image of a new sandbox when none is named (doz up NAME, doz init, the UI's New sandbox). doz onboard writes the one you chose. |
| `defaults.base` | `node` | node \| python \| go \| rust \| java \| ruby \| dotnet \| debian \| ubuntu \| alpine | new sandboxes | `doz try --base` | The base image of this store: every tool you try (Quick try, doz try, the setup's first sandbox) is added to it as a layer when no base is named, so a second tool downloads nothing more. doz onboard sets it. New sandbox and doz_project.yaml keep a tool's own default base unless you choose one. |
| `defaults.projects_dir` | `~/doz-workspaces` | path ("" = automatic) | new sandboxes | — | The base folder of new sandboxes' folders: the web UI's New sandbox and Quick add, and doz new, share <projects_dir>/<sandbox name> (created when missing, like any folder given with --folder). doz create is isolated unless --folder; doz init uses the folder it runs in. In the web UI, Settings › Choose… sets it with the Mac's folder picker. |
| `defaults.account` | `mac` | mac \| none | a store that hasn't chosen | — | The Anthropic account of a store that has not chosen one: mac (this Mac's Claude Code login) or none. doz account default decides for a store once it has. |
| `defaults.permissions` | `standard` | standard \| locked \| open, or permissions like +web,-error-reports (doz net permissions) | new sandboxes | `doz create --allow / --network` | What a new sandbox's agent may do (its network, as permissions — doz net permissions): standard (talk to its AI model, update itself, install system packages and its base's language packages, use GitHub, send error reports), locked (its AI model only), open (everything, the web included), or standard with changes like +web,-error-reports. Stored by name: a Dozable update that adds a host to a permission reaches every sandbox that has it. |
| `defaults.github` | `off` | off \| read \| push | new sandboxes | `doz create --github off\|read\|push` | "Use GitHub as you" for new sandboxes: off, read (git and gh signed in as you on GitHub, read-only) or push (also push and make changes) — the Access step's choice (doz access set --github). A sandbox can differ: doz create --github, github: in doz_project.yaml, or its permissions later (doz net allow\|deny NAME github:as-you). Proxied sandboxes only. |

### `[agent]`

| key | default | values | applies | overridden by | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `agent.prompt` | `true` | boolean | next session | — | Tell the agent where it runs: a short facts block appended to its system prompt (the sandbox, its /workspace share, the network, credentials) and the doz skill, written at every session start. Your own template: agent-prompt.md beside this file. |
| `agent.history` | `keep` | keep \| agent-default | next start or wake | — | Conversation history in sandboxes. keep: Dozable asks each agent to keep its conversations — an agent that deletes old ones by itself (Claude Code after 30 days) is told not to, by a key in its own settings file, set only where you have not set one. agent-default: each agent follows its own rule (Dozable takes back only a key that still holds its own value). A value you set in the agent's own settings file is always kept. Each agent's recipe can choose its own (Recipes), and so can a project (history: in doz_project.yaml) or one sandbox (doz config set --sandbox NAME history VALUE). Set once in each sandbox when it next starts or wakes; doz config show --agent ID shows what each value does in that agent. |

### `[updates]`

| key | default | values | applies | overridden by | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `updates.mode` | `notify` | off \| notify \| auto | next command | `$DOZ_UPDATES` | Updates: notify (at most once a day, and when doz ui opens, look for a newer doz and say how to upgrade — one line on a terminal, a banner on the dashboard), auto (also install it: brew upgrade, or the signed download for a tarball install — only while no sandbox runs and no session is attached, else it notifies; then: restart to apply, doz daemon restart), or off (never look). Never a downgrade; a feed that does not verify is ignored. |
| `updates.channel` | `stable` | stable \| beta \| canary | next command | — | Which releases you are offered: stable, beta (beta and stable) or canary (every build, first). A Homebrew install's own formula (doz, doz-beta, doz-canary) decides while this is not set; doz upgrade --channel switches both. |

### `[telemetry]`

| key | default | values | applies | overridden by | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `telemetry.send_anonymous_usage_stats` | `true` | boolean | next command | `$DOZ_SEND_ANONYMOUS_USAGE_STATS`, `--no-send-anonymous-usage-stats / --send-anonymous-usage-stats` | Official builds send anonymous usage statistics: at most once a day, counts and ranges about how Dozable itself is used (commands by name, failures by exit code, which agents, bases and network presets new sandboxes use, setup sizes as ranges, start and wake times rounded to 50 ms, how long sandboxes ran and slept as ranges, which features were used, this Mac's macOS version, chip family, memory and cores as ranges) with a random install id — never a name, path, host, command argument, file or anything from inside a sandbox. false (or DO_NOT_TRACK=1, or --no-send-anonymous-usage-stats on one command) sends nothing and records nothing. doz telemetry show prints exactly what would be sent. Builds from the open-source repository send nothing whatever this says. |
