[Security model](https://dozable.com/docs/security-model.md).

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/the-workspace-view

# The folder view (`dozview`)

`/workspace` inside a sandbox is not your shared folder itself: it is a live view of it, served by a small
Dozable program, **`dozview`**. This page is what that program is, what it does, and how to look inside it.
When the folder holds a `.dozignore` or a `.dozreadonly`, the view also applies those rules — see
[Folder rules](https://dozable.com/docs/workspace-rules.md). Without either file it applies nothing: every file is there, as on
your Mac.

## Why every shared folder goes through it

A program working inside `/workspace` — an agent, a shell, a dev server — **keeps its folder when the
sandbox wakes from hibernation** (and after a daemon restart, which hibernates). The plain share cannot do
that: a hibernation disconnects it, and the sandbox has to connect it again on wake, so a program that was
inside it is left in a folder that no longer exists. Codex then fails every turn with
`invalid cwd: No such file or directory`; a shell says `No such file or directory` for `ls .`. The view is
never disconnected — it reconnects to your folder underneath — so nothing inside notices the wake.

**What it costs.** Most of the time nothing you would notice. The first look at many files after a start or
a wake is slower — measured on 2,000 small files:

| | through the view | the plain share |
|---|---|---|
| the first `find` of the tree after a start | about 0.19 s | about 0.02 s |
| `stat` of 1,000 files not looked at in the last second | about 0.1 s | about 0.02 s |
| reading every file | about 0.4 s | about 0.25 s |
| the same `find` again, or 8 programs reading at once | about the same | |

So a `git status` on a big repository, right after a start or a wake, takes noticeably longer the first
time; after that it is about as fast as before.

**Turning it off.** `doz config set folder.view off` (every sandbox), or for one sandbox
`doz create … --folder-view off`, `folder_view: off` in its `doz_project.yaml`, or
`doz config set --sandbox NAME folder.view off`. The folder is then shared directly — a little faster,
but a program working inside `/workspace` loses its folder at every wake from hibernation and has to be
restarted ([Restart session](https://dozable.com/docs/terminals-and-sessions.md#restarting-or-ending-a-session)). A folder with a
`.dozignore` or `.dozreadonly` always uses the view.

**When it takes effect.** At the sandbox's next start — never under programs that are running. A sandbox
that was already running when you upgraded (or turned the setting on) changes over at its next start, or at
its next wake from hibernation (whose wake would have cut its programs off anyway). Its first such wake is
still the old one; restart the session if a program complains.

**If the view cannot start**, the folder is shared directly instead (never an empty `/workspace`): the
start says so, and `doz doctor` warns "folder view" for that sandbox. `doz ls --json` reports how each
running sandbox's folder is served (`folderView`: `live`, `rules`, `direct`, `next-start` or
`fallback`).

## Who can write

Inside the sandbox, every file in `/workspace` appears to belong to the sandbox's own user — `agent` in
the agent images — and that user can change whatever your Mac account can change in the folder, files only
you may read included. Root can too. On your Mac, everything the sandbox writes belongs to you, as
before.

Any **other** user inside the sandbox (for example `node`, or `doz exec --user NAME`) can read the folder but
not write it through the view. With `folder.view` off the plain share lets every user in the sandbox
write, as your Mac account.

**Sandboxes started before Dozable 0.33.1** run an older view, under which the agent could not write
`/workspace` at all: "Permission denied", and git refused the repository ("detected dubious ownership").
Sleeping and waking such a sandbox keeps the old view (the wake says so); shut it down and start it again
(`doz shutdown NAME` then `doz start NAME`) and it gets the new one.

## What it does

- Your Mac folder reaches the sandbox as usual, but it is mounted privately at `/run/doz/raw/<id>`, inside
  a folder only root can enter.
- `dozview` presents that folder at `/workspace` (Linux FUSE — a program acting as a file system). Every
  file operation in `/workspace` goes through it, and it checks the path against the rules first:

  | the path is | what happens |
  |---|---|
  | in `.dozignore`, mode **lock** (the default) | listed as `----------`; every read, write, rename and listing is refused — "Permission denied", for root too |
  | in `.dozignore`, mode **hide** | not listed; "No such file or directory" |
  | in `.dozreadonly` | listed and readable; every change is refused (an ordinary user sees "Permission denied", root "Read-only file system") |
  | anything else | passed straight through to your Mac folder, both ways |

- **Always read-only to the agent's user**, whatever the rules say: `.dozignore` and `.dozreadonly` themselves (an
  agent cannot edit its own rules), and — unless your `.dozreadonly` says `!name` — `doz_project.yaml`,
  `doz_project.yml` and `.git/hooks`. Root in the VM can lift it (a mask, not the boundary); a fenced session on the Mac
  guards `.git/hooks` and `.git/config` with its fence instead.
- **Rules are read from the shared folder itself.** Edit `.dozignore` on the Mac and the sandbox follows
  within about a quarter of a second; `dozview` also drops anything the sandbox's kernel had cached about
  the affected names.
- **On a case-insensitive Mac volume** (every default one), matching ignores case and Unicode form, so
  `cat SECRET.ENV` does not read a locked `secret.env`. That only ever covers more than Docker would.

## Two processes

`ps` in the sandbox shows `dozview` twice. They are one daemon in two parts:

| process | job |
|---|---|
| the **supervisor** (the lower pid) | holds the connection to the kernel. If the worker dies — a crash, or someone killing it — it starts a new one within about 0.1 s and `/workspace` stays mounted. If the mount itself goes, it mounts a fresh view. |
| the **worker** | answers the file requests, on 6 threads, so a busy agent is not served one request at a time. |

A shell whose current folder is a *subfolder* of `/workspace` may need to `cd` again after a worker restart;
a request in flight at that moment is lost.

## Sleep, hibernate and wake

`dozview` is an ordinary process in the sandbox, so pause, sleep and hibernate keep it, with its rules.
After a hibernation the share underneath must be connected again: on wake, Dozable re-mounts the private
share and signals `dozview` to reconnect, in the same step. Three safeguards make that safe:

1. It never re-reads the rules over a broken connection — it keeps the last rules.
2. If a request finds the connection broken before the signal arrives, it repairs it itself and retries.
3. It never reconnects to anything that is not your shared folder — during the moment of the re-mount the
   path is an empty folder, and adopting it would show an empty `/workspace` with no rules.

A wake takes no measurably longer with the view than without.

## Cost

As above: looking at many files for the first time is slower than the plain share — a tree of 2,000 files
takes about 0.1–0.2 s more to walk the first time. Once looked at (for about a second), names are close to the
plain share's speed. With rules, hiding a big folder often makes a whole-tree walk faster than before.

## Looking inside

| to see | run |
|---|---|
| the rules, the mode and whether the view is running | `doz ignore show NAME` |
| which line decides a path | `doz ignore check NAME PATH` |
| the processes | `doz exec NAME -- ps` |
| the mode, case setting and owner Dozable gave it | `doz exec NAME -- sh -c 'cat /run/doz/view/*.conf'` |
| its log (rule reloads, reconnects, worker restarts, lines that did not parse) | `doz exec NAME -- sh -c 'tail /run/doz/view/*.log'` |

Its files are in `/run/doz/view/`: the `.conf` Dozable writes (the mode, whether matching ignores case, and the
user the files are shown as belonging to),
its `.state`, its `.pid` (the supervisor's) and its `.log`. The program is copied into the sandbox at
`/usr/local/lib/doz/bin/dozview` — it never runs from your shared folder.

## Not a security boundary

Root in the sandbox can stop `dozview`, or reach the private share directly. The view keeps an agent from
stumbling into files you listed; the virtual machine is the boundary. See [Security model](https://dozable.com/docs/security-model.md).

## About the program

A small static Linux program written in C, with no outside libraries — it speaks the kernel's FUSE protocol
itself rather than using the usual FUSE library (whose licence would complicate shipping it inside Dozable).
The copy Dozable ships is checked to rebuild byte for byte from its source.

See also: [Folder rules](https://dozable.com/docs/workspace-rules.md) · [Troubleshooting and FAQ](https://dozable.com/docs/troubleshooting-and-faq.md).

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/prompts-for-your-agent

# Prompts for your agent

Your Mac's own coding agent — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor — can install Dozable, set it up and run
sandboxes for you. This page gives you prompts to paste, in order: install, set up, brief it once, then
three things worth using sandboxes for. [Letting another agent drive Dozable](https://dozable.com/docs/letting-another-agent-drive.md)
explains the rules underneath (`--json`, exit codes, why destructive commands need `--yes`).

**Keep the decisions yours.** Every prompt below tells the agent to stop and ask before it chooses an
account, widens network permissions, or deletes anything. Your Mac's agent runs `doz` with *your*
permissions — treat it as you would at the keyboard.

## 1. Install

Paste:

> Install Dozable (the `doz` command) on this Mac with Homebrew, following
> https://github.com/dozable/dozable/blob/main/docs/manual/02-install-upgrade-uninstall.md.
> When it is installed, run `doz --version` and `doz doctor --json` and tell me what they say.

What it will run:

```sh
brew trust --tap dozable/tap
brew install dozable/tap/doz
doz --version
doz doctor --json
```

## 2. Set up

Onboarding checks the Mac, prepares the base image every tool is added to, adds keys, writes the settings and can
make a first sandbox. The choices are yours, so the prompt makes the agent ask:

> Set up Dozable with `doz onboard`. Before you run it, ask me which base image to prepare (Node.js is the
> default; `doz base ls` lists the others) and whether to make a first sandbox now (claude, pi, opencode or none).
> Then run it without questions, using my answers, and show me `doz onboard --status` when the base is ready. Do
> not change any other setting, and never ask me for a key in the chat — I add keys myself with `doz account add`.

What it will run (for example):

```sh
doz onboard --yes --base node --first none
doz onboard --status
```

Preparing the base the first time takes a few minutes (a download, once); each tool is added to it the first time
it is used.

## 3. Brief it once

Paste the briefing from [Letting another agent drive Dozable](https://dozable.com/docs/letting-another-agent-drive.md#the-briefing)
into your project's `CLAUDE.md` (or `AGENTS.md`). From then on, every session in that project knows how to
use `doz` safely, and the prompts below can stay short.

## Three use cases

### A. A risky change, done by an agent in a sandbox

A dependency upgrade, a big refactor, a migration: let a sandboxed agent do the work on your project folder
while your Mac's agent watches, with a restore point to fall back to.

> In a Dozable sandbox called `upgrade`, upgrade this project to the latest major version of our test
> framework and get the test suite passing. Take a restore point before you start. Let a Claude inside the
> sandbox do the work (run it detached) and check on it every few minutes. When the tests pass, show me
> the diff on my Mac and a summary of what changed. If the sandboxed agent is refused a website, tell me
> which and why — don't allow it yourself. Hibernate the sandbox at the end.

What it will typically run:

```sh
doz create upgrade --image claude-code --folder "$PWD" --json
doz point take upgrade before-upgrade
doz run upgrade --detach -- claude -p "Upgrade the test framework to its latest major version and make the tests pass"
doz sessions upgrade --screen claude
doz exec upgrade --json --timeout 1200 -- sh -c 'cd /workspace && npm test'
doz hibernate upgrade
```

The changes land in your folder as they are made (`/workspace` is your project), so you review them with
`git diff` — and `git checkout .` undoes them if you don't like them.

### B. Jail an untrusted agent

An agent you don't trust yet — a new agent CLI, an unfamiliar model, a tool someone sent you, or code that
runs on its own: run it in a sandbox that shares none of your folders, holds none of your logins, can't
reach the Mac's clipboard, browser or files, and reaches the internet only where you allow it.

> I want to try the agent <AGENT> but I don't trust it. Jail it in a Dozable sandbox called `jail`:
> **isolated** (no folder of mine shared), the lab image, network **locked**, no Claude account, no GitHub,
> no SSH agent, and the clipboard, browser and file bridges off. Take a restore point, then install the
> agent inside and start it detached on this task: <task>. Check on it every few minutes and tell me what
> it is doing. When it is refused a website, show me `doz net jail --json` and what it wanted — I decide
> what to allow, you never do. When I say so, copy out what it produced and delete the sandbox.

What it will typically run:

```sh
doz create jail --image lab --isolated --network locked --account none --github off --ssh-agent off \
  --clipboard off --browser-bridge off --open-files off --json
doz point take jail before-agent
doz exec jail --json --timeout 900 -- sh -c 'cd ~ && <install the agent>'
doz run jail --detach -- <the agent's command>
doz sessions jail --screen <session>
doz net jail --json
```

And what you run yourself, when you decide it may reach its model's API:

```sh
doz net allow jail site:api.example.com
```

What the jail gives you:

| it cannot | because |
|---|---|
| read or change your files | `--isolated`: `/workspace` is the sandbox's own folder |
| use your Claude login, GitHub or SSH keys | none are attached — and credentials never enter a sandbox anyway; the proxy holds them |
| touch the Mac's clipboard, open pages or open files | the three bridges are off |
| reach anything you did not allow | `locked`: every connection goes through the proxy and is refused unless allowed; each refusal is on record |
| leave a mess you can't undo | the restore point: `doz point revert jail before-agent --yes`; `doz rm jail --yes` removes everything |

Root inside the sandbox is still only root inside a virtual machine — that is the boundary, not the
agent's good behaviour. See [Security model](https://dozable.com/docs/security-model.md).

### C. Let an agent work on a project that holds secrets

Your project folder has an `.env`, credentials or customer data the sandboxed agent should never read.
[Folder rules](https://dozable.com/docs/workspace-rules.md) keep it out of them, without moving anything.

> Before we use a sandbox on this project, add a `.dozignore` at the project root that keeps the agent out
> of `.env*`, `secrets/` and `*.pem`, and a `.dozreadonly` that lets it read but not change `deploy/`.
> Show me what each path resolves to with `doz ignore check` before creating anything. Then create a
> sandbox called `feature` on this folder, confirm in the sandbox that `.env` is listed with no
> permissions and can't be read, and start a Claude in it on this task: <your task>.

What it will typically run:

```sh
printf '.env*\nsecrets/\n*.pem\n' > .dozignore
printf 'deploy/\n' > .dozreadonly
doz create feature --image claude-code --folder "$PWD" --json
doz ignore check feature .env secrets/api.key deploy/prod.yaml src/app.ts
doz exec feature --json -- sh -c 'ls -la /workspace; cat /workspace/.env'
doz run feature --detach -- claude -p "<your task>"
```

Locked files stay visible as `----------` so the agent knows they exist and leaves them alone (the
sandboxed agent is told so). The rules are a guard against accidents, not a security boundary — see
[The folder view](https://dozable.com/docs/the-workspace-view.md).

## When something goes wrong

| what happened | what to tell your agent |
|---|---|
| a `doz` command seems to hang | "Use `doz exec`, `doz run --detach` and `doz sessions --screen`, never an interactive `doz attach` or `doz up`." |
| exit code 6 (daemon unavailable) | "Run `doz doctor --json` and tell me what it says." |
| a site is refused | "Show me `doz net NAME --json` and the suggestion; I'll decide." |
| the sandbox is in a state you didn't expect | "Show me `doz ls --json` and `doz inspect NAME --json`." |

See also: [Letting another agent drive Dozable](https://dozable.com/docs/letting-another-agent-drive.md) ·
[Getting started](https://dozable.com/docs/getting-started.md) · [Troubleshooting and FAQ](https://dozable.com/docs/troubleshooting-and-faq.md).

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/sound

# Sound

> **Not in public releases yet.** The releases on Homebrew and GitHub do not include sound: `--sound` says so. This
> page describes a build that carries the sound kernel (`make release PUBLIC=0`).

A sandbox can have sound: programs in it play through your Mac's speakers and, if you want, record from its
microphone. It is a setting, `sandbox.audio`, off unless you choose it:

| value | what the sandbox gets |
|---|---|
| `off` (the default) | no sound device — exactly as every other sandbox |
| `speakers` | the Mac's speakers; its microphone records silence, and macOS is never asked about it |
| `on` | the Mac's speakers and its microphone, once macOS allows it |

## Make one

```sh
doz create a1 --image lab --sound on      # or --sound speakers; --audio is the same as --sound on
doz start a1
doz exec a1 -- doz-sound test
```

In the dashboard: **New sandbox › Bridges › Sound**. In a project file: `audio: on`. To give every new sandbox
sound: `doz config set sandbox.audio speakers`.

Sound is a device in the sandbox's virtual machine, so it is chosen when the sandbox is created. Afterwards a sandbox
can move between `speakers` and `on` (`doz config set --sandbox a1 sandbox.audio on`) — from its next start; a wake
keeps what it slept with — but not to or from `off`: for that, create a new sandbox.

A sandbox with sound boots its own Linux kernel: the same one every sandbox uses, with ALSA and the virtio sound
driver added. It ships with doz (never downloaded), and `doz doctor` says whether this doz carries it. It is
kata-containers' kernel 6.18.15-186 (kata 3.28.0: its config and patch, unchanged) with four options added —
`CONFIG_SOUND`, `CONFIG_SND`, `CONFIG_SND_VIRTIO`, `CONFIG_SND_PROC_FS` — and nothing else; its recipe, the complete config and the source offer are in Dozable's source (`Guest/sound-kernel/`)
and in a release's `licences/sound-kernel/`. It is built from source reproducibly — anyone can check it: `make
sound-kernel` builds it (twice, in a throwaway Ubuntu sandbox) and compares its sha256 with the one doz pins.

## Inside the sandbox

Dozable's managed tools ([Managed tools](https://dozable.com/docs/the-tools-layer.md)) sets a sandbox with sound up at every start and wake:
ALSA's tools (`aplay`, `arecord`), an `/etc/asound.conf` that makes the sound card ALSA's default (one program
at a time can play, and one can record — a second gets "Device or resource busy"), and `doz-sound`:

| command | does |
|---|---|
| `doz-sound info` | the sound card, its devices, the default, and the microphone (the Mac's, or why it is silent) |
| `doz-sound test` | plays a quiet tone (under a second), records 3 seconds, says the level, plays it back |
| `doz-sound rec FILE [SECONDS]` | records a WAV file (5 seconds unless you say) |
| `doz-sound play FILE` | plays a WAV file |
| `doz-sound tone FILE` | writes a quiet test tone (a WAV, under a second) to play |

Any program that uses ALSA's default device works the same way.

## The microphone and macOS

macOS asks about the microphone for the **app that started doz** — Terminal, iTerm, your editor — not for doz
itself. It asks once; after that its answer stands until you change it in System Settings › Privacy & Security ›
Microphone.

**A sandbox records from the Mac's microphone only if macOS allowed it before the sandbox started.** The microphone
is part of the sandbox's virtual machine, fixed when it starts and kept through Pause, Sleep and Hibernate (a wake
keeps the microphone it went to sleep with). Otherwise — not asked yet, denied, or the question left unanswered — the
sandbox records **silence**, and `doz-sound` says why.

When doz asks is a setting, `sandbox.microphone_ask`:

| value | doz asks macOS | then |
|---|---|---|
| `first_recording` (the default) | when a program in a sandbox with `on` first records | that recording is silent: once you allow it, **Shut Down and Start** the sandbox — doz says so in the sandbox's terminals and on the dashboard |
| `first_start` | when a sandbox with `on` starts | the start waits for your answer (at most a minute), so the first recording already has the microphone |

```sh
doz config set sandbox.microphone_ask first_start
```

With `first_recording`, a sandbox whose sound is `on` starts with a silent microphone while macOS has no answer, and
doz watches it for a program that records (a recording stream of its sound card that runs — `arecord`, `doz-sound`,
any ALSA program). The first one makes doz ask: macOS shows its question ("Terminal would like to access the
microphone"), and doz says in the sandbox's terminals and on the dashboard that this recording is silent and that,
once you allow it, Shut Down and Start makes the sandbox record from the Mac. Nothing is asked again once macOS has
answered.

`doz doctor` says macOS's answer, which app it is for and when doz asks; the sandbox's Home in the dashboard says what
its microphone is.

Because nothing records from the Mac's microphone until macOS has said yes, pausing, sleeping or hibernating a
sandbox is always safe, whatever macOS's answer.

## Across pause, sleep and hibernation

Sound keeps going across Pause, Sleep and Hibernate, and after the daemon restarted: a program that was playing or
recording when the sandbox went to sleep carries on when it wakes, with nothing to restart.

## Known limitations

- A recording from the Mac's microphone can start with a short stretch of silence and contain a few single-sample
  ticks (`doz-sound` leaves them out of its level).
- Sound takes a moment to reach the speakers: with the standard tools' defaults, about three quarters of a second from
  playing a sound to hearing it back through the microphone; programs that use small buffers are much quicker.
- A sandbox with sound wakes from hibernation a little more slowly (about 0.07 s).
- One player and one recorder at a time.
- Codex's voice mode does not work in a sandbox yet: it sends its sound over the network as UDP (WebRTC), which a
  proxied sandbox does not carry.

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/codex

# Codex

OpenAI's **Codex** runs in a Dozable sandbox the way Claude Code does: ready to work, without approval
prompts (the VM and its network are the boundary), told where it runs, and with its credential kept on
your Mac — it never enters the sandbox. It can use **this Mac's own Codex login** (`mac` — nothing to
add: your ChatGPT plan, through Codex's own sign-in) or an **OpenAI API key**.

> **Public releases** include those two. Dozable's *own* ChatGPT sign-in (`doz account add NAME --chatgpt`,
> described further down) is only in builds from source: a public release says so and keeps an account an
> earlier build made, unused — use `mac` or a key instead.

## Quick start

If Codex is already signed in on this Mac (`codex login`, or the Codex app), there is nothing to add:

```sh
doz new --image codex                 # uses this Mac's Codex login (the account mac) — the default while it is signed in
```

Otherwise, sign in to Codex on this Mac (`codex login` — Dozable then reads that login, read-only), or use a key:

```sh
doz account add openai --openai-key   # it asks for the key, not echoed
doz account default openai            # Codex sandboxes that follow the default use it
doz new --image codex                 # a Codex sandbox, attached — Codex is running
```

In the dashboard: **New sandbox**, choose **Codex** as the agent (on any base). The account chooser
offers only OpenAI accounts; an OpenAI key can be typed in the masked field.

## The image

- `codex` is Node.js · Codex; any other base is `<base>-codex` (`python-codex`, `go-codex`,
  `alpine-codex`, or your Dockerfile's): `doz create my-app --agent codex --base python`.
- Codex is installed from its official linux-arm64 build (a single static program, the same on Debian
  and Alpine), checked against the integrity the npm registry publishes. `recipes.openai.codex.version` is
  `latest` (resolved when its image is baked) or an exact version like `0.160.1`.
- Codex's own state (its sessions, history and settings) is `~/.codex`, on the state disk: it survives
  shutdown and reset.

## How it starts

`codex` in a sandbox is Dozable's launcher, which:

- runs Codex with **approvals and Codex's own Linux sandbox off**
  (`--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`): the VM, the network permissions and the absent
  credentials are the boundary. Set `recipes.openai.codex.approvals` to `ask` (or run
  `doz run NAME -e DOZ_CODEX_PERMISSIONS=ask -- codex`) to keep Codex's own approvals; `codex` run as
  root always keeps them;
- marks the working folder trusted in `~/.codex/config.toml` (only when that folder has no entry
  there — your own choice is kept), so there is no trust screen;
- turns off Codex's update check (the image decides its version);
- gives Codex the sandbox's **facts** as its developer instructions, and the **`doz` skill** in
  `~/.agents/skills/doz/SKILL.md` ([Agents and accounts](https://dozable.com/docs/agents-and-accounts.md)). Your
  `AGENTS.md` files are never touched.

`codex exec`, `codex resume` and `codex fork` get the same; `codex login`, `codex mcp` and the other
subcommands run as they are.

## This Mac's Codex login (`mac`)

The least setup: a Codex sandbox uses the login of the Codex already signed in on this Mac, as Claude
Code sandboxes use the Mac's Claude login.

- **Dozable only reads it.** From `$CODEX_HOME/auth.json` (else `~/.codex/auth.json`) it takes the
  **access token** and the few account details Codex reads (plan, email, account id). It never uses or
  keeps the refresh token and never writes anything there: your Mac's Codex stays the one that renews
  the login. Nothing is copied into the sandbox — it gets placeholders, and the proxy puts the token in
  on the way to `chatgpt.com`.
- **It is the default** for Codex sandboxes while this Mac's Codex is signed in (`doz account ls` shows
  `mac` · `codex-mac` with its plan, email and expiry). Choose another per sandbox
  (`doz account use NAME ACCOUNT`) or for all (`doz account default NAME`); `doz account default mac --codex`
  makes it the default explicitly.
- **It must stay fresh.** Access tokens last about an hour; your Mac's Codex renews one when it is within
  5 minutes of expiry, whenever it runs — the Codex app's background server checks every few minutes, so
  while the app (or any `codex` session) runs, sandboxes stay signed in. A renewal reaches open sandboxes
  at their next request. With nothing running it expires, and Codex in a sandbox says: "your Mac's Codex
  login has expired — run codex on the Mac, or turn on the keep-alive". Never another account.
- **Keep-alive** (off by default): `doz config set --agent codex keep_alive true`. When the token is about to
  expire and a sandbox used it in the last 15 minutes, Dozable runs this Mac's own `codex doctor` once —
  no model call — which renews the login the way Codex itself does.
- **Not supported yet:** a Codex that keeps its login in the keyring (`cli_auth_credentials_store =
  "keyring"`) — use `doz account add NAME --chatgpt` instead; and a Mac Codex signed in with an API key
  — add the key as an account (`--openai-key`). `doz doctor` says which.

## Your ChatGPT plan, without the token in the sandbox (builds from source)

`doz account add NAME --chatgpt` signs **Dozable** in to ChatGPT — the same browser sign-in `codex login`
does, on your Mac. It is Dozable's own sign-in, separate from your Mac's: Dozable never reads or changes
your Mac's `~/.codex`. What must last is kept in your login keychain (`doz-chatgpt:NAME`): the refresh token
and the few account details Codex reads. The short-lived access token is kept only in Dozable's memory (a new
Dozable daemon renews it on first use). `doz account ls` shows the account's plan and email, never a token.

- **In the sandbox**, Codex's `~/.codex/auth.json` holds only **placeholders** (`doz_cred_…`) where the
  tokens go, written at every session start. The id_token's details Codex reads (your plan, account id)
  are there; its signature is not — nothing in the VM can be used anywhere else.
- **On the way out**, Dozable's proxy on your Mac puts the real access token into Codex's requests to
  `chatgpt.com` — only there.
- **Renewal happens on your Mac.** OpenAI's tokens last about an hour; Dozable renews them with the
  refresh token only it holds, and keeps the new one in the keychain. When Codex asks to renew (its
  request to `auth.openai.com`), the proxy answers it itself — the request never leaves your Mac.
- **No silent fallback.** If the sign-in has ended (or you took the account away), Codex's requests
  get Dozable's message saying what to do — `doz account add NAME --chatgpt --force` signs in again —
  never another account or a key.

An OpenAI API key works the same way on `api.openai.com`: the sandbox's `OPENAI_API_KEY` and
`auth.json` hold a placeholder; the proxy puts the key in.

## Permissions

A Codex sandbox has **Talk to OpenAI** (`model:openai`: `chatgpt.com`, `api.openai.com`, and
`ab.chatgpt.com`, Codex's metrics) on in every preset, and it can't be switched off there — Codex
couldn't work. Claude Code and pi sandboxes never get it. `auth.openai.com` itself is not allowed:
only Codex's renewal of Dozable's sign-in is answered there, by the proxy.

```sh
doz net my-app                 # the permissions, "Talk to OpenAI" among them
doz net allow my-app web       # e.g. let Codex browse the web
```

## Accounts

```sh
doz account add chatgpt --chatgpt          # sign in with ChatGPT (opens the browser on this Mac)
doz account add chatgpt --chatgpt --force  # sign in again (after the sign-in ended)
doz account add openai --openai-key        # an OpenAI API key (prompt or stdin)
doz account default chatgpt                # the default OpenAI account (Codex sandboxes that follow it)
doz account use my-app openai              # this sandbox uses the key (open sessions switch on their next request)
doz account verify chatgpt                 # renews the sign-in when it is due, and says how it stands
doz account rm chatgpt                     # also deletes its keychain item
```

The store has two defaults: the Anthropic one (`mac` out of the box) for Claude Code and pi, and the
OpenAI one (none until you choose) for Codex. `doz onboard`'s Models & keys step shows whether Codex
is signed in on this Mac, and takes an `openai` key or (official builds) `chatgpt` — or `doz onboard
--openai-account mac|chatgpt|openai-key|later`.

## Settings

| key | default | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `recipes.openai.codex.version` | `latest` | The Codex version its image is baked with. |
| `recipes.openai.codex.approvals` | `skip` | Codex's own approvals and sandbox in a sandbox: `skip` or `ask`. |
| `recipes.openai.codex.keep_alive` | `false` | Renew this Mac's Codex login near expiry (`codex doctor`) while a sandbox uses it. |
| `recipes.openai.codex.memory_mib` · `recipes.openai.codex.network` | 2048 · `agent` | A new Codex sandbox's memory and network. |

## Troubleshooting

| symptom | what to do |
|---|---|
| Codex says Dozable's sign-in has ended | `doz account add NAME --chatgpt --force` on your Mac; open sessions recover by themselves. |
| "your Mac's Codex login has expired" | Run `codex` on the Mac (any prompt), or `doz config set --agent codex keep_alive true`. |
| "Codex needs an OpenAI account" when creating | `doz account add chatgpt --chatgpt` (or `--openai-key`), then `doz account default NAME` or `--account NAME`. |
| The sign-in's port is in use | Another sign-in (`codex login` on your Mac) is waiting — finish or cancel it, then try again. |
| Codex asks for approval for every command | `recipes.openai.codex.approvals` is `ask`, or Codex runs as root. |
| Codex can't reach a site | It's the network permissions: `doz net NAME` shows them; ask for the one it needs. |

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/doz-serve

# The dashboard on your other computers, tablets and phones (`doz ui --lan`)

`doz ui` is one dashboard. Without its LAN option it listens on `127.0.0.1` and nothing but this Mac can reach it.
With the LAN option the SAME dashboard, on the same port, also serves the other browsers of your home network — the
laptop on the couch, a second Mac, the iPad, a phone — at `http://<this Mac>.local:7443`.

```bash
doz ui --lan                          # this run
doz config set ui.lan true            # every run (then: doz ui restart, if one is running)
```

Nothing listens beyond this Mac until you turn it on, and it is only ever turned on here, on the Mac (`ui.lan` cannot
be changed from a browser). It runs until you press Ctrl-C (or run `doz ui stop` in another terminal). To keep it
running without a terminal open, start it in the background:

```bash
doz ui --lan --detach        # or -d: prints where it listens and an invite, then returns
doz ui status                # pid, since when, the addresses, the version, its log
doz ui stop
```

A detached `doz ui` belongs to no terminal — closing the terminal does not stop it; its output goes to
`<store>/ui.log`.

The earlier name of `doz ui --lan`, doz serve, still works for one release (it says so), and so do its subcommands
(share, devices, revoke, rename, status, log and stop).

## This Mac's browser and the others

**This Mac's browser** is signed in by the link `doz ui` opens (or `doz ui link`), at `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`, as
without the LAN option — and it can do everything, including typing a key and the windows on the Mac's screen (the
folder pickers, Open in Terminal).

**Every other browser** gets in once, with an **invite**, and then stays in until you remove it. An invite is three
things at once — use whichever suits the device:

- a **QR code** — point a phone's or tablet's camera at it;
- a short **access code** like `Y14G-99K3` — type it on the dashboard's sign-in page;
- a **link** — open it in the other browser.

Whichever is used first lets ONE browser in, within five minutes; the other two stop working. `doz ui --lan` prints an
invite when it starts (on a terminal) — its link by name (`http://<this Mac>.local:7443/…`) and by each of the Mac's
addresses (`http://192.168.1.20:7443/…`): `.local` names do not resolve the same everywhere, so use an address if the
name does not answer. For another invite:

```bash
doz ui share
```

or, on any browser that is already in (this Mac's too): **Devices › Add another browser**.

Which kind of browser a request comes from is decided for each request: only a connection from this Mac itself, to
`127.0.0.1:<port>` exactly, with no reverse proxy in between, is this Mac's browser. The same Mac reaching the
dashboard by `<this Mac>.local` or `localhost` is treated like any other browser (it needs an invite).

A browser that opens the dashboard without an invite sees the sign-in page and nothing else — no sandbox, no name, no
data. A request the dashboard refuses always gets an answer saying why — only a sandbox's connection is dropped
without one.

## What another browser can do

Everything the Mac's browser does — watch and drive sandboxes, open terminals in the browser, create sandboxes,
change their network, settings, images and resources — with two exceptions:

- **No keys or tokens over plain HTTP.** Adding an account's API key or setup token, a sandbox's own key or a GitHub
  token would send it across your network unencrypted, so the dashboard does not offer the field there and refuses
  it. Add it on the Mac (`doz account add NAME --api-key`, or this Mac's own browser), or reach the dashboard over
  HTTPS through your reverse proxy (below) — there it is allowed.
- **Nothing that opens a window on the Mac's screen**: the Mac's folder and file pickers, **Open in Terminal**, **Open folder** and the Files tab's Open items are
  not shown on another computer. Type the folder's path instead, and use the browser's own terminals.

**Chat** is not shared with another browser unless you say so on the Mac: `serve.chat` is `off` (they do not see it),
`read` (they read the rooms, with nothing they can send or change) or `write` (they also post, react, edit, delete,
reveal and attach). A browser that may write acts as you in chat — the verified human whose words your agents act on —
and each thing it sends is a line in `doz ui log` (never what it said). See [Chat](https://dozable.com/docs/chat.md#chat-on-your-other-browsers-servechat).

**Workspaces and Agents / Bots** are shown to another browser as to the Mac's own, except what is on this Mac's sessions:
while `serve.mac_sessions` is `off` it does not see the loose sessions on this Mac, a workspace's agents on this Mac, the
lines of its log about them, or who is working — Home, **Loose agents** and a workspace's page say how many were left
out. A workspace's brief follows `serve.chat`, as its room does: `off`, the page says "the brief is not shared with this
browser"; `read`, it is shown; `write`, it can also be edited (its announcement in the room speaks as you; each edit is a
line in `doz ui log`, never the text). Another browser never makes, starts, stops, puts to sleep, wakes, finishes, archives,
restores or deletes a workspace, adds or ends a worker or changes a bot, and never puts an agent in a workspace or takes one
out — whatever `serve.chat` and `serve.mac_sessions` say, that is only the Mac's own browser (the **New workspace** wizard,
**Start**, **Sleep**, **Wake** and the rest of a workspace's **⋯**, **Put in a workspace…**, **Add a worker**, **End…**) or a
terminal on the Mac (`doz workspace new`, `start`, `sleep`, `wake`, `finish`, `archive`, `delete`, `adopt` and `release`,
`doz worker add` and `end`); another browser sees the wizard's and Add a worker's addresses as a notice and those
buttons disabled, with the command instead. A workspace's **Network & secrets**, **Folders &
points**, **Activity** and an agent's **Can do** are shown too, with the same rule for this Mac's sessions; another browser
sees how many secrets each agent holds, never their names, cannot remove an ended session on this Mac (that is this Mac's
own browser, or `doz sessions @mac --forget-ended`, whatever `serve.mac_sessions` says), and cannot allow a site for a session on this Mac (that is
`doz net allow @mac --session SESSION site:HOST` on the Mac). The isolation guide is the same on every browser. See
[Sessions on this Mac](https://dozable.com/docs/sessions-on-this-mac.md#in-the-dashboard).

**Your Macs** (the machine picker — "Dozable · studio ▾") is the same list on another browser as on this Mac: a phone
switching between your Macs is what it is for. It holds names and addresses only; picking a Mac opens that Mac's own
dashboard, where the browser needs that Mac's own invite. Adding or removing a Mac is done on this Mac, with
`doz ui macs`.

`ui.lan` and the `serve.*` settings — who can reach the dashboard — are changed only on the Mac, with `doz config set`.

A workspace's runs can be listed from another browser, and a past run's messages read there only when `serve.chat`
allows reading chat. Archiving or removing a room, and writing a run's archive again, happen only in this Mac's own
browser (or with `doz chat room …` and `doz workspace runs …` in a terminal on the Mac).

## Adding this Mac to another Mac's list

To open this Mac's dashboard from another Mac's machine picker, put this dashboard on the network first (`doz ui --lan`,
or `doz ui publish tailscale`), then, **on the other Mac**:

```bash
doz ui macs add studio studio.example.ts.net      # its Tailscale name (published: https), or
doz ui macs add studio studio.local:7443          # its LAN name or address and port
```

Give the address only — a sign-in link is refused and not kept. `doz ui macs add` checks once that this dashboard
answers (`doz ui macs check` again later). Then pick **studio** in the other Mac's picker: a new tab opens this
dashboard's sign-in page, and this Mac lets that browser in once with an invite, as any other (`doz ui share` here).
See [Your other Macs](https://dozable.com/docs/the-dashboard.md#your-other-macs-the-machine-picker).

## The browsers that are in

```bash
doz ui devices              # name, when let in, last seen, from where, which browser
doz ui rename ID "Kitchen iPad"
doz ui revoke ID            # or --all
```

The **Devices** page (on every browser that is in, and on this Mac's) lists the same, with **Remove** and **Rename**,
and the recent activity. A removed browser is signed out at once — its pages say so and its terminals close — and
needs a new invite to come back. A new link for this Mac's browser (`doz ui link --rotate`, `doz ui --new-link`) signs
out this Mac's pages only; the other browsers stay in.

Every change another browser asks for, every terminal it opens, every admission and every refusal is written to an
audit log — never a key, a code or what was typed:

```bash
doz ui log
```

## Where it listens

By default (`serve.bind = lan`) on every network interface of this Mac (Wi-Fi, Ethernet, the Thunderbolt Bridge) and
on Tailscale — never on a sandbox's network. A sandbox can never reach the dashboard: a connection from a sandbox's
network is dropped before anything is read, and the proxy that carries a proxied sandbox's traffic refuses the Mac's
own addresses on the dashboard's port, whatever the sandbox's network policy says. This Mac's own browser is served
at `127.0.0.1` whatever `serve.bind` says.

With the LAN option the dashboard announces itself with Bonjour as "Dozable on <this Mac>" (`serve.advertise`), so
Safari's Bonjour list and other devices can find it.

The port is the dashboard's one port, `ui.port`. While `ui.port` is 0 (automatic), the LAN option uses `serve.port`
(7443): with other browsers it never moves by itself — their sign-ins, an installed app and a bookmark belong to it.
When another program holds it, `doz ui` refuses and names that program.

```bash
doz config set ui.port 8443
```

## On your tailnet, at its own https address (Tailscale)

If you use Tailscale, one command puts the dashboard on your tailnet at an address of its own, with a real
certificate — so it can be installed as an app on your other devices and takes keys and tokens:

```bash
brew install tailscale          # once: Dozable runs its own Tailscale node from it
doz ui publish tailscale        # the dashboard at https://dozable-<this Mac>.<your tailnet>.ts.net
```

The first time, it shows Tailscale's sign-in link: open it, approve the new device, and the command carries on by
itself (not approved within five minutes? run the same command again to continue). It then says the address, and the
next step: run `doz ui share` on this Mac to let a browser on another device in, once — the address is on your tailnet
only, and every browser still needs an invite.

What it does, in one step:

- It runs **Dozable's own Tailscale node**, from Homebrew's `tailscale` (it does not need to be linked). The Mac's own
  Tailscale — the app or the `tailscale` command — is left exactly as it is. The node keeps its state in the store and
  is kept running by a LaunchAgent of yours, so it comes back after a restart.
- It names the node `dozable-<this Mac's local hostname>` (`--name` chooses another).
- Tailscale serves `https://<name>.<your tailnet>.ts.net` to the dashboard; plain `http://` there redirects to it. The
  redirect answers on a second port of this Mac's, on `127.0.0.1` only, picked the first time and kept; nothing needs
  administrator rights.
- It sets the dashboard up for it: a fixed `ui.port`, `ui.lan` on, `serve.bind` `loopback`, `serve.public_origins` the
  address and `serve.trusted_proxies` `127.0.0.1,::1` — then restarts the dashboard. Chat on other devices stays as
  `serve.chat` says.

Run it again any time: it re-applies everything (after you changed `ui.port`, say, or when `doz doctor` says plain
`http://` does not redirect — as it did for a dashboard published with version 0.51.14, where Tailscale refused the
redirect). Check it:

```bash
doz ui publish status      # the node, its sign-in, what it serves, the settings, and whether the address reaches the dashboard
doz doctor                 # the same, as rows
```

Take it off again with `doz ui unpublish tailscale` — the dashboard is this Mac's only again (`ui.port` is kept). Add
`--logout` to also sign the node out of your tailnet and remove its state; publishing again then asks you to sign in
again, as a new device.

While it is published, the doz daemon keeps the dashboard running: it starts it in the background when the daemon
starts (at login, with `doz daemon login-item on`) and again if it stops unexpectedly. `doz ui stop` is your word: after
it the daemon leaves the dashboard stopped until you start it again (`doz ui --detach`). `doz ui publish status` says
which.

## HTTPS behind your own reverse proxy

If you already run a reverse proxy at home (Caddy, Traefik, nginx, Nginx Proxy Manager, a Cloudflare Tunnel …), put
the dashboard behind it: your proxy does HTTPS, and through it the dashboard can be installed as an app (with its
offline page) and takes keys and tokens.

Tell `doz ui` three things:

```bash
doz config set serve.public_origins https://doz.home.example   # the address your proxy serves it at
doz config set serve.trusted_proxies 127.0.0.1,::1             # your proxy's address (here: on this Mac)
doz config set serve.bind loopback                             # a proxy on this Mac: listen on 127.0.0.1 only
```

For a proxy on another machine of your network, set `serve.trusted_proxies` to that machine's address and
`serve.bind` to this Mac's address the proxy connects to (or leave it `lan`).

The dashboard believes `X-Forwarded-Proto`, `X-Forwarded-Host` and `X-Forwarded-For` ONLY from the addresses in
`serve.trusted_proxies`; from anyone else they are ignored, and the public address is refused. A request that came
through a proxy is never treated as this Mac's own browser, even from a proxy on this Mac. When it starts it prints
the upstream your proxy should use and what is missing. Check the whole path:

```bash
doz doctor
```

— its `dashboard via https://…` line fetches each public address from this Mac and says whether it came back to this
dashboard, over https, through a trusted proxy.

What your proxy must do: pass the `Host` header (or `X-Forwarded-Host`), set `X-Forwarded-Proto` and
`X-Forwarded-For`, pass WebSocket upgrades (the terminals), and not buffer responses (the live updates are a
server-sent event stream).

### Caddy

```caddyfile
doz.home.example {
	reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:7443 {
		flush_interval -1
	}
}
```

Caddy passes `Host`, sets the forwarded headers and upgrades WebSockets by itself; `flush_interval -1` keeps the live
updates unbuffered.

### Traefik (file provider)

```yaml
http:
  routers:
    doz:
      rule: "Host(`doz.home.example`)"
      entryPoints: [websecure]
      service: doz
      tls: {}
  services:
    doz:
      loadBalancer:
        servers:
          - url: "http://127.0.0.1:7443"
```

Traefik passes `Host` and the forwarded headers and upgrades WebSockets by default.

### nginx (and Nginx Proxy Manager's custom configuration)

```nginx
map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade { default upgrade; '' close; }

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name doz.home.example;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/doz.home.example.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/doz.home.example.key;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:7443;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
        proxy_buffering off;
        proxy_read_timeout 1h;
    }
}
```

`proxy_buffering off` matters: with nginx's default buffering the live updates arrive late or not at all.

### Cloudflare Tunnel

```yaml
# ~/.cloudflared/config.yml
tunnel: <your tunnel id>
credentials-file: /Users/you/.cloudflared/<your tunnel id>.json
ingress:
  - hostname: doz.example.com
    service: http://127.0.0.1:7443
  - service: http_status:404
```

`cloudflared` runs on this Mac, so `serve.trusted_proxies` is `127.0.0.1,::1` and `serve.public_origins` is
`https://doz.example.com`. A tunnel puts the dashboard on the Internet: put Cloudflare Access in front of it too.

The Caddy and Traefik configurations above are the ones Dozable's own tests ran in front of the dashboard (terminals,
live updates, the installable app, keys over https, `doz doctor`); the nginx and Cloudflare ones follow the same rules.

## The macOS firewall and Local Network privacy

- **Firewall** (System Settings › Network › Firewall): when it is on, macOS asks once whether `doz` may accept incoming
  connections — answer **Allow**. A `doz` installed with Homebrew is signed, and with the firewall's "Automatically
  allow downloaded signed software" (on by default) it is allowed without asking. With "Block all incoming
  connections" nothing on your network can reach the dashboard; `doz ui --lan` says so when it starts. It never
  changes your firewall's settings.
- **Local Network privacy**: accepting connections from your network needs no permission. Announcing with Bonjour is
  done on behalf of the app you run `doz ui` in (Terminal, iTerm2, your editor); if macOS has refused that app Local
  Network access, `doz ui` says it was not announced — browsers still reach it by address and by `<this Mac>.local`.
  To announce it: System Settings › Privacy & Security › Local Network, allow that app, or set `serve.advertise` to
  false.

## Settings

| setting | default | what |
|---|---|---|
| `ui.lan` | false | serve your other browsers too (`--lan`, `--no-lan`, `$DOZ_UI_LAN`) |
| `ui.port` | 0 | the dashboard's one port; 0 = automatic (`--port`, `$DOZ_UI_PORT`) |
| `serve.port` | 7443 | the port with the LAN option while `ui.port` is 0 (`$DOZ_SERVE_PORT`) |
| `serve.bind` | `lan` | `lan`, `loopback`, or this Mac's addresses (`--bind`, `$DOZ_SERVE_BIND`) |
| `serve.public_origins` | — | your proxy's https addresses |
| `serve.trusted_proxies` | — | your proxy's addresses or networks |
| `serve.advertise` | true | announce with Bonjour |
| `serve.mac_sessions` | `off` | what these browsers may do with the sessions on this Mac: `off`, `watch` or `interactive` ([Sessions on this Mac](https://dozable.com/docs/sessions-on-this-mac.md#in-the-dashboard)) |
| `serve.chat` | `off` | what these browsers may do with chat: `off`, `read` or `write` — writing acts as you ([Chat](https://dozable.com/docs/chat.md#chat-on-your-other-browsers-servechat)) |

All of them but `serve.mac_sessions` and `serve.chat` (at once) apply when `doz ui` starts again (`doz ui restart`). See the [Settings reference](https://dozable.com/docs/settings-reference.md).

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/try-and-search

# Trying agents, and what Dozable supports

`doz try` takes you from nothing to talking to an agent in one command. `doz search` tells you whether Dozable runs
something, and how. Both use the same choices as `doz new`, `doz create` and `doz up`, and `--dry-run` shows what any
of them would make before anything is made.

## Try an agent: `doz try`

```sh
doz try opencode                   # OpenCode, from nothing: prepared, made, started and attached
doz try pi --base python           # any choice option works (here: pi on the Python base)
doz try                            # a numbered list of the agents — coding agents, then AI tools — with your keys and whether each is ready
doz try --tag terminal-tool        # only those of a kind (coding-agent, ai-tool) or a category
doz try opencode --dry-run         # make nothing: print the plan
doz try opencode --rm              # delete it when you leave, without asking
doz try opencode --keep            # keep it running when you leave, without asking
doz try opencode -d                # make and start it, but don't attach (it is kept)
```

**Offered now:** Claude Code, pi, Codex and OpenCode (OpenCode 1 and 2), with OpenRouter as the gateway. The other
agents and AI tools in this manual are **unpublished** in this version of Dozable: they are in no list, and
`doz try`, `doz new` or `doz create` of one says so. A sandbox you already made with one keeps working — its image,
its key and its settings — and so does a Vercel AI Gateway key you already added.

A try is the fast way to make a sandbox, with safe defaults. What it makes is an **ordinary sandbox** — nothing marks it
as a try afterwards; you keep it, sleep it or delete it like any other:

- **A new empty folder of its own** — Dozable makes `try-<agent>` in your projects folder (`defaults.projects_dir`,
  `~/doz-workspaces` unless you set another) and shares it at `/workspace`, so what the agent makes is on
  your Mac. It is never one of your folders: a folder of that name that holds anything is skipped (the try is named
  `try-<agent>-2`). `--isolated` shares no folder at all (`doz get try-opencode /workspace/FILE` copies a file out —
  see [Terminals and sessions](https://dozable.com/docs/terminals-and-sessions.md)); `--folder DIR` uses a folder you choose.
- **Your Mac's clipboard and its apps**, as in any sandbox: what the agent copies reaches your Mac's clipboard (also
  from agents that copy with `xclip`, `xsel` or `wl-copy`), and it can open a file it made, or a link, on your Mac.
  The try's first line says so:

  ```
  try-grok · Node.js · Grok Build · a new empty folder ~/doz-workspaces/try-grok (not one of yours), at
  /workspace · copy to your Mac's clipboard: on · open files on your Mac: on · open links in your Mac's browser: on
  ```
- **A new sandbox's network** — `defaults.permissions`, **Standard** unless you changed it: its AI model, updating
  itself, software packages (apt, npm, PyPI …) and GitHub; not the web at large. `--network locked` keeps it to its
  model alone; every other choice option works too. ([Why Standard](https://dozable.com/docs/permissions-and-network.md#the-default).)
- **This store's base** (`defaults.base`, Node.js unless you set another): every tool you try is added to it as a layer, so a second tool downloads nothing more. `--base` picks another for this one. Its approval prompts are off.
- **Your key for its provider** — the provider's default account.
- **Named `try-<agent>`**, then `try-<agent>-2`, ….

**When you have no key yet**, a terminal shows **What you need**, the same card for every agent, made from the agent's
recipe:

1. **Paste a key** (hidden) — kept in your Mac's login keychain; the sandbox only ever gets a placeholder.
2. **A key you keep in 1Password, AWS Secrets Manager or a program** — `op://…`, `aws:arn:…`, or a command; read on
   your Mac when needed, never stored (see [Agents and accounts](https://dozable.com/docs/agents-and-accounts.md)).
3. **Signing in inside the agent** — offered only where that sign-in can work in a sandbox, and labelled: the sign-in
   lives in that sandbox, and deleting the try deletes it. (Grok Build's own sign-in uses hosts Dozable keeps out, so
   it is shown, not offered.)

It also says where to get a key. While you deal with the key, the image is already being prepared.

**When you leave** (the agent exits, or you detach with Ctrl-] twice), it asks:

```
Leaving try-grok — [S]leep / [d]elete / [k]eep running [S]:
```

**Sleep** (Enter) hibernates it: everything is kept on disk and it holds no memory; `doz wake try-grok` (or
`doz attach try-grok`) brings it back where it was.
**Delete** removes it and everything in it. Its folder goes too when it is empty; when the agent left files there,
it asks (the default keeps the folder and says where it is), and off a terminal it keeps it and says so. `--rm` does
the same without asking. **Keep running** leaves it as it is. This is no special rule of a try: `doz rm` and the
dashboard's Remove… do the same for **every** sandbox whose folder Dozable made (see
[Sandboxes and their lifecycle](https://dozable.com/docs/sandboxes-and-lifecycle.md)).

**Off a terminal** (a script, `--json`, `-d`) `doz try` asks nothing and does not attach: it makes and starts the sandbox,
keeps it, and prints how to attach. With no key it stops and says how to add one.

## In the dashboard: Quick try

**Quick try** (beside New sandbox on the Sandboxes page, or `#/try` and `#/try/grok` in the address bar) is the same
try in the browser, with the same defaults and the same plan. It covers the whole window; **Close** (or Esc) returns
to where you opened it.

- **Two sections** at the top of the left pane: **Coding agents** and **AI tools**, each with how many it holds. A
  search that matches something in the other section says so ("2 in AI tools"), one click away.
- **Search and filters** below: type a name, a maker, an alias, `tag:headless` or `tag:terminal-tool` — the same
  matching as `doz search`, and forgiving (`agy` finds Antigravity CLI). The pills narrow the section — **Ready** (its
  key is here), then the section's categories (a terminal tool, a personal agent, a framework, evaluation, MCP …): any
  of the categories you press. The count says how many match; when none do, it says so, suggests a near name, and
  clears in one click. Superseded agents, then the ones that are coming, come last.
- **Cards or a list**: the toggle beside the count; the dashboard remembers your choice in this browser.
- **Each agent's mark** is a plain black-and-white sign — a neutral lettermark, not the maker's logo (their brand terms
  do not allow it here).
- **The chosen agent** on the right: its version and how long ago it was released, whether it is current (a
  superseded one says what replaced it, with a link to try that instead), **What you need** — its key, or, when there
  is none: paste one in a masked field (kept in your Mac's keychain; turned off with `ui.allow_secret_entry = false`),
  or the command to run for a key you keep in 1Password, AWS or a program. Then **the plan** (its name, base, network,
  its new empty folder — not one of yours — and what reaches your Mac), the same as a command to copy (`doz try opencode`),
  and what it can reach.
- **Where it gets its model** — **Try…** opens its setup. A tool that can use more than one provider (pi, OpenCode, and
  most of the recipe tools) shows ONE list: its providers, then the gateway (OpenRouter — one key,
  models from many makers), each with its key status. Its own provider is chosen; choose any other the same way. The
  chosen one shows its key (a choice when you have several, or "Add another key"), or a field to paste one, where to get
  a key and the command for a key kept in 1Password, AWS or a program. Then **Model**: the source's own list —
  a gateway's public list, read by Dozable on this Mac once a day — to search by name, maker or id, with each model's
  context and price per million tokens and the default marked; an id it does not list can still be typed. The plan
  names the model, and **Same in Terminal** is the command (`doz try pi --gateway openrouter --model …`). New Sandbox
  asks the same in its Account step, and writes the choice to `doz_project.yaml` (`model_source:`, `model:`).
  OpenCode 2 also lists **OpenCode Zen** (free models), marked "no key needed": chosen, it needs no key and no account,
  Start is ready at once, and its model list shows each free model with its data terms as OpenCode's docs state them
  (`doz try opencode --provider opencode-zen`). It lists **OpenCode** too — an OpenCode key, for OpenCode Zen's paid
  models and OpenCode Go (`doz try opencode --provider opencode`), its model list OpenCode's own (Go first).
- **Nothing is prepared while you browse.** **Start** makes it, starts it and opens its session: a first start
  prepares its image, and its terminal area shows the progress (the steps, the one under way and the last lines of the
  build) until the session is there. Its page is an ordinary sandbox's page: Sleep and Hibernate are in its action bar,
  and ⋯ › **Remove…** deletes it — and its folder too while that folder is empty.
- **Keyboard:** `/` searches, ↑ and ↓ move through the results, Enter starts. On a phone the list comes first and an
  agent opens its details, with a back control.

`doz try --ui opencode` opens it from a terminal: it starts `doz ui` in the background when none runs; with a dashboard
page already open, that page goes to the Quick try (no new tab, as `ui.open_browser` says); otherwise a new one opens
there.

## The guide

Every agent and tool comes with a **guide**: what it is, the facts of your sandbox, the first steps and some tips.

- **In the dashboard**, the sandbox page's details have a **Guide** tab, the last of its tabs. It
  says what kind of thing it is and how to use it here; **This sandbox**: its version (Dozable's pin), the provider and model
  with the account it uses (your key stays on the Mac), what the network lets it reach (with a link to Network), the
  folder and where its settings live; **Start here**: the first steps, each command with **Copy** and **Run** — Run
  types it into the sandbox's session and presses Enter (for an agent with its own screen, into a shell beside it: open
  one with New shell), **Type** types a command you change first; **Good to know**: tips, its docs, and when Dozable last
  checked the recipe. The first step is always the one Dozable checks the recipe with, so it is known to work.
- **In a terminal**, `doz guide NAME` prints the same (`--json` as data). `doz try` prints "Start here" before it
  attaches to a tool whose session is a shell, and the first login shell in such a sandbox shows the steps once.
- **Fabric** comes with its patterns (some 260, from its own release, checksum-verified when its image is baked):
  `fabric -l` lists them, `fabric -p summarize` uses one — nothing to download first.

## Is it supported? `doz search`

```sh
doz search opencode                      # OpenCode — supported · key: xAI (you have work-xai) · try it: doz try opencode
doz search opencod                       # nothing called 'opencod' — did you mean opencode?
doz search grok                          # Grok Build is unpublished in this version of Dozable
doz search cursor-cli                    # Cursor CLI — coming: …
doz search                               # everything: supported, then coming
doz search tag:multi-vendor-models       # agents with a capability
doz search --tag api-key --level any     # every agent, with that tag at any level
doz search opencode --base alpine        # is it supported on that base?
doz search opencode --details            # what it installs, the hosts it may reach, its keys, what is kept out, tags
doz search opencode --json               # the directory entry, and your key and image state beside it
```

It matches agents (by id, alias, title or publisher), key providers (`xai`, `google`, …) and bases (`alpine`, …).

**Is it current?** Under each agent, a second line says its latest release as your Mac last saw it — `latest 1.3.3 ·
released 10 Oct 2026 (2 days ago) · active` — and, when its maker has moved on, its standing:

```
Gemini CLI — supported · key: Google AI (Gemini API) (you have google) · try it: doz try gemini
    latest 0.63.0 · released 6 Oct 2026 (6 days ago) · active
    Superseded by Antigravity CLI — Google retired Gemini CLI for personal accounts; it still works with a paid Gemini API key · instead: doz try antigravity
```

- **active**: a release in the last 3 months; **quiet**: none for 3 months; **stale**: none for 6 months;
  **deprecated**: its maker marked that release deprecated (that wins).
- The Dozable daemon looks up each agent's latest release about once an hour while it runs (the same check that keeps
  images up to date). Looking — `doz search`, `doz try`, the Quick try — never asks the internet; before the first
  check it says *not checked yet*.
- A tool Dozable installs from one pinned release download or a hash-locked set of Python packages (Fabric, AIChat,
  Goose, Crush, Tau, …) is not looked up: its line says the pin — *pinned 1.4.518 — Dozable installs exactly this
  release* — and a newer one comes with a Dozable update.
- **Superseded** agents still work and stay selectable; they are listed after the current ones, and `doz search` of
  one lists what replaces it too. `doz try` of one says so first. **Antigravity CLI** (alias `agy`) is Google's lead
  agent; **Gemini CLI** is superseded by it (both are unpublished for now).

### Antigravity CLI

Unpublished for now (see above).

Google's terminal agent, installed from Google's own release (checked against its published SHA-512), on Debian-based
bases (not Alpine yet). It uses a **Gemini API key** (`doz account add google --provider google`); Dozable never offers the
Google sign-in. Its approval prompts are off (`antigravity.permissions = ask` keeps them), its updater is off, and its
telemetry setting is off. It reads Google's feature switches at start-up, and sends its usage log to
`play.googleapis.com` every few seconds (its own setting does not stop it); both are allowed.

**What it is**: every agent, and every one that is coming, is a **coding agent** or an **AI tool**, with one or more
categories — `personal-agent`, `terminal-tool`, `framework`, `browser-agent`, `mcp`, `research`, `evaluation`,
`workflow`, `local-models`, `chat-app` (and `coding-agent`). `doz search --tag ai-tool`, `doz search --tag mcp`
(coming ones included), `doz search NAME --details` ("what it is: AI tool · terminal tool").

**Tags** describe capabilities (`multi-vendor-models`, `api-key`, `vendor-sign-in`, `free-tier`, `resume`, `musl`,
`open-source`, `headless`, `gateway:openrouter`, …). Each tag has a level per agent: `documented`, `verified`,
`experimental`, `no` or `unknown`. By default only `documented` and `verified` count; `--level` changes that.

**Exit codes**, for scripts and for agents on your Mac:

| code | meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | supported (or a plain `doz search`) |
| 8 | supported, but not with what you asked (a base it does not run on) |
| 6 | known, but not in this Dozable: coming, or not possible |
| 2 | nothing by that name (it suggests the closest) |
| 64 | usage |

The whole table, the same for every command: `doz help exit-codes`.

## A tool's major version

Some tools come in more than one major release line, each a recipe of its own — OpenCode 1 and OpenCode 2. The tool's
name is the one Dozable recommends; you can always choose another:

```sh
doz try opencode                   # the major Dozable recommends (a release it checked)
doz try opencode@1                 # OpenCode 1, kept up to date within 1.x
doz try opencode@2.0.28            # exactly that release (checked against the registry before anything is made)
doz create my-app --agent opencode@1      # the same in new, create and up — and in doz_project.yaml: agent: opencode@1
```

- **Recommended, never "latest"**: the recommended major is one whose recipe passed Dozable's checks; Dozable moves it to a
  new major only once that one has.
- **A sandbox keeps its major.** It records what it was made as (`opencode@2.0.29`). Later recommendations never move
  it, and a reset keeps its major. The other major is a new sandbox.
- **A project file keeps its major too.** What Dozable writes for later — a plan's `doz_project.yaml`, `doz init`, New
  Sandbox — records the major the name resolved to (`agent: opencode@2`), so `doz up` on it next year makes the same
  major. A file you write by hand with the bare name (`agent: opencode`) keeps meaning the recommended major; `doz up`
  says which one when it makes the sandbox.
- **Where you see them**: a try's first line, `--dry-run` and the sandbox's Guide say which release it is and how to get
  the other one (`OpenCode 1 1.19.0 (recommended) — OpenCode 2: doz try opencode@2`). `doz search` marks each major
  (`(recommended; also @2)`), and the `doz try` list shows the tool once. In the dashboard, Quick try has one card per
  tool, with a **Version** choice in its Try setup; New Sandbox shows the tool once, with its majors under it.
- An exact release that does not exist, or a major that does not, is refused with the choices there are
  (`opencode has opencode@1 (recommended) and opencode@2 — not @9`).

## A tool's full name

Every tool also has a full name: its vendor and its product, like a container image's (`anthropic/claude-code`,
`openai/codex`, `earendil-works/pi`, `anomalyco/opencode`). The short names (`claude`, `pi`, `codex`) stay the everyday
ones; the full name says whose tool you mean, and works everywhere a short one does:

```sh
doz try anthropic/claude-code               # the same as doz try claude
doz try anomalyco/opencode@1                # with a major or a release, as above
doz create my-app --agent openai/codex      # new, create, up, --image, doz_project.yaml's agent:, the dashboard's plan
doz search anomalyco/opencode2              # search finds it by its full name
doz try mine/acme/tool                      # one of your own recipes: mine/VENDOR/PRODUCT
doz try hub/acme/tool                       # a community source's: SOURCE/VENDOR/PRODUCT
doz try doz.sh/anthropic/claude-code        # Dozable's recipe directory, doz.sh — the same as anthropic/claude-code
```

- **Whose recipe.** A name without a source is Dozable's recipe (`dozable/anthropic/claude-code` says it in full). Your own
  recipes are `mine/VENDOR/PRODUCT`, a community source's `NAME/VENDOR/PRODUCT` — the source's name as you added it. Their
  plain id still works too. A full name that is not the recipe's is refused with the one that is
  (`acme/tool: Acme Tool is yours — mine/acme/tool`; `openai/claude-code: claude-code is not openai's — its name is
  anthropic/claude-code`).
- **The product** is the tool's own name, not a short one: `anthropic/claude` is refused, naming
  `anthropic/claude-code`. A tool with majors is named by its family's name (`anomalyco/opencode`, the recommended
  major) or with `@MAJOR`.
- **Where you see it**: `doz search` puts each tool's full name beside its title (and `--details` on its own line), the
  `doz try` list too, `--dry-run` says the recipe a sandbox is made from (`recipe: dozable/anthropic/claude-code@2.1.299`),
  the sandbox records it (`doz ls --json`: `recipeRef`) and its Guide says it under This sandbox. In the
  dashboard, Quick try shows it as **Full name** in a tool's details.
- **doz.sh.** `doz.sh` is Dozable's recipe directory, where its signed recipe catalogue is published. `doz.sh/VENDOR/PRODUCT`
  (with `@MAJOR` or `@VERSION` if you like) names the same recipe as `dozable/VENDOR/PRODUCT` and `VENDOR/PRODUCT`, and
  wherever a name is typed — the command line, `doz_project.yaml`, the dashboard's plan, `doz recipe show` — what you typed
  is kept. It names a recipe your doz already has: typing it fetches nothing. Your own and a community source's recipes are
  not in it (`doz.sh/acme/tool` is refused with `mine/acme/tool`, its right name).
- **Refused**: any other host (`example.com/…`: only doz.sh is a recipe directory — add a community catalogue with
  `doz recipe source add` and name it by its source), `doz.sh/PRODUCT` and four-part names (a name in doz.sh is
  `doz.sh/VENDOR/PRODUCT`), digests, and `:` after a name (`NAME:PATH` is `doz get`, `put` and `cp`'s — a release is `@`).

## One set of choices

`doz new`, `doz create`, `doz up` and `doz try` take the same choice options, named after the keys of
[`doz_project.yaml`](https://dozable.com/docs/projects.md):

| option | what it chooses |
|---|---|
| `--agent`, `--base`, `--dockerfile` | the agent and its base (`--image` is the shorthand for both); a tool's major or release: `--agent opencode@1`; its full name: `--agent anthropic/claude-code` |
| `--permissions` | what the agent may do: `standard`, `locked`, `open`, `+web`, `-error-reports`, `site:HOST` or `site:HOST:PORT` (`--allow` is the same) |
| `--network` | `agent`, `locked`, `open`, `bake`, `nat` or `none` |
| `--account`, `--key` | the account, and custom keys beside it |
| `--github`, `--ssh-agent` | GitHub as you, your SSH agent |
| `--folder`, `--isolated` | a folder of your Mac at `/workspace`, or none |
| `--cpus`, `--memory` | resources |
| `--clipboard`, `--browser-bridge`, `--open-files`, `--tmux`, `--ignore-mode`, `--folder-view`, `--agent-sudo` | the per-sandbox settings |

`doz new my-app` names the sandbox (`--name` still works). `doz init` takes `--agent`, `--base` and `--dockerfile`
and writes them as the file's own keys.

## See it first: `--dry-run`

```sh
doz new --agent opencode --dry-run
doz create my-app --agent pi --base python --permissions +web --dry-run
doz up my-app --dry-run
doz try opencode --dry-run --json
```

The plan has three parts:

- **the command** that makes it, showing only what differs from your defaults;
- **the same choices as `doz_project.yaml`**, so a sandbox you like can become a project;
- **what it can reach**, in plain words, from the same rules the proxy will apply ("Talk to xAI (api.x.ai, 4 API
  paths)", "No package installs (Locked)", "Kept out whatever you choose: …", "A new empty folder … (not one of
  yours)", "Copy to your Mac's clipboard: on", "Open files on your Mac: on").

It also says whether the image is ready, which account and key it uses (where the key comes from, never the key),
and anything in the way, with the fix. `--json` gives the same plan as data. Looking never starts the daemon.

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/more-agents

# More agents: Antigravity CLI, Grok Build, OpenCode, GitHub Copilot CLI, Qwen Code, Goose, Kilo Code CLI, Mistral Vibe, Factory Droid, Dirac, Kimi Code, Cline CLI, OpenHands CLI, Letta Code, Docker Agent, Nanocoder, mini-swe-agent, Open Interpreter, Crush, MiMo Code, CodeWhale, Maki, oh-my-pi, Tau, Gemini CLI

> **Unpublished for now.** Of the agents on this page only **OpenCode** (`doz try opencode`, OpenCode 1 and 2) is
> offered in this version of Dozable; the others are unpublished — in no list, and `doz try grok` (or `doz new`,
> `doz create`) says so. A sandbox you already made with one keeps working: its image, its key and its settings. The
> rest of this page describes them as they work when published.

Beside Claude Code, pi and Codex, Dozable runs agents from other makers. Each uses an **API key** — most of them of the
provider or gateway you choose (`--provider` / `--gateway`, or the Quick try's “Where it gets its model”; `--model` picks the
model; see [Other AI tools](https://dozable.com/docs/ai-tools.md#providers-and-gateways)). The key stays on your Mac and the sandbox only ever
gets a placeholder, which Dozable's proxy swaps for the key on the way out — and only to that provider's or gateway's
own API.

```sh
doz try antigravity      # Google's agent (alias: agy)
doz try grok             # xAI's agent
doz try opencode         # OpenCode, the open-source agent, on xAI or another provider or gateway
doz try copilot          # GitHub Copilot CLI with your own key (no Copilot plan)
doz try qwen-code        # Qwen Code (alias qwen), on xAI or another provider or gateway
doz try goose            # Goose, on xAI or another provider or gateway
doz try kilo             # Kilo Code CLI (alias kilocode), on xAI or another provider or gateway
doz try mistral-vibe     # Mistral Vibe (alias vibe), on xAI or another provider or gateway
doz try droid            # Factory Droid (alias factory), no Factory account, any provider or gateway
doz try dirac            # Dirac, a Cline-derived agent, on xAI or another provider or gateway
doz try kimi-code        # Kimi Code (alias kimi), on xAI or another provider or gateway
doz try cline            # Cline CLI, on xAI or another provider or gateway, no Cline account
doz try openhands        # OpenHands CLI, on xAI or another provider or gateway
doz try letta-code       # Letta Code (alias letta), local backend, on xAI or another provider or gateway
doz try docker-agent     # Docker Agent (alias cagent), its built-in coding agent, on xAI or another provider or gateway
doz try nanocoder        # Nanocoder, on xAI or another provider or gateway
doz try mini-swe-agent   # mini-swe-agent (alias mini), on xAI or another provider or gateway
doz try open-interpreter # Open Interpreter (alias interpreter), on xAI or another provider or gateway
doz try crush            # Crush (Charmbracelet), on xAI or another provider or gateway
doz try mimo-code        # MiMo Code (Xiaomi, alias mimo), on xAI or another provider or gateway
doz try codewhale        # CodeWhale (formerly DeepSeek TUI), on xAI or another provider or gateway
doz try maki             # Maki, on xAI or another provider or gateway
doz try omp              # oh-my-pi (a pi derivative), on xAI or another provider or gateway
doz try tau              # Tau (Hugging Face's Python port of pi), on xAI or another provider or gateway
doz try gemini           # Google's earlier agent (superseded by Antigravity CLI)
doz search google        # what Dozable runs with a Google key, each with its latest release
```

The first `doz try` of each asks for the key (a paste, or where you keep it: 1Password, AWS, a command — see
[Keys from 1Password, AWS or a command](https://dozable.com/docs/agents-and-accounts.md#keys-from-1password-aws-or-a-command)), prepares the
agent's image once (a minute or so) and starts it. A try is Standard, like any new sandbox: the agent reaches its model,
software packages and GitHub, and, below, the few hosts its maker's program calls when it starts — not the web at large. [Trying agents](https://dozable.com/docs/try-and-search.md) has the rest.

## Antigravity CLI (Google)

Google's terminal agent and **the one to use with a Google key** (`doz try antigravity`, or `agy`).

- **Installed** from Google's own release for linux-arm64, checked against the SHA-512 Google publishes with it.
  Debian-based bases only for now (not Alpine). It is closed source; Dozable installs it from Google, it does not
  redistribute it.
- **Key:** a Gemini API key (`doz account add google --provider google`; get one at https://aistudio.google.com/apikey).
  Dozable never offers the Google sign-in: it keeps its token in a keyring inside the machine.
- **Set up for you:** approval prompts off (`antigravity.permissions = ask` keeps them), its updater off, its
