  telemetry setting off.
- **Its first start is yours:** it asks you to pick a colour scheme, then to accept Google's **Terms of Service &
  Data Use** — data sharing is ticked by default and you can untick it. Dozable never accepts those terms for you;
  `doz try antigravity` says so first, and so does the first step of its Guide.
- **May reach:** the Gemini API (its model); Google's feature switches for it (`antigravity-unleash.goog`) when it
  starts; its usage log to `play.googleapis.com`, every few seconds. Its own telemetry setting does not stop that log,
  and Dozable allows it rather than blocking it.

## Grok Build (xAI)

xAI's own agent (`doz try grok`), on an **xAI API key** only: it checks its key with xAI's API when it starts and
will not run without an xAI key or sign-in, so another provider's or gateway's key cannot stand in.

- **Installed** from the npm registry's linux-arm64 package, integrity-checked. Debian, Node and Alpine bases.
- **Key:** an xAI API key (`doz account add xai --provider xai`).
- **Set up for you:** approval prompts off, its auto-updater off, its telemetry and feedback off; copying to your
  Mac's clipboard works (Dozable tells it the terminal takes OSC 52).
- **May reach:** xAI's API (the paths Grok Build uses, and its key-less start-up check of `api.x.ai/`), and its release
  notes on `x.ai` when it starts.
- **Kept out, whatever you choose:** xAI's sign-in hosts (Dozable never offers the sign-in).

## OpenCode (open source)

An open-source terminal agent that works with many model providers (`doz try opencode`). Dozable offers it on the
key of the provider or gateway you choose: **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** — and OpenCode 2 also on an **OpenCode** key (below); on xAI the model is `xai/grok-build-0.1`.

- **Installed** from the npm registry's linux-arm64 package, integrity-checked. Debian and Node bases (not Alpine yet).
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (`doz account add NAME --provider xai` — or `openrouter`, `vercel-ai-gateway`, `google`; `--api-key` for Anthropic, `--openai-key` for OpenAI); the sandbox only gets a placeholder.
- **No key at all (OpenCode 2):** OpenCode Zen's free models — `doz try opencode --provider opencode-zen`, or
  **OpenCode Zen** in the try setup (marked "no key needed"). No account is used and nothing of yours is added to
  its requests. The model list shows each free model with its data terms as OpenCode's docs state them (some keep
  nothing, some are used to improve the model) — the free models OpenCode's docs list that this release of OpenCode can
  use without a key; `doz models --provider opencode-zen` lists them, and `--model`
  chooses one (default `big-pickle`). Only OpenCode's model requests to `opencode.ai` are allowed — not its Console or
  its sign-in. A key you add with OpenCode's own `/connect` is stored inside the sandbox; a key added in Dozable stays on
  your Mac.
- **An OpenCode key (OpenCode 2):** one key serves **OpenCode Zen** (pay as you go — models `opencode/…`) and
  **OpenCode Go** (the subscription — models `opencode-go/…`): `doz account add oc --provider opencode` (a key from
  opencode.ai/auth; Dozable cannot check it without spending, so it is not checked), then
  `doz try opencode --provider opencode`, or **OpenCode** in the try setup. The default model is
  `opencode-go/kimi-k2.7-code`; `--model opencode/claude-sonnet-4-6` (or any other in `doz models --provider opencode`)
  picks a Zen model. The sandbox gets only a placeholder in `OPENCODE_API_KEY`; the key goes ONLY to OpenCode's model
  requests on `opencode.ai` and to the one read of your key's OpenCode Console settings that OpenCode makes when it
  starts (`GET /console/api/v2/config`) — a placeholder sent anywhere else on `opencode.ai` is refused, whatever the
  network allows.
- **Set up for you:** its auto-update, session sharing, language-server downloads and the online model list off; the
  model set in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (written only when it is not there yet). Its plugin kit is not
  downloaded into `~/.config/opencode` when it first starts (it is only for plugins you write; `cd ~/.config/opencode
  && npm install @opencode-ai/plugin` adds it). OpenCode asks no approval questions by default.
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch), and, for
  OpenCode 2, OpenCode Zen's and OpenCode Go's model requests on `opencode.ai` (under `/zen/v1/` and `/zen/go/v1/`, and
  from OpenCode 2.0.32 under `/inference/`) and, with an OpenCode key, `GET /console/api/v2/config`.
- **Use:** `opencode` (its TUI), or `opencode run "…"` for one answer.

## GitHub Copilot CLI (GitHub)

GitHub's terminal agent, run in its own **bring-your-own-key** mode (`doz try copilot`): it talks to your model with
your key and never signs in to GitHub, so no Copilot plan is needed. Dozable points it at the provider or
gateway you choose: **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** (on xAI the model is `grok-code-fast-1`).

- **Installed** from the npm registry's linux-arm64 package, integrity-checked. Debian and Node bases (not Alpine yet).
  It is GitHub's software under its own licence; Dozable installs it from npm, it does not redistribute it.
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (`doz account add NAME --provider xai` — or `openrouter`, `vercel-ai-gateway`, `google`; `--api-key` for Anthropic, `--openai-key` for OpenAI); the sandbox only gets a placeholder.
- **Set up for you:** approval prompts off (`--allow-all`; `copilot.permissions = ask` keeps them), its offline mode
  (no GitHub sign-in, no calls to GitHub) and its auto-update off.
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch).

## Qwen Code (Alibaba Qwen)

Alibaba Qwen's open-source agent, a Gemini CLI fork (`doz try qwen-code`, or `qwen`). Its free Qwen sign-in ended in
April 2026; Dozable runs it in its **OpenAI-compatible mode**, pointed at the provider or gateway you choose: **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** (`--provider` / `--gateway`, or the Quick try's “Where it gets its model”; `--model` picks the model).
On xAI the model is `grok-code-fast-1`.

- **Installed** from the npm registry, integrity-checked; it needs Node 22 (the Node and Debian bases; not Alpine).
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway; the sandbox gets a placeholder in its own variable and in
  `OPENAI_API_KEY`. Dozable sets `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and `OPENAI_MODEL` for the choice at each session.
- **Set up for you:** approval prompts off (`--approval-mode=yolo`; `qwen-code.permissions = ask` keeps them), its
  auto-update and usage statistics off, and its download of the public model catalogue (models.dev) off — it uses the
  catalogue it ships with.
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch).

## Goose (Agentic AI Foundation)

The open-source agent from Block, now an Agentic AI Foundation project (`doz try goose`), on the key of the
provider or gateway you choose: **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** (its own providers; on xAI the model is `grok-code-fast-1`).

- **Installed** from its GitHub release (the static linux-arm64 build), checked against the SHA-512 Dozable recorded.
  Every base, Alpine included.
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (`doz account add NAME --provider xai` — or `openrouter`, `vercel-ai-gateway`, `google`; `--api-key` for Anthropic, `--openai-key` for OpenAI); the sandbox only gets a placeholder.
- **Set up for you:** it runs without asking (`GOOSE_MODE=auto`, its default), its keyring off (it would keep secrets in
  the sandbox), its telemetry off.
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch).
- **Use:** `goose` (a session), or `goose run -t "…"` for one task.

## Kilo Code CLI (Kilo Code)

Kilo Code's terminal agent, an OpenCode derivative (`doz try kilo`), on the key of the provider or
gateway you choose: **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** (on xAI the model is `xai/grok-build-0.1`).

- **Installed** from the npm registry's linux-arm64 package, integrity-checked. Debian and Node bases (not Alpine yet).
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (`doz account add NAME --provider xai` — or `openrouter`, `vercel-ai-gateway`, `google`; `--api-key` for Anthropic, `--openai-key` for OpenAI); the sandbox only gets a placeholder.
- **Set up for you:** its auto-update, sharing and online model list off; its usage telemetry off
  (`experimental.openTelemetry: false` — Kilo sends it by default); its Kilo Gateway provider off, so it does not call
  Kilo's servers. In its TUI, Kilo asks before running commands (its own default); `kilo run --auto` does not.
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch).

## Mistral Vibe (Mistral AI)

Mistral AI's terminal agent (`doz try mistral-vibe`, or `vibe`). Vibe takes any OpenAI-compatible or Anthropic
provider, and Dozable names the one you choose: **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** (`--provider` / `--gateway`, or the Quick try's “Where it gets its model”; `--model` picks the model). On xAI the model is `grok-build-0.1`. Mistral's own
models need a Mistral key, which Dozable does not hold yet.

- **Installed** from PyPI with every dependency hash-pinned, into its own Python (Debian base; not Alpine).
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (a placeholder in the sandbox). Vibe's Mistral key and sign-in
  (`vibe --setup`) are not offered.
- **Set up for you:** its telemetry, update checks and auto-update off (`VIBE_ENABLE_*`); the provider and model are
  set for the choice the same way at each session (`VIBE_PROVIDERS`, `VIBE_MODELS`, `VIBE_ACTIVE_MODEL`), not in its
  settings file.
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch).
- **Use:** `vibe` (a session), or `vibe --trust --auto-approve -p "…"` for one task.

## Factory Droid (Factory)

Factory's terminal agent (`doz try droid`) in its **airgap mode**, on the key of the provider or gateway you
choose: **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** — no Factory account, and none of Factory's servers. Droid takes it as a custom model, which
Dozable sets in its settings at every run (on xAI, `grok-build-0.1`).

- **Installed** from Factory's download server (its linux-arm64 build), checked against the SHA-512 Dozable recorded.
  Debian and Node bases (not Alpine: Factory publishes a glibc build only).
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (`doz account add NAME --provider xai` — or `openrouter`, `vercel-ai-gateway`, `google`; `--api-key` for Anthropic, `--openai-key` for OpenAI); the sandbox only gets a placeholder.
- **Set up for you:** airgap mode (`FACTORY_AIRGAP_ENABLED=1`): without it Droid calls Factory's API (sessions, usage,
  feature flags) and its telemetry even with your own model; with it, only the model. Its first start in a folder asks
  whether to trust it.
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch).
- **Use:** `droid` (a session; with approvals off, `--auto high`), or `droid exec -m "custom:$DOZ_MODEL" "…"` for
  one task.

## Dirac (dirac-run)

A Cline-derived terminal agent aimed at lower API cost (`doz try dirac`), on the key of the provider or gateway
you choose: **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** (on xAI the model is `grok-build-0.1`).

- **Installed** from the npm registry, integrity-checked. Node 22 on the Node and Debian bases (not Alpine: Dirac needs
  Node 22.13 to 24).
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (`doz account add NAME --provider xai` — or `openrouter`, `vercel-ai-gateway`, `google`; `--api-key` for Anthropic, `--openai-key` for OpenAI); the sandbox only gets a placeholder.
- **Set up for you:** its telemetry off (`telemetrySetting: disabled` — Dirac sends events to dirac.run by default)
  and its self-update off (`DIRAC_NO_AUTO_UPDATE=1`).
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch).
- **Use:** `dirac` (a session; with approvals off, `--auto-approve-all`), or `dirac --yolo "…"` for one task.

## Kimi Code (Moonshot AI)

Moonshot AI's terminal agent, the successor to kimi-cli (`doz try kimi-code`, or `kimi`). Kimi Code takes its model
from the environment (`KIMI_MODEL_*`), and Dozable names the provider or gateway you choose: **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** (`--provider` / `--gateway`, or the Quick try's “Where it gets its model”; `--model` picks the model). On xAI the
model is `grok-build-0.1`. Kimi's own models need a Kimi account or a Moonshot key, which Dozable does not hold yet.

- **Installed** from the npm registry, integrity-checked. Node 22 on the Node and Debian bases (not Alpine: it needs
  Node 22.19 or later).
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (a placeholder in the sandbox, in its own variable and in
  `KIMI_MODEL_API_KEY`), read on each request and never written into `~/.kimi-code/config.toml`.
- **Set up for you:** its telemetry and self-update off (`KIMI_DISABLE_TELEMETRY`, `KIMI_CODE_NO_AUTO_UPDATE`). At each
  start it asks Moonshot for its public client settings; Dozable keeps that request out quietly, and Kimi Code does
  without them. Its first start in a folder asks whether to trust it.
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch).
- **Use:** `kimi` (a session; with approvals off, `--auto`), or `kimi -p "…"` for one task.

## Cline CLI (Cline)

Cline's terminal agent (`doz try cline`), on the key of the provider or gateway you choose: **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** — no Cline account.
Dozable puts the provider and model on its command line (`cline -P xai -m grok-build-0.1` on xAI).

- **Installed** from the npm registry's linux-arm64 package, integrity-checked. Debian and Node bases (not Alpine).
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (`doz account add NAME --provider xai` — or `openrouter`, `vercel-ai-gateway`, `google`; `--api-key` for Anthropic, `--openai-key` for OpenAI); the sandbox only gets a placeholder.
- **Set up for you:** its telemetry and self-update off (`telemetryOptOut`, `autoUpdateEnabled: false`,
  `CLINE_NO_AUTO_UPDATE`), and its ClinePass notice. When it starts it asks for feature flags (its PostHog host), its
  recommended models (api.cline.bot) and the models.dev catalogue; Dozable keeps those requests out quietly, and Cline
  does without them. Cline approves its own tool calls by default (its
  `--auto-approve` is on unless you pass `--auto-approve false`).
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch).
- **Use:** `cline` (a session), or `cline "…"` for one task.

## OpenHands CLI (OpenHands)

OpenHands' terminal agent (`doz try openhands`). Its LLM settings come from the environment (`--override-with-envs`,
in Dozable's command), set for the provider or gateway you choose: **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** (`--provider` / `--gateway`, or the Quick try's “Where it gets its model”; `--model` picks the model). On xAI the model is `grok-build-0.1`.
Nothing is written to its settings.

- **Installed** from its GitHub release (the linux-arm64 build), checked against the SHA-512 Dozable recorded. Debian and
  Node bases (not Alpine: OpenHands publishes a glibc build only).
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (`LLM_API_KEY` and its own variable, the same placeholder in the
  sandbox). OpenHands Cloud's sign-in is not offered.
- **Set up for you:** its model price list read locally (`LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP`, not fetched from GitHub) and
  its banner off.
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use), and two reads no setting
  turns off: its public skills (a git clone of
  github.com/OpenHands/extensions at each start) and its latest release on PyPI (a notice only; Dozable installs the
  pinned release).
- **Use:** `openhands` (a session; with approvals off, `--always-approve`), or
  `openhands --override-with-envs --headless -t "…"` for one task.

## Letta Code (Letta)

Letta's memory-first coding agent (`doz try letta-code`, or `letta`) on its **local backend** — no Letta account, its
agents and memory kept in the sandbox (`~/.letta`) — on the key of the provider or gateway you choose: **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** (on xAI the model is `xai/grok-4.3`; `grok-build-0.1` is
not in its catalogue).

- **Installed** from the npm registry, integrity-checked. Node 22 on the Node and Debian bases (not Alpine: it needs
  Node 22.19 or later).
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (`doz account add NAME --provider xai` — or `openrouter`, `vercel-ai-gateway`, `google`; `--api-key` for Anthropic, `--openai-key` for OpenAI); the sandbox only gets a placeholder.
- **Set up for you:** its telemetry and self-update off (`LETTA_CODE_TELEM=0`, `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER`). When its TUI
  starts it may ask Letta Cloud for its health and an account balance; Dozable keeps those requests out quietly, and it
  does without them. Letta asks before running commands (its own default).
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch).
- **Use:** `letta` (a session), or `letta --backend local --new-agent -p "…"` for one task.

## Docker Agent (Docker)

Docker's YAML-defined agent runner, formerly cagent (`doz try docker-agent`), as a program in the sandbox — Docker
Desktop is not used. A session runs its built-in coding agent (`docker-agent run coder`) on the key of the provider or
gateway you choose: **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** (on xAI the model is `xai/grok-build-0.1`); your own agent files run the same way (`docker-agent run ./agent.yaml`).

- **Installed** from its GitHub release (the static linux-arm64 build), checked against the SHA-512 Dozable recorded.
  Every base, Alpine included.
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (`doz account add NAME --provider xai` — or `openrouter`, `vercel-ai-gateway`, `google`; `--api-key` for Anthropic, `--openai-key` for OpenAI); the sandbox only gets a placeholder.
- **Set up for you:** its telemetry, self-update, tour and setup wizard off. At each run it reads the public models.dev
  catalogue; Dozable keeps that request out quietly, and it does without it.
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch).
- **Use:** `docker-agent` (a session; with approvals off, `--yolo`), or
  `docker-agent run coder --exec "…"` for one task.

## Nanocoder (Nano Collective)

A local-first terminal agent (`doz try nanocoder`), with a provider at the base URL of the one you choose: **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** (on xAI the model is `grok-build-0.1`).

- **Installed** from the npm registry, integrity-checked. Node 22 on the Node and Debian bases.
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (`doz account add NAME --provider xai` — or `openrouter`, `vercel-ai-gateway`, `google`; `--api-key` for Anthropic, `--openai-key` for OpenAI); the sandbox only gets a placeholder.
- **Set up for you:** its context size given (`NANOCODER_CONTEXT_LIMIT`). It reads the public models.dev catalogue for
  prices when it needs them; Dozable keeps that request out quietly, and it does without it. Its first start in a
  folder asks whether to trust it.
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch).
- **Use:** `nanocoder` (a session; with approvals off, `--mode yolo`), or
  `nanocoder run "…" --trust-directory --plain` for one task.

## mini-swe-agent (SWE-agent team)

A minimal bash-only coding agent from the SWE-agent team (`doz try mini-swe-agent`; its command is `mini`), on an
key of the provider or gateway you choose, through LiteLLM: **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** (on xAI the model is `grok-build-0.1`).

- **Installed** from PyPI with every dependency hash-pinned, into its own Python (Debian base; not Alpine).
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (`doz account add NAME --provider xai` — or `openrouter`, `vercel-ai-gateway`, `google`; `--api-key` for Anthropic, `--openai-key` for OpenAI); the sandbox only gets a placeholder.
- **Set up for you:** LiteLLM's price list read locally (not fetched), and cost tracking that does not stop on a model
  without a price.
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch).
- **Use:** `mini` (a session; with approvals off, `--yolo`), or
  `mini -t "…" --yolo --exit-immediately` for one task.

## Open Interpreter

Open Interpreter, rebuilt as a Codex CLI derivative (`doz try open-interpreter`; its command is `interpreter`), on an
key of the provider or gateway you choose: **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** — a Codex-style provider Dozable names on its command line
(`-c model_providers…`, `-m`; on xAI the model is `grok-build-0.1`).

- **Installed** from its GitHub release (the static linux-arm64 build), checked against the SHA-512 Dozable recorded.
  Every base, Alpine included.
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (`doz account add NAME --provider xai` — or `openrouter`, `vercel-ai-gateway`, `google`; `--api-key` for Anthropic, `--openai-key` for OpenAI); the sandbox only gets a placeholder.
- **Set up for you:** its analytics, plugins, apps and update check off (without them it calls ChatGPT's and GitHub's
  servers).
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch), and one read when its TUI starts: Codex's announcement tips file on GitHub.
- **Use:** `interpreter` (a session; with approvals off, `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`), or
  `interpreter exec --skip-git-repo-check "…"` for one task.

## Crush (Charmbracelet)

Charmbracelet's terminal agent (`doz try crush`), on the key of the provider or gateway you
choose: **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** — its model and provider set in its settings at every run (on xAI, `grok-build-0.1`). Its licence is FSL-1.1-MIT: each release becomes MIT two years on, and until then it forbids a
competing use — running it in your own sandbox is not one.

- **Installed** from its GitHub release (the static linux-arm64 build), checked against the SHA-512 Dozable recorded.
  Every base, Alpine included.
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (`doz account add NAME --provider xai` — or `openrouter`, `vercel-ai-gateway`, `google`; `--api-key` for Anthropic, `--openai-key` for OpenAI); the sandbox only gets a placeholder.
- **Set up for you:** its metrics and provider auto-update off (`CRUSH_DISABLE_METRICS`,
  `CRUSH_DISABLE_PROVIDER_AUTO_UPDATE`; without them it calls Charm's catalogue and Hyper hosts).
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch), and GitHub's API for one read: its latest release, asked at each run.
- **Use:** `crush` (a session; with approvals off, `--yolo`), or `crush run -q "…"` for one
  task.

## MiMo Code (Xiaomi)

Xiaomi's terminal agent, an OpenCode derivative (`doz try mimo-code`, or `mimo`), on the key of the provider or gateway you
choose: **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** (on xAI the model is `xai/grok-build-0.1`). Its code is MIT, with Xiaomi's use restrictions beside it.

- **Installed** from the npm registry's linux-arm64 package, integrity-checked. Debian and Node bases (not Alpine yet).
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (`doz account add NAME --provider xai` — or `openrouter`, `vercel-ai-gateway`, `google`; `--api-key` for Anthropic, `--openai-key` for OpenAI); the sandbox only gets a placeholder.
- **Set up for you:** its usage analytics off (`MIMOCODE_ENABLE_ANALYSIS=false` — by default it posts to
  tracking.miui.com, which is never allowed), its online model list, auto-update and sharing off.
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch).
- **Use:** `mimo` (a session; with approvals off, `--dangerously-skip-permissions`), or
  `mimo run "…"` for one task.

## CodeWhale

A provider-neutral terminal agent, formerly DeepSeek TUI (`doz try codewhale`), on the key of the provider or gateway you choose:
**Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI** or **OpenRouter** — its built-in providers (on xAI the model is `grok-build-0.1`; it has no Vercel AI Gateway provider).

- **Installed** from its GitHub release (the static linux-arm64 build), checked against the SHA-512 Dozable recorded.
  Every base, Alpine included.
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (`doz account add NAME --provider xai` — or `openrouter`, `vercel-ai-gateway`, `google`; `--api-key` for Anthropic, `--openai-key` for OpenAI); the sandbox only gets a placeholder.
- **Set up for you:** its usage telemetry and update check off (`CODEWHALE_TELEMETRY=0`, `CODEWHALE_NO_UPDATE_CHECK`),
  its onboarding skipped. Its TUI refreshes the models.dev catalogue when it starts; Dozable keeps that out quietly, and
  it uses the catalogue it has.
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch).
- **Use:** `codewhale` (a session; with approvals off, `--approval-policy never`), or `codewhale exec "…"` for one task
  (`--auto` lets it use tools).

## Maki

A Rust terminal agent with Lua plugins (`doz try maki`), on the key of the provider or gateway you choose:
**Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default) or **OpenRouter** — its own providers, the model on its command line (on xAI, `xai/grok-build-0.1`).

- **Installed** from its GitHub release (the static linux-arm64 build), checked against the SHA-512 Dozable recorded.
  Every base, Alpine included.
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (`doz account add NAME --provider xai` — or `openrouter`, `vercel-ai-gateway`, `google`; `--api-key` for Anthropic, `--openai-key` for OpenAI); the sandbox only gets a placeholder.
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch), and GitHub's API for one read: its latest release, asked when its TUI starts. It also
  fetches the models.dev catalogue then; Dozable keeps that out quietly, and it does without it.
- **Use:** `maki` (a session; with approvals off, `--yolo`), or `maki -p "…"` for one task.

## oh-my-pi

A batteries-included derivative of pi (`doz try omp`), on the key of the provider or gateway you choose:
**Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** — its built-in providers, the model on its command line (on xAI, `xai/grok-build-0.1`).

- **Installed** from its GitHub release (the linux-arm64 build), checked against the SHA-512 Dozable recorded. Debian
  and Node bases (not Alpine yet).
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (`doz account add NAME --provider xai` — or `openrouter`, `vercel-ai-gateway`, `google`; `--api-key` for Anthropic, `--openai-key` for OpenAI); the sandbox only gets a placeholder.
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch). When it starts it checks for a newer release and asks several model gateways for
  their public model lists (Kilo, Venice, ZenMux, Command Code, Charm Hyper, Alibaba Model Studio, a model
  catalogue); no setting turns that off, so Dozable keeps those requests out quietly, and it does without them.
- **Use:** `omp` (a session), or `omp -p "…"` for one task.

## Tau

Hugging Face's Python port of pi (`doz try tau`), on the key of the provider or gateway you choose:
**Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI** (the default), **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** or **Vercel AI Gateway** — its own providers, named on its command line (on xAI, `grok-build-0.1`).

- **Installed** from PyPI into its own Python environment: Dozable's Python and exactly the packages Dozable locked, each
  checked against its recorded hash. Debian and Node bases (not Alpine yet).
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (`doz account add NAME --provider xai` — or `openrouter`, `vercel-ai-gateway`, `google`; `--api-key` for Anthropic, `--openai-key` for OpenAI); the sandbox only gets a placeholder.
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given (any of those it can use, so you can switch). Its update check and its model catalogue refresh are turned off.
- **Use:** `tau` (a session), or `tau -p "…"` for one task.

## Gemini CLI (Google) — superseded

Superseded by Antigravity CLI: Google retired Gemini CLI for personal accounts; it still works with a **paid** Gemini
API key. Dozable keeps it, listed after the current agents; `doz try gemini` says so first.

- **Installed** from the npm registry, integrity-checked. Node, Debian and Alpine (on Alpine its shell tool runs
  without a terminal).
- **Key:** a Gemini API key, as Antigravity CLI. Never the Google sign-in (Google's terms forbid third-party tools from
  using it).
- **Set up for you:** approval prompts off, usage statistics off, auto-update off.

## Coming: CodeBuddy Code, Every Code

Two agents Dozable had recipes for are **coming** again, because their first screen is a sign-in Dozable cannot offer
(`doz search` says why):

- **CodeBuddy Code** (Tencent) asks you to sign in to a CodeBuddy account at its first screen, even with Dozable's model
  set.
- **Every Code** (just-every, a Codex CLI fork) shows a ChatGPT sign-in whenever it has no login file, whatever
  provider is set.

Each comes back when it can start on the model Dozable gives it.

## What each one calls — the network profiles

Dozable keeps a **network profile** of every agent: a fresh try with the network open and every request logged, its
first start and a short task, and for each host and path it called, a decision — allowed (and why), allowed by its
path only, turned off by the agent's own setting, or refused. The recipes are checked against these profiles on every
build, so an agent never meets a refusal on a normal first run, and a new release is profiled again before anything
new is allowed (`make profile-agents` in the source tree; `make agent-currency` says which agents moved).

## Is it current?

`doz search`, `doz try` and the Quick try show each agent's **latest release** as your Mac last saw it — the version,
the day it came out, how long ago, and **active** (a release in the last 3 months), **quiet** (none for 3),
**stale** (none for 6) or **deprecated** by its maker — and its **standing**: current, or superseded by another
agent. See [Is it current?](https://dozable.com/docs/try-and-search.md#is-it-supported-doz-search).

## New agents without a new doz — the recipe catalogue

Every agent Dozable runs is described by a **recipe**, and each version of doz carries its own set. Dozable can also
publish its recipes on their own, as a **recipe catalogue** on its recipe directory, `doz.sh`, so a new agent
or a fix to one reaches you without a new release of doz:

- **Where from.** doz asks `doz.sh` for it, at most once a day, and reads every file from the same place. The request carries
  doz's version in its user agent and nothing else. (Earlier builds asked the update site, and keep their own recipes.)
- **Signed.** doz uses a catalogue only when it is signed with Dozable's own key — the one that signs its updates — and
  every file in it is exactly what was signed. Anything else is ignored, whole.
- **Checked like the built-in recipes.** A catalogue that fails any check doz runs on its own recipes is ignored whole
  (never used in part), and `doz doctor` says why. A catalogue can add agents and update them; it never takes one away,
  so a sandbox you made keeps working.
- **Claude Code, pi and Codex are always your doz's own** — a catalogue never changes them.
- **When it applies.** While doz's daemon runs it looks for a newer catalogue at most once a day, quietly (offline is
  fine). A new one applies when the daemon next starts — by itself once nothing is running, or `doz daemon restart`. A doz
  older than a catalogue needs keeps its own recipes, and doz never uses a catalogue older than the recipes it carries.
- **Where you see it.** `doz doctor`'s `recipes` line says what this doz uses: `embedded (doz 0.37.24)` — its own — or
  `catalogue 3 from 2026-10-26`, and whether a newer one is waiting.

Until Dozable publishes a catalogue, every doz simply uses its own recipes. A build you make yourself from the source
always uses its own.

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/ai-tools

# Other AI tools

> **Unpublished for now.** Every tool on this page is unpublished in this version of Dozable: in no list, and
> `doz try fabric` (or `doz new`, `doz create`) says so. So is the **Vercel AI Gateway**: OpenRouter is the gateway
> offered now (`--gateway openrouter`). A sandbox you already made with one, and a Vercel key you already added, keep
> working. The rest of this page describes them as they work when published.

Beside the coding agents, Dozable runs AI tools that are not coding agents: command-line tools that answer a prompt,
prompt toolkits, agent frameworks. Each is tried like an agent (`doz try TOOL`) and uses an **API key** of a provider
or a **gateway** Dozable offers. The key stays on your Mac; the sandbox only gets a placeholder, which Dozable's proxy swaps
for the key on the way out, and only to that provider's or gateway's own API.

```sh
doz try fabric                                  # Fabric, on its default (a Google AI key)
doz try shell-gpt --provider openai             # ShellGPT on an OpenAI key
doz try gptme --gateway openrouter --model anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6
doz try aichat --dry-run                        # the plan: its model, and every provider and gateway it can use
doz try stitch                                  # Google Stitch's command line, on a Stitch API key
doz search gemini                               # what Dozable runs with a Google key
```

## Providers and gateways

Most tools here can talk to more than one: **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **xAI**, **Google AI** (the Gemini API), and the
gateways **OpenRouter** and **Vercel AI Gateway** (one key, many models — their model names are `creator/name`). Which
ones depends on the tool: each section below lists them, its default first. Choose one with `--provider` (or
`--gateway`) on `doz try`, `doz new`, `doz create` and `doz up`, or in the Quick try's setup (“Where TOOL gets its model”, then the model picker) and New Sandbox, or in doz_project.yaml (`model_source:`, `model:`);
`--model` picks the model (the default is the provider's or gateway's: `grok-4-1-fast`, `gpt-5.4-mini`,
`gemini-2.5-flash`, `claude-sonnet-4-6`, `openai/gpt-5.4-mini` …).

- **The key is a key of that provider or gateway**: `doz account add NAME --provider openrouter` (or
  `vercel-ai-gateway`, `xai`, `google`), `--api-key` for Anthropic, `--openai-key` for OpenAI — never a Claude
  subscription or a ChatGPT sign-in. The sandbox's account decides which one it talks to; `doz account use NAME ACCOUNT`
  switches it (from its next session).
- **Dozable sets the tool's own settings** for the choice (a base URL, a model, its provider switch) at every session and
  `doz exec` — a value you set yourself wins — and nothing is baked into the image, so one image serves every choice.
- **The key only ever goes to that provider's or gateway's own hosts.** The tool may reach the others' (so you can
  switch), but a placeholder sent to any other host is refused.
- The default models were chosen from the providers' published names; a model a provider has renamed or retired is
  refused by the provider itself — choose another with `--model`.

### Which models: `doz models`

```sh
doz models --gateway openrouter               # OpenRouter's models: id, context, price in and out per million tokens, tools
doz models --gateway vercel-ai-gateway sonnet # Vercel AI Gateway's, narrowed to those matching "sonnet"
doz models --gateway openrouter --refresh     # read the list again now
doz models --provider xai                     # a provider: the model Dozable checked
```

- **A gateway publishes its list**, and Dozable reads it on this Mac — never from a sandbox — at most once a day, keeping
  the last one (offline, the last list stays; `--refresh` reads it now and starts Dozable's background process when it
  is not running). `--json` gives it as data.
- **A provider lists its models only with a key**, so `doz models` shows the model Dozable checked for it; any other id
  that provider names may still be given with `--model`.
- **A `--model` a gateway does not list is used as given**, with a note on the closest ids it does list:
  `note: openai/gpt-5.4-mni is not in OpenRouter's model list — did you mean openai/gpt-5.4-mini, …? (used as given)`.
  Lists change every week, so it is never refused for that.

A tool that answers and exits opens a **shell** as its session, with the tool on the PATH. Type its commands there.

## OpenClaw

A self-hosted personal agent with shell and file tools. Its own docs recommend running it isolated: in a sandbox its
tools act on the sandbox, not your Mac.

- **Installed** from the npm registry, integrity-checked, on Node 24, which Dozable installs for it (Debian-based bases
  only). The image is large (about 1.3 GB).
- **Key:** Google AI (default), Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI or OpenRouter — OpenClaw's own providers, which read the key's
  usual variable. Its models are `provider/model` (`google/gemini-2.5-flash` by default); Dozable puts the chosen one in
  `DOZ_MODEL`.
- **Use:** one headless turn — `openclaw agent exec "a task" --auth-env-only --model "$DOZ_MODEL"`. Its auto-update is
  off (`OPENCLAW_NO_AUTO_UPDATE`).
- **May reach:** those providers' APIs (the key goes to the chosen one only).
- **Later:** its Gateway (the TUI, the Control UI on port 18789, chat channels such as Telegram or Slack) is a
  background service with a web page, which Dozable does not run or forward yet. You can start it by hand in a second
  session (`openclaw gateway`), but nothing keeps it running and the Control UI is not reachable from the Mac.

## nanobot

A small personal agent in the terminal (an OpenClaw-style assistant its authors keep auditable).

- **Installed** from PyPI with every dependency pinned by its hash, on Dozable's own Python (Debian-based bases).
- **Key:** xAI (default), OpenAI, Google AI, OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway. nanobot is set up with its custom
  OpenAI-compatible provider whose base URL, key and model come from `DOZ_MODEL_BASE_URL`, `DOZ_MODEL_API_KEY` and
  `DOZ_MODEL`, which Dozable sets for the choice (`~/.nanobot/config.json`, keys written only when not there yet).
- **Use:** `nanobot` opens its terminal UI (the session); one headless turn is `nanobot agent -m "a task"`.
- **May reach:** those providers' and gateways' APIs, and OpenAI's public tokenizer file (`openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net/encodings/…`), which
  the token counter it uses downloads at the first turn.
- **Later:** its gateway (chat channels) and web UI need a background service and a forwarded port.

## gptme

A terminal agent with shell, Python and file tools.

- **Installed** from PyPI with every dependency pinned by its hash, on Dozable's own Python (Debian-based bases).
- **Key:** xAI (default), Anthropic, OpenAI, Google AI, OpenRouter, or Vercel AI Gateway (through its OpenAI-compatible
  `local` provider). Dozable sets `MODEL` to `provider/model` for the choice (or `--model`).
- **Set up for you:** its confirmation prompts off (`--no-confirm`; `gptme.permissions = ask` keeps them).
- **Use:** `gptme` (the session); one headless run is `gptme --non-interactive "a task"`.
- **May reach:** those providers' and gateways' APIs, and OpenAI's public tokenizer file (as nanobot).
- **Later:** its browser tool needs Chromium in the image; `gptme-server`'s web UI needs a forwarded port.

## llm

Simon Willison's command-line tool for prompting models (and logging every prompt to SQLite).

- **Installed** from PyPI with every dependency pinned by its hash, on Dozable's own Python (Debian-based bases), with the
  `llm-grok` plugin, which talks to xAI.
- **Key:** xAI (default, through `llm-grok`) or OpenAI (its own models). Dozable sets `LLM_MODEL` to the chosen model.
- **Use:** the session is a shell. `llm "a question"` (or `-m MODEL`).
- **May reach:** xAI's and OpenAI's APIs. Other providers need plugins, which are not in the image.
- **Later:** `llm install` (more plugins) needs PyPI at run time, which no permission offers yet.

## ShellGPT

A command-line assistant (`sgpt`) that answers questions and turns requests into shell commands (`sgpt --shell`).

- **Installed** from PyPI with every dependency pinned by its hash, on Dozable's own Python (Debian-based bases).
- **Key:** xAI (default), OpenAI, Google AI (its OpenAI-compatible endpoint), OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway. ShellGPT
  speaks OpenAI's API; Dozable points it at the choice (`API_BASE_URL`, `DEFAULT_MODEL`) and puts the key's placeholder
  under `OPENAI_API_KEY` too — it still works only on the chosen API.
- **Use:** the session is a shell. `sgpt "a question"`, `sgpt --shell "find large files"`.
- **May reach:** those providers' and gateways' APIs.

## ZeroClaw

A personal-agent runtime in one Rust program, with shell, file and web tools.

- **Installed** from the project's linux-arm64 release on GitHub, checked against the SHA-512 Dozable recorded (Debian-based
  bases).
- **Key:** xAI (default), OpenAI, Google AI, OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway. ZeroClaw is set up
  (`~/.zeroclaw/config.toml`, keys written only when not there yet) with one OpenAI-shaped provider and one agent,
  `main`, at full autonomy — the sandbox is the boundary. Dozable points the provider at the choice (its uri, model and the
  key's placeholder) through ZeroClaw's own environment overrides.
- **Use:** the session is `zeroclaw agent -a main`; one headless turn is `zeroclaw agent -a main -m "a task"`.
- **May reach:** those providers' and gateways' APIs.
- **Later:** its gateway, web dashboard and chat channels need a background service and a forwarded port.

## AIChat

An all-in-one LLM command line: a chat REPL, a shell assistant (`-e`), roles, sessions.

- **Installed** from the project's static linux-arm64 release on GitHub, checked against the SHA-512 Dozable recorded.
  Every base, Alpine included.
- **Key:** xAI (default), Anthropic, OpenAI, Google AI or OpenRouter — its built-in clients, with no config file
  (`AICHAT_PROVIDER`, `AICHAT_MODEL`: `xai:grok-4-1-fast` by default, or `-m`).
- **Use:** the session is its REPL; one question is `aichat "a question"`, a shell command `aichat -e "list big files"`.
- **May reach:** those providers' APIs.
- **Its playground:** run `aichat --serve` in a session; the sandbox's **Open AIChat web** button (or
  `doz open NAME`) opens it in your Mac's browser — see [Web ports](https://dozable.com/docs/web-ports.md).

## tgpt

A small terminal chat client.

- **Installed** from the project's static linux-arm64 release on GitHub, checked against the SHA-512 Dozable recorded.
  Every base, Alpine included.
- **Providers:** **Google AI** (the default — its Gemini provider, `AI_PROVIDER=gemini`), **OpenAI**, **xAI**,
  **OpenRouter** and **Vercel AI Gateway** (its OpenAI provider at the chosen source's chat endpoint, `OPENAI_URL`,
  `OPENAI_MODEL`).
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (a placeholder in the sandbox). On Google AI, Dozable's proxy sends the
  key as Google's `x-goog-api-key` header — checked against a stand-in provider, not yet against Google itself.
- **Use:** the session is its interactive mode (`tgpt -i`); one question is `tgpt -q "a question"`.
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given. Its key-less "free" providers are other companies' services, which Dozable does not allow
  by default.

## smolagents

Hugging Face's library for agents that write and run Python, with its `smolagent` command. Its own README says its
built-in Python executor is not a security boundary and recommends a sandbox — this is one.

- **Installed** from PyPI (with its toolkit and OpenAI extras) with every dependency pinned by its hash, on Dozable's own
  Python (Debian-based bases).
- **Key:** xAI (default), OpenAI, Google AI, OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway, through its OpenAI-compatible model:
  `smolagent "a task" --model-type OpenAIModel --model-id "$DOZ_MODEL" --api-base "$OPENAI_BASE_URL"` (Dozable sets both
  for the choice; the key's placeholder is also `OPENAI_API_KEY`).
- **Set up for you:** Hugging Face Hub telemetry off (`HF_HUB_DISABLE_TELEMETRY`).
- **Use:** the session is a shell.
- **May reach:** those providers' and gateways' APIs. Its web-search tools reach the open web only when you allow it.

## Agent Development Kit (Google)

Google's Python framework for building agents (`adk`).

- **Installed** from PyPI with every dependency pinned by its hash, on Dozable's own Python (Debian-based bases).
- **Key:** a Gemini API key, read by Google's genai SDK (`GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=FALSE`: the API key, never Vertex AI).
- **Use:** the session is a shell. Write an agent (a Python package folder whose agent module defines `root_agent`), then
  `adk run FOLDER` talks to it in the terminal.
- **May reach:** the Gemini API.
- **Later:** `adk web` (its dev UI) and `adk api_server` need a forwarded port.

## promptfoo

A command line for evaluating and red-teaming prompts and LLM apps. A red-team run sends attack prompts with your key —
in a sandbox the key stays on the Mac.

- **Installed** from the npm registry, integrity-checked, on Node 22 (Debian-based bases).
- **Key:** xAI (default), OpenAI, Google AI, OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway: its `openai` provider is pointed at the
  choice (`OPENAI_BASE_URL`, the key under `OPENAI_API_KEY`) — `providers: ["openai:chat:MODEL"]` in a config, the model
  in `DOZ_MODEL`; on xAI its `xai` provider works too.
- **Set up for you:** its telemetry and update check off (`PROMPTFOO_DISABLE_TELEMETRY`, `PROMPTFOO_DISABLE_UPDATE`).
- **Use:** the session is a shell. `promptfoo eval -c promptfooconfig.yaml`.
- **May reach:** those providers' and gateways' APIs. **Kept out, quietly:** `r.promptfoo.app` — with its telemetry off, promptfoo still sends one
  "telemetry disabled" event each run; no setting stops it, so Dozable refuses it without counting it as a refusal.
- **Later:** `promptfoo view` (its web viewer) needs a forwarded port.

## clai (Pydantic AI)

Pydantic AI's command line for chatting with models.

- **Installed** from PyPI with every dependency pinned by its hash, on Dozable's own Python (Debian-based bases).
- **Providers:** **xAI** (the default), **Anthropic**, **OpenAI**, **Google AI**, **OpenRouter** and **Vercel AI
  Gateway** — Pydantic AI's OpenAI-compatible model at the chosen source's base URL (`OPENAI_BASE_URL`), or its
  Anthropic model (`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`). Dozable puts the model on its command line (`-m openai-chat:MODEL`; on xAI,
  `grok-4-1-fast`), unless you give your own `-m`.
- **Key:** an API key of that provider or gateway (a placeholder in the sandbox, also under `OPENAI_API_KEY` or
  `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`).
- **Use:** one question is `clai --no-stream "a question"`.
- **May reach:** the API of the provider or gateway it was given.
- **Later:** `clai web` (its chat page) needs a forwarded port.

## Fabric

A prompt toolkit: crowd-sourced "patterns" applied to text you pipe in.

- **Installed** from the project's own linux-arm64 release on GitHub, checked against the SHA-512 Dozable recorded when it
  pinned the release. Debian, Node and Alpine bases.
- **Key:** Google AI (default: `doz account add google --provider google`; get one at https://aistudio.google.com/apikey),
  Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI or OpenRouter — its own vendors. Dozable sets `DEFAULT_VENDOR` and `DEFAULT_MODEL` for the choice
  (over the ones in `~/.config/fabric/.env`, written only when not there yet).
- **Patterns** come with it: its release's some 260 patterns, checksum-verified when its image is baked, in
  `/opt/fabric/patterns` (`CUSTOM_PATTERNS_DIRECTORY`) — `fabric -l` lists them; `fabric -U` (from GitHub) is not needed.
- **Use:** `echo "some text" | fabric "summarise this"`, `cat notes.txt | fabric -p summarize` — or the sandbox page's Guide.
- **May reach:** those providers' APIs.
- **Its REST API:** run `fabric --serve` in a session; the sandbox's **Open Fabric REST API** button (or `doz open NAME`)
  opens its API reference in your Mac's browser — see [Web ports](https://dozable.com/docs/web-ports.md).

## Google Stitch CLI

Google Labs' command line for Stitch, Google's UI design service: it generates and edits app screens from a prompt (on
Google's side, with Gemini) and prints their ids and links. It is a client of the hosted service — every command is a
call to Stitch.

- **Installed** from the npm registry, integrity-checked, on Node 22 (Debian-based bases).
- **Key:** a **Stitch API key** (it starts `AQ.`), made in Stitch's settings at https://stitch.withgoogle.com —
  `doz account add stitch --provider google-stitch --no-verify`. Not a Gemini or Google Cloud key (`AIza…`), which Stitch
  refuses. Generation uses your Stitch account's quota.
- **Not offered:** its Google sign-in (`stitch login`), which would keep Google tokens in the sandbox. The API key covers
  projects, screens and design systems.
- **Use:** the session is a shell. `stitch find projects --json`;
  `stitch generate screen --new-project "My app" --prompt "A sign-up screen" --device MOBILE`. Every command takes
  `--json` and `--dry-run`.
- **May reach:** Stitch's API only (`stitch.googleapis.com`). It has no update check; its client header's telemetry is off.
- **Preview:** `stitch serve -p PROJECT --port 3000` serves a project's screens; `doz ports add NAME 3000` opens them on
  your Mac — see [Web ports](https://dozable.com/docs/web-ports.md).

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/web-ports

# Web ports: opening a sandbox's web page on your Mac

Some tools serve a web page from inside the sandbox: a chat playground, a workflow editor, the dev server of the app
you are building. A **forward** makes such a port reachable in your Mac's browser, at `http://127.0.0.1:PORT/` —
on this Mac only, never on your network.

```sh
doz ports my-app                 # the sandbox's forwarded ports: each one's URL on this Mac and whether it listens
doz ports add my-app 3000        # forward the dev server on port 3000 too (kept until you remove it)
doz open my-app                  # open its first web port in your browser (signed in, when the tool says how)
doz open my-app 3000 --print     # or print the URL
doz ports rm my-app 3000         # stop forwarding it
```

In the dashboard, a sandbox's header has an **Open** button for each web port while the sandbox runs, and its
Overview tab lists every forward with its state.

## Where the ports come from

- **The tool's own.** A tool whose recipe declares a web port gets it forwarded in every sandbox made from it — for
  example AIChat's playground (`aichat --serve`, port 8000, opened at `/playground`). Run the server in a session;
  its Open button works as soon as it listens.
- **Yours.** `doz ports add NAME PORT` forwards any port a program you start listens on — a dev server, a notebook,
  a dashboard. `--title` names its button; `--path` is what `doz open` opens. At most 16 per sandbox.

## Pages that ask you to sign in

Some web pages ask for a sign-in that the tool hands out in the sandbox. OpenCode 2's web app is one: `opencode pair`
prints a link that works once, for five minutes. When a tool's recipe says how to get that link, **Open signs your
browser in for you** — in the dashboard and with `doz open`:

1. Dozable runs the tool's own sign-in command in the sandbox (`opencode pair`), as the sandbox's user.
2. It takes the link the command printed for that port, keeps its path, and opens it at your Mac's port for the
   forward — so it works even when the port on your Mac moved.
3. Your browser lands on the page, signed in.

The link is a one-time secret: Dozable never shows it, logs it, keeps it or sends it anywhere but your browser.
`doz open NAME PORT --print` prints the page's plain address instead (without signing in).

If the sign-in does not work (the command failed, took longer than 15 seconds or printed no link), Dozable says why
and opens the page as it is; you can still sign in by hand, as `doz ports NAME` describes. Open on another device
(through `doz ui --lan`) never signs in: the page is on your Mac.

## When it listens

A forward listens **while the sandbox runs**. When the sandbox stops, sleeps or hibernates, its listeners close at
once; when it starts or wakes again — and after Dozable itself restarts — they come back by themselves. `doz ports`
says `stopped` until then.

The port on your Mac is the sandbox's own when it is free. When another program on your Mac already uses it (or it is
below 1024), Dozable picks a free one, says so (`moved`), and keeps it for next time.

## What a forward can and cannot do

- **This Mac only.** It listens on `127.0.0.1` (and `::1`), never on the network. Other programs on this Mac can reach
  it, as they can any local server — a tool with its own sign-in still asks for it.
- **Inbound only.** It carries your browser's requests to the program in the sandbox. It does not let the sandbox
  reach anything: what the program itself may reach is still decided by the sandbox's [network](https://dozable.com/docs/permissions-and-network.md).
- **No key crosses it.** Your keys are swapped in by Dozable's proxy only on the sandbox's own outbound requests; a
  forward never touches them. A page that shows its environment shows a placeholder, which is useless anywhere else.
- **From another device** (the dashboard through [`doz ui --lan`](https://dozable.com/docs/doz-serve.md)), `127.0.0.1` is that device, not your
  Mac: the button says the port is on the Mac instead of opening it there.

How it works: each connection your browser makes is relayed into the sandbox by Dozable's small helper there, to the
program's own `localhost`. A program that listens on `127.0.0.1` or `0.0.0.0` inside the sandbox both work.

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/your-own-recipes

# Your own recipes, and community catalogues

Every tool Dozable runs comes from a **recipe**: a YAML file that says how the tool is installed, how it runs, which
key it uses and what it may reach. Dozable ships its own. You can also write **your own**, and add **community
catalogues** — recipes someone else publishes, signed with their key.

A recipe that is not Dozable's is labelled everywhere it is shown: **yours**, or **community · NAME** — in
`doz search`, in `doz try`'s list, in the plan, and on the dashboard's Quick try and New Sandbox. It can never use the
name of one of Dozable's own recipes.

## Your own recipe

```sh
doz recipe new mytool --from opencode     # a copy of one of Dozable's recipes, renamed — a good start
doz recipe new mytool                     # or an empty one to fill in
doz recipe check mytool                   # does it meet the minimum requirements for a community recipe?
doz try mytool                            # use it like any other
```

The file is `~/.config/doz/recipes/mine/mytool.yaml` (your settings folder). Edit it with any editor — the first line
points editors at the format's schema, so they check it as you type. The format is in the repository's
`docs/recipes/RECIPE-FORMAT.md`.

`doz recipe add ./tool.yaml` copies a file in as one of yours, after it passes the check. `doz recipe ls` lists yours
and every catalogue's: where each came from, whether it is in use (or why it was refused), and whether it was checked.

## The minimum requirements for a community recipe

`doz recipe check` goes through them one by one, then gives one verdict. Every recipe that is not Dozable's must meet
them, or it is not used:

- it is a schema 2 recipe, read strictly, and passes every rule Dozable's own recipes pass;
- its name is none of Dozable's, and it is not a built-in agent;
- its maker, its link (https), its licences and a description are filled in;
- its text is plain: no control or direction characters, a short name and description;
- every download is pinned with its checksum — and Dozable installs exactly that release, never a newer one;
- it has a guide and a check turn;
- it names no credential, and holds nothing shaped like a key;
- it hides nothing: no hosts kept out silently, no hidden hosts it may reach — only permissions you see;
- it wears no mark from Dozable's icon registry, and belongs to no family of versions.

**`doz recipe check mytool --full`** also builds and tries it for real, on this Mac, in a scratch folder (minutes the
first time — the image is built there and kept for the next run). It uses fake keys and a stand-in for the model
provider, so no real key is involved: the image is built at its pinned release, its verify commands run, a fresh
sandbox's first screen is read (no setup wizard, sign-in or consent question), its check turn runs and must answer,
its guide's steps run, and Dozable checks that only a placeholder of the key is in the sandbox and that the placeholder
sent anywhere else is refused. It does not check the tool's status reports, its web ports, every model provider it can
use, or a tool that answers only through a tool call.

A pass is recorded with the checksum of the file that passed: `doz recipe ls` says when the file has changed since.

## Community catalogues

```sh
doz recipe source add https://example.com/v1/recipes.json --key BASE64KEY
doz recipe source ls
doz recipe source rm example
```

Adding one shows its publisher's key **fingerprint** (`SHA256:…`) and asks whether it is the one the publisher gave
you — compare it with what they publish. Nothing is downloaded before you confirm. In a script, give the fingerprint
you checked: `--fingerprint SHA256:…`.

A catalogue is used **whole or not at all**: if it is tampered with, signed with another key, or offers a name that is
already taken (by Dozable, by yours, or by a catalogue added earlier), none of it is used, and `doz recipe source ls`
says why. Dozable looks for a newer catalogue once a day while its daemon runs.

Before a sandbox of a community recipe is made, Dozable says whose recipe it is, what its image build installs and
reaches, and asks once for each version of it. `doz recipe trust NAME` says yes ahead, for scripts. On the dashboard,
Quick try's setup shows the same under **Whose recipe** before Start. Your own recipes are said, never asked.

## When a change applies

When no Dozable daemon is running, a change to your recipes or catalogues is used at once. While one runs, it applies at
its next start — `doz daemon restart` — so every command keeps using what the running daemon uses. A running dashboard
shows it after `doz ui restart`.

## Removing one

`doz recipe rm mytool` and `doz recipe source rm NAME` never break a sandbox made from the recipe: it is kept,
unpublished — it is offered nowhere, and a new sandbox of it is refused, but every sandbox made from it keeps working,
and its name stays theirs. `doz recipe ls --all` lists the kept ones; `doz recipe rm mytool --forget` drops one once no
sandbox uses it.

## Publishing a catalogue

A catalogue is the same format as Dozable's own recipe catalogue, signed with **your** key. From a checkout of the
Dozable repository:

```sh
swift Scripts/update-key.swift community-key ~/keys/my-recipes.key      # once: prints the public key and its fingerprint
make publish-recipes COMMUNITY=1 RECIPES_DIR=~/my-recipes UPDATE_KEY_FILE=~/keys/my-recipes.key UPDATES_DIR=~/my-site
```

It compiles every `*.yaml` in `RECIPES_DIR`, signs the catalogue with your key, checks that Dozable would use it
(`doz recipe source verify`), and writes `v1/recipes.json` and `v1/recipes/<serial>/` into your site's folder — never
pushed unless you add `PUSH=1`. Publish your public key and its fingerprint where people can compare them. Run
`doz recipe check --full` on each recipe before you publish it.

Your recipes never use Dozable's keys or its usage statistics: nothing about a recipe that is not Dozable's is counted.

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/dotfiles

# Your dotfiles

A new sandbox has a stock shell: no aliases, no prompt of yours, no editor settings. Point Dozable at your
**dotfiles** — a git repository of them, yours or someone else's — and every new sandbox gets them at its first
start, so a shell in any sandbox feels like yours.

## Setting it up

One setting, `sandbox.dotfiles`, for every new sandbox:

```bash
doz config set sandbox.dotfiles https://github.com/you/dotfiles   # a repository over https
doz config set sandbox.dotfiles ~/dotfiles                        # or a folder on this Mac that is a git repository
doz config unset sandbox.dotfiles                                 # none again (the default)
```

A sandbox can have its own instead: `doz new --dotfiles PATH|URL` (also `doz create`, `doz try` and `doz up`),
`dotfiles:` in its `doz_project.yaml`, or `--dotfiles none` for a sandbox without them. In the dashboard, the
**Settings** page takes a repository's URL (a folder on your Mac is set from the Mac, with `doz config set`); New
sandbox's review shows the repository, the commit it will get and what will run.

Nothing changes for anyone who does not set it.

## What happens

- **Fetched on your Mac.** Dozable fetches the repository with your Mac's own `git`, so a private repository works
  with the login your Mac already has — and that login never reaches the sandbox. A sandbox gets the commit its
  repository was at when it was made; that commit is recorded with the sandbox.
- **Only the files go in** — copied in from the Mac at the first start, into `~/.local/share/doz/dotfiles`. The
  sandbox's network is not used. (A folder on your Mac: its last commit — changes not committed are not included.)
- **Applied as the sandbox's user**, the way GitHub Codespaces does it:
  - if the repository has an install script, it runs — the first of `install.sh`, `install`, `bootstrap.sh`,
    `bootstrap`, `script/bootstrap`, `setup.sh`, `setup`, `script/setup` — from the files' folder, for at most 5
    minutes. Its output is in the boot log (`doz console NAME --steps`, the sandbox's Boot logs) and all of it in
    `~/.local/share/doz/dotfiles.log`. A script that fails is said; the sandbox still starts;
  - with no script, every dotfile and dot-folder at the top of the repository is **linked** into your home
    (`~/.bashrc` → the repository's `.bashrc`).
- **Once.** The sandbox remembers the commit it applied: later starts and wakes do nothing. A reset (which gives the
  sandbox a fresh system disk) applies them again at its next start.

## What is never touched

The link pass never replaces a file that is already there — yours stays, and `doz dotfiles NAME` lists it as kept.
The one exception is the image's own stock copy: a file that is byte-for-byte the one in `/etc/skel` (Debian's stock
`.bashrc` and `.profile`) is replaced by yours and kept beside it as `.bashrc.doz-stock`.

It never touches **Dozable's own** files either: the agents' settings and state (`~/.claude`, `~/.claude.json`,
`~/.codex`, `~/.pi`, `~/.config/opencode`, `~/.agents`, each tool's own folders), the agents' launchers in
`~/.local/bin`, and Dozable's state (`~/.local/state/doz`). A folder that holds one of them — `.config`, `.local` —
is linked entry by entry instead (`~/.config/nvim`, `~/.local/bin/mytool`), never as a whole. The repository's own
files (`.git`, `.github`, `.gitignore`) are not linked, and submodules are not fetched.

An install script is different: it is code you chose, and it runs as the sandbox's user, with the sandbox's network
policy — Dozable does not police what it does.

## Trust

Dotfiles are code that runs in the sandbox. So the first time a repository's commit would be applied, `doz` says what
will run and asks — once per repository and commit:

```
[doz] dotfiles: https://github.com/you/dotfiles at 3f2a9c41d0be (bash: aliases) — code that runs in the sandbox, as its user, at its first start:
  9 dotfiles linked into ~ — never over a file that is there, never over Dozable's own: .bashrc, .gitconfig, .vimrc, …
  the files are copied in from this Mac; no credential of yours enters the sandbox
Apply these dotfiles in the sandbox? [y/N]
```

Without a terminal (a script, `--json` in a pipe) it refuses and names the command that says yes ahead:

```bash
doz dotfiles trust https://github.com/you/dotfiles --commit 3f2a9c41d0be…   # this commit
doz dotfiles trust                                                         # the setting's repository, at its head now
```

## Seeing and updating them

```bash
doz dotfiles my-app            # the repository, the commit, what it does, how the last run went
doz dotfiles my-app --update   # move to the newest commit and apply it — now when it runs, else at its next start or wake
```

`--update` asks again for a commit you have not said yes to. With a repository that has no script, a file the new
commit removed loses its link, and a new one is linked. A sandbox that had no dotfiles takes the setting's with
`--update`.

The sandbox's page shows its dotfiles on its Home (**Folder**: the repository, the commit, how the last run went),
and the agent is told about them in its facts ("Dotfiles: the user's dotfiles … are applied in this home").

## Not covered

Dozable runs your repository's own script — it has no special support for chezmoi, stow or yadm beyond that (your
`install.sh` can call them). Secrets do not belong in dotfiles: anything in the repository is copied into every sandbox.

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/claude-code-other-models

# Claude Code with other models — a gateway, or a model server on your Mac

Claude Code talks to Anthropic by default: this Mac's Claude login, a setup token or an Anthropic API key, exactly as
in [Agents and accounts](https://dozable.com/docs/agents-and-accounts.md). It can also get its model from:

- **a gateway** — OpenRouter: one key, models from many makers, through the gateway's Anthropic-compatible endpoint;
- **a model server on this Mac** — Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp's `llama-server`, LiteLLM, vLLM or oMLX, reached by
  its port. No key.

Anthropic supports Claude models only. Another maker's model through a gateway or your own server is yours to judge —
it may not handle Claude Code's tools as well.

## Through a gateway (OpenRouter)

Add the gateway's key once — it stays in this Mac's keychain, like every key:

```
doz account add my-or --provider openrouter
```

Then try Claude Code through it, with a model by the gateway's name for it:

```
doz try claude-code --gateway openrouter --model anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6
```

`doz models --gateway openrouter` lists the gateway's models. The sandbox gets the gateway's address and a
placeholder in `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`; Dozable's proxy on the Mac swaps in the real key, and only on the way to
openrouter.ai. A placeholder sent anywhere else is refused. A Claude subscription is never used this way: the
gateway key replaces it.

## A model server on your Mac

Start the server on your Mac first (`ollama serve`, LM Studio's server, …), then:

```
doz try claude-code --provider local --local-port 11434 --model qwen3-coder
```

- `--local-port` is the port the server listens on (Ollama 11434, LM Studio 1234, llama-server 8080, LiteLLM 4000,
  vLLM and oMLX 8000).
- `--model` is the server's own name for the model (`ollama list`, LM Studio's list). Every alias Claude Code uses
  (and its subagents) gets that model, so it never asks your server for a Claude model it does not have.
- There is no key: Claude Code is given a fixed word in `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, which the local servers ignore.

`doz models --provider local` lists the servers known to work, with the port each uses by default.

The servers must speak **Anthropic's Messages API** (`/v1/messages`) — Ollama (0.14 or later), LM Studio (0.4.1 or
later), llama-server, LiteLLM, vLLM and oMLX do. A server that speaks only OpenAI's chat API (`mlx_lm.server`) needs
a translator in between: not yet.

In a project file:

```yaml
model_source: local
local_port: 11434
model: qwen3-coder
```

### What the sandbox can reach on your Mac

A sandbox has no network of its own: everything it sends goes through Dozable's proxy, which runs on your Mac. So:

- **One name, one port.** The sandbox reaches your server as `http://mac.dozable.internal:PORT`, for the port it was
  made with — the proxy sends that to `127.0.0.1:PORT` on your Mac. Any other port of that name is refused, and a
  sandbox made without a port cannot resolve the name at all.
- **Nothing else on your Mac.** `127.0.0.1`, `localhost` and `::1` through the proxy are refused for every sandbox,
  whatever its network — Open included — and so are your Mac's other addresses (a server listening on all of them is
  still reached only by the name above) and link-local addresses. (Inside the sandbox, `localhost` is the sandbox's own.)
- It is not a network permission: no preset or edit widens it. The sandbox's Network tab says it ("This Mac: port
  11434 only"), and so does the agent's own description of its sandbox.
- `doz doctor` checks that something answers on each such port.

The port is chosen when the sandbox is made. It is one entry of the sandbox's list of this Mac's ports: other
services on your Mac can be opened beside it (`--host-port PORT`, `doz net allow NAME host:PORT`), and
`host.dozable.internal` is the same route as `mac.dozable.internal` — see
[This Mac's ports](https://dozable.com/docs/permissions-and-network.md#this-macs-ports). The model server's own port belongs to its model
source: it stays open as long as the sandbox uses it.

## In the dashboard

Try (Claude Code's setup) and New sandbox (its Account step) show **Where Claude Code gets its model**: Anthropic
with its usual account choice, OpenRouter with its key, and **A model server on this Mac** with a port (one click
for the known servers) and the model. The sandbox's page shows where its model comes from ("via OpenRouter · model
…", "via this Mac's port 11434 · model …"). Accounts & keys says a server on your Mac needs no key.

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/bundling-doz-in-an-app

# Bundling doz in an app

**Most people do not need this page.** If you want Dozable on your Mac, install the `doz` command with Homebrew
([Installing, upgrading and uninstalling](https://dozable.com/docs/install-upgrade-uninstall.md)). This page is for people who build a Mac
app that runs sandboxes through Dozable, and carries `doz` inside the app to do it.

Every release of `doz` comes in two flavours, built from the same source at the same version:

| file on the releases page | what it is | who it's for |
|---|---|---|
| `doz-VERSION-macos-arm64.tar.gz` | the **command-line release** — what Homebrew installs | people |
| `doz-VERSION-macos-arm64-helper.tar.gz` | the **helper build** — the same daemon, made to live inside an app | app authors |

Each has its `.sha256` beside it, and a `.dSYM.zip` with its symbols (so a crash report from it can be symbolicated).

## Concepts

- **The daemon** is the `doz` process that owns a store's virtual machines and answers on `<store>/daemon.sock`. The
  helper build runs the very same daemon as the command-line release, speaking the same protocol: an app talks to it
  over that socket, as the `doz` command itself does. See [the daemon and its protocol](https://github.com/dozable/dozable/blob/main/docs/DOZABLEKIT.md) (the section
  "The doz daemon": JSON lines, one request, progress events, one answer).
- **The helper build** is that daemon with the parts a person uses at a terminal left out. The app is its interface.
- **The layout contract** is the folder an app copies whole into its bundle. Within a minor version (all of
  `0.37.x`, say) nothing in it moves or is renamed.

## How the helper build differs

| | command-line release | helper build |
|---|---|---|
| the daemon, `daemon.sock`, its protocol, every sandbox operation | ✓ | ✓ the same |
| read-only commands (`doz ls`, `doz inspect`, `doz doctor`, `doz daemon status`, `doz --version`) | ✓ | ✓ |
| the web dashboard (`doz ui`, `doz ui --lan`) | ✓ | — not built in: `doz ui` says it is "not in this build" |
| the setup wizards (`doz onboard`, `doz init`) and `doz try` | ✓ | — not built in (the same answer) |
| updates itself (`doz upgrade`, the daily check, `updates.mode`) | ✓ | — never: `doz upgrade` refuses, and it never looks for updates. Your app updates it |
| anonymous usage statistics and `doz signup` | ✓ (you can turn them off) | — never: not built in, so it sends nothing. What your app sends is your app's choice |
| `RELEASE` file says | `public` | `helper` |
| the daemon's status reports `flavour` | `cli` | `helper` |
| the pinned Linux kernel inside | ✓ | ✓ |
| stripped, with its symbols published as a `.dSYM.zip` | ✓ | ✓ |
| signed with Dozable's Developer ID (team `KJ8QMLWB97`), notarised, the virtualization entitlement | ✓ | ✓ the same |

Both carry the pinned Linux kernel, so a new Mac's first sandbox needs no kernel download (it used to fetch a
release archive of about 0.6 GB to keep 16 MB of it). The first start of a store copies the kernel into the store and
checks it; nothing is downloaded from kata-containers.

## Get it and verify it

From the project's GitHub releases page (`dozable/dozable`), take the helper tarball and its `.sha256`, then:

```sh
shasum -a 256 -c doz-VERSION-macos-arm64-helper.tar.gz.sha256
tar -xzf doz-VERSION-macos-arm64-helper.tar.gz
codesign --verify --strict doz-VERSION-helper/libexec/doz/doz
codesign -dv doz-VERSION-helper/libexec/doz/doz 2>&1 | grep TeamIdentifier=KJ8QMLWB97
```

Pin the version AND the sha256 in your build: the helper runs with the virtualization entitlement, so a tarball
whose checksum or team does not match must stop your build.

## The layout contract

```
doz-VERSION-helper/
├── README.md                         what this is, and a link to this page
└── libexec/doz/                      copy this folder WHOLE into your app
    ├── doz                           the program (signed, with the virtualization entitlement)
    ├── VERSION                       its version, one line
    ├── RELEASE                       helper
    ├── DozableKit_DozableKit.bundle/ the small Linux programs each sandbox uses (deckhold, doznet, dozview, tmux), and skills/ (doz skill show)
    ├── manual/                       this version's user manual: its pages, llms.txt, llms-full.txt, VERSION (doz docs)
    ├── kernels/vmlinux-6.18.15-186   the pinned Linux kernel (GPL-2.0, unmodified)
    └── licences/                     LICENSE, NOTICE, THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES.txt; kernel/: the kernel's source offer
```

`doz` finds everything beside its own (resolved) executable, so the folder works wherever it lands, as long as it
stays whole. The command-line release has the same `libexec/doz/` plus `bin/doz` (a link) and the dashboard's
bundle, `DozableKit_DozableWeb.bundle`.

## Rules for an app that carries it

1. **Copy `libexec/doz/` whole** to `YourApp.app/Contents/Resources/Helpers/doz/`. Not `Contents/MacOS/`: the daemon
   starts itself again from its own executable, and must find its parts beside it.
2. **Never re-sign it.** Its signature carries the virtualization entitlement; your app does not need that entitlement
   at all. Sign your app WITHOUT `--deep` (which would re-sign the helper and drop the entitlement).
3. **Replace it by rename, never in place.** Copy the new folder beside the old one and rename it over: a daemon still
   running the previous copy keeps its own file. Overwriting a running daemon's program makes macOS refuse its VMs.
4. **Give it its own store and its own settings.** Pass `--store` (or set `DOZ_STORE`) to a folder of your app's
   (`~/Library/Application Support/<your bundle id>/doz-store`, say), and set `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` to a folder of your
   app's, so it never shares a store or `doz.toml` with a person's own `doz`. Keep the store's path short: the socket
   path `<store>/daemon.sock` must fit in 103 bytes.
5. **One daemon per store.** The daemon holds `<store>/daemon.lock` for its whole life. Start it with
   `doz daemon start --store DIR`: it starts one detached (or finds the one already running) and answers with its
   status. While the lock is held, a daemon is there or is exiting: wait for `daemon.sock` to answer rather than start
   another process.
6. **Check whom you are talking to.** The status the daemon answers (the `ping` request, or `doz daemon status --json`)
   carries `version`, `protocolVersion` and `flavour`. Refuse a daemon whose version is not the one you carry, or whose
   `flavour` is not `helper` (a person's command-line `doz` pointed at your store), and say so.
7. **Updates are yours.** Ship a new helper with a new version of your app. The helper never replaces itself.

A minimal handshake over the socket:

```
→ {"v":1,"op":"ping"}
← {"ok":true,"result":{"version":"0.37.41","protocolVersion":1,"flavour":"helper","pid":4242,…}}
```

## The kernel and its source

Both tarballs carry Linux `vmlinux-6.18.15-186` exactly as kata-containers 3.28.0 builds it, checked against its
sha256 on every start. It is GPL-2.0: its provenance and Dozable's written offer of its source are in the tarball
(`libexec/doz/licences/kernel/`) and in the repository ([`Guest/kernel/PROVENANCE.md`](https://github.com/dozable/dozable/blob/main/Guest/kernel/PROVENANCE.md)).
If you redistribute the helper, keep `licences/` with it — it is part of the layout for that reason.

## Settings

The helper reads the same settings as the command-line release (see [Settings reference](https://dozable.com/docs/settings-reference.md)),
from `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/doz/doz.toml`. `updates.mode` and `updates.channel` have no effect: it never updates itself.

## Troubleshooting

| symptom | what to do |
|---|---|
