| "cannot boot a VM", or `doz doctor` says the entitlement is missing | The helper was re-signed (an app signed with `--deep`?). Copy it again from the tarball. |
| `doz upgrade` says "this doz belongs to …" | That is the helper build: the app that carries it updates it. |
| `doz ui` says it is "not in this build" | The helper has no dashboard. The `doz` command from Homebrew has it. |
| A wake fails with "this daemon's program was updated underneath it" | The helper's file was overwritten while its daemon ran. Replace it by rename (rule 3); `doz daemon stop`, then retry. |

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/sessions-on-this-mac

# Sessions on this Mac

Every other page of this manual is about sandboxes: a program in its own small Linux machine, with a network that
reaches only what you allow and none of your keys. This page is about the one exception. **`@mac` is this Mac
itself.** A session there is held exactly like a sandbox's — you can detach from it, attach again from another
terminal, type into it from a script, read its screen, see what its agent is doing, end it and restart it — but the
program runs on your Mac, as you.

Use it for the work that has to happen on the Mac: building a Mac or iOS app with Xcode, driving the Simulator, an
agent working on a project that only builds here. Use a sandbox for everything else.

A new session on this Mac is **fenced** by default. **Fenced** means: macOS's own sandbox (Seatbelt) holds the
program and everything it starts to its project folder, its own temporary files and caches, and Dozable's proxy for
the network. Your Keychain, your secrets and your other folders are closed to it. `--unfenced` opts one session out —
then nothing is around it at all, and it acts as you. A workspace's manager and workers run fenced unless you choose a
micro VM or name unfenced. What the fence does and does not block is said plainly below ([What the fence
is not](#what-the-fence-is-not)) and in the [Security model](https://dozable.com/docs/security-model.md).

Each fenced session has a fence of its own — its own proxy, its own placeholders, its own profile — and shares none of it
with another session. A workspace's **fenced place** (Space files, 39) is a policy, not a shared box: two agents in one
fenced place are two sessions with two fences, each built from the place.

## Where an agent runs: the three choices

Every agent — a sandbox you make, a workspace's manager or worker — runs in one of three places. This table is the one
comparison; other pages point here.

| | **micro VM** (a sandbox) | **fenced** on this Mac (the default for a workspace's agents) | **unfenced** on this Mac (as you) |
|---|---|---|---|
| what holds it | its own Linux virtual machine: its own kernel and disk | macOS's own sandbox, around the program and everything it starts | nothing |
| files it reaches | the one folder shared at `/workspace` | its project folder (and folders you name with `--write` / `--read`), its own temp and caches; reads your tools | all of yours |
| network | only through Dozable's proxy, by its permissions; never this Mac's addresses | the same | all of yours |
| your keys and logins | never inside: a placeholder, swapped on the way out | the same; the Keychain closed (`--keychain` opens it) | yours, as you |
| memory | its own allocation (1 GiB for a plain shell, 2 GiB for an agent image; `--memory`), given back when it hibernates | a program on your Mac: what it uses | the same |
| start | a first start may prepare its image (minutes, once); then ~0.4 s to boot, ~0.3 s to wake | a program starting: about a second | the same |
| pick it when | the work is Linux work, or you want the strongest wall (a tool that installs things, a render, untrusted code) | the work has to happen on the Mac (Xcode, the Simulator, a Mac-only build), or you want no VM | signing and notarising, or anything that needs your Keychain and networking whole — knowingly |

What each wall does and does not stop is in the [Security model](https://dozable.com/docs/security-model.md); a sandbox's lifecycle is in
[Sandboxes and their lifecycle](https://dozable.com/docs/sandboxes-and-lifecycle.md).

## The idea, in plain words

A fenced session may change its project, and nothing else of yours that something unfenced would later run or load.
Its temporary files, its tool caches, its agent's settings folder and its git settings are its own, kept in a folder
Dozable makes for that session — so nothing it writes there can be picked up later by your own terminal, your own
Claude Code or your Xcode. The only thing it shares with you is the project folder itself: that is its work, and
you review it as you would any change.

Everything else follows from that rule:

- **Reads:** the system, your tools (what your `PATH` finds, Homebrew, toolchains, Xcode) and your `~/.ssh/config`
  and public keys. Not your home's other files: not `~/.ssh`'s keys, `~/.aws`, `~/.config`, `~/Library`, your shell
  history, your other projects.
- **Writes:** the project folder, and folders you name with `--write`.
- **Network:** only through Dozable's proxy, by the session's permissions — the same switches a sandbox has
  ([What the agent can do](https://dozable.com/docs/permissions-and-network.md)). Every connection is logged. Never this Mac's own
  addresses.
- **Keychain:** closed. `--keychain` opens it (signing as you needs it — and then it could read your saved logins too).
- **Logins:** Claude's and GitHub's reach the program as placeholders; the proxy puts the real one in on the way out,
  so the program never holds your token.

## Five ways to start one

The dashboard's **This Mac › New session on this Mac…** offers these five; each card shows exactly what it opens and the
command (Dozable never starts a session for you from the page — you run the command in a terminal on the Mac).

| case | what it is | the command |
|---|---|---|
| **Plain agent** | an agent on one folder: its own temp and caches, your Keychain closed, the network through the proxy | `doz run @mac -d --session agent --folder ~/src/app -- claude` |
| **Web / Node development** | the same, and the ports of your dev server — it may listen on them, and your browser and tests reach them | `doz run @mac -d --local-port 3000 --folder ~/src/site -- claude` |
| **Swift / Xcode development** | builds into the session's own DerivedData; optionally **Run in the Simulator** (`--simulator`) and **Sign with my Apple identity** (`--keychain`) | `doz run @mac -d --xcode --folder ~/src/MyApp -- claude` |
| **Signing & notarisation** | no fence: Apple's signing and notary tools need your Keychain and their own networking | `doz run @mac -d --unfenced --folder ~/src/MyApp -- zsh -l` |
| **Unfenced** | no isolation at all — your files, Keychain and network, as if you typed it yourself | `doz run @mac --unfenced --session shell` |

More you can do with the command line (cards may come later): `--write DIR` for a second repository, `--ssh-agent` for
git over ssh with your keys, `--permissions locked` for a research session that reaches only its AI model.

## Starting one

```bash
cd ~/src/my-app
doz run @mac -d --session agent -- claude          # fenced, in the folder you are in
doz run @mac -d --session build --xcode -- zsh -lc 'xcodebuild -scheme MyApp -derivedDataPath "$DOZ_DERIVED" -scmProvider system build'
doz run @mac --unfenced --session shell            # no fence; no command: your login shell, attached
doz run @mac --dry-run -- claude                   # what it would be able to do — nothing is started
```

- `--session` names it (at most 32 characters); without it, the program's name.
- `--folder` is the project folder. Fenced, the default is **the folder you are in**, and your home itself, `/`, a
  folder that holds your home, or Dozable's own folders are refused (a fenced session must have a project folder).
  Unfenced, the default is your home.
- `-d` starts it and returns (exit 0 once it started); without `-d`, `doz run` attaches to it, as for a sandbox, and
  **exits with the program's exit code** when the program ends — also when it ends at once, before the attach (it
  shows the program's last screen first); 128 + N for a program killed by signal N; 0 when you detach.
- There is no `--user`: a session on the Mac runs as you.
- The program starts without a shell in front of it; say `-- zsh -lc '…'` for one.

`doz run @mac` prints one line saying what it opened — fenced: `[doz] fenced: reads and writes ~/src/my-app; its own
temp, caches and Claude Code settings; network through Dozable's proxy (standard permissions); your Keychain, secrets
and other folders closed — doz run @mac --unfenced for none of this`; unfenced, that it has no isolation.

**Which one is used:** `--fenced` or `--unfenced` on the command, else the environment variable `DOZ_MAC_FENCE`
(`on` or `off`), else the setting `mac.fence` (`on` by default). A flag that only a fenced session has (`--keychain`,
`--xcode`, `--local-port`, …) means fenced; with `--unfenced` it is refused.

| flag (fenced) | what it opens | setting for the default |
|---|---|---|
| `--keychain` | your Keychain (signing; and so your saved logins) | `mac.keychain` (`off`) |
| `--read DIR`, `--write DIR` | one more folder, read-only or read-write (never your home, `~/.ssh`, `~/.config`, `~/Library` or the store) | `mac.fence_read` (read-only, relative to your home) |
| `--permissions` | what it may reach: `standard`, `locked`, `open`, a permission, `-PERMISSION`, `site:HOST[:PORT[,PORT]]` | `mac.permissions` (`standard`) |
| `--local-port N` | it may listen on, and connect to, `localhost:N` — a dev server, a sign-in callback | — |
| `--host-port N[:tag]` | it may reach a service on this Mac — a message server, a local API — through its proxy, as `host.dozable.internal:N` (`:tag`: requests name the session) | `network.host_ports_live` (live changes) |
| `--secret VAR,src=PATH,to=HOST:PORT[,header=NAME][,file=FILEVAR]` | a token for one service, held by Dozable: the session sees a placeholder in `VAR` (and a file named by `FILEVAR`), swapped on requests to exactly `HOST:PORT` (below) | `network.placeholders_plain_http` |
| `--agent-config private\|shared` | the agent's settings folder (below) | `mac.agent_config` (`private`) |
| `--history keep\|agent-default` | what happens to its conversations (below) | `agent.history` |
| `--account NAME\|mac\|none` | the Claude login the proxy swaps in | `mac.account` (`mac`) |
| `--github off\|read\|push` | GitHub as you, through the proxy (read refuses pushes) | — |
| `--ssh-agent` | your SSH agent, for listing keys and signing only | — |
| `--xcode`, `--simulator` | Xcode's build services; the Simulator too | — |
| `--open-url`, `--open-files`, `--clipboard` | the bridges (below) | `mac.open_url`, `mac.open_files`, `mac.clipboard` |

## Its files

Each fenced session has a folder of its own, `~/Library/Application Support/Dozable/fence/…/SESSION/`, which only it
(and Dozable) uses:

- **`tmp`** — its `TMPDIR`, emptied at every start.
- **`cache`** — every tool cache Dozable knows of (npm, pip, uv, Go, SwiftPM, Python, `XDG_CACHE_HOME`,
  `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`). Kept between starts, so the second build is warm; the first one starts cold. Emptied when a start
  opens MORE than the last one did (`--keychain`, `--simulator`, `shared`, another folder or port, wider permissions),
  so nothing written under narrower rules is used under wider ones.
- **`derived`** — Xcode's DerivedData (`$DOZ_DERIVED`).
- **`agent`** — the agent's own settings folder, when it is private.
- **`etc`** — what Dozable writes for it and it may only read: its git settings (your name, email and ignore file,
  taken from yours; nothing else of your git config), the certificate the proxy uses, its shell's start-up file.
- **`ssh/known_hosts`** — a copy of yours, made again at every start; host keys it learns stay here.

Your own temporary folder, `/tmp`, `~/Library/Caches` and `~/Library/Developer` are not writable from inside — the
exceptions are the few folders Apple's build tools insist on making in your temporary folder whatever they are told
(`swift build` and `xcodebuild` fail without them).

**Git, guarded.** Inside its folder a fenced program can commit, branch, fetch and push, but it cannot write a git
hook, rename a `.git` folder away, create one at the top, or point a repository's settings anywhere that would run
something the next time *you* use git there. Git settings it may add are the everyday ones (branches, remotes, `push
-u`, LFS, submodules); anything else — `core.hooksPath`, `core.fsmonitor`, a pager, an `insteadOf`, an unknown key — and
**the session is stopped at once**, the change taken out and kept aside:

```bash
doz sessions @mac                       # says: agent is STOPPED: a git config change …
doz sessions @mac --quarantine agent    # what was taken out
doz sessions resume @mac agent          # continue without it
```

The dashboard shows **Stopped: git config** on its tile, with **Review…** and **Resume**. A resume is refused while
the key is still there. Because every `.git` folder is protected, `rm -rf` of a clone fails inside a fenced session —
remove it from your own terminal.

## Its agent's settings folder: private or shared

For Claude Code (the agent whose recipe declares where it keeps its settings), there are two ways. Dozable knows the
agent by the program you start — `-- claude …`, also `-- env NAME=VALUE claude …` — but give variables with
`doz run -e NAME=VALUE` rather than through `env`, and start the agent itself rather than a script that starts it:

- **Private** (the default): the session has its **own** Claude settings folder. Your `CLAUDE.md`, skills, agents,
  commands and output styles are there as **read-only** links (one that points somewhere closed is not followed); its
  `settings.json` is a cleaned copy of yours — only a short list of safe keys, so no hooks, status line, MCP servers or
  plugins come along; it is made again at every start, so nothing the agent changes there survives. Your own
  `~/.claude` is closed to it. Your conversations of that folder are copied in at its first start, so `claude -c`
  finds them.
- **Shared** (`--agent-config shared`): it uses your **own** `~/.claude`. Convenient — everything you have set up
  is there — but **less isolated**: what it writes into your settings (a hook, a status line script, a plugin) runs the
  next time you use Claude Code yourself, outside the fence. Said when it starts, and in every view of it.

`mac.agent_config` sets the default for every agent; `recipes.anthropic.claude-code.mac_config` for Claude Code alone
(`follow` follows `mac.agent_config`).

**The Claude login** is swapped in by the proxy: `--account mac` (this Mac's own Claude Code login, the default),
`--account NAME` (one of `doz account ls`) or `--account none`. The program holds a placeholder, never your token, and
signs in with no prompt. Claude Code gets a short note in its prompt saying where it runs (`mac.agent_prompt`).

## Its conversations (transcripts and history)

A private settings folder is the session's, so its conversations would go when the session does. They don't: when the
session ends, is restarted, removed, or found gone, Dozable **copies its conversations back** into your own
`~/.claude/projects/<folder>/`, where a later `claude --resume` (or `-c`) in that folder finds them. Only the
conversation files are copied — never its memory, to-dos, settings or anything else — and only ones that are what they
claim to be (one per conversation, for that folder); anything else is named and left behind. A copy of yours is replaced
only by a longer version of the same conversation; otherwise both are kept.

What else happens follows the conversation-history setting (`agent.history`, per agent
`recipes.anthropic.claude-code.history`, or `--history` for one session):

- **`keep`** (the default): copied back, and **also kept in Dozable's own archive**:

  ```bash
  doz sessions @mac --transcripts agent                    # what was kept, when
  doz sessions @mac --transcripts agent --export ~/saved   # copies, with a manifest
  ```

  The dashboard's **Conversations** tab lists and downloads them.
- **`agent-default`**: copied back, where Claude Code's own rule decides how long they stay; nothing archived.

**Exporting.** `--export DIR` writes into a new or empty folder of yours: the archived conversations, the copies carried
back (only while they are still what was carried), and `manifest.json` (each file's name, where it came from, and the
sha256 of the original and of the copy). An **unfenced** Claude Code session's conversations are exported too: exactly
the ones Dozable saw it hold (each `/clear` or `/resume` adds one), from your own `~/.claude/projects/<folder>/` — never
another session's file in the same folder. A link is never followed, and every file is swept for chat tokens, as a chat
export is. Listing and exporting need no daemon and never start one.

A shared session writes its conversations straight into your own folder, and Dozable never changes your settings
there. A conversation written in a fenced session and continued outside it is still text the fenced agent wrote:
the end message says so.

### Discarding a session's conversations once a run's archive holds them

When a workspace finishes, its run's archive keeps a copy of each agent's conversations. Once that copy exists, you can
remove the session's own files too:

```bash
doz sessions @mac --forget SESSION --discard-transcripts
```

Each file goes only while it is exactly the copy the archive holds; a file that changed since is kept, and you are told
why. Nothing is discarded while the workspace's run is still open, and nothing for a session no archive holds. A finished
workspace's session starts fresh the next time you wake it.

## The network

The session's proxy decides by host name, with the permissions of a sandbox. This Mac's default for a fenced session
(`mac.permissions` = `standard`) is: its AI model, its own updates, GitHub, error reports, and the Node, Python, Go,
Rust and Swift package registries. `locked` is its model only; `open` is any site, still logged.

```bash
doz net @mac --session agent                    # its permissions and what it was refused lately
doz net allow @mac --session agent install:ruby site:api.example.com
doz net deny @mac --session agent github
doz net log @mac --session agent --denied --follow   # its connections
doz net log @mac --session agent --fence        # the fence's own refusals: files, programs, services
```

**This Mac's own ports, the chat server's included, are closed to it** unless it is given one: `--host-port PORT`
(or `doz net allow @mac --session S host:PORT`), reached as `host.dozable.internal:PORT` through its proxy. A
workspace's fenced manager or worker is given exactly one, the chat server's page port of its store, and nothing else
of this Mac's; its network beyond that is the workspace's preset (locked unless you chose another), by the same
permissions.

Changes apply to its next connection. Name lookups (DNS) are closed inside the fence — the proxy looks names up;
`localhost` still works. A program that ignores the proxy settings gets no network at all, rather than a direct one.
`--local-port N` is the way to listen: the program may listen on and connect to `localhost:N` only, so your
browser and tests reach its dev server there. `doz net log … --fence` shows the fence's refusals so far; it does not
follow new ones (`--follow` works for connections).

**Listening on any port** (a test server on a free port, a tool that picks its own): the setting
`mac.fence_loopback_listen` (`off` by default) lets a fenced session listen on any TCP port from its next start or
restart — your browser and other programs on this Mac reach it, another fenced session does not (it has only its
proxy), and UDP stays closed. Two limits come from macOS's sandbox and are said in the session's capabilities: it
cannot keep such a server to this Mac's loopback — one that listens on every address is reachable from your network
too (your firewall decides) — and the program still cannot connect to its own server from inside, because its only
way out is Dozable's proxy. When a test must reach its own server, give that port with `--local-port N`. The same
macOS limit holds for a `--local-port N` server that listens on every address.

```bash
doz config set mac.fence_loopback_listen on     # from the next session or restart
```

**Reaching a service on this Mac** — a message server another session runs, a local API — is `--host-port N`, a different thing
from `--local-port N`: `--local-port` is the session's OWN listener (it binds it; your browser reaches it), while
`--host-port` lets it reach someone else's listener on this Mac, through its proxy, by name:

```bash
doz run @mac -d --host-port 8780 -- claude      # inside: curl http://host.dozable.internal:8780/
doz net allow @mac --session claude host:8781   # one more, live (network.host_ports_live, on by default)
doz run @mac -d --host-port 8780:tag -- claude  # its plain-HTTP requests carry X-Dozable-Session: @mac/claude
```

`127.0.0.1:8780` stays closed inside the fence; only the name is the way, and only for those ports. The header is
identification, not authentication. `--unfenced` with `--host-port` is refused: an unfenced session already reaches
every port. The full rules: [This Mac's ports](https://dozable.com/docs/permissions-and-network.md#this-macs-ports).

**A token for that service** — `--secret` — never enters the session. `doz` reads it from a file of yours alone; the
session's variable (and, with `file=`, a file under its own folder, named by the second variable) hold a placeholder,
and its proxy puts the real token in its place on requests to exactly that host and port — over plain HTTP too, to this
Mac's ports (and Tailscale addresses) while `network.placeholders_plain_http` is on:

```bash
doz run @mac -d --host-port 8780 \
    --secret SERVER_TOKEN,src=~/.config/token,to=host.dozable.internal:8780,file=SERVER_TOKEN_FILE -- claude
# inside: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $SERVER_TOKEN" http://host.dozable.internal:8780/
```

The launch says `secret SERVER_TOKEN → host.dozable.internal:8780 (fp …)`. The file must be outside everything the
session may read (its folder, `--read`/`--write` folders, `mac.fence_read`); `-e SERVER_TOKEN=…` is refused; a restart
keeps the secret (a new placeholder each time), and so does a new daemon (it reads the keychain item again); the
secret and its keychain item go when the session's record is removed (`doz sessions end` of a session that has ended).
`--unfenced --secret` is refused. The full rules: [A secret for a service](https://dozable.com/docs/permissions-and-network.md#a-secret-for-a-service).

**A chat room.** Every fenced session has `dozchat` on its PATH — Dozable's chat client, a member of your chat rooms
with nothing to install (it reaches only what the session can already reach: the one file is all the fence opens for
it). With the page port and the participant's token given as above, `dozchat rooms`, `dozchat send room1 "…"` and
`dozchat listen` work inside: [Chat](https://dozable.com/docs/chat.md#participants-and-tokens). An unfenced session has no `dozchat`.

Under `locked`, macOS's certificate service is closed too, so tools that check certificates through it (Go programs,
`gh`) cannot reach anything; under `standard` it is open (it fetches revocation lists on the program's behalf).

**GitHub as you** (`--github read` or `--github push`): git and `gh` are signed in as you, through the proxy — your
token stays on the Mac; `read` refuses pushes. Without it, a push over https has no credential (git says how).
**Git over ssh** works through the proxy too; your keys only with `--ssh-agent` (list and sign — never added, removed
or read), and host keys it learns stay in the session.

## Tools inside the fence

| tool | fenced | how |
|---|---|---|
| git over https, LFS, worktrees, submodules | works | through the proxy |
| git over ssh, `ssh` | works | through the proxy; your keys only with `--ssh-agent` |
| GitHub (git, `gh`) | `--github read` or `push` | the proxy puts your token in |
| signed commits | ssh signing with `--ssh-agent`; gpg fails | your `gpg.*` settings are not carried in |
| Node, npm, pnpm, bun | work | caches in the session |
| curl, Python, pip, uv | work | |
| Go | works; `go install` lands in the session's caches | a host whose traffic the proxy reads (GitHub with `--github`) fails for Go programs |
| Swift, SwiftPM | `swift build --disable-sandbox` | SwiftPM's own sandbox cannot run inside another; binary packages need their host allowed |
| Xcode | `--xcode`, and `xcodebuild … -derivedDataPath "$DOZ_DERIVED"` | without it Xcode's DerivedData is closed; signing needs `--keychain` |
| Simulator | `--simulator` | a guard rail, not a boundary (below) |
| codesign, notarytool, tools that use Apple's own networking | fail | run them unfenced (the Signing & notarisation case) |
| Java | fails | no proxy for Java yet |
| Docker, Podman, VMs, `open`, `osascript`, `sudo` | refused | |
| headless Chrome, Playwright | `--no-sandbox`, browsers in the session | Chrome's own sandbox cannot run inside another |

The list of macOS services Claude Code and Xcode may use inside the fence is still being settled from real sessions;
a later version may open or close a few. `doz net log @mac --session NAME --fence` shows what was refused.

## Building Swift and Xcode projects in a fenced session

Start the session with `--xcode` (the dashboard's Swift / Xcode case). Inside it these work, and the wizard shows the same
lines, each with Copy (`doz run @mac --xcode --dry-run` prints them too):

```bash
swift build --disable-sandbox --cache-path "$XDG_CACHE_HOME/swiftpm" --scratch-path "$DOZ_DERIVED"
swift test  --disable-sandbox --cache-path "$XDG_CACHE_HOME/swiftpm" --scratch-path "$DOZ_DERIVED"
xcodebuild build -scheme MyApp -derivedDataPath "$DOZ_DERIVED" -scmProvider system
xcodebuild test  -scheme MyApp -derivedDataPath "$DOZ_DERIVED" -scmProvider system -destination "platform=macOS"
```

`--disable-sandbox` is needed because SwiftPM's own sandbox cannot run inside another. The session's own caches hold
SwiftPM's downloads, and `$DOZ_DERIVED` is its own build folder; `swift build` and `swift test` also work with the
default `.build` (leave `--scratch-path` out). Claude Code in such a session is told the same flags.

**When to go unfenced.** Signing and notarisation need your Keychain and Apple's own networking: use the Signing &
notarisation case. Simulator UI tests: what the Simulator launches runs outside the fence, so turn on **Run in the
Simulator** (`--simulator`) — a guard rail, not a boundary. Tools that need your Keychain: **Sign with my Apple
identity** (`--keychain`). Unfenced means your files, Keychain and network, as if you typed it yourself.

A test server that picks its own port (listening on port 0) needs the setting `mac.fence_loopback_listen` (off by
default, see The network): the session may then listen on any port, and a server on all addresses is reachable from your
network, not only from this Mac.

## Bridges

A fenced program cannot open things on your Mac itself (that would reach outside the fence), so Dozable does it for it,
as for a sandbox — each time announced in `doz attach` and the dashboard:

- **Open a URL** (`open`, `xdg-open`, `$BROWSER`): an http or https page opens in your browser (never `file:` or other
  schemes, never this Mac's own addresses; at most a few at a time). A sign-in whose callback is the program's
  `localhost:N` works when the session has `--local-port N`; otherwise it is refused before anything opens, and the
  message names the flag.
- **Open files**: a document from its folder opens in your app (never a program, a link out of the folder, or an app
  bundle).
- **Clipboard**: it can put text on your clipboard (OSC 52), never read it; each copy is announced with its first
  characters, so a command planted for you to paste is visible.

`--open-url off`, `--open-files off` and `--clipboard off` turn one off for a session; while it runs,
`doz sessions bridges @mac agent --open-url off` (or the switches on its dashboard panel) changes it at once. An
unfenced session's program opens things itself, as before; its copies reach your clipboard as from any session.

## What it can do, at a glance

```bash
doz sessions @mac --capabilities agent    # one line per capability: its state, what it opens, when it can change
doz run @mac --dry-run --xcode -- claude  # the same, for a session before it starts
```

The rows: the fence (fenced, fenced (Xcode), guard rail (Simulator), no isolation), the Keychain, the network, the
agent's settings folder, history, the Claude login, GitHub as you, the SSH agent, the three bridges, and the folders it
can write and read. Each says whether it can change **live** (the network's permissions, the bridges) or **at the next
start**. `--json` has them as `capabilities`, for unfenced sessions too. The dashboard shows the same rows on a
session's **What it can do** tab, and up to four as chips on its tile.

## What the fence is not

Said plainly, so you can decide:

- **Not a virtual machine.** It is macOS's own sandbox around one program and what it starts, running as you. A
  sandbox (`doz new`) is a separate machine; prefer it when the work does not need the Mac.
- **Your project files are its work.** It can change anything in its folder — a `Makefile`, `package.json`'s scripts,
  a test — and what you run there later, unfenced, runs that. Review its changes as you would anyone's.
- **Names and sizes of files are visible everywhere** (not their contents).
- **Other programs' command lines are readable.** Any program you run can read the command line (not the
  environment) of your other programs, fenced or not — never put a password or token on a command line.
- **The Simulator is a guard rail, not a boundary.** With `--simulator`, the Simulator and the apps it launches run
  outside the fence.
- **`--keychain` and `shared` open real doors**: your saved logins, and your own Claude Code settings.
- **A git setting is taken out within a second** — between its write and the stop, an unfenced git run in that folder
  could still read it once.
- **macOS's certificate service** checks certificates for it under `standard`.

## Looking, typing, attaching

```bash
doz sessions @mac                            # the sessions: state (fenced, no isolation …), what the agent is doing, folder, command
doz sessions @mac --json                     # each with its folder, argv, when it was opened, its fence and capabilities
doz attach @mac build                        # Ctrl-] opens the menu (d detach · n next · p prev · s sessions)
doz sessions screen @mac build               # its screen as text, now
doz sessions send @mac agent --text 'run the tests' --enter
doz sessions wait @mac agent --until idle,done,blocked,error --timeout 90   # has it stopped working?
```

These are the same commands as for a sandbox's sessions ([Terminals and sessions](https://dozable.com/docs/terminals-and-sessions.md)).
Looking (`doz sessions @mac`, `screen`) never starts a daemon. `doz ls` ends with one line for this Mac: how many run,
fenced or not.

## What `@mac` is, and is not

- **It is a place, not a sandbox.** Its name starts with `@`, so it can never be a sandbox's name (those are `a-z`,
  `0-9` and `-`). Only the session commands take it — `doz run`, `doz attach`, `doz sessions` — and `doz net` for a
  fenced session (`--session`). Every other command (`doz exec`, `doz start`, `doz sleep`, `doz key`, …) refuses it.
- **Its environment is built new.** The program gets `HOME`, `USER`, `LOGNAME`, `SHELL`, `TMPDIR`, `LANG`, `LC_*`,
  `TERM=xterm-256color`, `COLORTERM=truecolor` and `PATH` — nothing else of the environment `doz` was started from.
  `PATH` is your login shell's, read once. A fenced session adds its own: the proxy, its caches, its certificate, its
  agent's settings folder (and no `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` unless `--ssh-agent`); an unfenced one gets your `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`. Add
  what you need with `-e NAME=VALUE`. The markers that tell a program it runs inside Claude Code (`CLAUDECODE`,
  `CLAUDE_CODE_*`) are never passed on, and `-e` refuses them; a fenced session also refuses `-e` of a login
  (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, `GH_TOKEN`, …) — the proxy brings those.

## In the dashboard

`doz ui` has an **On this Mac** page (in the sidebar under **This Mac**, after Sandboxes — tagged with how many run with
**no isolation**, when any do; `#/mac/here`, a session's own `#/mac/here/SESSION`), and **This Mac › Sessions** ends with an
On this Mac section. A session that is an agent of a workspace is also under that workspace in the sidebar. Each session is a tile with its picture, what its
agent is doing, its folder and its chips — **Fenced**, **Fenced (Xcode)**, **Guard rail (Simulator)**, **Keychain
open**, **Shared config**, **GitHub: push**, or **No isolation** — and marks for news: network waiting for a daemon,
refusals seen, **Stopped: git config**. A session whose own command line bypasses its permissions says **permissions
bypassed**.

- **Watch** (or a click on the picture) opens it below, **watching**: nothing you type reaches it. Its tabs: the
  screen, **What it can do** (the capabilities; the bridges' switches change live), **Network** (its permissions,
  read-only, with the `doz net` commands; its connections and the fence's refusals), **Conversations**.
- The pane's two-state toggle, **Watching** | **Controlling**, says which it is and switches: Controlling attaches for
  real (the tile's **Control** does the same). It is offered only to a browser that may type into these sessions, and
  only while the session runs. **Restart…** and **End…** ask first.
- **Remove…** on an ended or gone session's tile, and **Remove all ended…** in the page's header (this Mac's own browser
  only), forget them: the dialog names each, says a gone one can no longer be restarted, and their conversations are
  carried back first. A running session, or one that is an agent of a workspace, is never removed here (its workspace
  forgets it). In a terminal: `doz sessions @mac --forget-ended` (it lists them and asks once; `--dry-run` only says, with
  no daemon; `--yes` does not ask) or `--forget SESSION`. A second run forgets nothing.
- **New session on this Mac…** (this Mac's own browser) is the five-case guide above (its folder starts as the newest
  session's, never a temporary folder): it shows the command, **Copy**,
  and **Open in Terminal** for the plainly fenced cases (Plain agent, Web / Node, Swift / Xcode without the Simulator
  or the Keychain, private settings). Anything with less of a fence is copy-only, so no single click starts it.

**Your other browsers** (the dashboard's LAN option, [The dashboard on your other devices](https://dozable.com/docs/doz-serve.md)) do not get
these sessions unless you say so — a browser on your network typing into one is typing on your Mac. The setting
`serve.mac_sessions` decides, on the Mac (never from a browser):

| `serve.mac_sessions` | what another computer's browser may do |
|---|---|
| `off` (the default) | nothing — the page and its entry are not there |
| `watch` | list them and watch them (read-only); no typing, no Restart, End, Resume or bridge switches |
| `interactive` | everything this Mac's own browser does with them, except New session and Remove |

```bash
doz config set serve.mac_sessions watch        # applies at once
```

This Mac's own browser (`doz ui` on the Mac) always has them. A sandbox never reaches any of it.

## Bypass only when asked

Dozable never adds a flag that skips an agent's permission questions for a session on the Mac. If the command you give
asks for it itself — `claude --dangerously-skip-permissions`, `claude --permission-mode bypassPermissions`,
`codex --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` — that is your choice and it is allowed, and the session is marked
**permissions bypassed**: once on `doz run`'s output, and in `doz sessions @mac` (and `"bypassed": true` in `--json`)
for as long as it is listed. Fenced, the fence still holds; unfenced, such an agent can harm your Mac.

## Sleep, logout, restart

- **Sleep and closing the lid: kept.** Each session is held by its own small process (`deckhold-mac`), which simply
  pauses with the Mac.
- **The daemon: not needed to keep them.** The holders are not the daemon's children. `doz daemon stop` says how many
  sessions on this Mac keep running; the next daemon finds them again (same program, same screen). A fenced session's
  network waits for a daemon: its connections are served when one runs again.
- **Logout and restart: gone.** Logging out or restarting the Mac ends every program, sessions on the Mac included.
  Afterwards `doz sessions @mac` lists them as **gone**; `doz sessions screen @mac NAME` shows the screen saved last,
  and `doz sessions restart @mac NAME` starts the same program again in the same folder. The variables you gave with
  `-e` are not kept (they might be secrets): give them again with a new `doz run`.
- **Claude Code comes back on its own conversation.** Dozable notes which conversation a Claude Code session holds
  (from Claude's own record of it, nothing else of its folder) and a restart resumes exactly that one: a session
  started as `claude --session-id ID --remote-control admin` restarts as `claude --resume ID --remote-control admin` —
  the same conversation, and with it the same Remote Control session. A session that never talked is opened again with
  its `--session-id`; with nothing known, Claude continues the folder's newest conversation (`--continue`), or starts
  a new one when the folder has none. `--fresh` starts a new conversation.
- **A restart that fails says why.** When the program dies at once (within two seconds), `doz sessions restart`
  fails with "exited at once (exit N)" and the program's own last lines, and `doz sessions screen @mac NAME` shows
  that run's screen — never an older one.
- **A program that ended keeps its last screen.** `doz sessions screen @mac NAME` of an ended session shows what it
  left on its screen, and says "ended (exit N)" — until you end (forget) or restart it.
- **A restart keeps the session's mode.** A fenced session restarts fenced, with the same grants and its folder made
  again; one opened unfenced — every session opened before fenced became the default included — restarts unfenced.
- `doz sessions end @mac NAME` ends a program (hang-up, then terminate, then kill; fenced, every process of its fence,
  even ones that detached). Ending one that has already ended or is gone forgets it.

## Upgrading from a version without the fence

- Sessions you opened before keep running, and keep their mode when restarted: unfenced.
- A new `doz run @mac` without a flag is now fenced. A script that needs the old behaviour — calling `doz` from inside
  the session, using your Keychain, reaching any host, writing outside its folder, running from your home — passes
  `--unfenced` (or set `doz config set mac.fence off`). A fenced session's refusal says what was refused and names
  `--unfenced`.
- An older `doz` does not know `--unfenced`: check `doz run --help` before relying on it in a script.

## The Keychain, and a daemon started over ssh

An unfenced program (or a fenced one with `--keychain`) uses your login Keychain only when the doz daemon runs inside your
logged-in session. A daemon started from an ssh connection runs where the Keychain is locked: `doz doctor` says so, and
the fix is `doz daemon restart` from a terminal on the Mac itself. macOS may also ask about a session's program on behalf
of `doz` ("doz wants to access your Documents folder") — the dialog names `doz` because it started the holder.

## Uninstalling

`doz nuke` ends every session on the Mac. `doz uninstall` asks whether to end them (`--yes` ends them); left running,
no `doz` can reach them again once the store is gone.

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/the-menu-bar-app

# The menu bar app

Dozable's daemon is the background process that runs your sandboxes. The menu bar app, **Dozable.app**, puts it in
your Mac's menu bar: whether it is running, which version, how many sandboxes are up — and Start, Stop, Restart and
Open Dashboard, one click each, and **Start at Login**. It has no chat and no settings of its own; everything else is
`doz` and the dashboard.

It comes with doz (Homebrew and the release tarball carry it) and does nothing until you install it.

## Install it

```sh
doz app install
```

This copies the app that came with your doz into `/Applications` (into `~/Applications` when you cannot write to
`/Applications`). Then open **Dozable** from Finder, Launchpad or Spotlight — or install and open in one go:

```sh
doz app install --open
```

It has no Dock icon and no window: look for its icon in the menu bar, at the top right of the screen. It is signed
and notarised by Dozable, so macOS opens it without a warning.

`doz app install` checks the copy before it installs it (its signature, that it is Dozable's, that it is the version of
your doz) and then swaps it in whole — a copy that is already running keeps running the version it started with until
you open it again. `--dest DIR` installs it somewhere else.

## What the menu shows

The first line is the daemon's state:

| the menu says | what it means |
|---|---|
| Daemon running · 0.50.7 | It runs, and this is its version. The next line says whether it stays running with nothing open ("Always on") and how many sandboxes run. |
| Daemon stopped | Nothing runs. **Start Daemon**, or any `doz` command, starts it. |
| Daemon stopped until a doz command starts it | You stopped it with `doz daemon stop` (or the menu): it stays stopped until you start it — "or your next login" when a login item starts it at login. |
| Daemon started from ssh — it cannot read your Keychain | It was started over ssh, where your login Keychain is locked, so it cannot use your Claude login. **Restart Daemon** starts a new one from your desktop session, which can. |
| Daemon runs an older build (0.50.6) — Restart to update | doz was upgraded while the daemon ran. **Restart Daemon** switches to the new version. |
| doz is not installed | The app found no doz (it looks at `/opt/homebrew/bin/doz`, `/usr/local/bin/doz` and `~/.local/bin/doz`). **How to Install doz…** opens this manual's install page. |
| doz 0.50.3 is older than this app needs | Upgrade doz (`doz upgrade -y`). Meanwhile the menu still shows the state and offers Start, Stop, Restart and Open Dashboard. |

The icon is filled while the daemon runs, outlined when it is stopped, a warning triangle when a Restart is due, and
hollow when there is no doz.

## What it does

- **Start Daemon** — the same as `doz daemon start`.
- **Stop Daemon…** — the same as `doz daemon stop`. When sandboxes are running it asks first: they hibernate, and wake
  when you use them again. Sessions on this Mac keep running.
- **Restart Daemon** — the same as `doz daemon restart`: stop (sandboxes hibernate), then start on the current version.
- **Open Dashboard** — the same as `doz ui --detach --open`: the dashboard opens in your browser, signed in. The
  sign-in link goes straight from doz to your browser; the app never sees it.
- **Start at Login** — see below.
- **Quit Dozable Menu** — quits the app only. The daemon and your sandboxes keep running.

The app runs `doz` for each of these, so it does exactly what the command does — including refusing what the command
refuses (it shows doz's reason in the menu). It never starts the daemon just by looking: the state is read with
`doz daemon status`, which never starts one.

The menu refreshes when you open it (and every two seconds while it is open), once a minute while it is closed, when
your Mac wakes, and after every action.

## Start at Login

One switch for both: with **Start at Login** checked, the daemon starts when you log in (from your desktop session, so
it can read your login Keychain) and the menu comes back too. Nothing is set up until you click it.

The first time, macOS shows a notice ("Login Item Added") and lists **Dozable** under System Settings › General ›
Login Items & Extensions. At login, and every 15 minutes after, the app runs the same short doz command doz's own login
item runs: it starts the daemon if none runs (and you did not stop it), then exits. The daemon itself is never a login
item.

| the menu says | what it means |
|---|---|
| ✓ Start at Login | On. Click to turn it off (the daemon keeps running; it just will not start at your next login). |
| Start at Login | Off. Click to turn it on. |
| ✓ Start at Login (set by doz — click to let this app hold it) | doz's own login item starts the daemon (`doz daemon login-item on`). Click to let the app hold it instead: the app's item replaces doz's, and the menu comes back at login too. |
| Start at Login — needs approval: Open System Settings… | Dozable is switched off under System Settings › Login Items (or macOS waits for your OK). Click to open that page and switch it on. |
| Start at Login — open the copy in Applications (doz app install) | This copy runs from somewhere else (a download, Homebrew's folder). macOS keeps a login item only for an app that stays in one place: run `doz app install` and open the copy in Applications. |
| Start at Login — needs doz 0.50.8 | Your doz is older than this needs. Upgrade doz (`doz upgrade -y`). |

There is only ever one login item for the daemon: when the app holds it, doz removes its own, and `doz daemon login-item`
says "the Dozable menu bar app starts the daemon at login". Turning Start at Login off, or removing the app
(`doz app uninstall`), gives it back to you: `doz daemon login-item on` adds doz's own again. If you delete the app
yourself without `doz app uninstall`, macOS may keep its login item listed (it does nothing without the app) — switch it
off in System Settings; `doz daemon login-item on` works again either way.

Start at Login uses the default store (the one `doz` uses with no `--store`) and the doz installed by Homebrew or in
`~/.local`. A Dozable release runs only a doz signed by Dozable.

## Updates

The app updates with doz. After `doz upgrade` (or `brew upgrade`), the menu shows the new version and then offers
**Update Menu Bar App (old → new)**: it installs the copy that came with the new doz and reopens the app. When a newer
copy is already installed but the old one is still running (after `doz app install` without `--open`), the menu offers
**Restart to Update (old → new)** instead: it quits the running copy and opens the new one. The same, from Terminal:

```sh
doz app install --open
```

## Remove it

```sh
doz app uninstall
```

This turns Start at Login off when it was on, quits the app and removes it from `/Applications` (and
`~/Applications`). The daemon keeps running. `doz uninstall`, which removes all of Dozable, removes the app too.

## Where to look

```sh
doz app status        # the copy that came with doz, where it is installed, whether it runs
```

The app writes one line per doz command it runs to the system log — the command and its result, nothing else. To read
it: `log show --predicate 'subsystem == "com.dozable.app"' --last 1h`.

From an ssh session you can see what the menu would show without the screen, and Start at Login as macOS reports it:

```sh
/Applications/Dozable.app/Contents/MacOS/Dozable --dump-menu
/Applications/Dozable.app/Contents/MacOS/Dozable --login-status
launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/com.dozable.app.daemon | head -20
doz daemon login-item           # who starts the daemon at login
```

## Not yet

- It shows the default store only (the one `doz` uses when you give it no `--store`).
- Its icon is a placeholder.

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/chat

# Chat

Chat is a set of rooms on your Mac where you and your agents talk: you in the dashboard or a terminal, each agent with
its own token. An agent can be a program in a sandbox, a session on this Mac, a bot on another machine, or anything
else that can make an HTTP request. Messages, reactions, direct messages, attachments and who is here are all kept on
your Mac, in the store.

The chat server is a small program the doz daemon runs and keeps running while chat is on. It never starts a sandbox
and never leaves your Mac on its own: an agent reaches it, it does not reach out — except to call a webhook bot you
added (below).

**A workspace's workers and its manager need chat:** they take their task and talk in the workspace's room, so
`doz workspace start` refuses a workspace with a declared worker or a manager until chat is on. Without chat you drive the
agents yourself. Turning chat on is the person's choice — an agent driving Dozable should ask before it does.

**Each store has its own chat:** its own server, ports, rooms, participants and tokens. A token of one store means nothing
to another, and an agent must talk to the server of the store it belongs to ([A second
store](13-resources-and-disk-space.md#a-second-store)). Who makes each token, and how to replace or revoke one, is on
[Tokens and identity](https://dozable.com/docs/tokens-and-identity.md).

## Turning it on

```bash
doz chat on --name ada        # chat on; you are ada in chat (your name is chosen once)
doz chat status               # on, ready, its ports, you and the participants
doz chat off                  # the chat server stops; rooms and messages are kept
```

`doz chat on` starts the daemon if it is not running and waits until the chat server is ready. The setting it turns on
is `chat.enabled`. Wherever the dashboard says chat is off — the Chat page, a workspace's room and its set-up list, the
New workspace wizard — this Mac's own browser offers **Turn chat on** (with your name the first time), which does the
same; another computer shows the command. Turning chat off is `doz chat off`, in a terminal.

The chat server listens on this Mac only (127.0.0.1), on two ports: the **page port** (`chat.page_port`, 8790), where
agents call `/agent/…` with their token, and the **line port** (`chat.line_port`, 8791), one JSON message per line,
also with a token. `doz config set chat.page_port N` (or `line_port`) moves it: the daemon restarts the chat server
within a few seconds, and `doz chat status` says it is restarting until the new server has the new port.

If you never set a port and another program already uses its default (a second Dozable on this Mac, say), chat takes a
free port instead and saves it in your settings, so it stays the same next time. `doz chat on` and `doz chat status` say
so: "page port 8790 was taken by another program; chat uses 8792 (saved in your settings)". A port you set yourself is
never moved: if it is taken, chat says which setting to change.

**You never have a token.** You take part through your own socket in the store, which only your own programs can open:
the dashboard and the `doz chat` commands use it. Nothing on the network acts as you.

## Rooms, from a terminal

```bash
doz chat rooms                       # the rooms and their members
doz chat room room1 @bot1 @bot2      # make a room with these members (and you)
doz chat send room1 "the build is green"
doz chat read room1 --last 20        # the room as you see it; --follow keeps showing what comes
```

A room called `general` is there from the start. In the composer (and with `doz chat send`) the chat server's own
commands work too: `/room`, `/invite @name`, `/remove @name`, `/archive`, `/dm @name text` (a direct message), `/hold`,
`/react`, `/edit`, `/delete`, `/avatar`. `/protocol` in the dashboard shows the message protocol without sending
anything.

## Participants and tokens

```bash
doz chat add bot1                    # an agent that polls; its token is shown once
doz chat add bot2 --to-file ~/bot2.token
doz chat who                         # name, kind, token or none, how it is reached, rooms, presence
doz chat token bot1 --new            # a new token (the old one is refused at once)
doz chat remove bot2                 # it leaves every room; its token is refused
doz chat add bot3 bot4 bot5 --to-dir ~/tokens   # several at once: each token in ~/tokens/NAME.token
doz chat remove bot3 bot4 --yes      # several at once (asked once without --yes)
```

The running chat server takes participants added or removed, and a new token, **without a restart**: nobody else is cut
off, and `doz chat status` says how many changes it took that way. A removed participant's token is refused at once, and a
receive it had waiting ends. Several names at once are added (or removed) together or not at all. A new participant is in
no room until it is invited (`/invite @NAME`); a name you removed and add again is back in the rooms it was in. Changing a
port, how a participant is reached (`doz chat set`) or a webhook entry still restarts the chat server, for under a second.

A token is shown once (or written to a new file with `--to-file`); doz keeps only its hash. `--from-stdin` gives a
participant a token it already has. `--kind KIND` labels how its messages are shown (`agent` by default).

A participant with a lasting identity — its agent program, where it runs, a token Dozable keeps for it — is an **Agent /
Bot**, made and changed with `doz bot` (see [Agents / Bots](https://dozable.com/docs/agents-and-bots.md)); `doz chat who` marks it `· bot`, and
`doz chat remove`, `token` and `set` on it name the `doz bot` command instead.

An agent with a token takes part over HTTP on the page port:

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "http://127.0.0.1:8790/agent/receive?wait=30"
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"room":"room1","message":{"content":"done — see the report"}}' http://127.0.0.1:8790/agent/send
```

**An agent in a Dozable sandbox or fenced session** has `dozchat` on its PATH — a chat client Dozable puts in every one,
with nothing to install. Give it its token as a secret and the page port as a port of this Mac; the session only ever
sees a placeholder:

```bash
doz chat add bot1 --to-file ~/.config/chat/bot1.token
doz run @mac --host-port 8790 \
    --secret CHAT_TOKEN,src=~/.config/chat/bot1.token,to=host.dozable.internal:8790,file=CHAT_TOKEN_FILE -- bash
# inside: dozchat rooms · dozchat send room1 "hello" · dozchat listen
```

Every agent Dozable starts itself — a workspace's manager and workers, and the sessions of an adopted agent — is given
its token and this store's chat address (`CHAT_URL`, with the page port `doz chat status` shows) by Dozable, with
nothing for you to do. For an agent you start yourself, as above, `dozchat` reaches `http://host.dozable.internal:8790`
unless `CHAT_URL` says otherwise (on this Mac with no proxy set,
`http://127.0.0.1:8790`; add `-e
CHAT_URL=http://host.dozable.internal:PORT` when the page port `doz chat status` shows is another). Its commands are
those of the one-file Python client Dozable publishes for agents elsewhere (`docs/chat/client/chat_client.py`); `dozchat
--help` lists them.

## Reading and exporting a whole room

`doz chat read ROOM` shows the latest messages (`--last N`, at most 500). For a time window, however many messages it
holds, give `--since` (and `--until`): an ISO 8601 time or day, Unix seconds, or a time ago (`30m`, `2h`, `7d`).

```bash
doz chat read room1 --since 2026-11-20 --json        # every message since that day, oldest first, as one JSON array
doz chat export room1 --to ~/exports/room1           # every message, its attachments and a manifest
doz chat export room1 --to ~/exports/today --since 1d
```

`export` writes into a new or empty folder of yours (never inside doz's store): `room1.jsonl` (one message per line, as
the chat server gives them), `attachments/ID/NAME` (each fetched as you; one that is gone is listed instead) and
`manifest.json` (the room, the window, the count, each file's sha256 and size). Every file is swept before it is written:
a live chat token in it — pasted into a message by mistake — is replaced by "[a chat token of NAME, removed by doz]",
and the export names whose it was with the fix (`doz chat token NAME --new`), never the token itself. Both need the
chat server, which runs while the daemon does: with no daemon they say so and start nothing.

In a room, a message can name participants with `@name`; a direct message (`/dm @bot1 …`) is seen only by those it
names — and by you, if you choose to reveal it (the room records that you did).

## Webhook bots

A bot can be called instead of polling: the chat server sends it each message meant for it.

```bash
doz chat add bot1 --webhook                     # called at the entry bot1
doz chat webhook set bot1 --from-file ~/bot1.entry
doz chat webhook status                         # each entry: set or not, where, a fingerprint, when it was set
doz chat webhook remove bot1
```

An entry is two lines: the address the chat server calls, then the `Authorization` value it sends (an empty line: none).
It is kept in your login keychain — never in a file, a log or `--json` — and only you, on this Mac, can set it.
`--webhook-entry NAME` lets several bots share one entry. The bot still sends with its own token.

## Claude Code sessions on this Mac

The chat server can write each message for a Claude Code session straight into that session's own inbox, so the session
hears it whether it is busy or idle, with nothing for it to keep running:

```bash
doz chat add bot1 --inbox --to-file ~/.config/chat/bot1.token   # the Claude Code session named bot1 (--session S for another name)
doz chat set bot1 --deliver inbox    # or turn an existing participant into one (--kind claude-session if it is not one)
doz chat set bot1 --deliver poll     # back to polling; its token, rooms and history are kept either way
doz chat who                         # DELIVERY inbox; PRESENCE working, idle or not running
```

To find the session, the chat server reads your `~/.claude/sessions` (Claude Code's own records of its running sessions)
and writes to the one session it delivers to; `doz chat status` and `doz doctor` say so while any participant is reached
this way. A message for a session that is not running is marked failed ("no running Claude session with that name").

**This reaches Claude Code sessions run on this Mac without a fence.** A fenced session keeps its Claude Code records
inside its own folder, out of the chat server's sight: a fenced session polls with `dozchat` instead (above).

The session answers with `dozchat`, which doz puts on your PATH: `dozchat send room1 --re MSG_ID "…"`, as the message it
was handed says. It needs its token in its environment when it is started — never on a command line:

```bash
CHAT_TOKEN_FILE=~/.config/chat/bot1.token claude
```

On this Mac, with no proxy set, `dozchat` reaches `http://127.0.0.1:8790`; if your page port is another, add
`CHAT_URL=http://127.0.0.1:PORT` (`doz chat add … --inbox` prints both lines).

## Agents on other machines

An agent on another machine needs three things: this Mac's address on your tailnet, the chat port, and **its own
token** (made on this Mac: `doz chat add NAME --to-file F`, or `doz bot new NAME --isolation elsewhere`). **Its replies
must go back to the server the message came from**: every Dozable — another Mac, or another store on this one — has its
own chat server, and a reply posted to another one lands in that server's rooms, unseen here. Two settings let agents on
your other machines take part over Tailscale:

```bash
doz config set chat.remote_listen 100.64.0.7    # this Mac's own Tailscale address
doz config set chat.remote_agents 100.64.0.8    # each other machine allowed, exactly
```

**Turning the remote listener on opens both chat ports on this Mac's Tailscale address to the machines named in
`chat.remote_agents` — as agents with their own token only, never as you.** On those addresses the page port answers
only `/agent/…` calls and attachments, each with a participant's token; the line port always needs a token; no one
coming from there is ever you. `doz chat status` and `doz doctor` say, one line per address:
"Also listening on 100.64.0.7 (page port 8790, line port 8791) for 100.64.0.8 — agents with a token only." once it is
so, "starting…" until then, and "not an address of this Mac now (is Tailscale up?)" when Tailscale does not have it.

## Bringing in another chat's history

```bash
doz chat off
doz chat import ~/chat-copy --dry-run           # what it would do, and what stops it; writes nothing
doz chat import ~/chat-copy                     # rooms, messages, reactions, attachments, holds, avatars
```

The copy is checked before anything of it is used, and nothing secret comes across (no token, no webhook entry). The
names in it must already be participants (the dry run prints the `doz chat add` commands, or use `--add-missing`).
Nobody is woken by what is imported. The store's own history is never overwritten unless you say `--replace`, and then
it is kept aside, not deleted.

## In the dashboard

While chat is on, the dashboard shows **Chat** in the sidebar, after This Mac. It has the rooms, a room's messages as
they come (headings, lists, code, tables and links render; anything else stays text), who is here, and a composer:
**Enter** sends, **Shift+Enter** starts a new line, `@` offers the room's members and `/` the commands.

On a message:

- **React** with the smile button (the chat server's reactions, or any emoji); click your reaction again to take it off.
- **Edit** your own message with its pencil, or press **Up** in an empty composer; **Enter** saves, **Esc** stops.
- **Delete** any message from its menu (⋮), with a box to tick first. A line saying who deleted it stays in the room;
  agents that had it are told to disregard it.
- **Reveal** a direct message between agents: you read it, and the room records that you did.

**Attachments**: the clip, a paste or a drop on the room. Each file is at most 20 MB (a bigger one is refused before it
is sent); several can go with one message. PNG, JPEG, GIF and WebP pictures show in the message and open in a gallery
(the arrow keys step through the room's pictures); anything else, an SVG or a web page too, is a download that never
opens as part of the dashboard.

The room's menu (⋮ beside its name) holds agent-only chatter (**/hold**: after a number of agent messages in a row,
messages to agents wait until you post) and changes your avatar (a letter, a shape or an emoji, in a colour).

You are "here" in chat while the Chat page is open (and for a few seconds after you leave it), not just because the
dashboard is open. Messages to you are marked delivered then.

### Pop a room out

The button with the arrow out of a box, at the top right of a room (on the Chat page and on a workspace's Room tab), opens
that room in a window of its own: the room alone, the same messages, composer, asks and people, the height of the
window. Clicking it again brings the same window forward; each room has one window. Cmd-click (or a middle click) opens
it in a tab instead. The window's address is `/chat#/ROOM`, so a bookmark or a reload opens the same room, and a draft
you were typing is kept.

The window loads only chat: it opens quickly and leaves the rest of the dashboard alone. **Open in the dashboard** goes
back to the room there. A room you read in a window counts as read in the dashboard too, and two windows on one room never
mark it unread again. You can answer an ask and turn chat on from the window. If the window was signed out, it says so:
sign in on the dashboard, then come back to the window.

Keep it to about four windows at once, with the dashboard on a page other than Chat. Over plain HTTP a browser opens at
most six connections to one address, and each window holds one of them open. Too many windows and new messages arrive
late, or a window says its stream is paused (use **Reconnect** there).

## Chat on your other browsers: `serve.chat`

With the dashboard on your network (`ui.lan`, [The dashboard on your other computers, tablets and phones](https://dozable.com/docs/doz-serve.md)), the setting
`serve.chat` decides what those browsers may do with chat. It is set on this Mac only:

```bash
doz config set serve.chat off      # the default: they do not see chat at all
doz config set serve.chat read     # they read the rooms; nothing they can send or change
doz config set serve.chat write    # they also post, react, edit, delete, reveal and attach
```

**A browser that may write acts as you in chat: it is the verified human, and your agents take its words as yours.**
An agent with tools does what you ask of it, so a phone that may write can instruct every agent in your rooms, read
the direct messages it reveals and change the holds. Keep it `off` or `read` unless you need to write from another
browser. With `read` the composer and every control that changes something are off there, and the page says why. With
`write`, each thing such a browser sends is a line in the dashboard's audit log (`doz ui log`): which browser, which
action, never what it said. This Mac's own browser always has chat.

## Closing, archiving and removing a room

A room a workspace made is **closed** when the workspace finishes: it can be read, and a post is refused until the
workspace is reopened. `doz chat rooms` shows each room's state. When a workspace is finished you can put one of its rooms
away and then remove it for good — only after its history is copied into the store and checked:

```bash
doz chat room archive ROOM
doz chat room rm ROOM          # asks for the room's name; a tombstone stays (doz chat rooms --gone)
```

A loose room (made outside your workspaces) needs `--loose`; a room a workspace only linked is never removed this way.

## Asks: a question that waits for a decision

An agent can **ask** instead of just writing: a message of kind `ask` with one or more questions, each with options to
pick (one, or several), and room for an answer in your own words. It waits for a **decision**. Every ask can be declined,
every ask expires (in 24 hours unless it says sooner, at most a week), and on expiry the answer is decline — so nothing
waits for ever and nothing is taken as a yes.

- **Who decides.** You, by default: the room's people at the time of asking. An agent can name other deciders, but a bot
  only when you gave it the **decider** role, and never itself. Only you give the role, and only here:

  ```bash
  doz chat set bot2 --role decider      # bot2 may be named as a decider, and decide
  doz chat set bot2 --role none         # taken away again
  doz chat who                          # a decider's KIND ends "· decider" (--json: roles)
  ```

- **How to decide.** In the dashboard, an ask is a card in its room: pick an option (a letter key picks it), add your own
  words when it takes them, then Answer (or ⌘Enter); Decline asks for a reason, if you like. Asks are answered in this
  Mac's own browser for now; another computer sees the card without its controls. In a terminal:

  ```bash
  doz chat asks                          # the open asks of your rooms
  doz chat decide room1 12 B             # #12, by its letter (or its id, or its label); words after it if it takes them
  doz chat decide room1 12 use the other copy   # an answer in your own words
  doz chat decide room1 12 --decline not today
  doz chat ask room1 "Ship it?" --option yes=Yes --option no=No --decider bot2 --wait   # ask yourself
  doz chat withdraw room1 13             # an ask you asked
  ```

  A refusal says why in plain words ("It was already answered: decided by Bot2.") and exits 3 when the ask can no longer
  be answered by you — already answered (`already-answered` in `--json`), expired, withdrawn or its room closed
  (`invalid-phase`), or not yours to answer (`not-owned`). Or in the room, as a message: `/decide #12 A` (the option's letter or id, words after it if you like),
  `/decide #12 use the other copy` (an answer in your own words, when the question takes them) or `/decide #12 decline not
  today`. `#12` is the ask's short number on this Mac; the start of its id works too (`/decide 41fa46f4 A`). An ask of
  several questions is answered with its answers (an agent: `POST /agent/decide`), or declined with `/decide #12 decline`.
  The first decision wins; a refused one is told only to whoever sent it and is never written into the room.
- **Withdraw.** Only whoever asked: `/withdraw #12` (or `doz chat withdraw ROOM 12`).
- **An agent's asks.** An agent asks and answers with its own token: `dozchat ask ROOM "…" --option yes=Yes --option no=No`,
  then `dozchat ask-show ROOM #N --wait 60` for the outcome. Dozable never answers for it.
- **What the asker hears.** The outcome comes the way it takes messages (its webhook, `dozchat receive`, or its Claude Code
  session's inbox). A decision a bot makes is its own, shown as decided by it (decider role) — never as yours.
- **Limits.** One open ask per agent and room (`chat.ask_max_open`), and not the same question again for 10 minutes after a
  decline or an expiry (`chat.ask_cooldown_seconds`); `chat.ask_expiry_seconds` is how long one stays open when it names no
  time. `doz config set chat.asks false` turns asks off: an ask, `/decide` and `/withdraw` are refused, and open ones stay as
  they are until asks are on again.
- **A finished workspace leaves no ask waiting.** When its room closes, each open ask in it expires at once and its asker is
  told the room was closed; it cannot be decided, and once the workspace is reopened the same question can be asked again
  straight away.

## Notices from feeds

Some messages are from no one: a unit of work's outcome from its journal, this Mac's login expiring, a host the network
keeps refusing, an agent that crashed, the disk running low. Each is a **notice** from a **feed**, drawn as a card, and
goes to whoever can act on it — the journal's outcomes to the room, the rest to the manager (or to you). An agent is
handed a notice only when it is addressed to it. [Feeds and notices](https://dozable.com/docs/feeds-and-notices.md) says what posts where, how
to change it, and how a critical one reaches an idle session safely.

## What is not there yet

Room apps (a room's own page), notifications from the browser, and a separate address for attachments. The chat
server's command list and protocol (`/protocol`) say what each version speaks.

## See also

- [Feeds and notices](https://dozable.com/docs/feeds-and-notices.md)
- [Agents / Bots](https://dozable.com/docs/agents-and-bots.md)
- [Tokens and identity](https://dozable.com/docs/tokens-and-identity.md)
- [The dashboard](https://dozable.com/docs/the-dashboard.md)
- [The dashboard on your other computers, tablets and phones](https://dozable.com/docs/doz-serve.md)
- [Security model](https://dozable.com/docs/security-model.md)
- [Settings reference](https://dozable.com/docs/settings-reference.md) — `chat.*` and `serve.chat`

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/workspaces

# Workspaces

A workspace is an environment set up for getting work done: its agents, its rooms, the brief that says what the work is
for, and any folders it works on (usually projects). Work starts only once it is fully set up, and then goes one **unit
of work** (a run) at a time: each has a goal, a journal of what was done, and the lessons you approved from the ones
before ([Runs, the journal and lessons](https://dozable.com/docs/runs-the-journal-and-lessons.md)). Where each agent runs — a micro VM, fenced
on this Mac, or unfenced as you — is one setting of the workspace, not the first thing you decide.

```bash
doz workspace new demo --preset swift-tests --brief "Fix the failing test" --folder ~/code/demo --dry-run   # what it would make
doz workspace new demo --preset swift-tests --brief "Fix the failing test" --folder ~/code/demo
doz workspace start demo                                   # the set-up check, the brief posted, the first unit of work open
doz workspace finish demo                                  # the unit of work closed and archived (asks first)
doz workspace run demo "Now the flaky one"                 # the next unit of work, with the lessons so far
```

A *project* is something else: a folder (usually a repository) with its sandbox settings in `doz_project.yaml` (see
[Projects](https://dozable.com/docs/projects.md)). A workspace can work on several projects' folders, or on none.

Nothing you already have moves by itself. Your sandboxes and your sessions on this Mac are **loose agents** until you
adopt them into a workspace, and adopting one changes only the workspace's own record: the sandbox and the session stay
exactly as they were. The dashboard shows them (below, [In the dashboard](#in-the-dashboard)), makes and starts a
workspace in this Mac's own browser ([The New workspace wizard](#the-new-workspace-wizard)), and leaves the rest of what
changes one to the command line.

## Making one

```bash
doz workspace new demo --brief "Fix the build" --folder ~/code/demo
doz workspace new app --preset blank --brief "Fix the build" --folder ~/code/app --worker "Fix the failing test" --start
```

`doz workspace create` is the same command (an alias of `new`): the same flags, the same answer.

- `--brief TEXT` is the brief: what the work is for, in your words (at most 256 KiB). `--brief -` reads it from standard
  input, its last line break dropped (`echo "Fix the build" | doz workspace new demo --brief -` gives the brief "Fix the
  build"). `--prompt-file FILE` reads it from a file instead, exactly as it is (`-` for standard input). Give one of them:
  `--brief` and `--prompt-file` together are refused. `--ref PATH` or `--ref https://…` adds a reference to it
  (repeatable).
- `--preset NAME` starts from one of the presets ([Presets](#presets), below); the dry run's `--json` lists them
  (`presets`). A flag you give wins over the preset (`--network open`, a folder's `:rw`). Another name is refused (exit
  65, `invalid-value`, naming the presets) and nothing is made.
- `--worker "TASK"` declares a worker (repeatable): it is recorded on the workspace now — `doz worker ls` lists it
  with its task, **not started** — and `doz workspace start` starts it, as `doz worker add NAME --task "TASK"` would, where
  the workspace's new workers run (fenced on this Mac unless `--worker-isolation vm`). Each is named when it is declared,
  the first free `bot1`, `bot2`, …. Declaring needs nothing else — chat may be off — but a worker talks in the
  workspace's room, so the start refuses (exit 3, saying the declared worker needs chat) until chat is on and the
  workspace has its room (`doz workspace edit NAME --make-room`); `--no-room` with `--worker` is refused at once. One that
  still does not start is said in the start's answer and stays declared; the next start tries it again.
- `--folder DIR` adds a folder it works on (repeatable); the first is the main one. `DIR:ro` makes one read-only. Folders
  are optional: `doz workspace new notes --brief "Take notes"` makes a workspace with none.
- `--adopt NAME` (or `--adopt @mac/SESSION`) adopts a sandbox or a session at once (repeatable).
- `--new-folder` makes an empty folder `~/doz-workspaces/NAME` (in your projects folder, `defaults.projects_dir`) and
  makes it the main folder. It is offered, never forced: with no folder the manager works there anyway.
- `--from-project` fills in the network preset from the project file in the main folder (it needs a `--folder`); the
  file is only read, never written. A `--network` that differs from it is refused.
- `--manager BOT` makes one of your Agents / Bots its manager (see [The manager](#the-manager) below). Nothing is
  started yet.
- `--worker-isolation fenced|vm` is where its new workers run unless `doz worker add` says otherwise (fenced by default;
  never unfenced by default — a worker is unfenced only when you name it).
- `--network locked|standard|open` is the network its agents get (locked by default); the room is always added.
- `--dry-run` shows what would be made and makes nothing: a few lines, everything that would be refused, what the start
  would still need once it is made (each with its fix), and the commands that make it — the brief as a heredoc you can
  paste. It never starts the daemon; it exits 0 when nothing is refused, else as `new` would.
- `--start` starts it as soon as it is made (`doz workspace start NAME`). If the start is refused, the workspace stays
  made and setting up, and the refusal says what is missing.
- `--request-id ID` makes it safe to run again: see [Retrying safely](#retrying-safely) below.

It prints the workspace. A new one is **setting up · you**: it has never started, and you drive it. The work starts
once the workspace is fully set up, with `doz workspace start`.

### Presets

A preset fills in three choices for you — where the manager and new workers run, the network and whether folders are
added read-only — and nothing else. It installs no tool, makes no agent and allows no site beyond its network preset.

| preset | the manager and new workers | network | folders | what it does not cover |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `blank` | as you choose (fenced unless you say) | as you choose (locked unless you say) | as you give them | — |
| `research` | fenced on this Mac | locked: its AI model only | added read-only | any website: allow each one (`doz net allow`) |
| `swift-tests` | fenced on this Mac | standard (its AI model, GitHub and the package registries, Swift's included) | as you give them | any other site: allow it |
| `mac-admin` | fenced on this Mac | locked: its AI model only | as you give them | anything else on the network: allow each site |
| `remotion-video` | micro VMs | standard, and `remotion.media` (where a render downloads Remotion's own browser) | as you give them | any other site — fonts or media a composition fetches, a browser's own background requests: allow what the work needs (`doz workspace show W --network` shows each refusal and the command) |

`--worker-isolation`, `--manager-isolation`, `--network` and a folder's `:ro` or `:rw` each win over the preset.
`--site HOST` (repeatable) adds a site every agent the workspace starts may reach on top of its network; a preset's own
sites join yours, and the dry run's `network:` line names them all.

### Retrying safely

`doz workspace new`, `doz worker add`, `doz workspace adopt` and `doz permissions grant` take `--request-id ID`: an id of
your own for this one request (1–128 letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `:` or `-` — a UUID is a good one). Run the same command
again with the same id and arguments and you get the first answer again, with `"replayed": true` in `--json`, and nothing
is made, added or granted a second time. It is for a script or an agent that did not see the answer — a timeout, a
dropped connection, a daemon restart — and cannot tell whether the first try worked: it simply runs the same command
again.

- The same id with different arguments is refused (exit 3, `request-id-reused`): the message names what differs (such
  as `--brief`), never its value. Use a new id for a new request.
- A first try that failed is not kept, so a retry runs for real.
- An id is kept for 24 hours from its first answer, in the store, so a daemon restart does not lose it. Each command has
  ids of its own: `r-1` for a `workspace new` and `r-1` for a `worker add` are two ids.
- Two runs with the same id at the same moment never both run: the second waits and gets the first answer.

### Its room
