# Space files

A **space file** describes a workspace in one YAML file, `NAME.space.yaml`, kept in git beside the work: its agents,
its rooms, the brief, any folders and sandboxes. Each thing in it is either **owned** — the space makes it — or
**external**: it exists already and is only referenced (`external:`). The file asks; Dozable decides: it holds the
workspace's record (see [Workspaces](https://dozable.com/docs/workspaces.md)), and every rule the daemon keeps holds for a file too.

Dozable reads, checks and plans a space file, sets the workspace up from it and takes it down again. Exactly what
applies one in this version:

| command | what it does with the file |
|---|---|
| `doz space plan -f FILE` | reads and checks it, and shows what `up` would do; changes nothing |
| `doz space up -f FILE` | applies it: shows the plan, then makes what is missing and opens a unit of work |
| `doz space down NAME` | takes it down at the end of the unit of work (`--purge` also removes what persists) |
| `doz space config FILE` | prints it merged with what it extends; changes nothing |

`doz space` is `doz workspace` under a shorter name: `doz workspace up -f FILE` is the same command as
`doz space up -f FILE`. **Plain `doz up` is something else** — a project's command ([Projects](https://dozable.com/docs/projects.md)): it reads
`doz_project.yaml` and never a space file. Saving a space file in the dashboard's editor never applies it either: `up`
does. Not in this version, and refused by the plan with exit 7 when a file asks for them: an owned **service**, a
**secret** for an agent Dozable starts, and an agent `permissions:` preset other than `standard` or `bypass`.

```yaml
doz: space/3
extends: ./my_doz_workspace_defaults.yaml   # settings every space shares (optional)
space: launch-video
brief: BRIEF.md
owner: ada

folders:
  repo: { external: ~/code/launch-video }
  scratch: {}                               # owned: made for each run, removed at down

agents:
  mira: { external: { bot: mira }, role: manager }
  writer:
    kind: claude-code
    isolation: fenced
    folder: repo
    prompt: Read BRIEF.md and draft the script.

chat:
  rooms:
    launch-video: { members: [owner, mira, writer] }

persist:
  team-chat: { room: launch-video }         # the room and its history carry over from one run to the next
```

## Looking at one

```bash
doz space config launch-video.space.yaml     # the file merged with what it extends, each value with its file and line
doz space plan -f launch-video.space.yaml    # what up would do: every step, the summary, what down will do
doz space up -f launch-video.space.yaml --dry-run   # the same plan, as up shows it
```

`doz space` is `doz workspace` under a shorter name: `doz workspace plan -f FILE` and `doz workspace config FILE` are the
same commands. Without `-f`, the one `*.space.yaml` in the current folder is used; with two or more there, name one.
`--profile NAME` (repeatable) includes the things the file marks `profiles: [NAME]`.

Looking never starts the daemon and changes nothing. With no daemon running, what only a running daemon knows — whether a
session or a bot runs now, the chat server's rooms — is marked "not known", and nothing is refused for it.

## What is read

- **The file**, then each **defaults file** it `extends:` (a list is applied in order, each after the files it extends;
  a loop is an error naming the chain). A defaults file (`doz: space-defaults/3`, or `space-defaults/3.1`, which holds the same) holds only `persist`, `archive`,
  `approvals` and `agent_defaults`: never agents, rooms, sandboxes, services, folders, secrets or the owner, so
  inheriting never starts anything the space file did not write.
- **`NAME.space.override.yaml`** beside the file, when there is one: good for paths that differ from Mac to Mac.
- **`${VAR}`** in values, from the environment or the `.env` beside the file (`${VAR:-default}`; `$$` is a `$`). Never in
  keys and never under `secrets:`.
- Maps merge by key; lists replace; `null` removes an inherited value (`persist: { memory: null }`).

Every problem is reported at once, as `file:line`, with what to write instead; an error stops everything (exit 65, an invalid
document; `--json` says `"error": {"code": "invalid-document", …}`) and nothing is done. A warning does not stop it.

### The version line: space/3.1

A file starts with its version line. **`doz: space/3.1`** is space/3 with a few keys of Dozable's own; everything else
reads the same. A file that says `doz: space/3` is read exactly as before.

```yaml
doz: space/3.1
space: app
owner: ada
brief: { text: Fix the build }  # the brief written here; or brief: BRIEF.md, or { file: BRIEF.md }; refs: [...] beside it
about: { title: Work on a project, summary: A manager and a helper. }   # title, summary, description, icon, tags, category, needs
layout: { … }                   # where the editor draws things; a plan never acts on it
network: standard               # locked, standard or open, or { preset, allow: [HOST…] }
x-dozable: { lifetime: standing }   # not a 3.1 key: standing (what the space owns stays) or runs (it lasts one run)
folders:
  repo: { external: ~/work/app, main: true }   # the main folder (one at most)
agents:
  helper: { kind: claude-code, isolation: fenced, folder: repo, prompt: Fix the failing test., restart: on-failure }
  old: { external: { sandbox: my-sandbox } }   # an agent in a sandbox that exists: adopted, never started
```

- **`brief`** is a path, `{ text }` or `{ file }` — one of them — with optional `refs:`: files or folders the agents
  should read, or `http(s)://` addresses. A relative path is the space file's folder's (as the brief's file is) and `~/…`
  is your home; `up` records each one as an absolute path (the plan shows them so), and refuses one that is not there.
- **`about.title`** is the workspace's title. A top-level `title:` still reads in a 3.1 file, with a note; both is an error.
- **The top-level `network`** is the workspace's network: `up` records it as the workspace's default, which every agent
  it starts gets — the manager, workers, and an agent in a place that declares no network of its own (below) — and the
  workspace's Network card shows. `allow:` holds host names (no port). A file that says none is `locked`. A later `up`
  of a changed `network:` changes the workspace's default (the plan names the change); an agent already running keeps
  the network it started with until it starts again.
- An agent's own `network` outside a place, and **`restart`** (`no` or `on-failure`), are recorded and noted, not applied
  in this version.
- **The lifetime is not a 3.1 key**: it stays under `x-dozable` in either version and is never required (a file that says
  none is read as `runs`). A top-level `lifetime:` in a 3.1 file is refused (65) with the fix.
- **`agent_defaults: { where: sandbox }`** runs every agent that does not say where in the workspace's own VM, a sandbox
  the run makes (named `SPACE-vm`). On an agent, a place is `mac` or `sandbox:NAME`.
- **An agent's own `network`**: an unfenced agent has none (it acts as you), and an agent in a VM — the workspace's or
  a sandbox the space makes — shares the VM's, which is the workspace's (standard when the file says none). Either
  written otherwise is refused (65).
- An empty `refs`, `tags` or `allow` list is refused; leave the key out instead.
- A 3.1 key in a file that says `doz: space/3` is refused (65): change the version line to `doz: space/3.1`. A space/3
  file extends only `space-defaults/3` files.

A brief written in the file is kept with the workspace and posted at the first up; `doz workspace show W --brief` reads
it. `doz workspace doc W` (37) prints any workspace as a space/3.1 file.

### Dozable's other keys: `x-dozable`

A few things the format cannot say yet are written under `x-dozable`, at the place they belong; any other `x-` key is
ignored.

```yaml
x-dozable: { lifetime: standing }                             # the space's lifetime: standing or runs
folders:
  notes: { x-dozable: { lifetime: run } }                     # in a standing space: this one lasts one run
agent_defaults: { x-dozable: { isolation: vm } }              # where a workspace's new workers run (3.1: where: sandbox)
```

### Places: `x-dozable.places` and `where:`

A **place** is where an agent runs: a VM, a fenced session on this Mac, or an unfenced one that acts as you. Declare your
places under `x-dozable.places` and put each agent in one with `where:`:

```yaml
doz: space/3.1
agents:
  helper:   { kind: claude-code, role: worker, where: desk, folder: repo }
  reviewer: { kind: claude-code, role: reviewer, where: build, access: ro }
x-dozable:
  places:
    desk:    { isolation: fenced }                                  # on this Mac, behind Dozable's fence
    build:   { isolation: vm, image: claude-code, cpus: 4, memory: 8G }  # a sandbox of the space
    old-box: { external: { sandbox: old-review } }                  # a sandbox that already exists: only referenced
```

- **`isolation`** is `vm`, `fenced` or `unfenced`. Only a `vm` place has an `image`, `cpus` and `memory`; it is made by
  `up` as the space's sandbox (`app-build`), and every agent in it shares it.
- **A fenced place is a policy, not a shared box.** Each agent in it gets a fence of its own: its own proxy, its own
  placeholders, nothing shared with the other agents of the place — and each fence is built from the place:
  - **`view`** (`{ notes: ro, out: rw }`): more folders of the space, read-only or read-write. The agent's own folder
    (the workspace's main one) is always read-write; a view cannot make it read-only.
  - **`network`** (as the top-level `network:`: `locked`, `standard`, `open` or `{ preset, allow: [HOST…] }`): the
    fence's network; a place that declares none has the workspace's (the top-level `network:`, else `locked`). An agent
    in the place may write its own `network:` only to narrow it — a preset no wider and only hosts the place allows (otherwise 65); it narrows that agent's fence alone.
  - **`credentials`**: `github:read` (or `github`), `github:push` — GitHub as you, through a placeholder — and
    `ssh-agent`. A fence holds no key accounts (65).
- **A vm place** takes its `network` (none: the workspace's) and `credentials` (`github:read`, `github:push`, or a key
  account's name) when its sandbox is made; every agent in it shares them, so an agent's own `network:` must equal the place's (65). Its `view` can
  name only the workspace's main folder, read-write: a sandbox shares one folder, at `/workspace`.
- **An unfenced place enforces nothing**, so it declares no view, network or credentials (the plan refuses them, 65) and
  says so: the plan shows each as "none: acts as you". An agent is never put in an unfenced place by `agent_defaults`:
  it writes `where:` itself, and `up` asks you to confirm it, as for `isolation: unfenced`.
- **An external place** is `external: { sandbox: NAME }` and nothing else: an existing sandbox, never made or removed.
- **`where:`** names a place, or `mac`, or `sandbox:NAME` for a sandbox under `sandboxes:` — those two words are never a
  place's name. A name that is no place is refused, listing the places there are. `sandboxes:` entries are still read,
  as places with isolation `vm`.
- **A grant is never a place's.** `doz grant desk …` is refused: grant the agents in it (`doz grant helper …`).

`doz workspace plan -f FILE --json` lists the `places` (name, isolation, view, network, credentials) and each agent's
`where`; `doz workspace state W --json` lists each place with its sessions — in a fenced place, each with its own fence.

The keys space/3.1 now has were written under `x-dozable` too (`x-dozable: { brief: { text: … }, network: … }`, a folder's
`x-dozable: { main: true }`, an agent's `x-dozable: { restart: …, external: { sandbox: … } }`). That form is
**deprecated**: it is still read in this release, in either version, and the plan says, for each use, the key to write
instead. Writing a key both ways is an error.

## The plan

The plan lists the steps `up` will run, in order: the external things it checks (each must exist, or up stops before
changing anything — "nothing was changed"); the workspace it makes (its folders, its room, its manager); its other
rooms and scratch folders; the start, which opens a run; each owned agent, in the order written. Each step says what
`down` will do to it.

Its summary names **every risky setting with the file and line that set it**: an agent that is unfenced (it acts as
you, with full access to your user), one that bypasses permissions, what persists, `archive: off`, transcripts
discarded. A setting inherited from a defaults file is named as such: inheriting never approves anything.

- **Unfenced is never inherited.** `agent_defaults` cannot make an agent unfenced; each unfenced agent writes
  `isolation: unfenced` itself. An agent that bypasses permissions on this Mac must write its own isolation.
- **Unfenced is confirmed at every up**, wherever the setting came from (`--yes` answers on a terminal only).
- **A file asks; the owner grants.** `requests:` on an agent are recorded and shown ("requested, not granted"); you grant
  them with `doz permissions grant`. A file never grants anything.
- **The owner** must be you, as the chat server knows you.
- **A workspace made without a space file** is not taken over: `up` refuses a name already used by one (exit 4).

Not in this version, and said so in the plan: owned services (refused), a manager that is not an Agent / Bot (refused),
secrets for an agent Dozable starts (refused), a preset other than `standard` or `bypass` (refused), and `model`,
Remote Control, chat delivery, `resume: summary` and folder trust (noted, not applied).

## Up and down

```sh
doz space up -f launch-video.space.yaml            # the plan, then it is set up
doz space down launch-video                        # end the run; archive it; remove what the run made
doz space down launch-video --purge                # and what persists
doz workspace show launch-video --space            # "Defined by launch-video.space.yaml": up or down
```

- **`up`** shows the plan and makes what is missing: the folders it keeps, the workspace (or the changes the plan
  shows), its rooms, the run (started — the brief posted as your first message the first time only — or reopened when
  the space is down, its kept agents woken), the run's scratch folders, each agent. An agent that runs **unfenced**
  acts with full access to your user: `up` asks you about it on the terminal at every up, whatever set it — `--yes`
  answers that question on a terminal; with no terminal, `up` does nothing and exits 5. What the file **requests** for
  an agent (a role, grants) is recorded, never granted: `doz permissions grant` does that. `up` stops at the first step
  that fails (the rest are "not run"): exit 75 when steps before it were done (`--json`'s `partial` names what is done,
  what remains and the command that retries), exit 1 when nothing was; `up` again makes only what is missing.
- **The brief is the file.** The kick-off, `doz workspace show --brief` and the run's archive read `BRIEF.md` beside
  the space file; an edit on the workspace's page or with `doz workspace edit --prompt-file` is saved into it. `up`
  never writes it. The file must be yours, under your home, and no link.
- **`down`** asks first (`--yes`; no terminal and no `--yes`: exit 5). It archives the run — chat, transcripts, screens,
  usage — into the store and checks it, then removes what the run made, each only after its copy verifies: agents
  ended and forgotten (transcripts deleted only with `transcripts: discard`, and only files unchanged since), the run's
  scratch folders and rooms (a room leaves a tombstone). If the archive could not be written, nothing that holds work
  is removed. What `persist:` names is kept for the next run: a room closed with its history, a sandbox's disk, an
  agent's memory (a fenced agent's comes back in its next fenced session only). External things are never touched.
  With **`archive: off`** nothing is copied: what goes with no copy is listed before you confirm. A step that fails is
  said and `down` carries on (exit 75); `down` again does what is left.
- **`--purge`** takes it down first, then removes what persists — its rooms (archived first), sandboxes and kept
  memory — and releases the folders it kept: they leave the workspace and stay on disk.

Exit codes: 0 ok · 1 a step failed before anything was done · 2 something external missing · 3 not in a state to go
on (chat off, a workspace archived), or changed since the plan · 4 a workspace of that name made without a space file ·
5 not confirmed · 7 not in this version · 64 usage · 65 a problem in the file · 75 partly done (a step failed after
others were done). `doz help exit-codes` lists them all.

## While it runs

- **`doz workspace state NAME`** shows the space as it is now beside its file: each agent (running, asleep, gone after
  down, missing — and whether it is working, idle or waiting for you), its chat member, every folder, sandbox and room,
  what the workspace holds named like the space but not in the file, and what waits for you (a permission prompt, a
  sandbox that failed, an up that stopped part way), and each agent's condition (running, asleep, stopped, crashed, not
  started). A chat message's text is never in it. `--json` is the document the dashboard reads, with `kind`
  `WorkspaceState`, `schema` 1 and each agent's condition (37, "Every agent's condition"). With no daemon running it
  starts none, and every state says "not known". A workspace made without a space file answers too, from its record.
- **`doz workspace show NAME --space`** names the file and, read now, its size and sha256. **`doz workspace edit NAME
  --space-file F --if-match SHA`** saves F over that same file — only while it is still the one whose sha256 you read
  (changed since: nothing is written, exit 3). A save is never applied: `doz workspace up -f FILE` applies it. From the
  dashboard the file is saved only in this Mac's own browser.
- **`doz workspace runs NAME --frames RUN`** shows a run as it went: its state each time it changed (recorded when
  something happens, never on a timer; at most 2,000 frames a run, then only the last state). Down keeps them in the run's
  archive and checks them.

## The workspace drawn

In the dashboard a workspace a space file made is drawn from its file and what is running now: its agents, rooms, folders
and sandboxes in the file's layout, each marked as it is — running, asleep, missing, gone after down — and what waits for
you. The picture is on the workspace's **Home** tab, across the page — on no other tab: click it to open the file in the
space editor (below). Home and the Workspaces page show each workspace small beside its
name, and the sidebar shows it at the top of an unfolded workspace (the setting `ui.nav_thumbnails` turns the sidebar's
pictures off; the sidebar keeps no empty box while a picture is on its way). The picture follows what happens — an up or down, a save, a
sleep or wake from the dashboard, a sandbox starting or stopping — and is never read on a timer; a change made only in a
terminal to agents on this Mac shows the next time you open a page.

A file that doesn't read is drawn as a small warning, and the page adds what Dozable itself found wrong with it and the
command that checks it, `doz workspace up -f FILE --dry-run`. A workspace made without a space file shows a small tile on
Home and the Workspaces page and, on its Home tab, "Made without a space file — `doz workspace up -f FILE` draws it". Another computer sees the picture
only while `serve.chat` lets it read; otherwise it sees the tile, "Shown to another computer only with serve.chat read".

## Editing a space in the dashboard

A workspace's picture (or **Edit the space** beside it) opens its space file in the space editor, the whole window, at
its own address — `#/w/NAME/space`, which you can bookmark, reload or open in a new tab. The bar above it leads back to
the workspace, names the file, says **Saved**, **Unsaved** or **Read-only here**, and has **Text**, **Watch** and **Open in
a new window**.

- **The canvas** draws the file; you change it there, and its problems are listed and marked as you go — a problem in a
  defaults file it extends is named with that file. **Live** draws what is running now over it (the agents, their rooms,
  what waits for you — a permission prompt, an open Ask, which you can answer there), following what happens; it is never
  read on a timer. The runs strip under it steps through a past run's states.
- **Text** adds the YAML beside the canvas; it is loaded only when you ask for it, and your changes, undo and selection
  carry over. The dashboard remembers that you use it.
- **Saving** (**⌘S**) writes the file only if it is still the version you opened. If it changed since — in your editor or
  with `doz workspace edit` — nothing is written and the editor says **Changed elsewhere**; **Reload** reads the file as it
  is now (your changes there are lost). A save is never applied: "Saved. Not applied: Up applies it." — `doz workspace up
  -f FILE` applies it. A file too long to send from the page is saved with the command the page shows.
- **Unsaved changes are never lost without asking**: leaving the page asks first (**Stay** or **Leave**), closing the tab
  asks too, and a restart of `doz ui` waits to reload the page until the file is saved.
- **Watch** (`#/w/NAME/space/watch`) shows the drawing with Live on and nothing else, read-only — for a second screen.
- **Another computer** sees the file only while `serve.chat` lets it read, read-only: "Changed only in this Mac's own
  browser", with the command that changes it on the Mac. Only this Mac's own browser saves a space file.
- **A phone** shows the drawing and Live, read-only ("Edit on a wider screen").

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/history-and-retention

# History and retention

Dozable keeps a history of what happened on this Mac — every action on a sandbox, sessions, the daemon's runs and its
events, each sandbox's connections and network by minute, CPU, memory and disk samples, the use of your keys (by name),
workspace and permission logs, runs and their frames, and the times of chat messages and the outcomes of Asks — and
answers it as one timeline: `doz timeline`.

**Nothing of it leaves your Mac.** It lives in your store, readable only by you. No message text, Ask question, command
line, path, URL, query string, header or key value is ever kept in it. The hosts a sandbox connected to are kept only as
hidden details: they are never searched as text, never in a summary, and only shown when you ask for them by name
(`attr.dest:`).

## Looking at it

```bash
doz timeline                 # this Mac's name, each source, how long it is kept, and since when
doz timeline retention       # each source's days, who set them, the history file's size
doz timeline query FILE      # answer a timeline query (a JSON document; - reads stdin)
doz timeline tail FILE       # follow a query live (needs the daemon)
```

Looking never starts the daemon: with none running, `doz timeline` answers from the store. The history is filled by the
daemon as things happen; the first time it starts after an update, it reads everything already recorded in the
background, and answers say "indexing … %" until it is done.

This Mac's name in the history is the setting `daemon.mac_name`, "this Mac" by default — a name you choose, never the
Mac's network name:

```bash
doz config set daemon.mac_name studio
```

## How long each kind is kept

Each source has a setting, `timeline.SOURCE`, with four parts in days: single events, then counts by minute, by hour and
by day. `kept` keeps it until you delete it; each part is at least a day.

| Setting | Default | What |
|---|---|---|
| `timeline.actions` | `30/30/365/kept` | actions on sandboxes (start, sleep, wake, …) |
| `timeline.sessions` | `30/30/365/kept` | sessions opened and ended |
| `timeline.daemon` | `30/30/365/kept` | the daemon's runs |
| `timeline.network` | `30/30/365/kept` | connections and bytes per sandbox per minute |
| `timeline.workspace` | `90/90/365/kept` | workspace logs |
| `timeline.grants` | `365/365/365/kept` | permission decisions and grants |
| `timeline.runs` | `kept/kept/kept/kept` | a workspace's runs and a space's frames |
| `timeline.chat` | `30/30/365/kept` | chat message times and Ask outcomes |
| `timeline.daemon_events` | `7/30/365/kept` | the daemon's own events |
| `timeline.egress` | `7/7/90/365` | each connection: its host is kept 7 days; counts per sandbox (never a host) longer |
| `timeline.resources` | `7/7/365/kept` | CPU, memory and disk samples |
| `timeline.keys` | `30/30/365/kept` | your keys' use, by name |

```bash
doz config set timeline.egress 3/3/30/365    # each connection's host for 3 days only
doz timeline prune --dry-run                 # what each source would lose now
doz timeline prune                           # the daemon does this hourly by itself
```

Counts are kept before single events go, so a zoomed-out timeline still shows the time; before a source's "since" it
shows "not kept", never quiet time. How often samples are taken is `timeline.sample_seconds` (60; 0 = never); they are
read from this Mac's side, never by running anything in the sandbox.

**What is not bounded yet.** These settings bound the history file and the records the history added (the daemon's
events, each connection, samples, key use). Dozable's older records — the metrics of actions, sessions, daemon runs and
the network, the workspace and permission logs — are not trimmed by them yet: they keep growing as before. You can
clear the metrics in Resources (see [Resources and disk space](https://dozable.com/docs/resources-and-disk-space.md)).

## Starting the history again

```bash
doz timeline rebuild           # read every record again (removes nothing)
doz timeline rebuild --clean   # start the history file empty, then read every record again
```

The history file (`timeline.sqlite`) is made from the records, so deleting it — in Resources, or with `--clean` — loses
only the counts kept for time whose records are already gone.

---

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/runs-the-journal-and-lessons

# Runs, the journal and lessons

A **run** is one unit of work in a [workspace](https://dozable.com/docs/workspaces.md), from its start to its finish: a goal, the agents
working on it, the conversation in its room, and a **journal** that records what was done. When a unit of work ends you
can draw a **lesson** from it, and once you approve it, every later unit of work carries it. Dozable records all of
this; it never decides what the entries mean or enforces a process. The process is yours: you write it in the brief
(see [Bring your own process](https://dozable.com/docs/bring-your-own-process.md) for a worked example).

**On this page:** [Opening and finishing](#opening-and-finishing-a-unit-of-work) ·
[The journal](#the-journal) · [Kinds and their data](#kinds-and-their-data) ·
[Lessons](#lessons-and-the-work-description) · [What agents may write](#what-agents-may-write) ·
[How an agent writes the journal](#how-an-agent-writes-the-journal) · [Times](#times-utc-and-local)

## Opening and finishing a unit of work

The first `doz workspace start` opens the first run, with the brief as its goal; after a finish, `doz workspace run`
opens the next.

```bash
doz workspace run demo "Fix the failing test"   # a run with this goal
doz workspace run demo                          # a run whose goal is the brief
doz workspace run demo "Again" --follows 2026-11-23-1 --source run:2026-11-23-1
doz workspace run demo "Look first" --no-start  # open the run, start nothing
doz workspace runs demo                         # each run, its goal, its archive and its totals
doz workspace runs demo --archive RUN           # write a run's archive again
doz workspace finish demo                       # close the run and archive it (asks first; --yes in a script)
```

`run` posts the opening message in the workspace's room as your message — the brief, the lessons to apply, and this
run's goal when you gave one (below) — and then starts its agents as `doz workspace start` does; `--no-start` starts
nothing. A finished workspace is reopened first: its rooms open to new messages again. An archived one is refused (`doz
workspace restore` first).

**One run at a time.** While a run is open, `run` is refused — exit 3, `run-open`, with `doz workspace finish W` as the
fix. Finish it first.

**`reopen` opens a run too.** `doz workspace reopen W` is the old name of `run`: the same command (it prints a one-line
note on a terminal, never with `--json`). So a `run` straight after a `reopen` is refused with `run-open`: the reopen
already opened one. `--dry-run` still shows reopen's plan, and `--if-plan SHA` reopens on that plan as before, starting
nothing.

Each run records what it is for and where it came from: its **goal** (`goalFrom`: `given`, or `brief` when you gave none),
its **source** (`--source KIND` or `KIND:REF`: `given`, `brief`, `run:ID`, `ask:TEXT`, `schedule:TEXT`; another kind exits
65), the run it **follows** (`--follows RUN`, a run of this workspace, else 65), who opened it (`owner`, or an agent's
name), the **revision** of the brief it read (1 when the workspace was made, one more for each edit of the brief or its
references), and its length (`usage.durationMs`). `--json` answers `{"kind": "WorkspaceRun", "id", "state": "open",
"goal", "goalFrom", "source", "follows", "openedAt", "openedBy", "revision", "usage"}`, and `doz workspace runs W --json`
carries the same fields on each run — a run opened by an older version has only its length. `doz workspace state W
--json` says whether a run is open (`conditions.run`: `open`, `id`, `since`, and `state` `open` or `closed`).

`doz workspace up -f FILE` (a space file, [Space files](https://dozable.com/docs/space-files.md)) opens a run each time it finds none open;
`up --no-run` sets everything up and starts its agents but opens no run — `doz workspace run W` opens one later (a space
with a scratch folder, which lives in a run, refuses it).

`doz workspace run` is not Docker Compose's `run`, which runs a one-off command in a service: here it opens a unit of
work.

**Finishing.** `doz workspace finish W` closes the run. It closes the workspace's own rooms to new messages — members can
still read them; the next `run` opens them again — and writes the run's evidence into Dozable's store: its messages, each
agent's conversations and last screen, its journal and the files attached to it, the usage and a timesheet. Nothing is
removed, and no program is run in your folders (commits are not collected). `--no-archive` writes none. What finish does
to each agent, and what it keeps, is on [Workspaces](https://dozable.com/docs/workspaces.md#sleep-wake-finish-archive-and-delete).

## The journal

Each run has a **journal**: an append-only, ordered list of entries that you and the workspace's agents write as the work
goes — a task, a claim on it, a criterion, a review against it, a finding, the outcome. Dozable records each entry and its
order. Its **outcomes and reviews that are not met** also appear in the workspace's room as a card, "from NAME's
journal", within seconds — never working notes, and never a secret; a space file can turn that off
([Feeds and notices](https://dozable.com/docs/feeds-and-notices.md)).

```bash
doz workspace journal demo add note "the build is green"                  # to the open run
doz workspace journal demo add review "c1 met" --data '{"criterion":"c1","met":"yes"}' --attach ~/src/demo/test.log
doz workspace journal demo add review "c1 not met after all" --data '{"criterion":"c1","met":"no"}' --supersedes 2
doz workspace journal demo                                                # the open run's entries (or: … demo RUN)
doz workspace journal demo --follow --json                                # one JSON line per event, as it happens
doz workspace wait demo --for journal.outcome --timeout 120               # until an outcome entry is written
```

- **Entries.** Dozable sets each entry's `id` (`RUN#SEQ`), `seq`, `at` and `by` (you are `owner`). A **kind** is any name
  of a–z 0–9 `.` `_` `-`; ten are known (below), and a known kind's `--data` fields are checked when present. Text and
  data pass the same leak sweep as exports: a chat token in them is replaced, and the entry says `"swept": true`. No agent
  may be named `owner`.
- **Corrections.** Nothing is edited. `--supersedes N` adds a correction of entry N: the same kind (another kind is exit
  65), by N's author — or by someone holding `journal.supersede`; you always may. The journal shows the original marked
  `superseded_by`.
- **Evidence.** `--attach FILE` copies a file from the run's folders into the run and records its hash, so a later edit
  never changes the record (10 MiB a file, 200 MiB a run, else exit 8). `--attach-ref FILE` records the hash of a large file
  without copying it (`"copied": false`). A file is read through no link and only from inside the workspace's folders.
  `--ref` points at another entry (`seq:N`, `entry:RUN#SEQ`), a message (`msg:SEQ`), a commit (`commit:SHA`, with whether
  its object is there) or an address (`url:…`, never fetched).
- **Only while a run is open.** With none open an entry is refused (exit 3, `no-open-run`); a finished run's journal never
  changes again. At finish the journal and its evidence go into the run's archive, and `doz workspace journal W RUN` still
  reads them.
- **Following.** `--follow` streams the workspace's lines: `hello` first, then each entry, each run opening and finishing,
  and the work description's changes and proposals, each with one cursor, `wseq` — resume with `--after-wseq N` and nothing
  is missed or repeated (`--after RUN#SEQ` for entries only; `--until-finish` ends at the run's finish). A clean close sends
  `end`; anything else means "reconnect". **`wait`** is level-triggered: an entry already written matches at once, and with
  `--after RUN#SEQ` only a later one does; it exits 124 on `--timeout`. Both need the daemon running and never start it
  (exit 3, `no-daemon` — `doz daemon start`).
- **Limits per run:** 10,000 entries; an entry's text and its data 64 KiB each; 32 references and 16 files on one entry.
  Past one, the entry is refused (exit 8), naming it.

## Kinds and their data

Any kind of your own is allowed; prefix it with your team's name (`acme.deploy`) so a kind Dozable adds later never
collides with it. The known kinds, and the `--data` fields Dozable checks when they are present (extra fields are kept):

| kind | what it records | `--data` |
|---|---|---|
| `note` | anything worth keeping | — |
| `task` | a piece of the work | `identity` (who it is for) |
| `claim` | someone takes a task | `task` (the task entry's id, `RUN#SEQ`) |
| `criterion` | what "done" means | `id` — **required**: `{"id":"c1"}`; `check` (a command for a process to run; Dozable never runs it) |
| `review` | a check against a criterion | `criterion` (its id), `met` (`yes`, `no` or `partly`), `subject` (the commit or tree reviewed) |
| `finding` | a problem found | `severity` (`low`, `medium` or `high`) |
| `outcome` | how the unit of work ended | `value` — **required**: `{"value":"accepted"}` (`accepted`, `accepted-with-issues` and `rejected` are the usual three) |
| `lesson` | a lesson drawn | `proposal` (a proposal's id) |
| `gate`, `hook` | Dozable's own | written by Dozable only |

`gate`, `hook` and every `dozable.` kind are written by Dozable only: anyone else, you included, is refused (exit 65). An
`outcome` or a `criterion` without its required field is refused (exit 65), saying which.

## Lessons and the work description

A workspace's **work description** is its brief plus its **addenda**: notes and lessons added after the brief without
rewriting it. **Every run carries the lessons**: its opening message in the room is the brief, then **Lessons to apply:**
with every accepted addendum (`- TEXT (from run R)`), then — when you gave the run a goal of its own — **This run's goal:
GOAL**. So a lesson learnt in one run is part of every later one, with or without a goal (`doz workspace run --json` says
how many it carried: `lessons`). `doz workspace doc W --json` shows them as `document.brief.addenda` — each `{run, at, by,
text}`.

**Changed in 0.52.52.** Before it, only a run with no goal of its own took the brief and the addenda: a run given a goal
skipped every lesson. A manual or a note older than 0.52.52 that says so describes the old rule.

```bash
doz workspace retro demo --propose --addendum "Run the linter before the tests"   # propose a lesson from the last run
doz workspace retro demo 2026-11-23-2 --propose --addendum "…"                   # …from that run
doz workspace proposals demo                       # every proposal: open, applied or declined
doz workspace decide demo pr-1a2b3c4d apply        # or decline
doz workspace edit demo --addendum "Keep the changelog" [--run RUN]   # add one directly: no proposal, no Ask
```

A **proposal** changes nothing until it is decided. Dozable asks you in the workspace's room — "Apply this lesson to the
work description of demo?" — even when the workspace is finished and its room closed. Answer **Apply** or decline there, in
the dashboard, with `doz chat decide`, or with `doz workspace decide`. Applied, the lesson becomes an addendum (from its
run, by whoever proposed it); declined, or left until the Ask expires, nothing changes. A proposal is decided once: deciding
it again exits 3 (`proposal-decided`). `--json` answers `{"kind": "WorkspaceProposal", "id", "origin": "retro", "state",
"change": {"addendum"}, "by", "at", "source": {"run"}}`; `proposals --json` is `{"kind": "WorkspaceProposals", "proposals"}`.

## What agents may write

You are never asked for permission. An agent is, and what it may do here comes from its **permissions**
([What agents may do](https://dozable.com/docs/workspaces.md#what-agents-may-do)):

- **Reading** its own workspace's journal is on by default (`journal.read`); you can withdraw it:
  `doz grant AGENT journal.read=never --in W`.
- **Writing** an entry needs `journal.write` (or `journal.write:KIND` for one kind only), attaching a file
  `evidence.attach`, and correcting another's entry `journal.supersede`.
- **Lessons:** `description.propose` (proposing one), `description.decide` (deciding one — its own proposals too) and
  `description.edit` (adding an addendum directly).
- **Units of work:** opening one needs `run.open` (`run` and `reopen`), finishing one `run.finish`.

Apart from reading, none of these is allowed for an agent until you grant it: the roles a workspace gives its manager and
its workers do not allow them, and for an agent an answer of ask is still a refusal (exit 9, `not-permitted`, naming the
permission). The `trusted-manager` preset allows `run.finish`. The **reviewer** role gives
`journal.write`, `evidence.attach` and `description.propose`, the usual three:

```bash
doz grant bot1 reviewer --in demo                     # it may write the journal, attach evidence and propose lessons
doz grant mira description.decide=allow --in demo     # mira may also decide them
doz grant mira run.open=allow --in demo               # it may open the next unit of work
```

These are enforced today, because an agent reaches Dozable only here: through the journal and the work description. The
other permissions are shown (`doz permissions show`, the dashboard's Can do tab) but not yet enforced — see [What agents
may do](37-workspaces.md#what-agents-may-do). An unfenced agent acts as you: it has `doz` and is held by none of this.

A space file can ask for these in its own config — `x-dozable: {permissions: {helper: [reviewer, description.decide]}}` —
and `doz workspace plan` shows each as a request ("Requested, not granted"): the file never grants anything; you grant with
`doz grant`.

## How an agent writes the journal

An agent in a workspace — its manager, a worker, an adopted agent — has no `doz`: it writes and reads the journal, and
proposes lessons, with `dozchat` and its own chat token. Every agent Dozable starts has both, and this store's chat
address (`CHAT_URL`); an adopted agent gets them in each session Dozable starts in its place after the adoption
([Tokens and identity](https://dozable.com/docs/tokens-and-identity.md)). Dozable knows who it is from the token, and decides by the same
permissions as above.

```bash
dozchat journal --json                                        # the open run's entries
dozchat journal add review "c1 met" --data '{"criterion":"c1","met":"yes"}' --attach /workspace/test.log
dozchat journal add outcome "accepted" --data '{"value":"accepted"}'
dozchat journal wait outcome --timeout 300                    # until an outcome entry is there (exit 124 at the timeout)
dozchat propose --addendum "Run the linter before the tests"  # a lesson: you decide it in the room's Ask
dozchat proposal decide pr-1a2b3c4d apply                     # needs description.decide
dozchat addendum "Keep the changelog current"                 # needs description.edit
```

An entry's `by` is the agent's name. A file to attach is named as the agent sees it — in a sandbox, a path inside a folder
the workspace mounts there — and is copied from that folder on this Mac; a path in no such folder is refused. An agent of
several workspaces names one with `--in W`. `dozchat`'s exit codes: 0 done; 2 usage; 3 refused — no open run, the run
closed, or a value refused; 4 not permitted (the permission is named) or the proposal decided already; 5 no answer from
the chat server; 124 a wait's timeout. With `--json` a refusal is `{"error":{"code","message","permission"}}` on stdout. A
chat participant that is no agent of a workspace is refused, and so is your own token: you use `doz`.

## Times: UTC and local

A journal entry's `at` — and every time in `--json`, `--follow` and a run's archive — is UTC, written as ISO 8601 with a
`Z` (`2026-11-24T03:12:09Z`). `doz workspace runs` prints its STARTED and ENDED columns in this Mac's local time, so the
two differ by your time zone.

## See also

- [Workspaces](https://dozable.com/docs/workspaces.md) — the workspace, its lifecycle and what agents may do
- [Bring your own process](https://dozable.com/docs/bring-your-own-process.md) — a worked example, three units of work
- [Chat](https://dozable.com/docs/chat.md) — rooms and Asks
- [Feeds and notices](https://dozable.com/docs/feeds-and-notices.md) — the journal in the room, and the Mac's own notices
- [History and retention](https://dozable.com/docs/history-and-retention.md) — `doz timeline` shows runs beside everything else

# Bring your own process: a worked example

Dozable does not come with a process. It gives you the parts — a workspace with a brief, a room, agents, units of work
(runs) and a journal for each, lessons that carry into the next — and you decide how they are used. This page walks
through one real shape of process from start to finish: **draft → render a still → review → revise**, over three units of
work, with two agents in one room and you deciding. Then it shows how to map a workflow you already have onto the same
parts.

Read [Runs, the journal and lessons](https://dozable.com/docs/runs-the-journal-and-lessons.md) for what each command does; this page shows
them working together.

**On this page:** [The set-up](#the-set-up) · [The process, in the brief](#the-process-in-the-brief) ·
[The first unit of work](#the-first-unit-of-work) · [Finishing and the lesson](#finishing-and-the-lesson) ·
[The second and third](#the-second-and-third-units-of-work) · [Reading it afterwards](#reading-it-afterwards) ·
[Your own workflow](#mapping-your-own-workflow)

## The set-up

The work: a short promotional video made with Remotion, one scene per unit of work. Two workers do it: **bot1** drafts
a scene and renders a still of it; **bot2** reviews the still against criteria you set. You have no manager here — you
drive, and you decide.

```bash
doz chat on --name ada                                     # workers talk in the room, so chat must be on
doz workspace new promo --preset remotion-video --prompt-file ~/video/promo/BRIEF.md --folder ~/video/promo \
    --worker "Draft each scene and render a still of it" --worker "Review each still against the criteria" --dry-run
```

The dry run says what it would make — the workspace, its room `promo`, two declared workers in micro VMs (the preset),
the standard network and `remotion.media` — and anything that would be refused. Then, in this order — make it, open the
first unit of work and set what "done" means, start the workers, grant them — so no worker ever looks at a unit of work
with no criteria:

```bash
doz workspace new promo --preset remotion-video --prompt-file ~/video/promo/BRIEF.md --folder ~/video/promo \
    --worker "Draft each scene and render a still of it" --worker "Review each still against the criteria"
doz workspace run promo --no-start   # the first unit of work open, its goal (the brief) posted; nothing started yet
doz workspace journal promo add criterion …   # what "done" means, one entry each (The first unit of work, below)
doz workspace start promo            # bot1 and bot2 started, into the open unit of work
doz grant bot1 reviewer --in promo   # both may write the journal, attach evidence and propose lessons
doz grant bot2 reviewer --in promo
```

A declared worker becomes an agent of the workspace when it starts, so it is granted right after the start (`doz grant`
before it refuses: the workspace has no agent of that name yet). Workers may read the journal from the start; writing
needs the grant (`reviewer` is the usual one — [What agents may write](https://dozable.com/docs/runs-the-journal-and-lessons.md#what-agents-may-write)).
An entry written in the moment before it is refused with exit 4, naming `journal.write`, and the agent tries again once
you have granted it — nothing is lost.

**The network.** `remotion-video` gives its micro VMs the standard network and `remotion.media`, where a render first
downloads Remotion's own browser. Anything else a composition fetches (a web font, a remote image) is refused until you
allow it — look, then allow exactly what it shows:

```bash
doz workspace show promo --network          # each agent's refusals, with the command that allows each
doz net allow promo-bot1 site:fonts.example.com
```

## The process, in the brief

The process is prose in the brief. Every agent reads it in the room at the start of each unit of work, so it is the one
place to say who does what, in which order, and what each step writes in the journal:

```markdown
# Promo video

Make a 30-second promotional video in /workspace, with Remotion. Each unit of work makes ONE scene; its goal names
the scene. With no goal, make scene 1, the title card.

The process, every unit of work:
1. bot1 writes a `task` entry for the scene, drafts it, renders a still (`npx remotion still`), attaches the still
   to a `note` entry and posts it in the room for bot2.
2. bot2 reviews the still against each `criterion` entry of this unit of work: one `review` entry per criterion
   (met yes, no or partly), and a `finding` for each problem.
3. If any criterion is not met, bot1 revises and renders again, and bot2 reviews again.
4. When every criterion is met, bot2 writes the `outcome` entry: accepted.
5. If something you learnt would help the next scene, propose it as a lesson.
Ask ada (in the room) when a choice is a matter of taste.
```

Each worker was also told its own task when it was declared; the brief says how the two fit together.

## The first unit of work

You set what "done" means for this scene — one `criterion` entry each, added in the set-up above between the run and
the start, so they are there when the workers read the unit of work:

```bash
doz workspace journal promo add criterion "The title reads at phone size" --data '{"id":"c1"}'
doz workspace journal promo add criterion "The logo is on screen for the last second" --data '{"id":"c2"}'
```

**bot1** (inside its micro VM, with `dozchat`) claims the work, drafts, renders and hands over:

```bash
dozchat journal add task "Scene 1: the title card"
npx remotion still src/index.ts Scene1 out/scene1.png
dozchat journal add note "draft 1 rendered" --attach /workspace/out/scene1.png
dozchat file send promo /workspace/out/scene1.png "Scene 1, draft 1 — ready for review"
```

A render can be long. An agent running it in its own session has no limit. If you run one yourself from the Mac,
`doz exec` stops after 120 s unless you pass `--timeout`, so start it in the background instead:

```bash
doz run promo-bot1 -d --session render -- npx remotion still src/index.ts Scene1 out/scene1.png
doz sessions screen promo-bot1 render     # how it is going
```

**A matter of taste: an Ask.** bot1 is unsure of the title's colour and asks you rather than guessing:

```bash
dozchat ask promo "Title colour?" --option a=Amber --option t=Teal
```

The Ask appears in the room as a card. Answer it there (pick **Amber**, then **Answer**), or from a terminal:

```bash
doz chat asks                  # the open asks, each with its short number
doz chat decide promo 4 a      # #4, option a
```

bot1 hears the decision (`dozchat ask-show promo #4 --wait 60` gives it as JSON) and goes on. An Ask nobody answers
expires — in 24 hours unless it says sooner — and the answer is then decline, so nothing waits for ever.

**bot2** reviews the still against each criterion:

```bash
dozchat journal add review "c1 not met: the title is too small on a phone" --data '{"criterion":"c1","met":"no"}'
dozchat journal add finding "the title is 48 px at 1080 wide" --data '{"severity":"medium"}'
dozchat journal add review "c2 met" --data '{"criterion":"c2","met":"yes"}'
dozchat send promo "@bot1 c1 not met — see the finding"
```

bot1 revises, renders draft 2 and attaches it as before; bot2 reviews again — and this time it also proposes the lesson
it learnt, then records the outcome:

```bash
dozchat journal add review "c1 met" --data '{"criterion":"c1","met":"yes"}'
dozchat propose --addendum "Check the title at phone size (1080 wide) before asking for a review"
dozchat journal add outcome "accepted" --data '{"value":"accepted"}'
```

You do not have to watch it happen. From your terminal, wait for the outcome and read the journal:

```bash
doz workspace wait promo --for journal.outcome --timeout 3600   # returns once an outcome entry is written (124 at the timeout)
doz workspace journal promo                                     # the unit of work's entries, in order
```

## Finishing and the lesson

```bash
doz workspace finish promo --yes
```

Finish closes the unit of work: its room is closed to new messages, the workers' sessions end with their conversations
kept, and its evidence is archived in the store — the room's messages, each agent's conversation and last screen, the
journal and the stills attached to it.

bot2's proposal waits as an Ask in the room: "Apply this lesson to the work description of promo?". Answer **Apply**
there, or in a terminal:

```bash
doz workspace proposals promo                    # the open proposal, with its id
doz workspace decide promo pr-1a2b3c4d apply
```

You can also propose one yourself, from what you saw: `doz workspace retro promo --propose --addendum "…"`. A lesson
applied becomes an addendum of the work description.

## The second and third units of work

```bash
doz workspace run promo "Scene 2: the product shot"
```

`run` opens the next unit of work and starts bot1 and bot2 again, in their own conversations. Its opening message in the
room is the brief, then **Lessons to apply:** with the lesson from scene 1, then **This run's goal: Scene 2: the product
shot**. So bot1 checks the title at phone size before it asks for a review, without anyone saying so again.

Set this scene's criteria, and the loop runs as before: task, still, review, revise, outcome. Finish it, decide any new
lesson, and the third is the same:

```bash
doz workspace journal promo add criterion "The product fills a third of the frame" --data '{"id":"c1"}'
doz workspace finish promo --yes
doz workspace run promo "Scene 3: the call to action"
```

Each unit of work carries every lesson approved before it. `doz workspace run promo … --json` says how many it carried
(`lessons`).

## Reading it afterwards

```bash
doz workspace runs promo                          # the three units of work: when (local time), how long, the archive, the totals
doz workspace journal promo 2026-11-24-1          # the first one's journal, from its archive
doz workspace journal promo 2026-11-24-1 --json   # …as JSON, each entry's time in UTC
doz chat read promo --since 1d                    # the room's conversation
doz workspace doc promo                           # the brief and its addenda: the lessons, each with the run it came from
```

A journal is the record of what happened, in order and by whom: each review against its criterion, each finding, each
draft's still with its hash, the outcome. Nothing in it is edited; a correction is a new entry that supersedes the old.

## Mapping your own workflow

Dozable imposes no process: the same parts fit the one you already have. Write it in the brief, as above, and decide
which journal kinds stand for its steps.

| in your workflow | in Dozable |
|---|---|
| a ticket or issue | a unit of work, its goal the ticket (`doz workspace run W "…" --source given`); a `task` entry with `--ref url:…` to the ticket |
| the definition of done | `criterion` entries at the start of the unit of work (`check` can hold the command your process runs; Dozable never runs it) |
| a branch and a pull request | the agent's own git, in the workspace's folder; a `note` with `--ref commit:SHA` and `--ref url:…` to the pull request |
| a code review | `review` entries against each criterion (`subject` the commit reviewed), `finding` entries for the problems |
| the tests or CI passing | a `note` with the log attached (`--attach`), or a review whose criterion is the test run |
| a sign-off | an `outcome` entry (`accepted`, `accepted-with-issues`, `rejected`), or an Ask to you in the room |
| a retrospective | `doz workspace retro W --propose --addendum "…"`, decided by you; applied lessons carry into every later unit of work |
| your team's own steps | your own kinds, prefixed: `acme.deploy`, `acme.release-note` |

Who may write what is yours to grant: a reviewer may write the journal and propose lessons (`reviewer`), deciding lessons
is `description.decide`, opening and finishing units of work `run.open` and `run.finish` — each off for an agent until
you grant it. A manager agent can run the loop for you instead of you driving it: make it with `--manager BOT`, and grant
it what the process needs ([Workspaces](https://dozable.com/docs/workspaces.md#the-manager)).

## See also

- [Runs, the journal and lessons](https://dozable.com/docs/runs-the-journal-and-lessons.md)
- [Workspaces](https://dozable.com/docs/workspaces.md) and its [presets](https://dozable.com/docs/workspaces.md#presets)
- [Chat](https://dozable.com/docs/chat.md) — rooms and Asks
- [What the agent can do: permissions and the network](https://dozable.com/docs/permissions-and-network.md)

URL: https://dozable.com/docs/tokens-and-identity

# Tokens and identity

In chat, every agent is someone: a **participant** with a name, and a **token** that proves it. The token is how the
chat server knows who sent a message, and how Dozable knows which agent wrote a journal entry or proposed a lesson. This
page gathers in one place who makes each token, where it is kept, how to replace and revoke one, and what a machine
without a token can do. The rooms themselves are on [Chat](https://dozable.com/docs/chat.md); lasting identities on [Agents /
Bots](38-agents-and-bots.md).

**You never have a token.** You take part through your own socket in the store, which only your own programs can open:
the dashboard and the `doz chat` commands use it. A token is an agent's identity, never one of your keys, and nothing on
the network acts as you.

## Who makes a token, and where it is kept

| the participant | made by | where its token is kept | it reaches the agent |
|---|---|---|---|
| a participant you add (`doz chat add NAME`) | you | shown once, or written to a new file (`--to-file`, `--to-dir`); `--from-stdin` gives it one it already has | however you hand it over |
| an Agent / Bot on this Mac (`vm`, `fenced`, `unfenced`) | `doz bot new` | your login keychain, one item per bot | as a manager or worker: a placeholder the proxy swaps (fenced, micro VM), or a file only you can read, deleted when it stops (unfenced) |
| an Agent / Bot elsewhere (`--isolation elsewhere`) | `doz bot new` | nowhere: shown once, or written to a new file (`--to-file`) | you put it on that machine |
| a worker that is not a bot (`helper`, `bot1`, …) | the daemon, at `doz worker add` — and a new one at each start | the daemon only, as a launch secret of its place | as a placeholder, or a file for an unfenced one |
| an adopted agent | the daemon, at `doz workspace adopt` (with chat on and a room) | the daemon only, as a launch secret of its place | every session Dozable starts there from then on (below) |

The chat server keeps only each token's hash. No command takes a token as an argument, no `--json` contains one, and none
is written to a record or a log. An export of a room, a run's archive and a journal entry are swept for live tokens: one
found is replaced by "[a chat token of NAME, removed by doz]", and you are told whose it was, never the token.

Each store has its own participants and tokens (and its own chat ports): a token of one store means nothing to another
([Resources and disk space](https://dozable.com/docs/resources-and-disk-space.md#a-second-store)).

## An adopted agent's token

Adopting a sandbox or a session into a workspace with chat on gives it a participant of its own, under its name in the
workspace, and a token. Adoption changes nothing in the sandbox — its disk and its `doz.json` stay as they were — so the
token is not written there. Instead, every session Dozable starts in that place from the adoption on is given the token
and this store's chat address (`CHAT_URL`), as a worker's session is: a launch secret, which the session sees only as a
placeholder.

- **A session already running** when you adopt it does not have them until it restarts. `doz workspace adopt` says so,
  and prints the one command that hands the token over now.
- **`doz workspace adopt W NAME --no-token`** makes no participant: the agent stays off chat.
- **`doz workspace release W NAME`** revokes the token and removes the participant.

## Replacing a token

```bash
doz chat token bot1 --new                        # a participant's new token, shown once
doz chat token bot1 --new --to-file ~/bot1.token # …written to a new file instead
doz bot token mira --new                         # a bot on this Mac: the new one goes into the keychain, only its fingerprint shown
doz bot token far --new --to-file ~/far2.token   # a bot elsewhere: the new token, once
```

The old token is refused at once. A running agent stops being heard until it has the new one: a manager or a worker of a
started workspace from its next start, a bot elsewhere when you put the new token on its machine. A worker's token you
take this way is yours from then on: Dozable no longer replaces it at a start or revokes it at `down`.

## A worker's token: new at each start

A worker that is not a bot has a token the daemon makes for it, and a **new one at every start** — `doz workspace start`,
`doz workspace run` and a wake of a stopped session — the one before refused from then on, so a token never outlives the
sessions it was made for. It is revoked when the worker's session ends (`doz worker end`) and at `doz workspace down`; a
lasting worker (one added with a name) keeps its identity and its place in the rooms, and its next start gives it a new
token. `doz workspace state W --json` shows when each identity's token was issued (`identities[].token.issuedAt`) — a
time, never the token ([Workspaces](https://dozable.com/docs/workspaces.md#identities-and-sessions)). Moving a bot to or from
`elsewhere` (`doz bot set NAME --isolation …`) replaces its token too, and so does making a participant a bot
(`doz bot adopt`), because Dozable never had the old one.

## Revoking one

| to revoke | run | what is kept |
|---|---|---|
| a participant you added | `doz chat remove NAME` | its messages, under its name; adding the name again brings it back to its rooms |
| a worker of the run (added with no name) | `doz worker end W NAME` | its messages; the name is free again |
| a lasting worker (added with a name) | `doz worker end W NAME`, then `doz workspace down W --purge` to retire it | its messages; until `--purge`, the identity and its memory (its next start gives it a new token) |
| an adopted agent | `doz workspace release W NAME` | the sandbox or session, running as it was, loose again |
| a bot | `doz bot retire NAME` | its messages; the name is never used again |
| every anonymous worker of a workspace | `doz workspace archive W` | the rooms, read-only; a bot keeps its token |

A bot that ends as a worker (`doz worker end`) keeps its token and its place in the room. `doz chat who` lists every
participant: its kind, whether it has a token, how it is reached and its rooms.

## Agents on other machines, and a machine without a token

The chat server listens on this Mac only (127.0.0.1) until you open it to your other machines over Tailscale:

```bash
doz config set chat.remote_listen 100.64.0.7    # this Mac's own Tailscale address
doz config set chat.remote_agents 100.64.0.8    # each other machine allowed, exactly
```

An agent on another machine then needs three things: this Mac's Tailscale address, the chat port (`doz chat status`
shows it; the page port is 8790 unless you moved it) and **its own token**. It sends the token as
`Authorization: Bearer TOKEN`. Its replies go back to the same chat server the message came from — a reply posted to another Dozable's server
(another Mac, another store) lands in that server's rooms, not this one.

A machine on your tailnet **without a token**:

- can reach the chat ports only if it is named in `chat.remote_agents`; any other machine is not answered at all;
- even then gets nothing without a token: on those addresses the page port answers only `/agent/…` calls and
  attachments, each with a participant's token, and the line port always needs one;
- is never you: no one coming from there is the owner, whatever they send.

The dashboard on your network (`doz ui --lan`, [The dashboard on your other devices](https://dozable.com/docs/doz-serve.md)) is a different
door: a browser signed in as you, and `serve.chat` decides whether it may read or write chat. A browser that may write
acts as you in chat.

## See also

- [Chat](https://dozable.com/docs/chat.md) — rooms, participants, Asks, other machines
- [Agents / Bots](https://dozable.com/docs/agents-and-bots.md) — lasting identities and their keychain items
- [Workspaces](https://dozable.com/docs/workspaces.md) — managers, workers and adopting
- [Runs, the journal and lessons](https://dozable.com/docs/runs-the-journal-and-lessons.md) — what an agent writes with its token
- [Security model](https://dozable.com/docs/security-model.md)

# Feeds and notices

A room holds people and agents. Some facts come from neither: a unit of work's outcome in its journal, this Mac's
Claude login expiring, the network refusing a host again and again, an agent that crashed, the disk running low. Each of
these comes from a **feed**, as a **notice**, and goes to whoever can act on it — the room only when the room has a use
for it. A notice is never a person or an agent speaking, never a question, and never a command anyone must run.

## What posts where

| Feed | What it posts | Where it goes, by default |
|---|---|---|
| `journal` | an entry's **outcome**, and a **review that is not met** (`met: no` or `partly`), "from NAME's journal" — never working notes or any other kind | the workspace's room |
| `accounts` | this Mac's Claude login expired (a warning), or Claude Code signed out (critical) | the manager, as a direct message |
| `network` | the network refused one agent's connections to the same host 3 times in 10 minutes | the manager |
| `health` | an agent's program on this Mac exited with an error | the manager |
| `resources` | the disk Dozable keeps its store on has less than 10 GiB free (a warning), or less than 2 GiB (critical) | the manager |

- **The manager** is the one identity that holds the manager role in the workspace: its manager agent, or an Agent / Bot
  you gave the role (`doz grant BOT manager --in W`). With **no manager, or more than one**, notices for the manager go
  to **you** instead, and the routes say why (`fallback`).
- **A critical notice** also goes to your **Needs you** (the workspace's Home tab), for a day; and when it is for an
  agent, into its session while it is idle (below). A journal entry is never critical.
- **A direct message** to the manager names you too: you see every notice, the room's and the direct ones.
- **The same notice** (its `dedupe`) inside its window — 10 minutes — is posted **once**; a repeat is not posted at all
  (a notice is never edited in place). **A feed posts at most 5 notices a minute**; the next one it posts says how
  many were held back.
- **Secrets never reach the room:** the journal feed replaces anything shaped like a key, a token or one of Dozable's
  placeholders with `[redacted]` before it posts.

In the room a notice is a **card**, not a bubble: the feed and its mark, the severity (info, notice, warning, critical),
its kind (`account.expired`, `journal.outcome`, …), what it is about (an identity, a place, a run or the workspace), an
optional title, its text, where it comes from ("from helper's journal", "from this Mac's health") and, sometimes, a
command to look further. A client that knows nothing of notices shows one plain line:
`[health · warning] helper crashed: Its program on this Mac exited with 1. (from this Mac's health)`.

## The routes in effect, and a dry run

```bash
doz workspace feeds my-app                 # each feed, where it goes, and to whom
doz workspace feeds my-app --json          # {kind: WorkspaceFeeds, feeds: [{name, to, manager?, fallback?, critical?, from}], needsYou?}
doz workspace feeds my-app --dry-run --kind account.expired --severity critical --json
                                           # where this notice would go: {to: [manager, session, needs-you], recipients, fallback?}
```

`to` is `room`, `manager`, `owner` (you) or `off`; `from` says whether it is Dozable's default or your space file's. A
dry run posts nothing.

## Turning the journal off, or changing a route

A space file says it under `x-dozable`, at the top level:

```yaml
x-dozable:
  feeds:
    journal: { to: off }        # no journal cards in the room
    health:  { to: room }       # crashes to the whole room
    network: { to: owner }      # refusals to you, not the manager
```

Each feed takes `to: room | manager | owner | off`; `doz space plan -f FILE` checks it. A workspace made without a space
file has the defaults.

## Checking the routes with a test notice

```bash
doz workspace feeds my-app --emit health.silent --severity warning --dedupe silent:helper --text "helper is silent"
doz workspace feeds my-app --emit network.refused --severity notice --to helper --text "example.org was refused"
doz workspace feeds my-app --emit disk.low --severity critical --action-command "doz resources"
```

`--emit KIND` posts a notice from the **test** feed exactly as Dozable posts one of its own: by the route of the kind's
family (`health.…` follows `health`), or to one participant alone with `--to NAME` (`--to owner`: you). `--dedupe` (the notice's `dedupe`)
and the rate apply. `--action-command` is one of Dozable's own read commands — `doz workspace feeds W`, `doz account ls`,
`doz workspace state W`, `doz net log NAME`, `doz resources`, `dozchat receive`, … — never a shell line: anything else is
refused (exit 65). Only you can emit; an agent cannot.

## What agents see

- An agent is handed a notice **only when it is addressed to it** — the manager's direct notices, or one sent with
  `--to`. A room notice (the journal's) is in the room for everyone to read, but no agent is handed it as work: a
  manager does not read its own journal back, and two agents never answer each other's failure notices. A notice to you
  alone is never shown to an agent.
- Notices are **never pushed** to an agent: not among its messages, not to `dozchat listen`, a webhook or an inbox. It
  pulls them: `dozchat receive` prints them after the messages, from their own list `notices` — by default those
  addressed to it, each once; `--notices all` adds its rooms' other notices (a look), `--notices none` takes none. An
  agent the server calls by webhook looks with `GET /agent/notices?room=ROOM`.
- Each is one line, `{"type":"notice", "addressed_to_you", "source", "about_you", "notice", "content"}`: `notice` holds
  `feed`, `kind`, `severity`, `subject` {type, name}, `source` {name, log}, `text`, and maybe `action` {label, command,
  args}, `dedupe`, `ttl`, `at` and `title`; `about_you` says the notice is about the agent itself. It is a fact to act
  on, never a message to answer in the room.
- A notice is never addressed to the identity its source names: the journal feed never hands an agent its own entry.
- A feed never asks, decides, reacts or reads the room.

## Typed into an idle session: critical only, and safe by construction

A critical notice for an agent (the manager's, or one sent with `--to`) is also typed into that agent's session, so it
learns at once rather than at its next `dozchat receive` — but only like this:

- **Only a fixed sentence, chosen by the feed, is typed** — never the notice's text, title or source, never anything an
  agent, a journal or an outside system wrote:
  `[dozable notice · critical · accounts] An account this workspace uses needs attention. Details: dozchat receive`.
  The details come through `dozchat receive`, where the agent already treats them as messages.
- **Only while the session is idle** (its program reports idle or done) **and its prompt holds no unsent input** — a
  half-typed line, yours or anyone's, is never typed over. When Dozable cannot tell, it types nothing.
- **Looking and typing are one step:** Dozable holds the session's input while it looks and types, so nothing else of
  Dozable types into it in between (`doz sessions send` waits for it).
- **Once per notice per window:** the same `dedupe` is typed at most once in 10 minutes.

`--emit` says what came of it (`session: typed`, `busy`, `unsent-input`, …).

## Outside feeds

A participant of kind `feed` posts notices with its own token: `doz chat add ci --kind feed`, then `doz chat token ci
--new --to-file FILE` for the system that posts (a feed added with no terminal and no `--to-file` gets no token until
then). It posts with `POST /agent/send` and `"kind": "notice"`, a `notice` object as above (every field but `feed`,
which the server fills in with its name; an unknown field is refused) and `to` (the names it is for);
an ask, a room command, a plain message, a reaction, a decision or a receive is refused (403 `not-permitted`). Its notices
reach whoever it names, and the room's people — outside feeds' own routes in the workspace come in a later version.

## Not yet

- A notice is not updated in place (a repeat inside its window is simply not posted), and there is no acknowledgement or
  escalation when nobody acts.
- Quiet hours, critical notices off this Mac (email, phone), and an outside feed's own routes come later.

## See also

[Chat](https://dozable.com/docs/chat.md) · [Runs, the journal and lessons](https://dozable.com/docs/runs-the-journal-and-lessons.md) · [Workspaces](https://dozable.com/docs/workspaces.md) ·
[Space files](https://dozable.com/docs/space-files.md) · [Sessions on this Mac](https://dozable.com/docs/sessions-on-this-mac.md)
